  - Stamped **v1.5.11** in all four places. Validated: tag balance, zero
    dead anchors, stale-claim sweep.

## [1.5.11] - 2026-08-19

Both training courses present as slides (TR-7).

### Added

- **Deck mode, and it is the default.** The courses now open on a cover slide
  and advance one screen at a time: a fixed bar with Back / Next, the module
  name and a per-module counter ("M5 · 1 of 7"), a progress rail, arrow-key and
  Home/End navigation, and a **Read as one page** escape that persists. 40
  slides for the operator course, 25 for the administrator course.
- **The slides are derived at runtime, not authored.** A script splits the
  finished document at the seams the content already has — every `h2`, every
  `h3`, every scenario and walkthrough block — and wraps each run in a section.
  **Neither fragment's markup changed.**

  That is the whole point: with JavaScript disabled, no slides are built, no bar
  exists, and the courses are byte-for-byte the scrolling pages that shipped in
  v1.5.7–v1.5.10. Print force-restores page mode for the same reason. So the
  Moodle File-resource download, the offline read and the accessibility fallback
  all keep working, and there is no second authored code path to drift from the
  first.
- **The hero becomes slide 0** — the course cover. Free, and it is most of what
  makes the thing read as a course rather than a document.
- Reaching a module's last slide **ticks its box in the progress strip**, so the
  two ways of tracking where you are cannot disagree. Sidebar TOC anchors select
  that module's first slide rather than scrolling to a hidden heading. Position
  and mode both persist per course.

### Changed

- **`training-harness-parity.test.ts` makes the duplicated harness an enforced
  invariant.** TR-D3 said revisit the duplication past ~300 lines and this took
  it well past — but the reason to duplicate (each page being a single
  self-contained file) does not weaken as the file grows, so extraction is still
  wrong. What changes at this size is the risk of a fix landing in one course
  only, which is invisible at runtime. The two harnesses must now be
  byte-identical apart from the documented storage-key difference, and the test
  also fails if a `tr-slide` section ever appears in authored markup.

### Fixed

- **A slide is focused on navigation so screen readers land on the new content**
  — and the manuals' global focus ring then drew an outline around the entire
  slide, which reads as a card border and made a short slide look like an empty
  box. The ring is suppressed for the slide container only; real controls keep
  theirs.

## [1.5.10] - 2026-08-19

The administrator course (TR-4).

### Added

- **`/training-admin.html`, seven modules.** A1 scopes and the host overlay, A2
  agencies, A3 runners, A4 access, A5 secrets, A6 in-app authoring, A7 external
  triggers and the four not-yets. It names the operator course as a prerequisite
  and repeats none of it, and it flags A2 and A4 up front as the two where an
  administrator's mistakes are expensive.
- **A2 teaches the half of the dispatch rule people miss.** Agency isolation is
  disjoint in *both* directions: a run carrying agencies goes only to a member
  runner, and a run carrying none goes only to a runner with **no** agencies.
  So adding a runner to an agency does not add capability — it *removes* that
  runner from the general pool, and every untagged run then queues silently.
  Scenario A1 is exactly that outage.
- **A4 teaches the same-grant rule from the code's own shape.** Scenario A3 gives
  Dana viewer-everywhere plus operator-on-Finance and asks about Tax: the answer
  is no, because Cronomicon never takes the verb from one grant and the territory
  from another. Also the tri-state (no grant = zero access, not everything), the
  case-sensitivity of AD group names, and the last-unrestricted-admin guard.
- **The harness is copied verbatim** from the operator course, per TR-D3 — same
  widget CSS, same script, only the localStorage key differs. The header comment
  says so, and says when to revisit.

### Fixed

- **The three usage guides are now covered by the palette drift guard.**
  `ansible-guide.html`, `bash-guide.html` and `powershell-guide.html` were never
  added to `DOC_FILES` when they were introduced, so their CSS went unguarded.
  They were clean, so this costs nothing and closes the gap — pulled forward from
  TR-5 while the file was open.

## [1.5.9] - 2026-08-19

The operator course is complete — M7, M8 and M9 (TR-3).

### Added

- **M7 · Reading results.** History's six tabs, the four filters, the trace ID as
  the thing to send when escalating, and the run drill-in. Four fields get their
  own treatment: Triggered by, Set off, the Queued-at/Started-at gap (a run that
  started late is a different problem from one that ran long), and the exit code
  — including the mapping nobody guesses, that **a warning counts as a success
  for anything reacting to the run**.
- **M8 · When something goes wrong.** A four-question triage order, the four
  things you can do about it, and **the stop disposition** — which is not
  bookkeeping: a dispositioned stop writes the chosen outcome into the run's
  status, so stopping a run "as a success" makes downstream success-reactions
  fire. Scenario 6 walks that consequence; scenario 7 covers the run that never
  appeared.
- **M9 · Bringing your own jobs across.** Explicitly skippable, for operators
  converting their own jobs. An eight-question conversion recipe, a worked
  example, and a five-item post-conversion checklist. The recipe's step 3 carries
  the migration's sharpest edge: an Automate Schedule calendar splits in two —
  run days into the cron expression, non-run days into a working calendar — and
  moving the whole thing across expecting it to drive the job means the job never
  runs.
- **Two new course figures**: `training-history-*` and `training-run-detail-*`,
  both themes.

### Fixed

- **M6 overstated the skipped/missed distinction.** It taught Missed as a
  separate result. It is not: a calendar veto and a missed fire are the *same*
  record type — result **Skipped** — distinguished by the reason line. The
  distinction is real and worth teaching, but it lives one field lower than the
  module claimed. Scenario 4 now teaches the habit that actually helps: on a
  skipped run, read the reason, never just the result.

### Notes

- **The drill-in figure deliberately excludes the log block.** Seeded runs carry
  no log file, and an empty log panel teaches nothing; the figure is cropped to
  the field grid and live tailing is covered in prose. A run was triggered to try
  to produce a real log rather than fake one — it did not land, and inventing one
  was not on the table.
- M9's worked example is **labelled illustrative** and points the reader at their
  own converted jobs. TR-Q7 (two real Automate Schedule jobs) remains open; when
  it resolves, the real examples should join or replace this one.

## [1.5.8] - 2026-08-19

Operator course modules M1–M4 and M6, and three new widget types (TR-2).

### Added

- **Five more operator modules.** M1 (one job becomes four objects), M2 (Git vs
  Cronomicon definitions), M3 (finding your way around), M4 (running a job) and M6
  (how runs start). With M0 and M5 from TR-1 the course now runs seven modules;
  History/triage and the migration module remain for TR-3.
- **`tr-walkthrough`, a CSS-only stepper.** Radio inputs drive which step shows
  via `:checked ~` sibling selectors, so the Run dialog's four states step
  through with **no JavaScript** — and the whole sequence prints. Added because
  TR-D8 removed the live sandbox: a dialog that unfolds across sections cannot
  be taught by one static hotspot, and this was a fraction of the cost of
  simulating it in HTML.
- **`tr-hotspot`, numbered pins over a figure.** Percentage-positioned so one
  coordinate set serves both themes and every viewport, each pin an anchor into
  the numbered list beneath — which is also what it degrades to in print.
- **`tr-sort`, a commit-then-reveal matcher.** Deliberately not drag-and-drop:
  the teaching value is deciding before you look, which a disclosure element
  delivers without a drag affordance that fails on touch or a keyboard trap.
- **Four new course figures** in `frontend/public/manual/`
  (`training-run-{collapsed,where,when,advanced}-{dark,light}.png`) — the Run
  dialog's successive states, cropped to the dialog, both themes.

### Notes

Two things the capture pass turned up, both now handled rather than worked
around:

- **The hotspot's coordinate space must be the image alone.** Pins first sat in
  a wrapper that also contained the `figcaption`, so every percentage was short
  by the caption's height and pin 2 landed on the Score header instead of the
  stat tiles. They now live in a `.tr-shotbox` that wraps only the images.
- **The seeded Dashboard is healthy, so it has no Recent errors block** — a pin
  pointing at it would have pointed at nothing. Rather than fake a failure, the
  legend's fifth entry names the absence and teaches the pattern: a section with
  nothing to say gets out of the way. The figure is captioned "on a good day".

## [1.5.7] - 2026-08-19

Onboarding training, first phase — the operator course opens (TR-1).

### Added

- **A training course now ships with the binary**, published at
  `/training-operator.html` and reachable from the manuals' sidebar. TR-1
  lands the harness plus two modules:
  **M0**, a Rosetta table translating Fortra **Automate Schedule** vocabulary
  into Cronomicon, and **M5**, targeting and blast radius, carrying three
  predict-the-outcome scenarios. The remaining eight operator modules and the
  administrator course follow in TR-2..TR-4.
- **The course is a body-only fragment on the existing GUIDES pipeline** — one
  entry in `vite-manuals-plugin.js` and no new infrastructure. It inherits the
  manuals' stylesheet, sidebar, TOC, theme toggle and Print button, and its
  widget CSS uses `var(--*)` exclusively so it carries **zero hex literals** and
  follows the light/dark toggle for free.
- **The interactive widgets are CSS-only.** Reveals, Rosetta rows and scenario
  options are all `<details>`, so the course works with JavaScript disabled, in
  print, and as a downloaded file — which is what lets Moodle serve it as either
  a URL or a File resource from the same artifact. The only script on the page is
  the localStorage progress strip, and it stays hidden unless storage actually
  writes, so it never shows a control that silently forgets.
- **SCORM was considered and rejected** (TR-D1): its one capability plain HTML
  lacks is the LMS completion record, which is explicitly not wanted here. What
  remained would have been a snapshot rotting outside version control.

### Changed

- **`GUIDES` is exported from `vite-manuals-plugin.js`**, and
  `runner-guide-wrap.test.ts` now derives its "every href resolves" allowlist
  from it. The allowlist had the guide basenames hardcoded and failed on the
  first entry added after it was written — a guard failing on a correct change
  rather than a wrong one. Adding a guide no longer requires editing the test.
- `documentation-palette.test.ts` covers `training-operator.html`. The training
  fragments are the first to author colour of their own (the runner guides carry
  none and inherit everything), so the guard is what keeps that true.

### Notes

Two wrapper behaviours were found by building this and are now documented in the
fragment's header, because both fail **silently**:

- The `<h1>` lift is anchored to the very start of the body, so a leading comment
  defeats it and leaves a duplicate title with no version chip. The `<h1>` must
  be the first thing in the file, ahead of any comment.
- The heading and code-block rewrites are blind regexes that run over comments
  too. An unclosed `h2` written inside the header comment matched forward to the
  first real closing tag and swallowed module M0 out of the sidebar TOC. Tag
  names in these fragments' comments must not be written in angle brackets.

## [1.5.6] - 2026-08-19

The Run dialog's "This run" rail names the chosen targets.

### Added

- **The Targets row itemizes an explicit subset.** When a run is narrowed to
  picked inventory groups or picked hosts, the rail's Targets row keeps its
  count phrase ("2 groups in dockerhost_cluster") and gains a quieter second
  line naming the actual picks ("dockerhost_carson, dockerhost_vegas") — the
  rail's question is "what will this run use", and a count answers how many
  without answering which. The names follow the SAME branch order as the
  phrase itself, so the two lines can never describe different selections; a
  raw `--limit` passes no names (the phrase already carries the literal), and
  a whole-scope run carries no detail line. Long lists cap at 140 characters
  with the full list in the row's tooltip. The summary model
  (`views/jobs/runSummary.ts`) gained the general `detail` row field, so
  future rows whose value is itself a summary have a vocabulary for their
  itemization.

## [1.5.5] - 2026-08-18

The Dashboard's attention strip can be dismissed.

### Added

- **A ✕ on the verdict strip's attention state.** Once you have seen that a job
  needs attention, the strip can be put away — there is no sense in a summary
  nagging through the twenty minutes spent fixing what it named. Two rules keep
  that safe:
  - **It returns the moment anything changes.** The dismissal stores a
    signature of the situation acknowledged — which jobs, at what severity, how
    many times, and when each last failed — and the strip reappears as soon as
    that signature differs. A new job failing, an existing one failing again, or
    a warning becoming a failure is a different situation. Dismissing silences
    what you have seen; it cannot swallow news. (`latestAt` is part of the
    signature deliberately: a job that failed twice and then had its older
    failure age out of the 24h window would return to a count of 1 and re-match
    a stale dismissal, hiding a failure newer than the one acknowledged.)
  - **It never hides the evidence.** Only the one-line summary goes; Recent
    errors still names every affected job, each row still linking into History.
- Remembered **per browser** in `localStorage`, alongside column layouts and
  widths — it survives a reload, applies across tabs on that machine, and is
  local to that person: dismissing does not silence the strip for colleagues.
  Private-browsing and hardened profiles that throw on storage access degrade to
  a per-page dismissal rather than crashing.

This restores, deliberately, the one behaviour the pre-v0.53.3 failed-run banner
had that Current status could not replace (CS-1) — re-showing after dismissal
when a genuinely new failure arrives — without bringing back the banner itself.

### Changed

- The attention strip is now two real buttons (the message, which jumps to
  Recent errors, and the ✕) instead of one `role="button"` container: an
  interactive element nested inside another is announced to nobody and reachable
  by no keyboard. Both are tab-reachable and activate on Enter/Space.
- User manual stamped **v1.5.5**, documenting the dismissal in §5.3 and the
  glossary.

## [1.5.3] - 2026-08-18

The Dashboard leads with its answer. VU2-1 and VU2-3 close the VU2 band's
Dashboard work (the visual-updates2 plan). The page exists to
answer "is everything okay?", and until now that answer was the last thing on
it — below the tiles and the timeline, rendered at title weight with an accent
edge precisely when nothing needed attention. Loud on a good day, buried on a
bad one.

### Added

- **A verdict strip at the top of the Dashboard.** One line, above everything
  else, in three states: quiet when all is well ("All 14 jobs healthy. Nothing

Note: the verdict strip deliberately does NOT name the next fire, though the

## [1.5.1] - 2026-08-18

A quieter Jobs catalog. First phases of the VU2 band
(the visual-updates2 plan, VU2-4 and VU2-5) from the design
review of the Dashboard and Jobs pages. The finding behind them: the list
surfaces spent most of their ink on values that are identical in every row —
twelve `GIT` badges, twelve em-dashes per empty column, three zero-count tabs
at full strength — while the job *name*, the row's actual identity, wrapped to
two lines. Nothing here changes what any page shows; it changes what each
thing is allowed to shout.

### Added

- **`EmptyCell`** (`components/ui.tsx`): the one vocabulary for a table cell
  with no value. Still an em-dash — a blank cell in a sortable column reads as
  a rendering failure — but fainter than `textMuted`, and labelled "no value"
  for assistive tech rather than announcing "em dash". Adopted across the
  catalogs: Jobs, Workflows, Runners, Scopes, History › Executions, and the
  three Env Vars tabs. Scope is deliberately table cells only: the `—` a
  formatter returns inside a value stays at full weight.
- **Muted zero-count tabs**: `TabBar` accepts `{ label, muted }` alongside the
  plain strings every other caller passes; Jobs dims a status tab whose count
  is 0. Never the active tab (you clicked it, so it must read as selected),
  and a dimmed tab stays clickable — "Failed (0)" is a real answer.

### Changed

- **Source badges are asymmetric now.** Git is the majority in every catalog
  that shows the column, so it renders as quiet text with no chip chrome;
  `AMADEUS` keeps the tinted chip. The interesting value is the minority one.
- **Job names no longer wrap.** The name cell is `nowrap` with an ellipsis cap
  rather than yielding its width to the `nowrap` columns beside it. (Raising
  the column's width *default* does nothing here — the table is
  `tableLayout: auto` inside a scroll wrapper, where a declared width is a
  hint content overrides; measured 153px → 173px with no new horizontal
  scroll, and the list gained a row.)
- **Jobs page subtitle** is now "Run your scripts on a schedule, across your
  hosts" — the old "Scheduled scripts synced from GitLab" described the
  plumbing and had been inaccurate since amadeus-source jobs arrived.
- **A job that has never run says so once.** The expanded panel's tail line
  listed every absent fact ("Not recorded: Next run · Scheduled ad-hoc run ·
  Last duration · …"); when a job has no runs at all it now reads "No runs yet
  — Run it to start recording history." and only the non-run absences keep the
  enumeration, which is where it earns its keep.

## [1.5.0] - 2026-08-18

Live log tailing for runner-executed jobs (wire protocol v12). EP-8 (v1.4.16)
made the log viewer follow a running job, which covers in-app SSH-executor
runs end to end — their log file is written line-by-line as output arrives.
Runner-agent runs still could not tail: the agent buffered the entire log
locally and streamed it to the server only after execution finished, so there
was nothing on disk for the viewer to follow. This release closes that half.

### Added

- **Runner agents stream logs mid-run (wire protocol v12)**: the poll
  assignment carries `liveLog: true`, inviting the agent to flush its pending
  log buffer every 2s during execution with an `X-Log-Partial: 1` header; the
  server persists the chunk and advances the resume offset without treating it
  as the end of the stream. The terminal sealed flush (trailing envelope) is
  unchanged. Additive in both directions: an old agent keeps its single
  end-of-run flush, and a new agent never sends a partial chunk to an old
  server (no `liveLog` on the assignment), which would otherwise finalize the
  run `log_stream_lost`.

### Fixed

- **History's run drill-in now notices a run finishing.** The drawer polls the
  run record while it is queued/running (and stops at terminal), so the header
  fields settle and the log viewer's tail switches itself off — previously a
  drawer opened mid-run kept its one-shot status forever and would have tailed
  indefinitely.
- **`streamLogs` now commits exactly the bytes each attempt sent** rather than
  the buffer's total size — with mid-run flushes the executor keeps appending
  lines while a POST is in flight, and committing the post-hoc total would
  silently skip those lines on the next flush.

---

## [1.4.16] - 2026-08-18

Stage EP-8 of the expanded-panels band — live log tailing. This closes the
band.

### Added

- **A running job's log now follows itself.** Open the log of a run that is
  still going — from History, a workflow step, or the recent-runs drill-in on
  Jobs and Runners — and new output appears as it is written, with a
  **Tailing** marker beside the heading. Scroll up to read something and it
  holds your position; a **↓ Resume following** control returns you to the
  tail. When the run finishes, the viewer takes one last read (so the final
  lines are never lost) and stops. A finished run's log behaves exactly as it
  always did — no polling, one fetch.
- **`GET /runs/{traceId}/log` accepts `?offset=`** and answers with an
  `X-Log-Offset` header. Following a log therefore transfers only what was
  appended since the last check rather than re-downloading the whole file every
  few seconds — which matters on a chatty Ansible run. Omitting the parameter
  returns the whole log exactly as before.

### Notes

- Following is a short poll rather than a streaming connection. Deliberate: a
  couple of seconds is imperceptible when watching a log, and a long-lived
  connection is the fragile thing to put behind an arbitrary reverse proxy.
- An offset past the end of a log is answered normally, not as an error, so a
  viewer whose position outlived a reaped or rotated log recovers instead of
  getting stuck.
- Nothing new is exposed: logs are redacted when they are written, so a partial
  read shows exactly what a full read would.

## [1.4.14] - 2026-08-18

Fix for 1.4.13, found by driving the real UI.

### Fixed

- **The panel Refresh button covered only part of its panel.** On seven of the
  eleven panels the button re-fetched the requests made by components *nested
  inside* the panel but not the panel's own — a job's Refresh re-issued two of
  its six requests, so the panel appeared to refresh while its main content
  stayed stale. Every panel now refreshes completely. (Cause: the refresh scope
  was opened inside each detail component rather than around it, and a React
  context reaches only descendants. Nothing automated caught this — the type
  checker and 928 unit tests all passed; a browser network trace found it. The
  placement is now pinned by two tests, one of which asserts the broken shape
  so the trap stays documented.)

## [1.4.13] - 2026-08-18

Stage EP-4 of the expanded-panels band — the Refresh button reaches the panels.
This is the visible half of 1.4.11 and 1.4.12.

### Added

- **Every expanded row now carries a Refresh button, top-right.** Eleven panels:
  Jobs, Workflows, Scripts, Schedules, Runners, History → Executions, workflow
  step detail, Scopes, the Agencies detail, and the three Env Vars tabs
  (Variables, Secrets, SSH Keys). Refresh leads each panel's action strip, so
  the harmless control is never next to Delete or Deregister, and it appears
  even on rows whose other actions you are not permitted — refreshing needs no
  permission.
- **One button covers the whole panel, not just its main request.** A job's
  panel alone issues five separate requests, two of them from components nested
  inside it; all of them re-fetch together.

### Fixed

- **Refreshing an Env Vars panel no longer closes it.** The three Env Vars tabs
  reused one reload routine for two different jobs — "re-read the rows" and
  "re-read the rows *and* collapse the open row", the latter being right after a
  create or delete. Wired to the new button as-is, it would have collapsed the
  panel it was asked to refresh. The two meanings are now separate.

### Notes

- Two surfaces that looked like expanded panels are not, and were deliberately
  left alone: the Activity feed's disclosure reveals a grouped entry's other
  timestamps, and Users & Access's expander reveals the rest of a login's AD
  groups. Neither is a detail panel, and neither has anything to refresh.

## [1.4.12] - 2026-08-18

Stage EP-3 of the expanded-panels band — the refresh mechanism and its control.
The button exists from this release; EP-4 puts it on the panels.

### Added

- **A `Refresh` control for a single expanded panel.** It re-fetches everything
  that panel shows — including requests issued by components nested inside it —
  without touching the rest of the page. Your expanded rows, filters, scroll
  position and unsaved drafts all survive, which is the difference between this
  and reloading. While work is genuinely in flight the button reads
  "Refreshing…" and is disabled, driven by a real count of outstanding requests
  rather than a timer that guesses.

### Changed

- **The top bar's "Refresh" is now "Reload page".** It does what it always did —
  a full browser reload that discards expansions, filters and drafts — but the
  word "Refresh" now belongs to the surgical per-panel control, and the tooltip
  says plainly what a reload costs. One word per concept. The user manual's two
  references were updated to match.

### Internal

- The refresh glyph moved out of the app shell into the shared component kit, so
  the two refresh affordances are drawn with one icon instead of a copy that
  drifts.

## [1.4.11] - 2026-08-18

Stage EP-2 of the expanded-panels band — the data-fetching hook learns to
refetch. Plumbing only: nothing visible changes in this release; the Refresh
button (EP-3/4) builds on it.

### Internal

- **`useGet` gains a third fetch mode, "refresh", and returns `refetch()`.**
  A manual refresh is neither of the modes that existed: "initial" flashes the
  loading skeleton over data the operator is reading, and the background-poll
  mode swallows its errors — which would let a failed refresh look identical to
  a successful one to the person who just asked for it. Refresh keeps the last
  good data on screen while the request runs (a separate `refreshing` flag
  serves the future button), and a failure surfaces as an error with the stale
  data still visible beneath it. A dependency change (a different job, a
  different trace id) remains a full initial load — a new identity must not
  briefly show the old one's data. Every existing call site is untouched.

Stage EP-1 of the expanded-panels band
— the Notes block in the Jobs and Workflows expanded views gets a readable
surface.

### Changed

- **Operator notes now sit on an opaque card.** The expanded row behind them is
  a translucent tint over the table, and the notes — the panel's only free-text

  uses the primary body text/background pair already in the contrast matrix (no
  new pair introduced), the five-line cap and bottom fade behave exactly as
  before, and the empty state ("+ Add a note") and the edit form are

Stage RS-5 — documentation. This closes the run-summary band.

### Documentation

- **The user manual describes the "This run" panel as it now behaves**: on a

  value — grouped as Answers, Where it runs, When and Advanced, and the

## [1.4.8] - 2026-08-14

Stage RS-3 of the run-summary band — the Run dialog's rail renders the summary.
This is the visible half of 1.4.7.

### Changed

- **The "This run" panel now says what the run will do, not just what you
  changed.** On a wide screen the Run dialog carries a panel beside the form; it
  used to list only your deviations from the job's defaults, which meant a stock
  job with an answer filled in showed **nothing at all** — the one surface whose
  job is to tell you what is about to happen was blank precisely when nothing
  unusual was happening. It now lists the answers, where the run goes, when, and
  any advanced options, always.
- **Changed things still stand out.** A setting you altered renders as a bordered
  card in the warning colour and names the default it replaced; a fact merely
  being stated renders flat and quiet. One axis, so "I changed this" reads at a
  glance against "this is how it is".
- **Answers and overrides show their values.** Previously an override appeared as
  a name with no value, which told you something had been changed without telling
  you to what.
- **The one-line recap above it is unchanged**, and so is everything below
  1200px, where the dialog keeps its stacked layout. The confirmation window is
  also untouched: it still lists deviations only, because its question really is
  "what did you change".

## [1.4.7] - 2026-08-14

Stage RS-2 of the run-summary band — the summary model. **No visible change**:
this is the piece the Run dialog's rail will render in RS-3, landed on its own so
the model and the layout can be reviewed apart.

### Added

- **A single function decides what a run summary says.** It takes the same state
  the run itself is submitted from, and returns the grouped answer — Answers,
  Where it runs, When, and Advanced — with each row marked as either something
  the operator changed or something merely being stated. Because it reads the
  submit state directly, the rail it will feed cannot drift from what the run
  actually does; that is a property of the shape rather than something anyone has
  to remember.
- **Overrides and extra variables carry their values, not just their names.** The
  existing list said an override had been set without saying what it had been set
  to, which is the gap this band exists to close. Long values are shortened for
  the narrow rail with the full text kept for the tooltip.
- **The Answers group always has a heading**, showing a quiet "this job declares
  none" when there is nothing to list. A group that silently disappears reads as
  "didn't load" rather than "nothing to say". Advanced is the one group that does
  vanish when unused, because no advanced options is the ordinary case.

### Notes

- Nothing calls this yet — the rail is RS-3. It ships with 24 tests covering the
  rules above directly, which is the point of it being a plain function: the
  surface it feeds sits inside a 3000-line dialog behind a width breakpoint and a
  review gate, and every rule would otherwise need all three staged to assert one
  string.

## [1.4.6] - 2026-08-14

First stage (RS-1) of the run-summary band.
Two pre-existing gaps in the Run dialog's confirmation path, both audit-adjacent
and both fixable without the rail redesign the rest of that band is about.

### Fixed

- **Sending a run to a different runner now counts as a change.** Pinning a run
  to another runner tag — or explicitly unpinning it from the one the job
  declares — produced no entry in the dialog's list of changed settings, never
  raised the confirmation window, and never reset an armed Run button. Runner
  targeting shipped after that list was built and nothing extended it, so all
  three places that read it missed the same fact. The confirmation window now
  names the pin against the job's default, and reads **unpinned** when a run is
  deliberately sent to the general pool. It stays absent on SSH runs, where a pin
  means nothing.
- **Editing an answer no longer leaves a run armed for the old one.** The Run
  button arms on the first press and commits on the second, and it is supposed to
  disarm the moment anything changes — a recap you have stopped agreeing with
  must never be confirmable. Prompt answers were not being watched, so typing a
  different value between the two presses left the button armed and the second
  press ran with the new answer against the old recap.

### Notes

- The plan also expected a same-length swap of two advanced options (trading
  check mode for diff) to leave the button wrongly armed. It cannot: any changed
  setting routes the press to the confirmation window instead of arming, so the
  armed state and a non-empty change list are mutually exclusive. The signature
  now hashes the changed settings by content rather than by count anyway — it
  costs nothing and stops the guard depending on that coupling holding.

A correction to the columns band's scope. Three tables were left out of the
1.4.3 adoption wave for a reason that turned out not to be true, and two of them
sit one tab away from tables that *had* adopted.

### Added

- **The Columns menu is now on every History tab.** Workflow Runs, Schedule
  Pushes and Git Sync join Executions and Change Log. Before this, tabbing
  across a single view made the button appear and disappear — 2 of 5 tabs had
  it. Schedule Pushes and Git Sync also gain resizable columns, which they never
  had.
- **The Workflow Runs table embedded in an expanded workflow row deliberately
  has no menu**, while the full History → Workflow Runs tab does. It is the same
  table in two places: inside a row you already chose to open it stays a fixed,
  narrow summary; as a view of its own it is yours to arrange. The two already
  kept separate widths and sort, and now keep separate arrangements too.

### Fixed

- **The last three copies of the table-header code are gone.** The 1.4.1 refactor
  was meant to leave exactly one; three views kept their own, two of them in the
  same view as siblings that had been converted. There is now genuinely one.
- **Two more hardcoded column counts.** The Workflow Runs table chose between
  the literals 5 and 9 depending on its display mode, and both had to be kept in

### Notes

- The band's plan excluded Git Sync and Schedule Pushes as "sub-5-column"
  tables. They have **5 and 6**. The exclusion appears to have followed from a
  survey that found tables by their column-width settings — which these two did

## [1.4.4] - 2026-08-14

Stage CO-5 — documentation. This closes the columns band.

### Documentation

- **The user manual documents the Columns menu**, as a new §3.4 alongside the
  other app-wide conventions: how to reorder and hide columns, that the first
  and trailing-actions columns are fixed and why, and what **Reset to defaults**
  puts back. It states plainly that the arrangement is **per browser** and will
  not follow you to another machine — otherwise the first support question is
  why a colleague's layout looks different.
- **It also says which sort is yours and which is the server's.** Column order
  and visibility are always applied in your browser; on the two History tables
  the *sort* is applied by the database across the whole history, which is why a
  sort there can change which rows appear at all.
- **The Critical column is documented** on the Jobs list, including that it is a
  display marker — Cronomicon does not run a critical job differently — and that it
  can be hidden like any other column.

### Fixed

- **Four documentation guard tests were failing and are now correct.** They
  pinned the manual's CSS by exact literal (`html[data-theme="dark"]{`,
  `font-display:swap`), so a reformat that added ordinary spaces broke them
  while the drift they actually guard against — a colour in the docs that the
  product's theme no longer defines — kept passing. Two of the four were
  self-checks that inject a fault and assert it is caught; with their anchor no
  longer matching, they were injecting nothing and passing an empty file, so
  they had quietly stopped guarding anything. Both now assert the injection
  landed before checking it was caught.

### Notes

- **The manual's version stamp moved from v0.57.24 to v1.4.4, and that
  overstates its coverage.** The columns material is current, but the manual
  still carries a content backlog from the whole 1.x line — reactions, working
  calendars, run-as credentials, annotations and runner targeting are all
  shipped and none are described. That reconciliation is its own piece of work,
  not part of this band.

## [1.4.3] - 2026-08-14

Stage CO-4 of the columns band — the adoption wave. The **Columns** menu that
shipped on Jobs and Workflows in 1.4.2 is now on **every catalog in the app**.

### Added

- **Arrange the columns on fifteen more tables.** Scripts, Schedules (Catalog,
  Inventory and Upcoming), History (Executions and Change Log), Scopes, Env Vars
  (Variables, Secrets and SSH Keys), Runners, SSH Targets (Host Registry and
  Bastion Configuration) and Recent Logins all carry the Columns menu now, with
  the same reorder, show/hide and reset behaviour, and the same per-browser
  storage.
- **Schedules columns can be resized too.** That catalog predated the resizable
  header entirely and rendered at whatever width its content implied; it now has
  proper column widths, which is what lets it be arranged and dragged like its
  siblings.

### Changed

- **"Reset columns" is gone from twelve toolbars**, replaced by the Columns menu
  it belongs inside. That button only appeared *after* you had already dragged a
  column, reset only widths, and had been copied into a dozen views. The menu is
  always there, and its **Reset to defaults** puts back the order, the visibility
  and the widths together.
- **Sorting on History is unchanged and still server-side.** Both History tables
  get their order from the database across the whole history, not just the page
  you are looking at. Arranging the columns is presentation only and does not
  touch that — which is deliberate: re-sorting a server-ordered page in the
  browser makes rows shear between pages.

### Fixed

- **The tables that were a cell short are consistent again.** Every column count
  in an adopting table — the header, the expanded-row span, the folder-tree row —
  is now derived from one place rather than typed out separately, which is what
  had let them drift apart in the first place.

### Notes

- Tables nested inside an expanded row (a job's recent runs, a workflow's run
  history) deliberately do **not** adopt: their container is already a choice you
  made, and a second column preference behind it would be indistinguishable from
  its parent's. The small four-and-five-column tables (Agencies, Roles, Access
  Grants, Git Sync, Schedule Pushes, Notifications, Service Accounts, Recycle
  Bin) do not adopt either — there is nothing there to arrange.

## [1.4.2] - 2026-08-14

Stage CO-3 of the columns band — the **Columns** menu. This is the surface that
makes 1.4.1's model usable: the Jobs and Workflows tables can now be arranged to
suit the work you actually do.

### Added

- **A Columns button on Jobs and Workflows**, beside the search and tag filters.
  It opens a list of every column in the table, where you can reorder them by
  dragging, and show or hide them with a checkbox.
- **Reorder by dragging within the list, or with the ▲/▼ buttons on each row.**
  The buttons are not a lesser path — they are the keyboard and screen-reader
  route to the same thing, and every reorder is announced.
- **Deliberately NOT by dragging the column headers.** A header already answers
  two gestures — click to sort, and drag its right edge to resize — and a
  horizontal drag is already taken. A third gesture on the same 30px target
  would need a movement threshold to disambiguate, and would fail by sorting the
  table when you meant to drag it. The list also has to exist regardless,
  because a hidden column has no header left to drag back.
- **The first column and a trailing actions column are fixed**, shown greyed in
  the list as "Always first" / "Always last" rather than omitted, so the
  constraint is visible instead of mysterious. Actions in column three is not a
  preference; a catalog whose leading column can be hidden stops being scannable.
- **The button says how many columns are hidden** ("Columns · 2 hidden"). On a
  shared workstation a preference silently in force is otherwise
  indistinguishable from missing data.
- **Reset to defaults** puts the table back — clearing the arrangement *and* the
  column widths you have dragged. "Put the table back" is one thought, so it is
  one button.
- **The preference is per browser**, like the column widths and the sort before
  it. It will not follow you to another machine.

---

## [1.4.1] - 2026-08-14

Stage CO-2 of the columns band — the column model. **No visible change**: this
is the machinery the operator-facing Columns menu (CO-3) needs, landed on its
own so the refactor and the feature can be reviewed apart. The Jobs and
Workflows tables render exactly as they did in 1.4.0 — verified pixel-for-pixel.

### Changed

- **A table's columns are now a thing.** Each column ties a stable key to the
  cell that renders it (`components/table.tsx`). Until now a table's header was
  one hand-written sequence, its row body was a second hand-written sequence
  matched to the first only by position, and the number of columns was typed out
  a third time in every `colSpan`. Nothing could be reordered, hidden or counted
  because nothing was addressable — and the three hand-kept copies of "how many
  columns are there" had already drifted into the bugs fixed in 1.4.0.
- **One table-header renderer replaces the per-view copies.** Jobs and Workflows
  each carried their own pair of header-cell helpers, and they had drifted from
  one another in ways nobody had decided. Both are gone. Fourteen more catalogs
  are queued to adopt the shared one.
- **Column order and visibility are stored per browser** under a new key, kept
  separate from the column widths you have already dragged — so this stage needs
  no migration and nobody loses a width. Nothing writes that preference yet; the
  Columns menu that will is CO-3.
- **A stored column order survives a release that adds a column.** Any order
  saved by a future menu is treated as a partial one: keys that no longer name a
  column are dropped, and a column added in a later release is re-inserted where
  its author placed it rather than vanishing for everyone who had a saved
  preference. This is the failure this stage most needed to design out — it
  would have surfaced months later as "the new column never shipped", and only
  for the people who had customised anything.

## [1.4.0] - 2026-08-14

First stage (CO-1) of the columns band. Surfaces a
job's or workflow's **critical** annotation as a column of its own. The rest of
the band (operator-arranged column order and visibility, CO-2..CO-5) follows on
the 1.4 line; this stage ships standalone and picks a defensible default
placement rather than waiting for the machinery that will let anyone change it.

### Added

- **Critical is a column now, on both catalogs.** The Jobs and Workflows tables
  carry a **Critical** column showing the operator annotation's critical marker.
  Previously the only way to see which jobs were marked critical was to read the
  chip tucked inside each row's Status cell — visible, but not something you
  could sort by or scan down.
- **Sort by it.** Clicking the column header floats the critical rows to the top,
  the same "worst first ascending" direction Status and Result already sort in.
  A criticality you have just set in the expanded panel sorts with everything
  else immediately, without waiting for a refresh.
- **It is visible by default**, which in a fleet with few annotations means a
  mostly empty column — that is deliberate. An empty column is how anyone learns
  the annotation exists; CO-2's Columns menu will be the remedy for anyone who
  disagrees. An un-marked row reads "—", the same as every other empty cell in
  these tables.

### Changed

- **The Critical chip moved out of the Status cell — it was not duplicated.** It
  now sits immediately *before* Status on Jobs and before Result on Workflows,
  which keeps the adjacency it was given for (both answer "how much should I care
  about this row") while making the fact addressable and sortable. Showing it in
  both places would have put one fact in two cells of the same row, and the two
  would drift the first time either was edited.

### Fixed

- **Folder rows in the Jobs browser were one cell short.** The folder tree's
  column count disagreed with the table's own header, so every folder row's
  "N items" cell stopped one column before the leaf rows beside it. The Workflows
  browser carried the same off-by-one. Both counts are now derived from the
  column set rather than typed by hand, so they cannot drift apart again.
- **The Jobs table's minimum width was stale by a whole column.** The Agency
  column (added in 0.56.3) had no width entry, so it rendered at no particular
  width and contributed nothing to the width the table refuses to compress below
  — which is what made it the column that got squeezed first on a narrow screen.
  The minimum is now summed from the column widths instead of being maintained by
  hand alongside them.

## [1.3.5] - 2026-08-14

### Changed

- **Runner placement is now authored in two places, not three.** The **Runner
  override** editor has been removed from a job's expanded detail panel. Where a
  job runs is decided when the job is built — the Composer's **Run on** field,
  or a Git job's YAML — and, for a single run, in the Run dialog's **Where it
  runs** section. A persistent editor on the detail panel was a third home for
  the same idea, and made a per-run decision into a standing one.
- **The panel still answers the question, it just doesn't take the answer.** The
  **Run on** row stays exactly where it was, next to **Executor**, and still
  names the runner tag with how much of the fleet is carrying it. Reading where
  a job goes never required an editor beside it.

### Removed

- **The operator runner-pin override is retired entirely** — the storage, the
  endpoint and its rung in the precedence chain, not just its editor. Migration
  **1090** drops `jobs.runner_tag_override`; `PUT /api/v1/job-runner-tag-override/{jobId}`
  and the `runnerTagOverride` field on the Job response are gone from the API;
  a job's pin resolves `per-run override → declared pin → unpinned`. A layer
  that no surface could write was worse than no layer: it left a rung nothing
  could set, inspect or clear, and the reason for the arm would have outlived
  anyone's memory of it.
- **What this costs, stated plainly.** A Git-sourced job's durable pin is now
  editable only in its repository — which was the argument *for* the operator
  layer, and it hasn't become wrong. When the pinned runners are gone and the
  work has to move now, the Run dialog's per-run pin sends a single run to
  another tag or to no tag at all, without touching the definition. That path is
  unchanged and is now the only one.
- **If an override was set**, dropping the column un-masks whatever the
  definition declares — including for a job someone had deliberately forced
  unpinned, which goes back to being pinned. Both the column and its writer
  shipped on 2026-08-14 and this drops on the same day, so in practice there is
  nothing to un-mask; the migration header carries the query to check before
  applying it to anything long-lived.

## [1.3.4] - 2026-08-14

### Fixed

- **A long note no longer takes over the expanded panel.** The **Notes** box on
  an expanded job or workflow now shows five lines and scrolls for the rest.
  Notes can run to 4096 characters, and a long one pushed everything beneath it
  — Executor, Run on, tags, the run history — off the bottom of the screen. The
  note itself is unchanged and still fully readable; only its box is bounded.
- **And it shows when there is more to read.** The last visible line fades out
  while the note continues below, and the fade goes away once you have scrolled
  to the end. Without it a fourteen-line note looked exactly like a five-line
  one: the scrollbar only appears while you are scrolling, and the cut landed
  neatly on a line boundary. A note that fits is never faded.

## [1.3.3] - 2026-08-14

Documentation for runner targeting (stage RT-4, the last of
the runner-targeting plan). **No code changes.**

### Changed

- **Runner Config Guide** gains *§4.7 · Tags — label a runner, then send work
  to it*: what a tag is for now that dispatch reads it, why pins name a tag
  rather than a runner, and how tags differ from capabilities (what a runner
  *is* versus what it can *do*). Its stuck-run table gains the two new reasons,

- **User Manual** documents *Run on* in the Run dialog and the *Runner

  Adds *Runner tag* and *Pin* to the glossary.
- **Administrator Manual** gains *§7.10 Runner pinning*: the two storage
  layers and who owns each, the four-rung precedence, the opposite sync rules
  the two adjacent columns follow, and the rules worth knowing before relying
  on it. Corrects §7.9, which still described runner tags as labels with no
  effect on dispatch.

### Notes

Both manuals still carry the **v0.57.24** stamp. That marks the last full
reconciliation, and this release did not perform one — it adds the runner-pin
material and fixes a statement that had become untrue. Other features shipped
since v0.57.24 remain undocumented in them.

## [1.3.2] - 2026-08-14

The runner pin gets its controls (stage RT-3 of
the runner-targeting plan). Everything the last two releases built
is now reachable without touching the API or the repository.

### Added

- **"Run on" in the Run dialog**, under *Where it runs* beside the executor. It
  pre-fills with the pin the job would use, so you can see where a run is going
  before you send it, and change it for this one run. **Run on any runner**
  releases a single run from a pinned job without editing the job — the answer
  when the tagged runners are down and the work still has to go somewhere.
- **A "Runner override" panel on job detail.** This is the one that works for
  jobs synced from Git, whose declared pin lives in a repository. Setting an
  override survives syncs; clearing it hands the job back to whatever Git says.
- **"Run on" in the job composer**, next to Executor, for jobs authored in
  Cronomicon.
- **Runs show the tag they were pinned to**, beside the runner that actually
  took them — what the run was waiting for, not only what eventually answered.

### Notes

- **Where a run is going is never guessed at.** When an override is in force,
  every surface that shows the pin says so and names what it is masking —
  "vlan-core (operator override; the job declares vlan-dmz)". A resolved answer
  shown without its reason is indistinguishable from a bug.
- **Masking a pin and clearing an override are different actions**, and the
  panel keeps them apart: one deliberately ignores what Git declares, the other
  restores it.
- **Pinning to a tag nothing is running is allowed, and says so.** The dialog
  warns that the run will queue until a matching runner appears, and does not
  block it — the runner may be enrolled minutes later.
- **The control is absent for the in-app SSH executor**, where there is no
  runner to select. Offering one there could only ever produce a rejection.
- Tag suggestions come with a live count of matching online runners, so picking
  a pin reads as picking capacity rather than typing a label.
