## [1.3.1] - 2026-08-14

You can now say which runner a job should use (stage RT-2 of
the runner-targeting plan). 1.3.0 taught dispatch to honour a pin;
this release is everything that sets one — the API, the Git round-trip, and the
precedence between them. **The controls arrive in 1.3.2; until then this is
reachable through the API and through Git YAML.**

A pin has two layers, deliberately, because it has two legitimate owners:

- **The declared pin** is part of the job. A Git-source job sets it with
  `spec.runner_tag`, so it lives in review next to `executor` and
  `target_host`, and — like `description` — Git overwrites it on every sync.
- **The operator override** is set in Cronomicon and **survives syncs**, like tags
  and annotations. It exists because a Git job's declared pin cannot be changed
  from the app at all, and the person who finds a placement problem is holding
  a running fleet rather than a merge request.

### Added

- **`spec.runner_tag` in job YAML.** An unusable value is warned about and
  ignored rather than failing the repository's sync, matching how a malformed
  `must_finish_by` behaves.
- **`PUT /api/v1/job-runner-tag-override/{jobId}`** — set, force-unpin, or
  clear the operator override. Same permission as tags and annotations: any
  signed-in user, because a pin can only ever *narrow* which runners may claim
  a run.
- **A per-run pin on the trigger API**, including the break-glass case: a run
  can be sent out unpinned even when its job is pinned. That is the answer when
  the tagged runners are all down and the work has to go somewhere.
- **Runs record the pin they were dispatched with**, so history shows what a
  run was waiting for and not merely which runner eventually took it.
- **Cronomicon-composed jobs carry the declared pin** through compose and through
  the Publish-to-Git builder.

### Notes

- **Precedence, highest first:** the per-run override, then the operator
  override, then the job's declared pin, then unpinned. It is resolved once
  when the run is created and frozen onto it, so a later change never
  retroactively moves a run that is already queued.
- **"Unpinned" is a decision you can record at every level.** Clearing an
  override is not the same as overriding a job to unpinned: the first restores
  whatever Git says, the second deliberately ignores it. The API keeps the two
  distinct rather than collapsing them.
- **Pinning a job whose runs use the in-app SSH executor is refused** (422).
  There is no runner in that path for a tag to select, so accepting the pin
  would run the job from the control plane while appearing to confine it to a
  network segment.
- **Tag matching ignores case.** Found while building this: `vlan-DMZ` in YAML
  now matches a runner tagged `vlan-dmz`, and a fleet can no longer end up with
  two tags that look identical and behave differently. Tags still display
  exactly as they were typed.
- **Scheduled runs, deferred runs, workflow steps and reactions inherit a
  job's pin automatically** — none of them needed changing, and none of them
  can drift from the rule the Run button uses.

---

## [1.3.0] - 2026-08-14

Runner tags start deciding where work runs (stage RT-1 of
the runner-targeting plan). A job or a single ad-hoc run can be
pinned to runners carrying a given tag — so a job that must reach a particular
network segment goes to a runner that sits on it, instead of to whichever
runner in the department happens to be free.

**Schema and dispatch only: no UI yet, and no API accepts a pin.** Nothing
changes for any existing job. This release lands the claim-query change on its
own so it soaks before the surfaces that populate it arrive in 1.3.1 and 1.3.2.

### Added

- **A `runner_tag` pin on jobs and on runs** (migration 1070), both optional
  and both empty by default.
- **Runner tags are now read by dispatch.** Tags have been editable from a
  runner's expanded row since 1.0; until now nothing acted on them. A run
  carrying a pin is offered only to runners carrying that tag.
- **Two new stuck-run explanations.** A pinned run that cannot be claimed says
  which of two things is wrong: *no runner in the fleet carries that tag* —
  a typo, or a runner nobody has tagged yet — or *runners carry it but none is
  online and otherwise eligible*. The two send you to different screens, which
  is why they are different sentences.

### Notes

- **Pinning narrows; it never widens.** A pin is applied on top of department
  isolation, not instead of it. Pinning a run to a tag that only another
  department's runner carries does not send the run there — it leaves the run
  queued, and says so. There is no combination of pin and tag that reaches a
  runner the department rules would deny.
- **A pin is not a reservation and not a priority.** It restricts who may take
  the work; it does not hold capacity, jump the queue, or bring an offline
  runner back. If every tagged runner is down, the run waits.
- **Tags are matched live, at claim time.** Removing a tag from a runner stops
  it taking pinned work from the next poll onward, and adding one starts it —
  no restart, and no effect on runs already in flight.
- **A pin belongs to the network, not to the machine.** Tags were chosen over
  naming a specific runner precisely because re-enrolling a host gives it a new
  identity: a pin naming that identity would break silently, where a tag simply
  applies to whichever runners carry it. Deregistering a runner drops its tags
  with it.

Rolling this migration back removes the pins and reverts the claim rule with
them, so previously pinned jobs become runnable from anywhere eligible again
rather than failing visibly. On a fleet where pins encode network reach, that
is worth knowing before rolling back.

---

## [1.2.7] - 2026-08-14

**Failure notifications now say who to call.** The last stage of the annotations
band (AN-4): when a job or workflow that
carries an operator annotation fails, the message names its contact and says so
if it is critical. **No schema migration and no API change.**

### Changed

- **Notification bodies carry the annotation.** A failure, a missed run or an
  SLA breach on an annotated definition adds up to two lines:

      Critical: yes
      Contact:  dba-oncall@corp.example

  Each line appears only when that field is set, and the notes themselves are
  not included — a notification is not where you read them. Both email and push
  carry it.
- **Workflows are covered as well as jobs**, so an annotated workflow's failure
  reports its contact the same way a job's does.

### Notes

- **Subjects are unchanged.** The `[Cronomicon] <name> FAILED` shape is untouched,
  deliberately: mail filters are keyed on it, and a silent change would break
  them at exactly the wrong hour. A `[CRITICAL]` prefix could be offered as an
  opt-in later if it is wanted.
- **An un-annotated definition's message is byte-for-byte what it was**, so
  nothing changes for anyone not using annotations.
- **An annotation never costs a notification.** If the lookup fails for any
  reason, the message is sent without the extra lines rather than not sent.
- **Where the definition cannot be identified, no contact is guessed.** An alert
  for a name shared by two departments' jobs goes out un-enriched rather than
  naming one of them — the same rule the rest of the app follows for ambiguous
  names.

---

## [1.2.6] - 2026-08-14

**Jobs and workflows can carry operator notes.** The visible half of the
annotations band (stage AN-3): what a
definition is for, whether it is critical, and who to contact when it breaks —
in the catalog, where you are already looking. **No schema migration and no API
change.**

### Added

- **A Notes section at the top of every expanded job and workflow.** It holds a
  Critical marker, a contact and free-text notes, with a line recording who last
  changed them and when. Any signed-in user can edit it — the same rule tags
  have always followed — and it is available on Git-sourced definitions too,
  where it is the only thing about the definition you can write from the app.
- **A Critical marker on catalog rows**, beside the status chip on both the Jobs
  and Workflows tables. It appears only when set; there is no marker for the
  ordinary case.
- **The Run dialog names the contact.** Running a job that is critical or has a
  contact shows both above the dialog's sections, with the first line of its
  notes. It is context, not a new confirmation step: nothing extra to tick, and
  the existing sections behave exactly as before.
- **Workflow search now matches notes and contact** as well as name and
  description. The Jobs search still matches names only — that list is paged by
  the server, where the same change is a larger commitment.

### Notes

- Notes are plain text. Newlines are kept; markdown is not rendered and URLs are
  not turned into links.
- Notes are stored in Cronomicon only, never written back to Git, and kept across
  syncs — they sit alongside the Git-owned description rather than replacing it.
- Clearing all three fields removes the annotation entirely rather than leaving
  an empty one behind.
- Marking something critical still changes nothing about how it runs. It is a
  label for people; failure notifications begin to mention it in the next
  release.

---

## [1.2.5] - 2026-08-14

The API half of operator annotations (stage AN-2 of
the annotations plan). **No schema migration and still no UI** — the
Jobs and Workflows pages do not show or edit annotations until AN-3. What lands
here is the read and write surface, so an integration can already set "who to
call when this breaks" ahead of the screens that display it.

### API

- **`PUT /api/v1/job-annotation/{jobId}`** and
  **`PUT /api/v1/workflow-annotation/{workflowId}`** — set a definition's
  annotation: `critical`, `contact`, `notes`. A full replace, not a patch.
  Session + CSRF, no role permission, matching the tags routes. Caps are
  enforced server-side (contact ≤256 chars, notes ≤4096); a breach is 400
  `invalid_annotation`.
- **Five additive fields on job and workflow rows**: `critical` always present,
  plus `contact`, `notes`, `notesBy` and `notesAt` when set. List rows carry
  `critical` and `contact` only — `notes` is detail-only, so a page of results
  does not carry up to 4KB per row. No removals or reshapes.

### Notes

Behaviours worth knowing before wiring anything to these routes:

- **Writing all three fields empty deletes the annotation.** An absent
  annotation and an empty one are meant to be indistinguishable; storing a blank
  would give every reader a second empty state ("annotated with nothing, by
  someone, at some time") that means nothing to an operator.
- **`notesBy` and `notesAt` are server-assigned** and ignored if sent.
  Attribution a client can set is attribution nobody can trust.
- **A recycle-binned definition can still be annotated.** It keeps its
  annotation through the bin, so being able to read a note but not correct it
  would be the strange state — and "why did this get binned" is exactly the note
  someone wants to leave at that moment. This matches how tags already behave.
- **`critical` still routes nothing.** It is carried and returned; it does not
  affect scheduling, queue priority or who gets paged. Failure notifications
  begin to mention it in AN-4.

---

## [1.2.4] - 2026-08-14

Groundwork for operator annotations — notes, a criticality flag and a contact
for jobs and workflows (stage AN-1).
**Schema only: there is nothing to see in the UI yet, and no API accepts or
returns an annotation.** This release adds the table those stages will write
to, so the migration lands and soaks on its own rather than alongside the
surfaces that depend on it.

### Added

- **An `annotations` table** (migration 1060), keyed on the definition's
  permanent id and holding a `critical` flag, a free-text `contact`, free-text
  `notes`, and who last changed them. One row per job or workflow, one table
  for both kinds.

### Notes

Three lifecycle properties are fixed by this migration and worth knowing before
the next stages make them visible:

- **Annotations are operator-owned and survive Git syncs.** They are not the
  YAML `description`, which stays Git-owned and is overwritten on every sync.
  The two coexist and neither writes the other — the same arrangement tags have
  had since 1.0.
- **Recycle-binning a definition keeps its annotation**, and restoring brings
  it back. Deleting one for good removes it.
- **Two same-named definitions in different departments keep separate
  annotations**, and deleting either leaves the other's intact.

Rolling this migration back destroys the annotations themselves. Unlike a
synced column there is no copy in Git to restore from, and re-running a sync
will not bring them back.

---

## [1.2.3] - 2026-08-14

Names that belong to two departments now say which one they mean, everywhere
they appear (stage R2F-3 of the rbac2-followups plan, completing the
band). **No schema migration and no runner protocol change.** If you do not run
duplicate job names, this release changes nothing you can see — which is the
point of the rule below.

### Added

- **Agency badges where a name would otherwise be ambiguous.** Run history,
  workflow runs, the activity feed, the Dashboard timeline and attention tiles,
  the Upcoming list, the reaction picker, calendar bindings, and the "used by"
  chips on Scripts and Schedules now render `deploy · FIN` instead of a bare
  `deploy` — **but only when the list you are looking at actually contains two
  definitions by that name.** A single-agency install, and every name that is
  not shared, keeps showing plain names.
- **Run dialogs name the job you are about to run.** "Run backup-daily" becomes
  "Run backup-daily · FIN" when two departments own a backup-daily.

### Fixed

- **The Dashboard folded two departments' failures into one tile.** The
  "needs attention" tiles grouped by job NAME, so two departments' same-named
  jobs merged into a single tile with a combined count — and clicking it opened
  a history filtered to both. Tiles now group by job identity and pivot history
  by it too.
- **The Workflows catalog could show the wrong department's agencies.** A
  workflow's Agency column is derived from its jobs, cached per page under a key
  that did not include the workflow's identity — so two same-named workflows got
  whichever set was computed last.

### Changed

- **Badges cannot reveal another department's catalog.** A name is qualified
  only when the collision is present in what you were already sent, which is
  filtered by your access before it reaches you. If the other department's job
  is invisible to you, so is the fact that it exists.
- **History rows from before identity tracking show plain names.** They cannot
  be attributed to either of two same-named jobs, so they say the bare name
  rather than guess — and they do not cause other rows to be badged either.
- **The `?job=` history filter is unchanged.** It remains an honest filter by
  name and may return runs of two same-named jobs; the rows carry their own
  badges. Links that know which job they mean now pass the identity instead.

### API

Additive fields only, no removals or reshapes: `jobUid`, `workflowUid` and
`agencies` on activity entries; `agencies` on workflow runs; `ownerUid` and
`ownerAgencies` on schedule rows, upcoming fires and calendar bindings; `uid`
and `agencies` on a schedule's `usedBy` entries. A script's `usedBy` stays the
plain array of names it has always been — the identity-bearing version is a new
parallel `usedByRefs`.

### Notes

Workflow step chips inside a graph still show plain step names; the graph itself
identifies the workflow, and qualifying steps would require threading the job
catalog into a presentational component for little gain. The workflow *pickers*
(1.3.0) are where a step's job is chosen and disambiguated.

---

## [1.2.2] - 2026-08-14

A workflow step can now say **which** job it means (stage R2F-2 of
the rbac2-followups plan). Since 1.2.0 two departments may own a job
of the same name, and a step naming one refused to run rather than guess —
correct, but it left a legal setup unbuildable. **No schema migration and no
runner protocol change.** Every existing workflow keeps working exactly as it
did; the new field is optional and nothing writes it to a graph you do not edit.

### Added

- **Pick a job, not a name.** The workflow editors — both the step list and the
  graph canvas — now record the job you picked, not just its name. Where two
  departments own a job of the same name, the picker shows each with its agency
  (`deploy · FIN`, `deploy · DSS`) so you can tell them apart, and the step you
  build runs the one you chose. A name that is not shared shows no badge: the
  common single-agency install looks exactly as it did.
- **Two steps in one workflow may now run different same-named jobs.** They are
  two references, and each resolves to its own job.

### Changed

- **Existing steps are left alone.** Opening a workflow and saving it does not
  rewrite the steps you did not touch — a step that references a job by name
  stays that way until you re-pick the job. The editor still shows you which job
  a name-only step resolves to, so nothing is hidden; it just does not change
  your graph behind you.
- **A step whose job was deleted refuses instead of substituting.** If you pinned
  a job and it is later deleted, the step fails with a clear reason. It does not
  fall back to another job that happens to share the name — re-creating a deleted
  job creates a *new* job, and running it in place of the old one silently would
  be worse than stopping.
- **Authorization resolves the same job execution will.** The compose-time
  permission check follows the pinned job, not the name — so it can never
  authorize you against one department's job while another's is what runs.
- **Git workflows still identify jobs by name.** A repository is a single
  namespace where names are unique, and an identity written into a YAML file
  would not survive being replayed into another installation. A hand-written
  `jobUid` in a git workflow is ignored, and the repository validator says so.

### API

`WorkflowStep` gains an optional `jobUid`. Write it together with `name` — the
pair must agree, and a `jobUid` naming a differently-named job is rejected with
422 rather than one half silently winning. Omit it for an unambiguous
name-only reference.

### Notes

The last deferred piece — disambiguation badges on the remaining
name-displaying views (R2F-3) — is still to come. Until then, the Jobs and
Workflows tables' Agency columns and the workflow pickers are where duplicate
names are told apart.

---

## [1.2.1] - 2026-08-14

Credential bindings now follow a job's permanent id (stage R2F-1 of
the rbac2-followups plan), closing the one behavioural defect that
same-named jobs could trigger. **No schema migration and no protocol change** —
if you run duplicate job names, upgrade promptly; if you do not, nothing about
this release changes what your installation does.

### Fixed

- **Editing one job's credentials no longer erases another's.** Two departments
  may own a job of the same name since 1.2.0, but the list of secrets, variables
  and keys a job consumes was still filed under that name. Saving one twin's
  bindings deleted the other's on the way — one department's edit silently
  destroying another's configuration — and opening either showed both sets
  merged together. Each job's bindings are now its own. Existing bindings are
  read and written unchanged; nothing needs re-entering.
- **A run injects its own job's credentials.** Every place that reads a job's
  bindings — dispatch to a runner, the in-app SSH executor, log redaction, the
  pre-flight check that refuses an unscoped run, the rule deciding which runners
  may claim a run, and the explanation of why a run is stuck — now identifies
  the job by the id frozen onto the run when it was queued. Previously a run of
  one twin could be gated on, and injected with, the other's credentials. The
  same correction applies to a job's `become` password and its referenced
  script, both of which were looked up by name.

### Notes

Where a caller genuinely cannot say which job it means, the old shared-by-name
behaviour is kept deliberately rather than guessing — a guess that deletes the
wrong department's bindings is the failure this release removes. Scripts keep
name identity permanently: they are a single catalog with no agency of their
own.

Reference *resolution* was never affected: which secret a run may read has been
decided by scope and department membership since 0.57, and an ambiguous
reference has always refused rather than picked. This defect was confined to
which job a binding LIST belonged to.

The other two deferred pieces — identity-valued workflow steps (R2F-2) and
disambiguation badges on the remaining name-displaying views (R2F-3) — are
still to come.

---

## [1.2.0] - 2026-08-13

**Two departments can now own a job of the same name.** This is the change the
whole 1.1.x series existed to make safe (stage R2-5, the final stage of
the rbac2 plan): the permanent id minted in 1.1.0 becomes the
primary key of jobs, workflows and schedules, and name uniqueness relaxes to
per-agency. **This is the largest schema migration since the dual-source
split; take a backup before upgrading, and soak it in staging first.**

### Added

- **Per-agency job and workflow names.** Creating `backup-daily` scoped to FIN
  no longer conflicts with DSS's `backup-daily`. The rule: a name must be
  unique within each agency its scope maps to, and a job or workflow in the
  "All" pool must be unique against everything, since All overlaps every
  agency. Git-sourced definitions keep one name per repository (the repo is a
  single namespace, and the sync validator now refuses a duplicate pair of
  YAML files instead of silently letting the last one win). Schedules keep
  their existing one-name-per-source rule: they have no agency of their own.

### Changed

- **Refusals stay deliberately vague.** A name conflict answers "name already
  in use" without naming the owning agency — a wordier message would let one
  department enumerate another's catalog by trying names. The one exception is
  a conflict with your own recycle-binned definition, where the actionable
  hint survives.
- **Everything that follows a definition follows its identity.** Delete
  cascades, pauses, schedule entries, reactions, bindings, revision history
  and log-folder codes are all keyed on the id, so deleting or renaming one
  twin never touches the other's. A reaction now follows its definition
  through a source move rather than being stranded by it.
- **Ambiguity refuses rather than guesses.** Wherever only a bare name is
  available and it now matches two definitions — a workflow step, an older
  runner's file-watch report, a token-authenticated trigger-by-name, a
  recycle-bin restore or purge — the operation is refused with an explicit
  message instead of silently picking one. Qualify the reference (step source,
  runner upgrade, restore one twin first) to proceed.

### Notes

Rolling back this migration refuses, loudly, if duplicate names exist — a
rollback that silently discarded one department's job would be worse than one
that asks an operator to rename first.

Two pieces of the original R2-5 scope ship separately rather than here, both
recorded in the plan: per-identity disambiguation badges across the remaining
name-displaying views (the Jobs and Workflows tables already carry their
Agency columns, which is where duplicate names are actually told apart), and
an identity-valued workflow step picker. Until the picker lands, a step
naming an ambiguous job refuses at run time rather than guessing — fail
closed, never fail wrong.

---

## [1.1.4] - 2026-08-13

The last two places that identified a job by name alone — the file-watch
trigger and alert targeting — now use its permanent id (stage R2-4 of
the rbac2 plan). Runner protocol goes to **v11**.

### Changed

- **A file arrival names the job by id.** When Cronomicon tells a runner to watch
  a directory, the instruction now carries the job's id, and the runner hands
  it back when a file lands. This was the only place in the runner protocol
  where something the *runner* reported chose which job the server started, so
  it is the one that most needed narrowing.
- **Alert rules remember which job you picked.** A rule targeting a job records
  that job's id, resolved from the name when you save the rule — you do not
  need to do anything differently, and existing rules were updated during the
  upgrade. A rule whose job name exists in both the Git and Cronomicon catalogs
  keeps matching by name, since there is no way to tell which one was meant.

### Upgrading

**Older runners keep working.** A v10 runner simply omits the id and the server
falls back to matching on the job's name and source, which is exactly correct
while job names are unique. Upgrade runners that use file-watch triggers before
the final stage of this work, which makes names ambiguous and turns that
fallback into a refusal rather than a guess.

Every runner will re-register once after upgrading. The protocol version is
part of a runner's configuration fingerprint, so changing it makes each agent
notice its configuration has moved and re-declare itself. This is expected and
needs no action.

### Notes

The server now fires from *its own copy* of the watch instruction rather than
from what the runner reported. The runner's report says which watch an arrival
belongs to; the server decides what that means. So a runner cannot select a
different job by reporting an id it was never given, nor by pairing one watch's
id with another's name — it can only match something it was actually asked to
watch, exactly as it could only ever report a path it was asked to look at.

---

## [1.1.3] - 2026-08-13

The rule that stops a job from overlapping itself now identifies that job by
its permanent id rather than by its name (stage R2-3 of
the rbac2 plan), and a real authorization gap in the workflow
composer is closed along the way.

### Fixed

- **The workflow composer checked the wrong job's permissions.** When deciding
  whether you may author a workflow, Cronomicon looked up each step's job
  alphabetically by source rather than by the order it will actually use when
  the workflow runs. For a Git-sourced workflow whose step name exists in both
  catalogs, that meant your access was checked against one job while a
  different, identically named job was the one that would run. Authorization
  and execution now resolve the step the same way, through one shared rule.

### Changed

- **"Do not let this job run twice at once" is now keyed on identity.** The six
  places that can start a job — a schedule, a manual trigger, a reaction, a
  workflow step, a skipped workflow step, and a watched file arriving — all
  build that key from the job's permanent id. Your own custom concurrency keys
  are untouched and still work exactly as before: they are how you deliberately
  make two different jobs share one gate, and Cronomicon does not rewrite them.
- **Runs already queued or running when you upgrade are carried across.** The
  gate compares keys as text, so runs in flight are rewritten during the
  upgrade to match what the new code computes. Without that, a job set to
  "Forbid" could have overlapped itself exactly once, during the upgrade.
  Finished runs keep their original key — that is the record of what happened,
  not a live value.

### Notes

Schedules are now matched to their job by id as well. As with the delete rules
in 1.1.2, that match keeps a name-based fallback, and here the reason is even
starker: a schedule entry that fails to match does not raise an error, it
simply never fires again. The tests for this deliberately verify that removing
the fallback breaks them.

One item planned for this stage was deferred: individual workflow steps do not
yet record the id of the job they point at. The step picker becomes id-valued
as part of the disambiguation work in the final stage, and adding a field
nothing writes would have been dead weight until then. The correctness problem
in that area — authorization and execution disagreeing — is fixed above.

---

## [1.1.2] - 2026-08-13

Everything that belongs to a job or workflow — its schedule entries, its pause,
its parked runs, its reactions, its log-folder code — now knows *which*
definition it belongs to rather than only what that definition is called
(stage R2-2 of the rbac2 plan). Behaviour is unchanged; this is the
groundwork that lets two departments own a job of the same name.

### Changed

- **The nine delete-cascade rules are now keyed on identity.** When you delete
  a job or workflow, the database removes its schedule entries, pause, parked
  runs, reference bindings and reactions — and it now finds them by the
  definition's permanent id instead of by name. Deleting one definition can no
  longer reach a same-named sibling's rows, which is precisely the accident
  per-agency naming would otherwise introduce.
- **Demo data now carries identities too.** The preview seeder writes
  definitions directly rather than through the normal authoring paths, so it
  had been producing id-less demo jobs; it now mints them exactly as a real
  create would, and seeded run history is attributed to them.

### Notes

Each cascade rule deliberately keeps a second, narrower fallback: rows that
somehow carry no identity are still matched by name. That is not
belt-and-braces. A cascade that silently stops working leaves orphan rows for
the *next* definition of the same name to inherit, and a rule that only matched
identities would have reintroduced exactly the failure this change exists to
prevent — for any row written by a path that had been missed. The fallback is
correct while names are unique and comes off in the final stage.

Two things were deliberately *not* moved yet, both for the same reason: the
file-sighting de-duplication constraint and the log-folder code's uniqueness
rule are the two places where a subtly wrong key does not merely mislabel
something but fires a duplicate run or reuses a folder. Both are exactly
correct as they stand while names are unique, and both move in the final stage
where the change is required and the table is being rebuilt anyway.

---

## [1.1.1] - 2026-08-13

Run history starts recording *which* job ran, not just what it was called
(stage R2-1 of the rbac2 plan, the plan that finishes AF-4b).
Like 1.1.0 before it, this is deliberately invisible: names are still unique,
every existing filter and view behaves exactly as it did, and nothing you do
changes.

### Added

- **Runs, workflow runs and the activity feed now carry the definition's
  permanent `uid`.** It is stamped when the run is created — the same rule
  the log-folder code follows — so a run stays attributable to the job that
  produced it after that job is renamed, re-created, or deleted. Existing
  history was filled in during the upgrade.
- **`GET /runs?jobUid=` and `GET /workflow-runs?workflowUid=`** filter history
  by that identity. The existing `?job=` and `?workflowName=` filters are
  unchanged and are staying: they filter by *name*, and a name will one day
  belong to more than one job. A job's own history panel now asks by `uid`.

### Notes

Three details worth knowing, because each is a place where the obvious
implementation would have been wrong:

The activity feed has no source column, so a name alone cannot always say
which definition was meant — the same name may legitimately exist in both the
Git and Cronomicon catalogs today. Activity rows therefore resolve their uid from
the run they describe when there is one, fall back to the name only when it is
unambiguous, and otherwise record nothing rather than guess. Attributing one
department's history to another's identity is worse than leaving a historical
row unlabelled.

The backfill runs now, while `(source, name)` still identifies a definition
uniquely. That window is the entire reason the remaining work is staged: each
stage moves a set of references onto the uid while names are still unique, so
no stage can be the one that breaks. A run whose job was already deleted keeps
a null uid — the name column still records what was asked for.

Nothing reads the uid to make decisions yet; the scheduler, the concurrency
gate, the runner protocol and alert targeting all still resolve by name. Those
are the next stages, and each ships on its own.

---

## [1.1.0] - 2026-08-13

Jobs, workflows and schedules gain a permanent identity (phase AF-4a of
the agency-first-rbac plan). This is the foundation for letting
two agencies use the same job name — a change that cannot happen while the
name *is* the identity — and it ships deliberately behavior-neutral: names
remain unique exactly as before, and nothing you see or do changes.

### Added

- **Every job, workflow and schedule now carries a `uid`** — assigned the
  first time Cronomicon sees the definition (whether it arrived from Git or the
  composer), returned by the API, and never changed afterwards: not by a
  sync, not by an edit, not by a restore from the recycle bin. Existing
  definitions received theirs during the upgrade migration. Unlike the
  numeric `id` (a database handle) and unlike the name (which a later phase
  will allow to repeat across agencies), the `uid` is the identity that
  survives — new integrations should key on it.

### Notes

The inventory pass that preceded this work mapped what "same name in two
agencies" actually touches: 21 name-reference columns across 15 tables, seven
delete triggers, roughly 300 query sites, the concurrency gate, the log-folder
allocator, the runner protocol and alert targeting — with ten edges that would
fail *silently* under a duplicate name. Migrating those edges onto the `uid`
is the remaining, staged work of AF-4; each stage is separately shippable
while names stay unique, which is what makes the staging safe. The plan
records the stages and the ranked risk list.

---

## [1.0.15] - 2026-08-13

A department can now administer its own access (band AF-3 of
the agency-first-rbac plan, specified in
the af3-delegated-governance plan). This completes the agency-first
arc: AF-1 made every job state its agency, AF-2 let a department author its own
work, and this lets a department decide who does it.

### Added

- **Delegated access administration.** Someone holding **Manage roles &
  access** for an agency — rather than globally — can now grant and revoke
  access within that agency. Three rules keep delegation from becoming
  promotion, all enforced server-side: grants may only name an agency you
  administer, "All scopes" stays with unrestricted administrators, and **you
  cannot grant a permission you do not hold yourself**. Editing or revoking an
  existing grant checks it both as it stands and as it would become, so a
  grant cannot be captured by re-pointing it.

  Practical note when setting this up: because you can only hand out what you
  hold, a departmental administrator's role must carry at least the
  permissions of the roles it is meant to assign. A role holding only Manage
  roles & access can grant nothing.

### Changed

- **Role definitions are now edited by unrestricted administrators only.** A
  role is shared by every agency — changing `operator` changes it everywhere —
  so it is not one department's to alter, and allowing it would have been a way
  around the rule above (add a permission to a role, then grant that role to
  yourself). Everyone who manages access still *sees* the roles, since knowing
  what a role carries is how you choose which to grant; the Roles card explains
  why its buttons are absent rather than failing on click. Note for existing
  installs: a scope-restricted administrator keeps grant administration and
  loses role editing.
- **The grant form offers only what you can give.** "All scopes
  (unrestricted)" no longer appears for a departmental administrator.

### Notes

Two items carried in the plan under this band were closed rather than built,
with the reasoning recorded in the sub-plan: per-agency gating of **Publish to
GitLab** (the object is a file in a shared repository reviewed as a unit, so
Git review is the real control), and splitting **viewer** into separate
View Jobs / View Schedules / View Run history permissions (enforceable, but
read visibility is currently one concept — your granted scopes — and dividing
it into verbs creates undesigned states such as an operator who may run a job
they cannot see). The second remains available as its own band if the need
becomes concrete.

---

## [1.0.14] - 2026-08-13

Authoring jobs and workflows becomes a permission you can grant to a
department, instead of something only a global admin can do (band AF-2 of
the agency-first-rbac plan, specified in
the af2-compose-permission plan). This is the change AF-1 was
built to make safe: because every job now states its agency, "may this person
author *here*" finally has an answer.

### Added

- **A seventh permission: Create jobs & workflows.** It appears in the Roles
  editor beside the other six, so "FIN composer — authors FIN's jobs, and
  nothing else" is now a role you can define. Granting it is **agency-bound**:
  the holder authors within the agencies their access grant covers, and is
  refused elsewhere. Existing roles are unaffected — only `admin` gains it on
  upgrade.

### Changed

- **Authoring is checked per job, not once at the door.** Holding the
  permission gets you into the composer; whether a *particular* job may be
  created, edited or deleted is decided against that job's scope. Editing
  checks both the scope a job is leaving and the one it is arriving at, so a
  job cannot be moved out of a department, nor captured into one, by anyone
  who could not already author it in both places. Workflows follow the jobs
  they drive: a workflow may only be authored by someone who could author
  every job in its graph.
- **Global (All) definitions remain admin-only.** A scheduled run of a job
  with no scope carries no agency to check, so authoring one stays with
  unrestricted administrators. Departmental composers see named scopes only —
  the All option is withheld from their scope picker rather than refused after
  the fact.
- **Shared authoring surfaces remain admin-only, deliberately.** Reusable
  schedules, working calendars, reactions, and the revision history and
  recycle bin all act on objects that belong to no single agency. Granting
  them to one department would mean retiming another's schedule, attaching a
  trigger to their job, or purging their deleted definitions — so this release
  does not widen them.

---

## [1.0.13] - 2026-08-13

Every job now states which agency it belongs to, and "everyone" is one of the
answers (band AF-1 of the agency-first-rbac plan). Departmental
visibility already worked — a restricted user only ever saw jobs in their
granted scopes — but a job whose scope was simply never filled in fell into
the global pool and was visible to all. That state is now a deliberate,
visible choice rather than a default.

### Added

- **"All agencies (global)" is a real option.** The composer's Scope field
  offers it as the first entry, with the consequence spelled out inline:
  visible to every agency, runnable by anyone who may trigger jobs. Picking it
  is a decision on the record; it stores exactly as before (no scope), so
  nothing about how global jobs run has changed.
- **The Agency column is sortable** on both Jobs and Workflows, so a
  department's work groups together. (Multi-value columns are normally left
  unsorted; this one is a deliberate exception, since a job carries at most
  one agency in practice.)

### Changed

- **A composed job must state its scope.** Creating or editing a job without
  answering the Scope field is refused — in the form, before anything is sent,
  with a sentence naming the All option. The API enforces the same rule
  (HTTP 422 on an absent or null `scope`); an explicit empty string remains a
  valid, deliberate "All". Editing an existing global job prefills All rather
  than re-asking, so no existing job needs revisiting.
- **The Agency column says "All", not "—".** An em dash reads as missing data,
  which is exactly how an accidentally-global job used to look. A global job
  now shows an "All" chip; an em dash is reserved for a job whose scope maps
  to no agency at all, with a tooltip saying so.
- **A scope with no agency mapping warns while you compose.** Advisory only —
  the save proceeds. Such a job is visible only to unrestricted admins, which
  is safe but usually means the scope→agency mapping in Settings is
  unfinished.
- **Git-source jobs are unaffected.** A job YAML with no `scope` still syncs,
  landing in All and recording a sync warning that names the file. A merged
  definition never goes out of service over a metadata field.

---

## [1.0.12] - 2026-08-13

Where a job's secrets and variables are declared moves to the composer, and
the Jobs expanded view starts telling the whole truth about what a run
receives (band JP-4 of the jobs-page-tweaks plan). No API,
schema, or server-side permission change.

### Changed

- **Secrets and variables are declared when you create or edit a job.** The
  composer has a **Secrets & variables** section beside SSH keys, with the
  same controls the Jobs detail used to carry — kind, reference name, and the
  optional *inject as* alias — validated against the job's scope while you
  author, and prefilled from the job's saved set when editing. Keys and
  references are written together in one request after the job saves, and
  skipped entirely when nothing changed, so an ordinary save still needs no
  extra permission. Practical effect: because composing a job is admin-only,
  changing an existing job's declared references is now an admin action;
  rotating the values themselves, managing a script's references, and adding
  a reference for one run are all unchanged.
- **The Jobs expanded view shows what a run actually receives, read-only.**
  The section now lists the *effective* set — the job's own references plus
  any declared on the script it uses, which is what dispatch injects — with
  each inherited row marked **from script**, since that is a Scripts-page
  edit rather than a job one. Rows still carry their resolution verdict. An
  **Edit in Composer** link appears for callers who may edit the job, and the
  section is omitted entirely for a job that uses no references, instead of
  showing an empty editor on every expansion. SSH keys keep their own field
  above, unchanged.

## [1.0.11] - 2026-08-13

Two Jobs-page readability tweaks (band JP-1/JP-2 of
the jobs-page-tweaks plan). Display only — no API, schema, or
permission changes.

### Removed

- **The two per-day analytics charts.** The Analytics panel's "Runs per day"
  bars and "Median duration trend" line are gone, from the Jobs expanded view
  and from History › Analytics alike (they were one shared component). What
  remains is the part operators actually read: the window picker (7d/30d/90d),
  the stat tiles — success rate, runs, suppressed, failures, median, p95,
  late, missed — and the most-common-failure list. The **Duration trend**
  sparkline at the top of a job's activity column is a different chart and
  stays. `/analytics/runs` still returns its per-day `buckets`; only the
  frontend stopped drawing them.

### Changed

- **Run inputs scroll past five.** A job declaring more than five run inputs
  now shows the first five and scrolls the rest inside the section, instead of
  growing the expanded view without limit — the same treatment Recent runs
  already gets. Five or fewer render exactly as before, with no scrollbar. The
  warning about required inputs that no scheduled run can fill stays outside
  the scroll area, where it cannot be scrolled out of sight.

## [1.0.10] - 2026-08-12

Two small composition workflows: reuse an existing job or an existing script
as the starting point for a new job, instead of re-entering everything from
scratch.

### Added

- **Clone a job.** Cronomicon-source rows on the Jobs page have a **Clone**
  action next to Edit (same gate: Compose capability, amadeus source). It
  opens the composer with every setting prefilled from the original — script,
  scope, target host, environment, run inputs, schedules, advanced fields,
  and the declared SSH-key bindings — but in create mode: the name arrives as
  `<original>-copy` and stays editable, and saving creates a new job while
  leaving the original untouched. Reactions are deliberately not copied
  (they attach to a job by name, so they would be wrong on the copy), and
  git-authored jobs refuse to clone with the existing read-only notice.
- **Create a job from a script.** The Scripts catalog's expanded detail has a
  **+ Create Job** button (Compose-gated, so viewers are never offered a
  dead end) that opens the composer with that script preselected and
  everything else blank.

## [1.0.9] - 2026-08-12

Hardening from the pre-merge review (band FX2-F of
the review-fixes2 plan). No behaviour changes — both items turn a
rule that existed only as hand-copied code into a single shared definition, so
the next copy cannot be forgotten.

### Changed

- **The per-job read gate is one helper, not a repeated block.** Every job
  sub-route that must 404 on a binned or out-of-scope job (without revealing
  which) carried the same ~12 lines by hand — and the file-arrivals route
  first shipped with that copy missing, which is a cross-scope information
  leak. `getJob` and the file-arrivals route now share `requireReadableJob`;
  routes that deliberately vary the shape (pause/resume's permission check,
  bindings' 404/403 split, tags' binned-allowed rule) keep their own guards,
  with the variations documented at the helper.
- **"A recycle-binned owner's schedule entries are not live" is stated once.**
  The SQL fragment encoding it was hand-copied between the schedules drain and
  the calendar binding collector — the same drift that produced the original
  defect class. Both now interpolate one shared fragment.

## [1.0.8] - 2026-08-12

Reporting and preview polish from the same pre-merge review (bands FX2-D/E of
the review-fixes2 plan): every fix here is about telling the
operator the truth — once, in the right place, with the right owner.

### Fixed

- **A held pending run logs its hold once, not every 15 seconds.** The
  "held by an admission gate" line re-fired on every promotion tick — about
  5,760 identical entries a day for a single paused job's deferred run —
  drowning real events. It now fires on the transition only, and again only
  if the run's reason for waiting actually changes.
- **A missed workflow run notifies as a workflow.** Notification rules that
  target a job by name also matched a same-named workflow's missed-run alert,
  paging the wrong operator; workflow-targeted rules could not match it at
  all. The alert now carries its owner kind and the "workflow" label in the
  subject, matching the missed-run detector's own alerts.
- **A deferred run keeps its "ad-hoc" badge while held.** Pausing (or
  binning) a job flipped its operator-scheduled deferral to look like a gated
  schedule fire on the Upcoming page, sending the reader hunting for a cron
  entry that doesn't exist. Who parked a run and why it is currently waiting
  are different facts; the row now shows both.
- **The cron preview enumerates sparse expressions honestly.** A leap-day
  cron (`0 0 29 2 *`) exhausted the preview's search budget and silently
  showed fewer upcoming fires than asked — or none, which read as "never
  fires" while the engine fires it fine. The search now skips month-by-month
  where the month alone rules a day out, the budget is restored to its
  pre-cut size, and when the horizon genuinely runs out the preview says
  "no fire found within the preview horizon" instead of rendering the same
  thing as "no more fires" — on all four surfaces that preview a cron.

---

## [1.0.7] - 2026-08-12

The pre-merge review's blockers (bands FX2-A/B/C of
the review-fixes2 plan). A high-effort adversarial review of the
v1.0.1–v1.0.6 sweep found its residue: not defects inside any band, but
interactions *between* them — a slide gated on the policy it feeds, a gate
policy judged under a different origin than the one that accepted the run, and
bin-filters reaching delete guards they were never meant for.

### Fixed

- **Enabling the session idle timeout no longer logs out every active user at
  once.** The activity clock only ran while the timeout was already on, so
  every session's "last seen" froze at login — and the moment an operator
  enabled the cap, every session older than the limit was judged against that
  login-time anchor and revoked simultaneously, the operator included. The
  clock now runs always, and flipping the cap on starts everyone's countdown
  at that moment rather than retroactively. The same fix covers switching
  "require re-authentication" off, and a transient failure to read the setting
  no longer counts as the operator re-enabling it (which would have handed
  every stale session a fresh window). The 8-hour absolute ceiling is
  unaffected.
- **A deferred run of a disabled job runs at its scheduled time.** Scheduling
  a run "for tomorrow" on a disabled job is allowed — a disabled job has
  always been runnable by hand — but the promotion applied the stricter
  automatic-run policy, so the system accepted the run and then held it until
  it expired as missed, paging on-call about a run it had agreed to. Promotion
  now honours the deferral's provenance: an operator's deferral inherits the
  by-hand exemption, while queued backlogs and reaction-triggered runs of a
  disabled job stay stopped — and a pause still holds *all* of them
  (deliberately: pause means "stop everything now", and a held run fires on
  resume).
- **Deleting a calendar again warns when a recycle-binned job still uses it.**
  The recycle-bin sweep taught the delete guard to ignore binned references,
  but a calendar delete is permanent while a binned job is recoverable:
  deleting its holiday calendar meant the restored job silently ran on every
  holiday it was configured to skip. The delete now blocks with the reference
  listed and marked "(in recycle bin)"; `?force=true` remains the informed
  override. Calendar pages still list only live references.
- **Marking a calendar global is blocked by binned references too.** The same
  asymmetry on the other guard: a calendar used as a run-day (`only`) list
  cannot also be global — the combination silences the job entirely — but
  binning the sole referrer first unlocked it, and the silence began on the
  job's restore with nothing connecting the two events.
- **Deleting a schedule notes the recycle-binned jobs it detaches.** Such a
  delete rightly proceeds without force (restoring the schedule replays the
  bindings), but it happened silently — and a restored job that lost its
  schedule a week earlier reads as data loss with no explanation. The Change
  Log and Activity entries now name the binned referrers and the remedy.

---

## [1.0.6] - 2026-08-12

Makes every schedule projection agree with the engine (band FX-F of
the review-fixes plan — the final band of the post-1.0.0 sweep).

### Fixed

- **The Workflows list now projects interval and windowed schedules.** It read
  only the cron expression, so an interval-mode schedule showed no next run at
  all and a windowed one showed a fire before its window opened — while the
  workflow's own detail page, which computes correctly, disagreed with the list
  about the same entry.
- **The cron editor's live preview honours day-of-month and month.** It matched
  only minute, hour and weekday, so the shipped "Monthly 1st 00:00" preset
  previewed as *daily* at midnight — wrong exactly where the operator is
  deciding. The preview now mirrors the engine's own cron rules, including the
  standard either/or behaviour when both day-of-month and weekday are
  restricted, and correct `*/N` stepping on day and month fields.
- **The preview no longer skips a midnight fire across a daylight-saving
  change.** Found while fixing the above: the day-skipping logic assumed
  24-hour days, so in European timezones the Monthly preset previewed a month
  late whenever the end of March fell on the transition Sunday.
- **The interval preview no longer shows a fire that has already happened**,
  matching the engine's strictly-after rule.
- **A one-time schedule's editor always shows the app-timezone hint.** The
  start field is the fire instant and is typed in the browser's timezone — the
  one place in the app where those can silently differ.

---

## [1.0.5] - 2026-08-12

Makes every promised surface real, or removes it (band FX-E of
the review-fixes plan). Each item here was something the API,
the settings page or the documentation offered that nothing behind it fed —
and a control that silently does nothing is worse than an absent one, because
an operator who set it believes it is working.

### Added

- **The file-arrival ledger is readable.** Since file triggers shipped, every
  arrival has been recorded — including the ones that started nothing, with the
  reason — as "the durable answer to 'the file landed, why did nothing
  happen?'". No screen or endpoint could show one; the answer lived only in the
  database file. Watched jobs now carry a File Arrivals panel on their detail
  page (and `GET /jobs/{id}/file-sightings`), and the ledger ages out on the
  runs retention window instead of growing forever.
- **The session idle timeout works.** The setting has been storable since
  General Settings shipped, and nothing enforced it — an operator could set a
  30-minute timeout, watch it persist, and believe their console locked. It is
  now enforced: an idle session expires, activity slides the window, and the
  "require periodic re-login" variant measures from login instead so activity
  does not extend it. The settings controls return alongside the enforcement.
- **A job's row now says why its run is waiting** ("no runner is online") and
  carries its next scheduled run on the list, not just the detail.

### Removed

- **The "notify on trigger" flag**, which had no backing storage, was never
  true, and still drew a badge in the workflow list. Nothing has ever notified
  anyone on trigger.
- **The Alertmanager configuration block** from the API description — no code
  ever read it, so an integrator configuring a webhook got silence.
- **The per-runner drain timeout field** from the API description; the real
  knob has always been per-request.

### Fixed

- **The RBAC pre-flight report's API description matched a report retired a
  year ago**, requiring eight fields the server no longer sends — a client
  validating responses against the description rejected every valid one. It now
  matches what the server returns, and a test keeps the two aligned.
- **Two security holes found in review before release:** the new file-arrivals
  endpoint shipped without the scope gate every other job route carries (a
  restricted operator could read any job's watched paths by guessing IDs), and
  the idle-timeout's sliding refresh would have quietly removed the eight-hour
  session ceiling — making a stolen session cookie immortal precisely when the
  operator had tightened policy. Both fixed; the ceiling is now enforced
  directly and tested.

---

## [1.0.4] - 2026-08-12

Stops a deliberately-stopped run from reporting itself as the last run (band
FX-D of the review-fixes plan).

When a working calendar, a pause or a concurrency policy stops a fire, Cronomicon
records it — that record is what lets you prove a job did not run on the
holiday, deliberately. But five places read the most recent record without
asking whether it ran, so a job stopped this morning looked like a job that ran
this morning.

### Fixed

- **A suppressed fire no longer impersonates the last run.** The Jobs and
  Workflows lists, both detail pages and the Schedules inventory now report the
  last fire that actually executed. The suppression is not discarded: each of
  those surfaces carries the most recent one separately, with its reason, so the
  evidence is still there without pretending to be a run.
- **A job suppressed today no longer reads as idle.** Because a suppression
  matched neither the healthy nor the failed side of the status rule, a job that
  succeeded yesterday and was stopped by a calendar today fell through to
  "idle" — dropping out of the success filter and out of its own count on the
  page.
- **Analytics counts runs, not suppressions.** "N runs in the last 30 days"
  counted stopped fires, so a job a calendar stopped every day read as fully
  active. Days on which everything was suppressed still appear in the chart —
  the day did happen, and a gap would read as missing data — but as a quiet day
  rather than a busy one, with their own count.
- **The RBAC pre-flight report no longer counts suppressions as activity.** A
  job stopped every day for a month reported "run 30 times, most recently
  yesterday", inverting the judgement that section exists to support.
- **Notification rules on "Run suppressed" can finally fire.** The trigger was
  accepted by the API but nothing could ever emit one, so a rule an operator
  created was silent forever. It is now offered in the notification form too.
  Rules set to "any outcome" deliberately do **not** match suppressions — a
  weekdays-only job is suppressed every weekend, and an existing rule should not
  become a weekend pager — and the high-frequency concurrency case is excluded
  for the same reason.
- **A run held back by a gate is no longer shown on the job page as a scheduled
  future run.**

### Changed

- Cancelling a workflow, or skipping a step after an earlier one failed, now
  records why. Those rows are surfaced as a job's most recent suppression, and
  without a reason they rendered as a blank next to a timestamp.

---

## [1.0.3] - 2026-08-12

Gives the six ways of starting a run one place that says which controls apply to
each, and closes the five gaps that had opened because there wasn't one (band
FX-C of the review-fixes plan).

Every producer — a schedule, a click, an API token, a reaction, a deferred run
coming due, a file landing — re-applied pause, calendars and the concurrency cap
by hand, so each new one had to reconstruct the list from the others. A
reconstruction that comes out one control short looks exactly like a correct
one, which is why these kept being found by review rather than by anything
failing.

### Fixed

- **A paused job can no longer be started by an API token.** The job trigger
  never checked pause at all, while the equivalent workflow route did — and the
  machine trigger endpoint runs through the same handler, so a service account
  could start a job an operator had explicitly paused. Clicking Run in the UI
  still overrides a pause, because pause exists to stop automation rather than
  the operator standing in front of it, but the Run dialog now names the pause
  in a confirmation first so the override is a choice.
- **A fleet-wide change freeze now stops a manual run and a workflow trigger.**
  Neither consulted working calendars, so a freeze that stopped every schedule
  could be walked straight through by hand. The workflow case was the sharper
  one: a frozen job refused while a workflow wrapping that same job fanned out
  normally. Scheduling a run for *after* the freeze is still allowed — it is
  re-checked on the day.
- **A deferred run is re-checked against pause, freezes and the catalog when it
  comes due.** Only the concurrency cap was judged at that point, so a job
  paused or disabled after someone scheduled a run for later still ran. Delays
  are unbounded and deferred runs survive restarts, so the decision has to be
  made at the moment the run actually starts.
- **A held run stays visible.** A deferred run held back by a pause or a freeze
  now appears on the Scheduling page with what it is waiting on, and can be
  cancelled there. If it eventually expires, the reason names the pause or the
  freeze rather than reporting an outage that never happened.
- **A file arrival is subject to change freezes**, and to the credential-binding
  check every other producer already applied — without which a watched file
  could start a run that no runner in the relevant department is able to claim.

### Changed

- Refusals now read the same wherever they surface. A file arrival stopped by a
  pause records the same sentence a suppressed schedule does, so an operator
  comparing the two is not left working out whether they mean the same thing.

---

## [1.0.2] - 2026-08-12

Closes the missed-run detector's remaining blind spots (band FX-B of
the review-fixes plan). 1.0.0 stopped the detector reporting a fire
that was *still* parked by the Queue policy; this release covers the one that
had already promoted, the one that never promoted at all, and the workflow
schedules it was never watching.

### Fixed

- **Stop reporting a late-promoted run as missed.** A fire the Queue
  concurrency policy parked writes no run row; when the gate clears, promotion
  deletes the parked row and creates the run stamped at *promotion* time. A fire
  expected at 02:00 that promoted at 02:06 was therefore invisible to both of
  the detector's checks — the parked row was gone, and the run looked too new —
  so it paged for a run that had just executed, and left a fabricated `skipped`
  row that then explained away every genuine miss for the rest of that day. The
  original fire instant is now carried onto the promoted run.
- **Report a parked run that never fires.** When a deferred or queued run passed
  the 24-hour catch-up grace it was marked missed internally and nothing else:
  no History row, no notification, no metric. A scheduled fire that never
  happened produced no signal anywhere an operator looks. It now records the
  same durable marker and raises the same alert as any other missed fire,
  timestamped at the instant the run was meant to happen.
- **Detect missed runs on workflow schedules.** Only job schedules were watched,
  so a workflow schedule that silently stopped firing was never reported.
- **Stop a job in the recycle bin from breaking a queued fire.** Holding a
  parked run for a binned job (1.0.1) overwrote the marker that recorded the run
  was queued, and cleared it on restore. A bin-and-restore therefore un-queued
  the fire: it read as a silent miss, dropped out of the concurrency-cap count,
  and lost its place in the Scheduling view. A queued run that is also binned
  now stays queued.
- **Prune missed parked runs.** Terminal `pending_runs` rows were never swept
  and accumulated indefinitely. Rows still waiting are untouched, so a run
  scheduled far ahead is never pruned out from under the operator who set it.
- **Target workflow alerts correctly.** A notification rule aimed at a job also
  fired for a workflow of the same name, and a workflow alert could not be
  targeted at all except by matching everything.

### Changed

- The Scheduling page no longer labels every parked run "ad-hoc". A run held by
  the concurrency policy or by the recycle bin is a scheduled fire waiting on a
  gate, not something a person deferred, and the `waitingOn` field says which.

---

## [1.0.1] - 2026-08-12

Closes the recycle-bin escapes found by sweeping the 1.0.0 defect classes across
the whole tree (band FX-A of the review-fixes plan). The 1.0.0 review
fixed the instances it found; this release fixes the siblings those instances
had, in the places nobody had looked yet.

### Fixed

- **Refuse to run a job in the recycle bin from a workflow step.** A workflow
  step resolved its job without checking `deleted_at` or `enabled`, so binning a
  job stopped every direct way to run it and left the indirect one open — any
  live workflow with a step naming that job still ran it, from any trigger. The
  step now fails with the reason recorded on its child run, keeps honoring the
  job's `continue_on_error`, and is not retried, since a barred job cannot become
  runnable between attempts. Two things this could not be: simply failing to
  resolve the job (an unresolved step name falls back to a synthetic `bash`
  definition carrying the workflow's own scope, so it would have run anyway, at
  the wrong scope), or filtering inside the source-precedence probe (which would
  have made a binned job fall through to the same-named job at the other source —
  a different definition entirely, reported as success).
- **Keep a schedule binding when the schedule and its referrer are restored in
  either order.** Restoring a schedule while its referring job was still in the
  recycle bin skipped that job's binding and consumed the tombstone that held
  it. Since the binding row is the only record that a job uses a schedule, the
  link was destroyed permanently — and which of the two orders an operator
  happened to pick was never surfaced to them. Bindings whose owner has been
  purged outright are still skipped.
- **Hold a parked run while its job is in the recycle bin instead of killing
  it.** Binning a job marked its deferred and queued runs `missed` — a terminal
  state no restore path revives — and explained it with "job no longer exists",
  which was untrue of a job sitting in the bin. Binning is reversible, so the
  parked run now waits and fires if the job is restored before its catch-up
  grace expires. A held run is shown on the Scheduling page as waiting on the
  recycle bin, so it stays visible and cancellable, and if it does expire the
  reason says so rather than only "past the grace".
- **Return 404 for `GET /workflows/{id}` when the workflow is binned**, matching
  the job route.
- **Refuse to author reactions onto a binned job or workflow.** A standing
  reaction written onto a binned definition went live, unannounced, whenever the
  definition was restored. This matches the job, workflow and schedule edit
  routes, which already refuse. Listing and deleting a binned definition's
  existing reactions still work — those are how an operator defuses one before
  restoring it.
- **Hide binned owners' entries from the Scheduling inventory and the upcoming
  projection.** A binned definition's schedule entries survive the soft delete
  by design, but the scheduler skips them — so the page promised runs that could
  never happen.
- **Exclude binned definitions from reference counts.** A definition in the
  recycle bin no longer blocks a schedule, calendar or scope from being deleted,
  no longer inflates a schedule's "used by" count, and no longer counts as a
  live schedule in the RBAC preflight report — which had been reporting binned
  jobs as actively firing, inverting the judgement that report exists to support.

### Added

- Add the `deleted_filter_sites` conformance test that `revisions_mount.go` has
  referred to since the recycle bin shipped and which was never written. It
  exercises every route that acts on a definition against a binned one, and
  carries a reasoned exemption list for the routes that legitimately do not
  refuse. Its absence is why this class of gap was found twice by review rather
  than by a test.

---

## [1.0.0] - 2026-08-11

First stable release. Feature-identical to the 0.57.32 fix band that preceded
it — the version number changes, the software does not. The seven feature bands
of 0.57.25–.31 (event triggers, SLA monitoring, revision history and recycle
bin, queue concurrency policy, sub-workflows, file-arrival triggers) had shipped
and been reviewed; this release is the point at which that surface was declared
stable.

Cronomicon follows [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/) from this release on.

### Fixed

- **Refuse to trigger a workflow sitting in the recycle bin.** `POST
  /workflows/{id}/trigger`, the token-authenticated name route and the pause
  endpoint all ran binned workflows; the equivalent job routes had been guarded
  since the recycle bin shipped.
- **Rebuild a schedule's runtime bindings when it is restored.** Binning a
  schedule detached the entries its referrers fire on and nothing replayed them,
  so a restored schedule silently stopped firing for every job that used it
  until someone re-saved the job. The delete now captures the bindings into its
  tombstone revision and the restore replays them in one transaction.
- **Apply pause and the fleet-wide concurrency cap to file-arrival triggers.** A
  paused job ran whenever a matching file landed, and arrivals could push the
  fleet past the operator's `maxConcurrent`. `scheduler.IsPaused` and
  `scheduler.AtCapacity` are now exported so every trigger producer can apply
  the same gates.
- **Stop reporting queued runs as missed.** A fire held by the Queue concurrency
  policy writes no run row, only a parked `pending_runs` row, and the SLA
  missed-run detector looked only at run rows — so a job whose gate stayed held
  past the five-minute grace paged an operator and then executed normally. The
  fabricated `skipped` row it left behind also masked every later miss that day.
- **Enumerate expected cron fires in the application timezone.** The missed-run
  detector walked schedule instants with a UTC cursor while the engine fires in
  the configured zone. On any non-UTC deployment it checked instants that never
  existed and skipped the ones that did.
- **Apply retries to sub-workflow steps.** `retries` on a `type: workflow` step
  validated, rendered in the canvas and documented that a failed child is
  re-triggered whole — but the child ran exactly once.
- **Propagate sub-workflow step outputs.** A sub-workflow step's outputs were
  accepted by both the server and the canvas as the source of a downstream
  `{fromStep}` input, and were always nil, so an empty string was injected into
  the next job's environment.
- **Compute the per-day median run duration.** `p50Ms` was declared in the
  analytics response, typed in the spec and consumed by the frontend, but never
  assigned, so the median-duration chart showed its empty state for every job.
- **Let a file-watching agent be told to stop watching.** The server sends a
  bare 204 exactly when the watch list has been retracted to empty, and the
  agent's 204 path returned before applying the watch set — so deleting a
  watched job while its runner was idle left the agent scanning those paths
  indefinitely.
- **Record queue-full refusals under the reason-keyed de-dupe rule.** Two jobs
  sharing a custom concurrency key could have a refusal swallowed, leaving no
  History row at all.
- **Render revision-history timestamps in the application timezone.** The
  revision panel used a raw `toLocaleString()`, the only place in the tree
  ignoring the app-zone convention.

### Changed

- Export `scheduler.IsPaused` and `scheduler.AtCapacity` so trigger producers
  outside the scheduler package can apply the same gates.

<details>
<summary>Release notes: what the eleven defects had in common</summary>

**Date:** Aug 11, 2026

**A full review of the seven bands that shipped as v0.57.25–.31 found ten
defects, writing the tests for them found an eleventh, and the shape of them is
more useful than the count.** Every finding here was verified against the source
before it was believed; one further suspicion — that the recycle bin let
sub-workflow references escape validation — was checked and found to be wrong,
because `validateWorkflowRefs` already refuses a binned target. The plan
document's §10 carries the full table.

**Three of the ten are the same defect in different clothes: a promise nothing
pinned.** A sub-workflow step accepted `retries`, validated them, and documented
that "a failed child is re-triggered whole" — then ran the child exactly once,
because the retry loop that job steps have was never written for workflow steps.
A sub-workflow step's outputs were accepted by both the server and the canvas as
the source of a downstream `{fromStep}` input — and were always nil, so
`resolveInputs` quietly injected an empty string into the next job's environment.
The per-day `p50Ms` on the analytics response was declared, typed in the spec,
consumed by the frontend, and never assigned by anything, so the median-duration
chart showed "not enough timed runs to plot a trend" for every job, forever.
Each of these passed review because the *declaration* was correct. A declaration
is not a behaviour, and the only thing that tells them apart is a test.

**Two are the multi-producer gate problem, which is now structural.** Cronomicon
has five things that can start a run — cron, a click, a reaction, a pending-run
promotion, and now a file arrival — and no shared seam where the gates are
applied. Every producer re-applies pause, the fleet-wide cap, calendars and
concurrency by hand, so the newest one missed two of them: a paused job fired
whenever a matching file landed, and file arrivals could push the fleet past the
operator's concurrency cap, because that cap is checked only at fire time and
nothing re-checks it at claim time. `scheduler.IsPaused` and
`scheduler.AtCapacity` are exported now so the fourth producer can call what the
other three do — but the real fix is one `enqueueGated` seam, and this is the
argument for building it.

**One is a feature interaction that no band could have caught by itself.** SLA
missed-run detection (v0.57.28) and the Queue concurrency policy (v0.57.29)
shipped a version apart and were each correct. But a queued fire writes no run
row at all — only a parked `pending_runs` row — and the missed-run detector only
ever looked for run rows. So a job whose gate stayed held past the five-minute
grace was reported missed, paged an operator, and then executed normally when
the gate cleared. Worse, the fabricated `skipped` row it left behind would go on
to "explain" every later fire that day, hiding real misses behind the false one.
The lesson generalizes: a band that adds a new *state* a run can be in has to
walk every reader of run state. Approval steps, when they revive, are exactly
this shape.

**A binned workflow could still be triggered and run.** Jobs and workflows are
twins nearly everywhere, and the recycle-bin work added `deleted_at IS NULL` to
four job paths and none of the workflow ones — so `POST /workflows/{id}/trigger`
happily ran a workflow sitting in the recycle bin, as did the token-authenticated
name route and the pause endpoint. An asymmetric guard reads as a complete one,
which is what let it survive.

**Restoring a binned schedule quietly stopped its referrers from firing.**
Binning a schedule detaches the runtime entries its referrers fire on, with a
comment promising they are rebuilt on restore. Nothing rebuilt them — and those
entries are the *only* record that a job references the schedule, so the
information was gone rather than merely detached. The restore returned 200, the
catalog showed the schedule live, and the job never ran on it again until
someone re-saved it. The delete now captures the bindings into its tombstone
revision and the restore replays them, inside one transaction, skipping owners
that have been deleted in the meantime.

**A file-watching agent could never be told to stop watching.** The server sends
a bare 204 exactly when there is no work, no control, no settings *and* no
watches — which is to say, precisely when the watch list has been retracted to
empty. The agent's 204 path returned before it applied the watch set, so the one
message that means "watch nothing" was the one message that could not clear
anything. Delete a watched job while its runner is idle and the agent kept
scanning those paths indefinitely, with the server warning on every arrival it
refused.

**And two smaller ones.** A queue-full refusal was recorded under the keyed
de-dupe rule instead of the reason-keyed one its own constant documents, so two
jobs sharing a custom concurrency key could have a refusal swallowed and leave
no History row at all — the invisible-failure mode this area of the code keeps
having to fix. The revision-history panel formatted timestamps with a raw
`toLocaleString()`, the only place in the tree ignoring the app-zone convention.

**The eleventh was found by writing the tests, which is the argument for writing
them.** The regression test for the queued-fire miss only passed when its cron
expression was rendered in UTC — and that workaround was the symptom. An
untagged cron expression carries no timezone, so it adopts the zone of whatever
instant it is handed; the scheduler hands it one in the application zone, and
the missed-run detector was handing it a UTC cursor. On a UTC deployment the two
agree and nothing is visibly wrong. Anywhere else the detector was checking
instants that never existed and never checking the ones that did — phantom
misses at one hour, real misses invisible at another. The test now pins it in a
zone offset by five and a half hours, so a regression that moves only the hour
cannot slip through.

Every fix ships with the test that would have caught it.

</details>
