## 0.57.31 — The file lands, the job runs

**Date:** Aug 11, 2026

**Cronomicon could start a run from a clock, a click, a Git push, another run, or
an API token — but never from a file appearing.** The workaround was to pad the
schedule and hope: run the importer at 02:00 because the upstream *usually*
delivers by 01:45, and when it doesn't, discover that tomorrow. Fortra's pitch
for file triggers is exactly that this pattern should not exist, and they were
right.

**A job can now declare where to listen.** A `watch:` block on the job spec —
beside `schedule:` and `requestable:` — lists absolute path globs. A capable
runner polls them; when a matching file's size has held steady, the job runs
with the path in `AMADEUS_WATCH_PATH`, `AMADEUS_WATCH_FILE` and
`AMADEUS_WATCH_SIZE`. The file itself is never copied anywhere (PF-Q2): the
job's script already runs where the file is.

**Polling, not inotify** — a decision worth recording because the plan sketched
the opposite. Three reasons, in order of weight. The stability window *already*
requires polling, since "size unchanged for N seconds" is a repeated stat by
definition, so inotify would be a second mechanism layered on one we need
anyway. inotify does not fire for changes made by another host on NFS, CIFS or
SMB — and a drop directory on a network share is the single most common shape of
this feature, so an event-driven watcher would silently do nothing in precisely
the deployment people reach for it. And polling adds no dependency to the agent
and no watch-descriptor limit to exhaust. The cost is latency bounded by the
scan interval.

**The stability window is not a nicety.** A file being written is visible long
before it is complete, so a watcher without one fires on a half-written CSV.
That is not a rare race — for anything large arriving over a network it is the
normal case, and it would have been this feature's first production incident.
Five seconds by default, per-path in YAML for large files over slow links.

**The security posture is inverted from what you might expect, deliberately.**
The *server* chooses the globs, so the *agent* is the thing that says no: a
runner watches only what falls inside its local `-watch-paths` allowlist,
checked on every scan against what the server sent. Without that, a careless or
compromised server could point a runner at a sensitive directory and learn what
lands there. An empty allowlist permits **nothing** rather than everything,
matching the scope-grant rule — and `-allow-watch` without any paths logs a
loud warning rather than watching in silence, because that state is otherwise
indistinguishable from the server never sending specs.

The reverse direction is guarded too: the server refuses a sighting for a path
it did not distribute to that runner, so an agent cannot widen its own remit by
reporting somewhere it was never asked to look. And watch distribution respects
agency isolation on the same disjoint rule `claimRun` uses — one department is
not told that a file landed in another's directory.

**The same file fires once.** De-duped on (job, path, size, mtime), so two
runners sharing an NFS mount both report the arrival and the job runs once —
for a job that ingests the file, firing twice is a double-import. A file
*replaced* at the same path fires again, which is the nightly-drop case; an
unchanged file sitting in the directory does not re-fire on every scan. The
de-dupe is a UNIQUE index rather than a check-then-insert, because two runners
reporting the same arrival in the same second is the ordinary case here, not the
race.

Every arrival leaves a **sighting row**, including the ones that produced no
run — a job that was disabled, deleted, or whose concurrency gate refused. That
row is the durable answer to "the file landed, why did nothing happen?", which
is otherwise unanswerable: there is no run to look at and the reason would live
only in a log line. Arrivals meet the concurrency gate like any other fire, so a
`Forbid` job does not start twice because two files landed, and a `Queue` job
parks the second.

**Declaring a watch is the opt-in** (decision, 2026-08-11). `requestable` gates
the service-account API, a different surface; requiring both would mean two
flags for one intent, with silence as the failure mode when an operator sets one
and not the other.

Wire protocol climbs to **v10**. Gated rather than merely additive, for the
reason v6 and v9 were: an older agent drops an unknown field silently, so an
operator who authored a watch would see a job configured to run on arrival that
simply never runs. A missing capability is visible; a dropped field is not.
Specs ride every poll rather than a one-shot control op, because they are
standing configuration — an edited watch must reach the agent with no operator
action, and a restarted agent must re-acquire the full set with no replay. That
also meant teaching the idle-poll path to return a body: a 204 would have
starved the one kind of runner this feature exists for.

Migration **960**, additive: `jobs.watch_json` and the `file_watch_sightings`
ledger. Enable per runner with `-allow-watch` and `-watch-paths`, or the
matching `AMADEUS_RUNNER_*` env vars now documented in the runner env example.

With this the PF roadmap closes except **HL** (approval steps), still deferred
pending the resumable-engine rework.

---

## 0.57.30 — A workflow can be a step

**Date:** Aug 11, 2026

**Reusing a common sequence meant copying it.** "Quiesce the app, snapshot,
verify" appears in four workflows; until now it appeared four times, and fixing
it meant fixing it four times. Workflow steps were jobs and only jobs. The
workaround was Reactions — but a reaction produces a new top-level run with no
shared linkage, no env passing and no cancel propagation, which is chaining, not
composition.

**`type: workflow` is a step that runs another workflow and waits for it.** The
child executes as a *real* workflow run — its own row, its own walk, its own
History entry, its own cancellability — linked to the parent by
`parent_workflow_run_id` and the parent step's node id. Deliberately not an
inlined expansion of the child's steps into the parent's graph: an inlined child
would lose its own identity and its own snapshot, and "which workflow failed"
would stop having an answer.

Its result enters the parent's name-keyed results map exactly as a job step's
does, so `{fromStep}` and branch conditions address it identically. That
indistinguishability is the whole point of a reusable component.

**The inheritance table (PF-Q12)** is written out in `subworkflow.go`'s header
rather than left to fall out of the code. The choices that will surprise people:
**env does not flow implicitly** — only the step's `inputs` cross the boundary,
because ambient inheritance is how a shared sub-workflow starts behaving
differently depending on who called it; **the parent holds no concurrency key
across the boundary**, since a parent that did would serialize every workflow
sharing a sub-workflow, the opposite of reuse; and **calendars are not
re-evaluated mid-descent**, because CAL's veto is a *schedule* concept applied
before a fire, and a sub-workflow step is not a fire — it is the parent already
running. Vetoing there would half-run the parent, which §2.6 already rejected
for a workflow's own step jobs. The actor *is* inherited: whoever triggered the
parent is accountable for everything it caused.

**Two guards, and both are needed.** Authoring in-app rejects a reference that
closes a cycle, walking the stored graph across both sources with the proposed
graph substituted in — modelled on the reactions cycle detector, including its
hard-won detail that the error must name the whole path, because "cycle
detected" is unactionable in a graph of any size. And a **runtime depth ceiling
of 3** refuses to descend further. Both exist because dual-source means the graph
can change between authoring and fire: a cycle can be closed by editing a
*different* workflow that the first check never saw. The ceiling is a Go constant
for the reason the reaction depth ceiling gives — a safety backstop is not a
tuning knob — and it composes with `reaction.MaxDepth` rather than sharing it,
since they count different things.

A refused descent — past the ceiling, or a dangling reference — **leaves a
terminal row saying why**, stamped where the child would have been. Without it
the parent would simply fail with the reason living only in a log line, which is
the invisible-failure shape this codebase keeps having to fix.

**Cancel propagates.** `CancelTree` recurses `parent_workflow_run_id`
depth-first. A child is its own run with its own walk goroutine, so cancelling
only the parent would stop the parent's *wait* and leave the child running to
completion, doing work nobody is waiting for.

On the canvas a sub-workflow is a **collapsed node** — one box, whatever the
child contains, with the child's own run detail to drill into. Inlining would
grow the parent's canvas without bound with someone else's graph, and re-grow it
whenever they edited theirs. It is offered in the editor palette everywhere
except as a bare parallel arm: `walkSteps` distinguishes exactly two arm shapes,
so wrapping it in a one-step sequence gives the same result today with no new
concurrency semantics to reason about, and the validator says so in those words.

**Git-authored workflows now get a structural warning (PF-Q23).** Their steps
have never been validated — they are parsed as `[]interface{}` and passed
through verbatim, so the whole WB-S5 vocabulary check applied only to in-app
graphs. Sub-workflow steps make that gap sharper, so the shape is checked at
sync — but a failure is a **log line, not a sync error**, following the
become-password advisory-warn precedent and PP-B2's rule that one broken
definition must not wedge the sync for everything else in the repo.

Migration **950** rebuilds `workflow_runs` to admit `trigger_kind='workflow'` —
reversing, deliberately and with the old comment replaced rather than left to
mislead, migration 890's recorded decision that *"a workflow is never triggered
by a workflow — there is no nesting"*. `runs.workflow_run_id` is a real foreign
key into that table with `ON DELETE SET NULL`, and FK enforcement is live during
migrations, so the rebuild's `DROP TABLE` fires that action and would NULL the
parent link on **every child run ever recorded** — History silently de-nesting
itself across the whole install, with nothing erroring. The link is stashed and
restored, the third time this recipe has been needed, and the round-trip test
asserts a pre-existing child link survives while an unparented run does not
acquire one.

**What deliberately did not change.** A restart still fails in-flight workflow
runs, parents and children alike — the orphan sweep needs no special case
because a nested run is just another `running` row. Workflow steps cannot
declare their own scope; the child resolves its own from its own jobs, as it
always has.

Ships SW-A through SW-E of the prod-features plan §6, resolving
PF-Q12, PF-Q13 and PF-Q23. With this the PF roadmap is complete except **ET-D**
(runner file-arrival triggers, which needs a wire-protocol bump) and **HL**
(approval steps, deferred pending the resumable-engine rework).

---

## 0.57.29 — Wait your turn, and the policy that never did anything

**Date:** Aug 11, 2026

**A job that must not overlap itself had two answers, and neither was the one
operators wanted.** `Allow` runs them concurrently. `Forbid` loses the fire —
recorded honestly as a skipped run, but lost. "Run it when the current one
finishes" had no expression at all, so people reached for longer cron intervals
and hoped.

**`Queue` is that third answer.** A Queue-policy fire that meets a held gate
parks instead of vanishing, and promotes when the gate clears.

Deliberately no new table and no new loop. The ad-hoc scheduling work
(v0.55.20) already built parking: `pending_runs` holds a frozen `EnqueueParams`
and a 15-second promoter that re-judges the concurrency cap and the gate before
firing. **A queued run is that same row with a different fire condition** —
"the gate cleared" rather than "the clock reached T" — and `promoteOne`'s
existing retry-not-fail behaviour on a held gate *is* the queue. Setting
`run_at` to now makes the row immediately due, so it retries every pass; it also
means AR's 24-hour catch-up grace applies verbatim, and a run queued behind a
permanently wedged job expires to `missed` rather than waiting forever (PF-Q10).

The queue is **capped at 3 per key**, and the cap is a Go constant rather than a
setting — the reaction depth-ceiling's reasoning verbatim: this is a safety
backstop, not a tuning knob, and exposing it invites raising it to 500, which
converts a contained backlog into an uncontained one. Three is small enough to
be obviously a queue rather than a buffer: it absorbs a slow run overlapping the
next fire or two, and refuses to accumulate a night's work that would all
stampede at 6am when the gate finally cleared. Beyond the cap the fire falls
back to Forbid's behaviour **and says so** in the run's reason, because a fire
that is neither run nor queued nor recorded is the invisible failure this area
of the codebase keeps having to fix.

**`Replace` is removed, because it never existed.** It was parsed by both write
paths, stored on the row, documented in the OpenAPI spec, and offered in the Job
Composer under the label *"Replace — cancel the running one"*. No code branch
anywhere read it. Every gate in the tree compared against `"Forbid"`. So a job
configured with the value that sounds strictest overlapped freely, and the
dropdown described a cancellation that never happened. Existing rows are coerced
to `Allow` by the migration, which changes nothing about how they actually ran.

Two things made that possible, and both are fixed. The vocabulary lived in **two
independent switch statements** — one in the Git sync, one in the compose API —
that each silently degraded an unrecognised value to Allow, so a `Queue` typed
into YAML would have become "overlap freely" with no error anywhere. There is
now one definition in `cronutil`, and the compose API **422s** an unknown policy
instead of quietly rewriting it. And nothing pinned the spec's enum to the
implementation: `TestConcurrencyPolicyEnumsAreHonoured` now asserts both
directions, exactly as the alert enums have since J-6 — a spec value with no
branch is how Replace survived, and a branch the spec forbids is how working
behaviour stays unreachable.

**`HoldsGate` replaced every `== "Forbid"` comparison.** A Queue run must carry
its concurrency key just as a Forbid run does, or nothing has anything to queue
behind and the policy silently degrades to Allow. That is four producers — the
cron fire, the manual trigger, the reactor and pending promotion — and getting
three of four right is the RX-25 failure mode all over again, so they now all
ask the same question.

The manual trigger answers differently for the two policies: **409 for Forbid,
202 for Queue**, with the queue depth. An integration that retries on a 409 must
not retry a run that is already going to happen.

**Priority** reorders the claim: higher first, ties oldest-first. Per-trigger
only (PF-Q11) — there is deliberately no job-spec default, because a standing
priority is how one job starves another permanently rather than merely going
first today. It is wired into **both** claim queries; the one in `sshexec`
serves every bash/perl/powershell/python run, so priority added only to the
runner's would have applied to a minority of runs and looked broken. The
covering index is re-cut `(status, executor, priority DESC, created_at ASC)` to
match the mixed-direction sort exactly, and the claim benchmark's mirrored query
moved with it.

Queued runs appear in **Scheduling → Upcoming** with a `queued` chip and a
cancel button. They needed their own branch there: a queued row's `run_at` is
when it *joined the line*, which is in the past, and the upcoming filter admits
only future instants — so without it a queued run sat perfectly alive in the
queue and appeared in no list at all. It reads "waiting for the gate" rather
than a timestamp, because nobody knows when it will fire.

**What deliberately did not change.** Promotion still applies exactly the gates
`promoteOne` always had — staleness, the global cap, definition existence, the
key. It does **not** acquire calendar or pause checks: `promoteOne` has never
had them (the reactor carries its own), and adding them here would change ad-hoc
and reaction behaviour as a side effect of a concurrency feature. Workflows have
no concurrency policy and so cannot queue.

Migration **940** rebuilds `jobs` — the expensive half — to widen the CHECK.
Read 890's header before touching it: no table holds an inbound foreign key to
`jobs` (verified), but `DROP TABLE` destroys the table's triggers and indexes,
and `jobs` now carries **five** delete-cascade triggers where migration 200's
caveat named two. All five and all three indexes are recreated, and the
round-trip test deletes a job afterwards to prove each cascade still fires —
because a rebuild that recreates four of five leaves a table whose deletes
silently stop cascading, and nothing complains until a recreated job inherits an
orphan.

Ships QP-A through QP-E of the prod-features plan §5, resolving
PF-Q10, PF-Q11 and PF-Q14.

---

## 0.57.28 — Noticing, as distinct from killing

**Date:** Aug 11, 2026

**Cronomicon could kill a job that ran too long. It could not tell you one was
running late — or that one had not run at all.** `timeout_seconds` has been
enforced since A12, in three places, and it does exactly one thing: it ends the
run. But "the nightly backup is still going at 6am" wants a person, not a
SIGKILL — the run may be perfectly healthy and merely slow, and killing it can
be the more destructive answer. And the failure mode with no signal whatsoever
was a schedule that simply never fired: History showed nothing, because nothing
is precisely what happened.

**Two soft deadlines, on the job spec.** `warn_after_seconds` for "this usually
takes twenty minutes", and `must_finish_by` — a wall-clock `HH:MM` in the
application timezone — for the half of the question a duration cannot ask, since
the run's start time is exactly what varies. A deadline earlier in the day than
the run's start resolves to tomorrow's, which is what makes "done by 06:00" on a
22:00 job mean what it looks like. Neither touches the run.

They could not reuse timeout's mechanism even if we wanted to. All three of its
enforcement points are in-process context deadlines held by whichever executor
owns the run, and for a runner-executed run **the server holds no goroutine at
all** — there is nothing to hang a deadline on. So this is a server-side scan
over `runs`, which has the side benefit of surviving a restart where an
in-memory timer would not. A run is warned exactly once: the scanner stamps
`sla_warned_at` and only alerts if that stamp is the one it just claimed, so two
schedulers cannot both page and a minute-by-minute scan cannot become a
minute-by-minute alert.

**The missed-run detector is the retrospective twin of the Score's hollow
marks.** The scheduler already projects next-fire times; this asks, after the
fact, whether each fire produced a run. It resolves expected times through
`ParseSpec` — the same resolver the engine fires by, activation windows included
— so "expected" cannot drift from "actual".

Its interesting property is how hard it works to stay quiet. A fire is reported
missing only when *nothing* explains it: no run row near the expected instant,
no suppression recorded for that definition and entry **anywhere that day**, and
the definition not paused, disabled or in the recycle bin. That day-wide clause
is doing real work rather than being lazy. Calendar suppressions de-dupe per DAY
(CAL-8's `dedupeDay`), so a `*/5` entry suppressed across a holiday leaves ONE
row standing for 288 expected fires — a detector demanding a row per fire would
have reported 287 misses for a job that behaved exactly as configured. Pause and
cap skips collapse per episode for the same reason. The cost is a real miss going
unreported on a day that also had a suppression; that is the right trade, because
a false 3am page destroys trust in an alert far faster than a late one does, and
the analytics view shows the gap either way.

Both scans follow the reactor's template rather than inventing one: a
settings-KV cursor, a 24-hour catch-up bound, and **a first pass that anchors and
scans nothing**. Without that last part, deploying this release would enumerate
every fire since the epoch and alert on all of them.

**The notification layer learned about events that are not run outcomes.** Until
now every notification described a run that had finished — `RunEvent.Status` was
matched against `runs.status`, and `running` was explicitly not an honoured
trigger. Two new triggers, `sla-breach` and `missed-run`, are matched by NAME,
and the `any` aliases deliberately do **not** cover them: an operator with an
"any run" rule asked about run outcomes, and silently widening it would have
converted every such rule into a pager the day this shipped. They ride the same
rules, transports, recipients and per-transport delivery stamps as everything
else, and they are offered in the Notifications dropdown — a trigger the
dispatcher honours but the UI cannot reach is the second half of the VF-15
defect the enum-conformance test exists to catch. Every alert also writes an
Activity row, so an install with no SMTP or Apprise configured can still SEE
that an SLA fired. Outcome `warning`, not `failure`: nothing failed.

**Analytics answers "is this getting worse?"** — the question neither the Score
(individual marks) nor DurationTrend (the last twenty runs) could. A new
endpoint computes success rate, duration percentiles, per-day outcome buckets
and failure clustering over a selectable window, **on demand** (PF-Q7): no
rollup tables, because a rollup is a second copy of the truth to keep in sync in
exchange for latency nobody has measured. It appears as a panel in the Jobs
expanded row and as a new **History → Analytics** tab — the fleet-wide view, and
the home the shipped Prometheus endpoint never had a UI for. Both use the same
component and endpoint, so they cannot disagree about how a rate is computed.

That rate is over **terminal outcomes only**. Counting calendar-skipped runs as
failures would make a correctly-suppressed job look broken, which is the exact
opposite of what the calendar feature exists to express; counting them as
successes would flatter a job that never ran. And a rate over nothing is `null`
rather than `0` — "no runs" and "everything failed" must not render the same.

Charts remain hand-rolled SVG. That is a constraint this codebase already chose
and this respects: theme tokens are read at render, colours are WCAG-AA-gated by
a test-enforced matrix, and a numeric `borderRadius` literal fails
`radius-tokens.test.ts` — a charting dependency would need shims for all three.

**Two indexes that were overdue.** `runs(started_at) WHERE status='running'` —
which the SSH orphan reaper has been running unindexed every minute since it
landed, so it pays for itself twice — and `runs(job_name, job_source,
created_at)` for the analytics range scan.

**What deliberately did not change.** `timeout_seconds` remains the only thing
that kills a run, in all three of its enforcement sites. Workflow-level SLAs are
not in this release (PF-Q20): a workflow's duration is a different question from
a job's, and the honest version needs the workflow-aware notification routing
that does not exist yet. The statistical flavour of "ran longer than usual"
(duration > N× the trailing median) is likewise deferred — the absolute
deadlines should be lived with first.

Migration **930** (additive: two nullable job columns, one on runs, two
indexes). Both **920 and 930 now drop their columns on the way down** rather
than leaving them: SQLite has supported `DROP COLUMN` since 3.35 and the bundled
driver is well past it, so a partial down bought nothing and would have wedged
any operator who rolled back and then forward again on "duplicate column name".

Ships SL-B through SL-E of the prod-features plan §3 — SL-A landed
in v0.57.25 — resolving PF-Q6, PF-Q7 and PF-Q20.

## 0.57.27 — Undo, for the definitions Git doesn't hold

**Date:** Aug 11, 2026

**A Git-source job has history, blame and undelete. An in-app one had none of
it.** Cronomicon-source Jobs, Workflows and Schedules were edited in place and
deleted outright; the config-change audit log records *that* someone changed
something, never a restorable picture of what. As the dual-source model pushes
more authoring in-app, "an admin fat-fingered the workflow editor at 4pm on a
Friday" stops being hypothetical.

**Every write now leaves a snapshot.** `definition_revisions` is an append-only
log of the compose input — what the operator actually authored — written
**inside the same transaction as the write it describes**, next to the
entity-code allocation and deliberately not next to the audit epilogue, which
runs post-commit and could leave a committed definition with no record of what
it replaced. A save that changed nothing writes nothing, so the history reads as
a list of changes rather than of button presses. Restoring a revision
re-submits it through the ordinary write path, which means the restored
definition is validated, audited and RBAC-checked exactly as a hand-typed edit
— and the restore code cannot drift from the write path, because it *is* the
write path.

The snapshot is the compose input rather than the database row for a reason
worth recording: there is no canonical serialization of a definition anywhere in
this codebase. No YAML marshaller exists (the Git path is parse-only),
`jobs.content_hash` is the referenced *script's* hash rather than the
definition's, and workflows have no hash column at all. The compose input is
already the exact shape the write path validates, so it needs no second
definition of "what a job is" to keep in sync.

**Delete is now a recycle bin.** Deleting an in-app definition stamps
`deleted_at` instead of removing the row. It leaves its catalog, stops firing,
and refuses runs and edits — but keeps its schedules, pauses, tags, reactions,
entity code and log folder, so restoring it is one UPDATE that loses nothing.

That last property is the whole design, and it has a sharp consequence.
**A soft delete is an UPDATE, so the AFTER DELETE triggers never fire** and the
definition keeps its `definition_schedules` rows. Nothing about the data
prevents the scheduler from registering the entry — only the `deleted_at`
filters now threaded through `reloadJobs`, `reloadWorkflows`, pending-run
promotion, the reaction gates, the three list endpoints, workflow step
validation and every path that acts on a definition. Deleting those bindings on
the way in would have been the easy fix and would have made every undelete
lossy. `TestReloadSkipsSoftDeletedDefinitions` exists to fail loudly if one of
those filters is ever dropped, and says in its own comment why: without it a
deleted job keeps running at 2am with nothing in the UI to explain it.

A binned definition still occupies its `(source, name)` primary key, so creating
a replacement 409s until it is restored or purged. That is accepted rather than
worked around — rename-on-delete would break the one-UPDATE restore — and the
409 now names the recycle bin instead of leaving the operator to guess.

**Purging is where the hard delete happens**: the row goes, the cascades finally
fire, and the entity code retires so a later definition of the same name mints a
fresh log folder. Deferred to here rather than done at delete time precisely
because a recoverable definition has not gone anywhere yet. Two new retention
knobs govern it — Recycle Bin (30 days) and Definition History (365, matching
Change Log). The reaper and the manual "Delete forever" button share one
implementation, so they cannot disagree about what permanent means.

**Schedules got the shared writer they never had.** Jobs and Workflows have had
a single `writeComposed*` body since A11; Schedules' create and update each
hand-rolled their own SQL, and **create ran its INSERT on the pool with no
transaction at all**. Survivable while it was a lone statement; not survivable
the moment a revision snapshot has to commit atomically with it. There is now
one `writeComposedSchedule` shared by create, update and revision-restore. The
transaction is a latent-bug fix that happens to arrive with this work.

Two smaller corrections fell out. A reaction watching a binned definition now
reports itself as `missing` — it will never fire, so calling it healthy was the
exact misreading that flag exists to prevent. And the Jobs and Workflows rows
grew a **History** affordance beside Edit and Delete, gated on the same
`amadeus-source` predicate; Git rows are unchanged, because their history is
Git's.

**What deliberately did not change.** Only amadeus-source definitions
participate — Git rows have Git. Reactions and schedule *bindings* are not part
of a snapshot in v1 (PF-Q21), and neither are Calendars or Scopes (PF-Q22);
both are stated rather than implied. Operator-owned tags are excluded from
restore (PF-Q8): they bypass Git-read-only by design and are edited through
their own endpoint, so rolling them back would silently revert tagging work done
since. `killJob` is the studied exception to the "binned means unreachable"
rule — it acts on a run, and binning a job mid-flight must not strand that run
un-killable.

Migration **920**, purely additive: one table plus `deleted_at`/`deleted_by` on
three, verified against the schema first — nothing in the tree carries an
inbound foreign key to jobs, workflows or schedules, so none of the 490 rebuild
checklist or the 830/890 cascade stash-and-restore applies. The down migration
is deliberately partial and says so: it drops the revisions table but leaves the
columns, because rebuilding three CHECK-laden tables from a down-migration is
the exact operation 890's header warns about, and resurrecting binned rows is
the safer failure.

Ships RH-A through RH-F of the prod-features plan §4, resolving
PF-Q8, PF-Q9, PF-Q21 and PF-Q22.

## 0.57.26 — Something other than a person can start a run

**Date:** Aug 11, 2026

**Every API call in Cronomicon rode a browser session.** A monitoring system that
detected a stuck queue, a ticketing tool closing a change, a CI pipeline that
had just published an artifact — none of them could start a job. The only
inbound webhook in the tree is GitLab's, and that one kicks a git sync rather
than authenticating anybody. The workaround was a human, which is the thing
automation is for.

**Service accounts** are the machine half of the identity story. Settings →
Service Accounts mints a named account carrying a role and either an agency or
the `*` sentinel — deliberately the same shape as an access grant, the same
one-shape-per-row rule, resolved through the same agency-to-scope expansion.
The token authenticates with `Authorization: Bearer amasvc_…`, no cookie and no
CSRF, and produces an **ordinary Identity**. That is the whole design: every
gate downstream — scope and verb, RB-26/RB-27's unscoped-job rules, unbound
references, connect-as, host and group subsetting, the concurrency cap, Forbid,
declared-input prompt enforcement — reads only the identity on the request and
needed no change to accommodate a token. A token is a principal, not a bypass.

`POST /api/v1/trigger/jobs/{name}` is the entry point, with a workflow twin. It
takes the same body as the Run dialog's endpoint, addressed by **name** rather
than rowid — an external caller holds a config file, not a row id — and
`?source=` disambiguates a name present in both sources. An ambiguous bare name
is a 409 naming the sources, never a silent pick of one. The route delegates to
the ordinary run handler rather than reimplementing it, because a second copy of
eight hundred lines of gates would drift on the first change to either. Runs
land with `triggerKind: webhook` — a value that has sat in the schema since
migration 890 with no producer, minted for exactly this — and an actor of
`svc:<name>`, so History, the change log and the activity stream all name the
account that started the work.

**`requestable` finally does something.** The field has been parsed from YAML,
persisted, and echoed on the job read model since A7, enforced by nothing and
hidden in the composer on the grounds that it did nothing. It is now the
per-job opt-in for external triggering: a service-account token is refused with
`not_requestable` unless the job carries it. Clicking Run in the UI is
unaffected — the question it answers is "may something outside the UI start
this", not "may this be started". The column defaults to 0, so **every existing
job is closed until an operator opts it in**, which is the correct default for a
surface reachable with a bearer token.

Wiring it turned up that it was never actually readable: `requestable` was
declared on the job read model but absent from the SELECT that fills it, so the
API always reported `false` — which means the composer's preserve-and-resubmit
round-trip had been silently clearing the flag on every edit, and the publish
builder omitted it from generated YAML entirely. Both are fixed; a field has to
be readable before it can be enforced.

**Revoking, not deleting.** An account name is the audit actor on every run it
ever triggered, so revocation stamps the row rather than removing it — the
registration-token precedent, for the same reason. `last_used_at` is stamped on
every successful authentication, best-effort and off the critical path: it is
the column that answers "is anything still using this token?", the question that
otherwise keeps dead credentials alive for years. Expiry is offered and
encouraged but not imposed, because a forced expiry means an integration stops
at 3am with nobody present.

**What deliberately did not change.** Calendar vetoes still do not apply to
triggers — they are a scheduler concept, they have never gated a manual run, and
a token trigger is morally a remote click; changing that would change manual
semantics too. Workflows have no `requestable` column, so the token's grant is
the whole gate there, and that asymmetry is recorded rather than papered over —
scope a workflow-triggering token narrowly. Minting sits behind **ManageRoles**
rather than ConfigureApp, because minting a service account *is* granting a role.

Migration **910** (additive: one table, no rebuild). Ships ET-A/B/C of
the prod-features plan §1, resolving PF-Q1, PF-Q15, PF-Q16 and
PF-Q17. File-arrival triggers (ET-D) remain future work.

## 0.57.25 — The steps the walkers could not see

**Date:** Aug 11, 2026

**A job inside a sequence arm ran as the wrong job, under the wrong scope, and
nobody checked whether you were allowed to run it.** PS-1 (v0.55.17) taught the
workflow engine that a parallel arm may be a serial chain, but it only taught
some of the walkers. `collectStepRefs` — the walk that feeds `lookupJobDefs` —
kept reading a parallel arm's own name instead of recursing into it, and had no
`sequence` case at all. A job nested in a sequence therefore never entered the
job-defs map, and `runJob` has a fallback for exactly that miss: it invents a
`jobDef{runType: "bash", scope: <the workflow's>}` and dispatches. So an Ansible
step ran as bash. A python step ran as bash. A job pinned to a target host,
carrying a timeout, a retry count, an ssh identity or a concurrency key ran with
none of them.

The same absence had a second consequence, and it was the worse one. The map
also backs `Engine.JobScopes`, which is what `workflowScopesPermit` consults to
decide whether an operator may trigger, patch or cancel a workflow. A job whose
scope never reached that list was a job whose scope was never checked — an
authorization hole that opened precisely when someone used the feature the
previous release had just shipped. Both halves are now pinned by tests that fail
loudly against the old walk.

While fixing the recursion we found the neighbouring case: `ValidateSteps` has
always legislated that an omitted `type` means `job` — a bare `{name: deploy}`
is a legal step — but every walker switched on `Step.Type` raw, so an untyped
step matched no case anywhere. It validated, got no node ID, resolved no job
def, and was **silently skipped at execution**: a step you wrote, the composer
accepted, and the engine quietly declined to run. A single `stepKind()` helper
now resolves the empty type in one place, and the engine agrees with the
validator about what a graph contains.

**Two more corners of the PS-1 ripple that were never closed.** The
`WorkflowRunStep.stepType` enum in the OpenAPI spec still read
`[system, job, parallel, branch]` — the spec forbade a value the server had been
emitting for six releases. And `StepChain`, the horizontal chain renderer, had
no `sequence` case: a sequence nested in an arm is routed to the canvas, which
is why this stayed invisible, but a *top-level* sequence under the ten-node
canvas threshold still arrived at the chain, fell through to the job default,
and drew the entire serial chain as one chip labelled "step". Both are fixed;
the chain now draws the sequence as a labelled container with its jobs inside.

**Paused and capped fires stop vanishing.** A calendar veto has left a durable
`skipped` row since CAL-6, but the two other reasons a scheduled fire silently
doesn't happen — the job or workflow is paused, or the global concurrency cap is
full — returned with nothing but a log line. That is indistinguishable from a
scheduler that died, which is exactly the question the coming missed-run
detector has to answer. All four gates now record, on both the job and workflow
paths, closing the gap CAL-32's own header flagged when it noted that
`fireWorkflow` "dropped even its concurrency-cap skips with a log line".

The de-dupe is the load-bearing part. `dedupeEpisode` keys on
`concurrency_key`, which PP-L8 assigns only to Forbid-policy runs, so every
Allow job carries NULL and a key-based rule would collapse nothing — a paused
`* * * * *` entry would have written some 1,440 audit rows a day. These
suppressions get a third mode, `dedupeEpisodeReason`, keyed on the definition
and schedule entry and matched on the reason, so each kind de-dupes only against
itself. That keeps CAL-8's independence rule intact in both directions: a pause
skip can never stand in for a cap skip, and neither can be mistaken for a Forbid
skip, whose rule stays key-based and therefore cannot see these deliberately
key-less rows at all.

**What deliberately did not change.** No schema, no migration, no new column —
`runs.status` has admitted `'skipped'` since migration 001 and the trigger-kind
vocabularies are untouched. The three reasons a fire is suppressed still record
under three different de-dupe rules rather than one, because CAL-8 established
that adding a reason means choosing its rule. Nothing about which runs execute
changed except the two cases that were wrong: a sequence-arm job now runs as
itself, and an untyped step now runs at all.

Groundwork for the prod-features plan §0.5 — the prerequisite band
ahead of the ET/RH/SL/QP/SW programs. Documentation caught up alongside: the
runner wire protocol is at **v9** (AGENTS.md claimed v6 in one place and v8 in
another), and migration 490's header note that `PRAGMA foreign_keys` is a no-op
during migrations now carries the retraction 830 and 890 earned the hard way —
enforcement is live, and `DROP TABLE` fires cascades.

## 0.57.24 — The Run dialog grows a second pane

**Date:** Aug 8, 2026

**On a wide screen, the dialog was narrow on purpose that no longer had one.** At
640px, everything about a run — the recap, the escape, the buttons — queued up
vertically beneath the sections, and the one thing the dialog computes that an
operator most wants while editing, the list of what they've changed, stayed
hidden inside the confirmation window until the first press of Run.

At 1200px and above, the Run dialog now widens to 960px and splits: sections on
the left, scrolling as before, and a fixed **"This run"** rail on the right.
The rail carries the recap sentence, then the **live deviations list** — the
same array that feeds the confirm window, in the same LABEL/detail dress —
then the error banner, the missing-answer escape, and Cancel/Run anchored at
the bottom. Tick check mode and a `CHECK MODE` row appears beside your hand
while you are still editing, not after you try to run. Below 1200px nothing
changes at all: the stacked footer from the recap-line work *is* the narrow
layout, not a degraded copy of this one.

Both layouts are composed from the same fragments — one recap, one escape, one
action row, built once — so they cannot drift apart, and resizing across the
breakpoint mid-edit just re-seats them: every setting survives, because the
state never lived in the layout.

**What deliberately did not change.** The deviation confirmation window still
fences every deviating run and still writes the `confirmation` audit key — the
rail makes it a formality, but whether it should go is a decision explicitly
deferred until this layout has been lived with. The review gate is likewise
untouched. Nothing about what a run submits changed.

This closes the Run-dialog rework: all
five phases shipped, v0.57.20 through this release. The two questions the plan
left open — the confirm window's fate and the review gate's meaning in a world
where targeting is always on screen — are now questions about a dialog that
exists, rather than a design.

---

## 0.57.23 — The section bars carry their own weight

**Date:** Aug 8, 2026

**Identical bars for unequal things.** After the regrouping, the Run dialog's
sections sat in the right order with the right contents — but the bars themselves
were interchangeable: same border, same ground, same title weight for the section
that genuinely needs the operator and the one most people open twice a year.
Hierarchy was carried entirely by the titles and the order. Worse, the "Add an
override" subgroup that moved inside Run inputs rendered *identically* to the
top-level sections below it, so a nested bar and a section read as the same rank
of thing.

Disclosure bars now come in three tones. **Run inputs** is primary — a firmer
border and title for the one section that asks the operator questions. **Where it
runs** and **When to run** are unchanged; they are the everyday middle. **Advanced
options** is quiet — smaller muted title, fainter border, transparent ground — and
so is the nested override subgroup, which finally looks like what it is: a detail
inside a section, not a fifth section.

One thing deliberately does not shrink: the collapsed summary text is the same
size in every tone. The quiet Advanced bar is where `CHECK MODE` and an active raw
`--limit` surface while the fold is shut, and the one fact that reinterprets the
whole run must not get smaller along with the bar that carries it — a render test
pins this.

Purely visual: no state, no behaviour, nothing on the wire. Every Disclosure in
the app lives in the Run dialog, so no other surface is affected.

This completes phases A–D of the Run-dialog rework
(the runtime-update plan): the recap line, the regrouping, helpers on
engagement, and now the weight tiers. The wide two-pane layout (Phase E) remains
designed but deliberately unscheduled.

---

## 0.57.22 — The Run dialog explains itself when asked

**Date:** Aug 7, 2026

**Every helper was individually good and collectively a wall.** One to three lines
of explanatory prose sat under nearly every control in the Run dialog,
permanently. What ansible's `-v` levels print. What tags do to a playbook. What
become escalates. What a host subset means for each run type. All accurate, all
worth saying — and all on screen at once whether or not the operator was touching
any of it, so an open section read as dense regardless of how ordinary the run
was.

The helpers now split by consequence, not by length. **What a control does** —
executor resolution, the connect-as precedence narrative, host and group
semantics, tags, verbosity, become, check mode, the raw `--limit` description —
appears when the operator engages with that control: focus lands inside the field,
or the control is no longer at its default. Leave it alone and it stays quiet.
**What could go wrong or leak** never hides: both plaintext-secret caveats, the
reserved extra-var guard, the invalid-subset and limit-conflict verdicts, the
unscoped-run wording, the incompatible-scope warning. Suppressing a warning until
someone engages with the control would be exactly backwards — the operator who
most needs it is the one not looking.

Nothing was deleted. The same words appear the moment a field is engaged, and the
danger tone is unsuppressible in the field component itself, so a call site that
opts into the quieter mode and classifies something wrong still cannot hide a
validation verdict.

Two helpers deliberately stayed on that the rule alone would have hidden. An Auto
job's "resolved from the job's Auto default" sentence discloses a resolution the
operator never made and cannot otherwise see, and the runner-only explanation
accounts for a card that is visibly disabled — neither is describing a control, so
both are exempt.

The effect is what it was meant to be: "Where it runs" and the whole ansible set
in Advanced each now fit on one screen at their defaults, where before either
filled the dialog.

---

## 0.57.21 — One home per idea in the Run dialog

**Date:** Aug 7, 2026

**Four identical bars, and the contents behind them had drifted.** Variables had
three homes — the declared prompts, the per-run environment overrides, and
ansible's extra-vars — distinguished only by helper text, even though one of them
silently outranks another. "Where it runs" carried targeting, transport and
identity in one ~2.5-screen fold, with the executor cards wedged between the
reference preflight and the host chips so that targeting was split in half by
something that isn't targeting. A field labelled "(advanced)" sat in that section
rather than in Advanced. And "When to run" — an everyday question — sat below
ansible's verbosity selector.

The sections now hold what their titles claim. **Run inputs** (renamed from
"Required variables", which was wrong: it counts optional inputs too) takes in the
per-run environment overrides as a collapsed subgroup directly beneath the answers
they outrank, so the precedence chain finally reads top-to-bottom on screen
instead of living in two folds and a code comment. **Where it runs** keeps the
executor and Connect-as — they answer "where does this run", and burying them a
fold deeper would have been worse — but gains two quiet subheadings, TARGETING and
CONNECTION, and the order to match: scope, references, hosts and groups are
contiguous, connection follows them whole. The raw `--limit` moved to
**Advanced**, where its own label said it belonged; its mutual exclusion with the
host and group pickers is state-level and survives the move untouched, the chips'
tooltip now points at where the pattern actually is, and the collapsed Advanced
summary names an active pattern so it can never be set with nothing on screen
saying so. **When to run** is promoted above Advanced.

A consequence worth stating: with the overrides gone, Advanced holds nothing but
ansible's options, so a bash or python run opens it to a sentence saying exactly
that and pointing at Run inputs — rather than to an empty box that reads as a bug.

**And the audit finally records the timing question.** "When to run" has existed
since the ad-hoc scheduling work but was never part of the reviewed-sections
record: a deferred run reached History only as a deviation, and a run that kept
the default looked identical to one where nobody considered timing at all. The
`when-to-run` key is now tracked and submitted, admitted by the server's allowlist
and declared in the API contract. It is purely additive — older clients never send
it, and runs stored before today still display their own keys verbatim. No
existing key was renamed: History shows stored envelopes as they were written, and
a rename would bifurcate old and new runs for nothing.

Nothing about what a run submits changed. Env merging, precedence, the raw-limit
exclusions and the prompt gating semantics are all untouched, and so is the
deviation confirmation window.

---

## 0.57.20 — The Run dialog says what it will do

**Date:** Aug 7, 2026

**The dialog computed the answer and hid it.** "What will this actually do" was a
sentence the Run dialog already knew how to write — the targeting phrase behind
the armed button and the deviation window's lead. Both are moments of commit: you
saw the sentence only after pressing Run once, having already made every decision
it describes. Before that press the dialog answered the question in fragments, one
per collapsed section summary, and the operator did the assembling.

The sentence is now permanent. It sits at the top of the commit bar, outside the
scrolling body, and reads from the same live state `submit()` sends, so it cannot
drift from the run: **ansible-deploy-app · all 2 hosts in Staging · via Runner ·
now**. Fragments carrying a deviation from the job's defaults — a host or group
subset, a raw `--limit`, a non-default executor, a scheduled instant, check mode —
take the warning or info accent, so the line also whispers that you changed
something. The armed second press still restates it, which at the instant of
commit is redundancy worth keeping.

**And the footer stopped shouting.** A missing required answer was stated four
times: the section summary, the button label, and an amber block that spelled out
the consequence *and* carried the escape checkbox. That block was pinned above the
buttons, roughly 120 pixels tall, listing inputs the operator could not see from
there — and because its list of names is unbounded, a job with a dozen missing
answers grew it further, which is the same pressure on the scrollport that moved
the commit zone out of the body in the first place.

The prose now lives in the answers panel, beside the rows it names, where the
distinction between "recorded as unanswered" and a `block` job's "there is no
override" is next to the thing it is about. Only the escape stays in the footer,
compressed to one line, because it ungates the Run button and has to be reachable
without scrolling. The recap carries the count and never the list. The practical
effect is a footer of fixed height: on a three-input job the reclaimed space is
enough for "When to run" to be on screen at all.

Nothing about what a run submits changed — this is the first phase of a larger
Run-dialog rework, and the regrouping,
helper-collapsing and weight tiers it plans are still ahead.

---

## 0.57.19 — An offline runner can come back

**Date:** Aug 7, 2026

**Offline was a one-way trap.** The poll handler answered every poll from an
`offline` runner with a drain op; the agent finished nothing (it had nothing),
logged "drain complete — exiting", and exited 0; systemd saw a clean exit and
left the unit stopped. Restarting the service just replayed the loop — a
48-millisecond lifetime per attempt. Nothing on any path wrote the row back to
`online`: registration only INSERTs, redeclare deliberately leaves status
alone, and the Resync op could never be delivered because the offline branch
returned before the delivery block. The only escapes were editing the database
by hand or a full deregister with a fresh registration token. The reaper's own
comment had promised otherwise all along — *"a reaped runner re-appears and
resumes its identity on the next register/poll"* — and so did the manage guide.
The re-admit half of that sentence was never implemented. Found in the field:
`ansible-rh8` read Offline with a heartbeat seconds old, because the poll that
refreshed `last_seen_at` was the same poll being told to drain.

Now an authenticated poll from an offline runner is treated as what it is —
proof of life. The bearer token is bound to the runner id, and after a drain
completes no agent process remains, so a poll can only mean a deliberate
restart: the operator saying "come back." The row flips to `online` (guarded,
so a concurrent deregister loses harmlessly), the stale drain deadline is
cleared, an activity row records the re-admission, and the same response falls
through to deliver pending resync, managed settings, and work — recovery is
one round-trip. The mid-long-poll status re-check gets the same treatment: a
runner that is inside a long-poll is by definition alive, so an offline flip
landing there (the reaper racing a live poll after a server outage) re-admits
instead of shutting down a healthy agent — which is what used to happen when
Cronomicon itself was down past the 5-minute threshold and came back.

`draining` keeps the drain op untouched: that is in-flight operator intent,
and it still resolves to offline by drain-complete or deadline. Deregister
remains the lock-out — a drained runner that should stay out of rotation is a
service you leave stopped. Server-side only: no agent change, no protocol
bump, no migration; every deployed agent recovers unmodified. Five regression
tests pin the loop end to end, including the reaper-offlines-then-poll
resurrection and the race edges. Manage guide updated; plan in
the runner-resurrection plan (RL-1, RL-Q1 option A).

---

## 0.57.18 — Deleting a job that something reacts to

**Date:** Aug 7, 2026

**A delete that could not be completed, refused for the wrong reason.** Deleting
a job or workflow that reactions watch is refused on purpose — a reaction that
disappeared because somebody removed an unrelated upstream would be a silent
loss of work you authored. The refusal names the reactions and can be overridden.
Neither of those reached the screen.

Two refusals share that button. One is "this definition is defined in Git", which
nothing here can clear. The other is "reactions watch this", which you can go
ahead with. They arrived indistinguishable, so the console picked the first and
told operators an in-app job was Git-authored — and offered no way to continue,
even though the answer was one request away.

Now the confirmation stays open, shows what the server actually said including
which reactions blocked it, and offers **Delete anyway**. Taking it deletes the
definition and keeps its watchers, which then read *missing* on Schedules →
Reactions: they cannot fire until you repoint or remove them. That is the same
end state a Git sync produces when it prunes a definition, which is why the state
exists at all — the difference is that here somebody chose it.

The Git-source refusal is unchanged and deliberately offers nothing to click,
because forcing it would fail. The two are now told apart by a machine-readable
code rather than by a status both share, and both delete routes document the
override in the API contract, which had never mentioned it.

Both manuals describe the flow and carry the v0.57.18 stamp. Found while writing
them: the gap was invisible from the API, which behaved correctly throughout, and
visible the moment someone had to write down what an operator should do.

---

## 0.57.17 — The runaway brake actually holds

**Date:** Aug 7, 2026

**A reaction chain that ran through a workflow's steps could loop forever.**
Reactions cap how deep a chain can go, and that cap is specifically meant to
catch the loops no up-front check can see — the ones that only exist because a
workflow runs the very job whose finishing starts the workflow. Those were the
loops it missed.

The counter was being reset. A workflow started by a reaction knew how deep it
was; the jobs it then ran did not, so each pass around the loop began again from
zero and the cap was never reached. A job step now carries its workflow's depth
— unchanged, because running a workflow's own steps is not another hop; the hop
was the reaction that started it.

**Only reachable if you opted in**, since a job running as a workflow step
raises no reaction unless you explicitly asked it to, which is off by default.
But that option existed, the loop it enabled was unbounded, and the brake meant
to stop it is the one thing standing between a mis-drawn graph and a system
running flat out.

The fix is fenced by a test that builds the loop for real — a workflow, the job
it runs, and a reaction pointing back — and lets the actual engine run it until
it stops on its own. Worth noting what makes this loop hard: as a picture of
reactions it is a single arrow, with nothing circular about it. It is only a
loop once you follow the workflow into the work it does.

**Docs.** Both manuals catch up with the whole reactions programme. The User
Manual gains §9.3 (what a reaction is, which outcome
to wait for, where to author one, the Reactions tab, the four brakes), §6.6
(stopping a run and recording what the stop meant, including the wedged
workflow step), a recipe for making one job run after another, the Trigger and
Stopped controls in History, and two FAQ entries. The Administrator Manual gains
§4.5 (the polled reactor, outcome normalisation, the five suppression gates,
migrations 880/890/900, and the runaway-chain Activity row), the Git
`spec.reactions` surface, the reactions endpoints, and the query that answers
"why did this reaction not fire" — because the delivery log has no console view,
which the manual now says outright rather than leaving to be discovered.

---

## 0.57.16 — Reactions on screen (RX, Phase D)

**Date:** Aug 6, 2026

**A reaction is invisible by design, and that is the problem this release
solves.** A workflow's coupling is drawn in its step graph. A reaction's lives
on the *other* definition, fires from no clock, and appears in no projection —
so until now the only way to know a job had downstream consequences was to
already know. Reactions now have a screen, and every place the feature made an
existing answer incomplete now says so.

**Schedules gains a fifth tab, Reactions** — the one canonical picture of what
triggers what, across jobs and workflows in every combination. Search either end
of an edge at once (you rarely know which side of the arrow the thing you are
looking for sits on), filter by owner, and switch to a grouped view that reads
the same list as *finishing this starts these* — because fan-out is the shape
that actually surprises people, and a list sorted by owner hides it. A reaction
whose watched definition has been deleted is flagged **missing** and counted at
the top: it can never fire, and one dangling edge in a long list is otherwise
invisible.

**Upcoming now bounds its own claim.** It projects instants; a reaction has
none. So the moment reactions shipped, Upcoming quietly stopped being the
complete answer to "what will run" — and the Dashboard's *"Nothing is scheduled
in the next 24 hours"* stopped meaning "nothing will run". Both now say which
question they are answering. That distinction matters most during a change
freeze, when a quiet dashboard is exactly what you would expect to see whether
or not a cascade is armed.

**Jobs and workflows show both directions of their edges.** *Reacts to* is the
easy half. *Reacted on by* — what this sets off when it finishes — is the half
nothing else in the product could show you, and the one you want at 3am when
you are deciding whether stopping a job is safe.

**History answers "why did this run?" by pointing.** A reaction-fired run names
the run that caused it and links to it; every run offers the reverse — *runs
triggered by this one*. A new **Trigger** filter narrows History to everything a
cascade produced. All of it is in the URL, so the answer to "what did last
night's failure set off?" is a link you can paste into an incident channel. Deep
in a chain, a run also says which hop it is.

**Reactions are authored where the definition is authored** — in the Job
Composer and the Workflow Editor, beside the schedules, because a reaction is
simply the fourth kind of trigger. The editor states the two things nobody
guesses: that a new reaction starts from *now* rather than catching up on
history, and that a minimum interval **drops** the events it blocks rather than
queuing them. A Git-defined job's editor points at `spec.reactions` instead of
letting you write something the next sync would erase.

**A review caught several things before this shipped.** Both because-of links
pointed at a route this app does not have, so every one of them rendered a blank
page — and the test that was supposed to cover them checked only the query
string, never the path. The reverse link reached job runs but not workflow runs,
so a reaction that started a workflow was silently missing from "what did this
run set off?". A failed load of a definition's reactions looked identical to
"there aren't any", which, since saving replaces the whole list, would have
deleted rows the editor never managed to read. And listing reactions filtered
only one end of each edge by what you are allowed to see, so scoped job names
could still be read off the other end. A screenshot sweep of the running app
also caught a grammar bug no test would ever have failed on.

**A runaway chain now reaches the Activity feed.** Hitting the depth ceiling
means a cycle that no static check caught — a defect in the graph or in the
checker, not a policy doing its job — so it is recorded where people actually
look rather than only in a table nobody queries. It deliberately reuses the
existing config-event kind: a new activity kind would have rendered fine in the
UI and been silently invisible to every SIEM, while the export still carried it.
Two audit surfaces disagreeing is the worst possible outcome for an audit
feature.

---

## 0.57.15 — Reactions become authorable (RX, Phase C)

**Date:** Aug 6, 2026

**v0.57.14 built the engine; this is how you tell it what to do.** Reactions can
now be authored through the API and through Git, and all four pairings work —
a job reacting to a job, a job to a workflow, a workflow to a job, a workflow to
a workflow. That was always one primitive rather than four, because both halves
were already modelled: the owner side is the same tuple a schedule entry uses,
and the target side is the same parked-run mechanism ad-hoc scheduling uses.
There is still no screen; that is the next phase.

**Authoring refuses the reactions that could never work.** A definition cannot
react to itself. An upstream that does not exist is rejected rather than written
and left silently inert. A cycle is refused with the full path named — "there is
a cycle somewhere" is not actionable in a graph nobody can see on one screen.
`killed` and `warning` are rejected as outcomes because normalisation has
already folded them into `stopped` and `success`, so accepting them would let
you write a reaction that can never fire. And the author has to be able to
*read* the upstream: without that check, someone with narrow access could bind
to a job they cannot see and read its fire timing as a signal for "did the
quarterly close succeed?".

**Deleting something another definition watches now asks first.** It returns a
conflict listing the reactions that point at it, with `?force=true` as the
explicit override — the same shape as deleting a bound calendar. Deleting the
definition that *owns* reactions still just takes them with it, no questions
asked, because a reaction on a definition that no longer exists could only fail
anyway. That asymmetry is deliberate: a reaction that vanished because somebody
deleted an unrelated upstream would be a silent loss of something you built.

**Reactions can be authored in Git, which matters most where it is least
visible.** Several deployments are air-gapped and author everything through the
repo; a trigger kind that only worked in-app would be missing from exactly the
installations under the strictest change control. A repo can also point a
reaction at an in-app definition and vice versa — cross-plane edges are settable
rather than assumed, because an installation running both sources is precisely
the one that wants them.

**Bad reactions are caught at merge-request time, not at sync time.** `amadeus
validate` checks everything checkable without a database — the name, the
outcome, the delays — so a typo fails in CI rather than at deploy. What needs
the database (does that upstream exist?) is checked at sync, where a bad
reference drops the whole definition and skips its prune rather than
half-landing it. A definition reacting to a sibling in the same repo validates
on the *first* sync: the repo is authoritative for its own definitions, so a
rule that only passed on the second sync would be a race, not a rule.

**A Git-defined job's reactions are edited in Git, and the app now says so.**
Authoring one in-app looked like it worked and then vanished at the next sync,
because a sync replaces a Git definition's reactions wholesale — deliberately,
so that it can never wipe an operator's own. That now returns a conflict
pointing at the `spec.reactions` key that does work, instead of quietly losing
what you wrote.

**A review caught several things before this shipped.** Listing every reaction
did not filter by what you are allowed to see, so a restricted operator could
enumerate scoped job names they have no access to. Reading one definition's
reactions ignored which source it came from, so for a name that exists in both
Git and in-app, editing them through the app would have duplicated the Git ones.
A transient database hiccup during a sync could read as "that upstream doesn't
exist" and drop a definition from the sync entirely. A minimum interval longer
than the run-retention window is now refused with the limit named, rather than
quietly disarming itself when the record it anchors on is pruned. And the API
now enforces the same name rule as YAML, so moving a reaction into Git cannot
fail on a name the app accepted.

**Two fixes that had to happen here.** Promoting a deferred workflow run
hardcoded its trigger as "manual" — harmless while ad-hoc deferral was the only
producer, and a lie in History the moment a second one existed, with the chain
depth resetting to zero on every hop and disarming the runaway ceiling. And a
pending workflow whose definition had been renamed away was silently consumed
rather than being marked missed, which is the guard the job path has always had.

---

## 0.57.14 — Jobs can react to each other (RX, Phase B — the engine)

**Date:** Aug 6, 2026

**Job-to-job coupling used to exist only inside a workflow.** The engine walks
its own step graph and reacts to the runs *it* started — so if `nightly-extract`
fired from its own cron, or from the Run dialog, or from a different workflow,
nothing downstream noticed. There was no `depends_on`, no `on_success`, no
trigger source anywhere whose event was "something finished."

A **reaction** is a fourth trigger kind, alongside cron, interval and one-shot:
*when X finishes with success / failure / stopped / any, run Y, optionally after
a delay.* This release ships the engine. There is no screen and no YAML for it
yet — those are the next phase — so **nothing changes for an installation until
the authoring surfaces land**.

**A reaction is edge-triggered, and that is the whole design.** It is not a
latch, it does not accumulate, and it cannot be inspected as "currently
waiting", because it never waits. It either observes a completion and fires, or
there is no event. A newly created reaction therefore fires on the *next*
matching completion and never retroactively on the most recent historical one —
which is also why the very first scan after upgrade deliberately looks at
nothing rather than discharging a retention window of history.

**Stopping something is its own outcome, and this is where v0.57.13 pays off.**
The two entity types don't share a vocabulary — workflows are binary, jobs have
five terminal states — so both are normalised to `success`, `failure` or
`stopped` before matching. A job warning counts as success; it ran and it
finished. `stopped` means a human ended it and *didn't say what it meant*, and
it exists because both simpler answers fail badly in opposite directions:
treating it as failure fires your rollback automation while you're already
hands-on fixing the thing, and treating it as nothing silently skips the
cleanup that releases a lock, exactly when something is already wrong. A stop
you *did* classify follows your classification — stop a run and record it as a
success, and a success reaction fires.

**A cancelled workflow reads as stopped even when its status says success.** A
soft cancel only halts the walk between steps, so a cancel arriving during the
final step is never observed and the run finishes green with the cancel flag
set. Reading the status there would cascade a success that happened only
because the cancel was a moment too late.

**Four brakes, because a feature that makes runs make runs needs them.** A
global calendar covering today suppresses a cascade — a fleet-wide freeze that a
chain runs straight through is worse than a schedule that does, because nobody
authored the chain to happen today. Entry-level calendar bindings deliberately
don't apply: those describe a schedule entry's clock, and a reaction has no
clock. A per-reaction minimum interval caps the storm case (a job on a
one-minute cron is 1440 downstream runs a day). A chain-depth ceiling of five —
a constant, not a setting, because exposing it invites raising it to 50 —
catches cycles that no static check can see. And catch-up is bounded at 24
hours, so a Monday-morning restart after a weekend outage doesn't discharge an
entire weekend of reactions at once.

**Every decision is recorded, including the ones that decided not to fire.** A
suppressed reaction writes a delivery row saying which gate stopped it and why —
naming the calendar and the day, or the interval, or the depth. "The cascade did
not run on Veterans Day, deliberately" is a query, not a log line. The row is
written *before* the verdict, so the record of having considered an event
survives a crash mid-decision.

**A reaction adds a producer, not a new way to run things.** It resolves into
the same parked-run mechanism ad-hoc scheduling already uses, so the global
concurrency cap, the Forbid policy and the does-this-still-exist check are
judged once, at the moment the run actually enters the system, by code that
already ran. The two gates that mechanism *doesn't* apply — pause and calendars
— the reactor applies itself. A reaction-fired job resolves its targeting,
its connect-as identity, its agencies and its executor exactly as a cron fire
does; a test pins that field by field, because the failure mode is a
reaction-fired run quietly targeting the wrong host.

**History can answer "why did this run?"** A reaction-fired run records
`reaction` as its trigger kind and carries the id of the run that caused it, on
the run row itself — not only in the delivery log, which is pruned with runs. It
also carries `AMADEUS_REACTED_TO_*` in its environment, which is the only data
that crosses a reaction edge: there is no output piping between definitions,
because workflows have no single outputs blob for it to generalise over.

**Two things a review caught before this shipped.** A reaction-fired run of a
`Forbid` job was building its concurrency key differently from the cron and
manual paths — a bare job name instead of a source-qualified one — which meant
two runs of a job whose entire purpose is never to overlap could run together.
And a reaction that decided to fire but couldn't (its job renamed, or refused
for credentials unbound at its scope) left a delivery row that couldn't be told
apart from a crash. Both are fixed, with the second earning a new `error`
verdict in migration `900` so the log can say what happened.

**Schema:** migration `880` adds the reaction and delivery tables; `890` rebuilds
`runs` and `workflow_runs` to admit the new trigger kind. That rebuild is the
risky kind — SQLite's `DROP TABLE` fires cascades, which would have wiped every
run's agency membership and blanked every workflow-to-run link — so both are
stashed and restored, and a test seeds real rows and proves they survive. The
two tables' trigger vocabularies still differ deliberately and were not
opportunistically unified.

---

## 0.57.13 — Stopping a run can say what it meant (RX, Phase A)

**Date:** Aug 6, 2026

**Kill becomes Stop, and Stop asks one question: what happened?** Until now,
ending a run recorded exactly one thing — `killed` — whether you stopped it
because it was destroying something, because it had already finished the work
and hung on a socket, or because you needed the host back. All three read the
same afterwards, and all three counted as a failure. The Stop dialog now offers
a disposition — **Stopped**, **Failed**, **Success**, **Warning** — and the run
records what you chose. There is no migration: all four are values a run could
already hold.

**The two halves of a stop are now separate, and both are kept.** `status` is
what happened; `killed_by` is the proof a human ended it. That second column has
always been written and was never read for anything but display — it is now the
answer to "did a person end this?", independently of what the run was recorded
as. A run can read **Success · stopped by operator@…**, which is a state the system
could not previously express.

**The payoff is a wedged workflow step you can get past.** A workflow treats a
stopped step as a failure and halts, so an operator whose step-three job was
hung — with its work already done — had no way to let steps four and five run.
Stopping it and recording it as a success now lets the workflow continue. An
*unclassified* stop still halts the workflow, deliberately: silence about what
happened is not the same as saying it was fine, and inferring the second from
the first is how a half-deployed system gets a green run.

**Nothing changes unless you choose a disposition.** The dialog defaults to
Stopped, the API defaults to `killed` when no body is sent, and an unclassified
stop still writes a `failure` activity outcome, still counts as danger in the
job health rollup, and still sorts where it always did. An older client, a
script, or the "Stop all queued" loop behaves exactly as it did before — and
that loop deliberately sends no disposition at all, because it clears runs that
never started and there is no work whose outcome anyone could assert.

**History gains a filter and a badge, and it needs both.** Dispositions create a
run that is genuinely a success *and* was ended by a person, which correctly
appears under the Success filter — so without a marker, "successful runs" would
quietly start including runs a human stopped, and History would become less
trustworthy than it was before this feature. Every run listing now carries a
**Stopped** badge naming who stopped it, and a **Stopped** filter (`?stopped=`,
mirrored into the URL like the calendar filter) answers "what did we stop last
quarter" — composable with Result, so "runs we stopped and then called fine" is
one link.

**A fix that outgrew its ticket: the kill write had no status guard.** A run
that finished between the operator's click and the write was silently
overwritten as killed — a live bug, independent of this feature. Stopping a run
now refuses with a 409 if it finished first, rather than rewriting a real
outcome as an asserted one. Auditing the rest of the terminal writers found the
same gap in three more: the runner's normal finalize, the drain-timeout path and
the orphan reaper all wrote a terminal status without checking the run was still
running. Each is now guarded, and each declines to re-emit a run-end it did not
win. Without that, a disposition would have been overwritten seconds later by
the runner's in-flight final log — on exactly the runs people stop. Runner load
accounting is deliberately *not* gated on winning the write: the runner really
did release its slot either way.

This is Phase A of the Reactions plan,
shipped on its own because it stands on its own. Reactions — jobs and workflows
that run when other jobs and workflows finish — need a vocabulary for what an
operator-stopped run *meant* before they can decide whether to fire, but nothing
here waits on that work.

---

## 0.57.12 — Working calendars, on screen (CAL, Phase 1C)

**Date:** Aug 6, 2026

**A holiday is now something you author, not something you write SQL for.**
v0.57.10 built the enforcement and v0.57.11 made it authorable through the API
and Git; this is the screen, and it completes the feature. Schedules gains a
fourth tab — **Calendars** — where a working calendar is created, filled with
dates, marked global, bound, and renewed. The minor bump is for the new
first-class primitive reaching the product; nothing changes for an installation
until somebody creates a calendar.

**Authoring eleven dates a year should not cost eleven gestures.** The editor
takes a single added day, a pasted block of `YYYY-MM-DD,label` lines, or a CSV or
`.ics` file — read in your browser, never fetched from a published holiday feed.
That is deliberate: several deployments are air-gapped, and an outbound call
would fail closed in exactly the environment that needs this most. A paste is not
all-or-nothing; bad lines are reported by line number and the good dates are
kept.

**Cronomicon still ships no holiday dates, in any form** — not a seeded calendar,
not an importable file. Every date is yours, so no list of ours can be silently
wrong for your organization. The consequence is stated where it lands rather
than buried: a calendar stops working when it runs out of days, and a *skip*
calendar that has run out simply stops suppressing, with nothing else anywhere
to tell you. So the list flags a calendar that has expired or is close to it,
and an expiring **global** calendar says so in a banner.

**Bindings are editable wherever a schedule is authored** — the Schedule
Builder, the Job Composer's inline schedules, and the Workflow Editor — as two
lists, "never run on days in" and "run only on days in". Naming one calendar in
both roles is refused inline, a global calendar cannot be picked as a run-day
list, and a binding whose calendar was force-deleted is shown as missing rather
than silently doing nothing. A **one-shot** schedule whose single instant lands
on a suppressed day is flagged while you are authoring it, because suppressing a
one-shot does not mean "not today" — it means the run never happens at all.

**A suppressed fire is visible in the one place it should be, and absent from
every place it shouldn't.** Upcoming strikes the instant through and names the
calendar and the day's label; the dashboard's "up next", the Score timeline and
the health score all exclude it, because a suppressed fire is not an upcoming
run. When a **global** calendar covers today, both Schedules and the Dashboard
say so by name — a fleet-wide freeze that nobody can see is this feature's worst
failure mode, and the quiet dashboard it produces looks exactly like an outage.

**History answers the compliance question by pointing.** Both the Executions and
Workflow Runs tabs gain a **Calendar** filter — one calendar, or any suppression
at all — and the filter is mirrored into the URL, so "every run suppressed by
`company-holidays` this fiscal year" is a link you can send someone. It matches
the structured column, never the wording of the message.
