**"Does this run on holidays?" is answered in one place** on a job's detail, a
workflow's detail and the schedule inventory: agreeing entries collapse to the
calendar name, disagreeing ones read "company-holidays (2 of 3 entries)". The
inventory also flags an entry pointing at a calendar that no longer exists.

**Two defects found while building it**, both invisible in the way this feature
exists to prevent. The Job Composer had been **dropping the activation window
and interval from every inline schedule on save** — authoring a windowed or
interval schedule there silently persisted a bare cron, with no error and no
sign. It was the same shape as the bug that once cleared activation windows on
every workflow save: a hand-written object listing the fields somebody
remembered. Both conversions are now single functions whose type requires a key
for *every* field of the wire format, so a field added to the API contract fails
the build until it is carried, with a test as the second half. Separately, the
two calendar fields were **missing from the inline-schedule shape in the API
contract**, so the server accepted bindings the generated client could not
express.

---

## 0.57.11 — Working calendars become authorable (CAL, Phase 1B)

**Date:** Aug 6, 2026

**Calendars stop being a SQL-only feature.** v0.57.10 built the enforcement —
a scheduled job could be told not to run on a holiday, and could prove it
didn't — but creating a calendar meant writing SQL. This is the half that makes
it real everywhere except the screen: the API, the Git YAML keys, the projection,
and the audit query. The Calendars tab and the binding pickers are the next
release.

**Calendar CRUD**, admin-only for writes and readable by any signed-in user.
Days are validated as real dates (Feb 30 is refused), de-duplicated and stored
sorted. Creating a calendar can carry its dates in the same call; editing its
metadata deliberately cannot touch them, so a description change can't silently
wipe a year of holidays. Deleting a calendar something still binds returns a
conflict naming what binds it, unless you explicitly force it.

**Bindings on every authoring surface.** A schedule entry — in an in-app job, an
in-app workflow, a first-class reusable schedule, or a Git-authored YAML file —
can now name calendars in either role. A first-class schedule carrying
`skipCalendars: [federal-holidays]` is a complete, reusable policy object: bind
the reference to forty jobs and all forty inherit it, and next year's dates are
added in one place.

**Three refusals, at every boundary, because each failure is silent.** An
unknown calendar name is rejected rather than dangling — a typo'd skip binding
just stops suppressing, and a typo'd run-day binding means the job never fires
again. A calendar named in both roles on one entry is rejected as incoherent
rather than redundant. And a global calendar cannot be used as a run-day list in
either direction (nor can a calendar bound that way be promoted to global) —
that combination yields a job that may only run on days it is also globally
forbidden from running on, reached by two individually sensible clicks. The Git
sync applies the identical rules and fails the sync with the same message the
API returns.

**The Upcoming projection now tells the truth.** It consults the same resolver
the scheduler does and marks the fires that will be suppressed, with the
calendar and the day's label — it does not hide them. Hiding them would have
been less work and would have thrown away the one view where a holiday gap is
worth seeing. What must exclude them is anything answering "what runs next",
which is the dashboard's job in the next release.

**"Does this job run on holidays?" has a single-place answer.** Binding lives on
the schedule entry, which is what makes it composable — but it means an auditor
would otherwise check every entry of a job. The schedules inventory now carries a
per-definition roll-up: entries that agree collapse to the calendar name, and
entries that *disagree* read "federal-holidays (2 of 3 entries)". The
disagreement is the case worth seeing, and a definition-level field would have
made it unrepresentable rather than visible.

**History answers the compliance question.** Filter runs — and workflow runs — by
the calendar that suppressed them, matching a real column rather than the wording
of a message, so rephrasing the reason can never break the audit query.

**Calendars report their own expiry.** Each one carries its newest date and how
many days of coverage remain, going negative once it has passed. Since Cronomicon
ships no holiday dates, an unrenewed calendar is this feature's likeliest
failure — a skip calendar whose last day is behind us simply stops suppressing —
and this is what the upcoming UI badges will read.

**Eight defects were caught by review before this shipped**, and they are worth
listing because most were the invisible kind. The audit roll-up leaked
out-of-scope job names and their compliance policy to restricted users through a
field the rest of the response correctly hid. Bindings on Git-authored *reusable*
schedules escaped validation entirely and were never written to the catalog row,
so an in-app job referencing a Git schedule silently lost its calendar policy.
The YAML normalizer dropped both new fields in a field-by-field rebuild —
the same shape of bug that once cleared activation windows on every workflow
save — which meant every Git-authored inline binding was being discarded between
the file and the database. The delete and global guards ignored bindings held by
reusable schedules. The global refusal was missing on create, reachable by
force-deleting a bound calendar and re-creating the name. Reference expansion
re-attached bindings without re-checking them. And the content hash could not
tell "never run on holidays" from "only run on holidays" — opposite rules,
identical digest. All are fixed, each with a test.

---

## 0.57.10 — Working calendars, enforcement core (CAL, Phase 1A)

**Date:** Aug 6, 2026

**A scheduled job can now be told not to run on a holiday, and can prove it
didn't.** This is the first of four phases (the calendar-update plan)
and it is deliberately the half with no screen: the schema, the resolver and the
two fire-time gates. Authoring a calendar still means writing SQL — the API is
Phase 1B, the Calendars tab is Phase 1C. Nothing changes for any existing
installation until somebody creates a calendar and binds it, which nothing in
this release lets them do through the UI.

**What a calendar is.** A named set of wall-clock dates, each optionally
labelled (`2026-07-03`, "Independence Day (observed)"). Not a time range, not a
cron, not a duration. A schedule *entry* — not a job — may name calendars in two
roles: `skip_calendars` suppresses a fire landing on any listed day, and
`only_calendars` suppresses a fire unless it lands on one. Both are legal
together and skip wins, which is how you say "only on fiscal-close days, but
never on a holiday".

**The day is a wall-clock day in the app timezone, never UTC.** This is the one
thing that had to be right and is easy to get wrong: matching in UTC would
suppress the wrong side of midnight for every deployment east or west of
Greenwich. A 23:30 local fire on a holiday is suppressed; the same instant read
as UTC would not be, and there is a test that says so in both directions.

**Suppression is recorded, not just logged.** A suppressed fire writes a terminal
`skipped` run carrying its reason, because the question this feature exists to
answer is "prove this job did not patch on Veterans Day, and that it was
deliberate" — and a fire that never happens leaves nothing behind. That is also
why the gate lives at `fire()` rather than wrapping the cron schedule: a
decorator that advances past excluded days cannot answer it.

**Change freezes are one flag, not N edits.** A calendar marked `global` has its
days unioned into every entry's skip set, whether or not that entry names it —
so "we are frozen for nine days" does not mean editing every schedule in the
system and remembering to unedit them. It is skip-polarity only by construction;
a global *only* calendar would be a fleet-wide outage behind one checkbox. The
freeze is named in every suppression reason it causes, so a job that stops firing
says why.

**A latent de-dupe bug fixed on the way through.** `recordSkippedFire` collapsed
repeat suppressions on "the most recent run for this concurrency key is already
skipped" — right for the Forbid policy it was written for, wrong for anything
else, and stated in terms of the last run's status rather than the episode it
belonged to. So any second reason for skipping silently inherited Forbid's rule:
a daily job across a three-day holiday weekend would have recorded one skip
instead of three, and an unrelated Forbid skip landing in between would have
swallowed the calendar skip entirely. The two rules are now explicit and
independent — Forbid still collapses per blocking episode, calendars collapse per
suppressed day — and adding a third reason means choosing its rule rather than
inheriting one. Calendar de-duping deliberately does *not* key on
`concurrency_key`: that column is only set for Forbid-policy runs, so a
minute-by-minute Allow-policy job would have written about 1,440 audit rows for
one suppressed day.

**Scheduled workflows can be suppressed too, and now leave a record.** They
previously left nothing behind at all — even a concurrency-cap skip was a log
line — so a workflow-shaped recorder had to be written; the job-shaped one
fabricates a bogus job run when handed a workflow. Suppressing a workflow's own
schedule entry suppresses the whole run; step jobs' calendars are not consulted,
because a workflow that half-runs is worse than either outcome.

**What calendars deliberately do not gate:** manual Run Now, workflow steps,
ad-hoc "when to run" instants, and webhooks. A human clicking Run on a holiday is
a human deciding to run on a holiday. Only scheduled fires are gated.

**Two schema notes.** `calendar_days` cascades from `calendars`, so a future
rebuild of that table has to stash and restore the days and re-create the foreign
key — the migration says so at length, because the RA-series learned it the
expensive way. And suppression provenance is a real column
(`suppressed_by_calendar` on both run tables), not a substring of the reason
text: the Phase 1B History filter queries the column, so a copy edit to the
message cannot silently gut the audit trail.

**Cronomicon ships no holiday dates, in any form** — not a seeded row, not an
importable file. Operators author their own and own them end to end, so a wrong
or stale list is never one we supplied. The direct consequence is that an
unrenewed calendar is this feature's likeliest failure: a skip calendar whose last
day has passed simply stops suppressing, and patching quietly resumes running on
holidays. The check that catches that is Phase 1B, and it is not optional.

---

## 0.57.9 — Membership stops being a wall (RB-22)

**Date:** Aug 5, 2026

**The Membership matrix is deleted.** It was rows × agency-columns over every
isolated entity — every scope, secret, variable, SSH key and runner — and its
row-name cell was never sticky. Past about a dozen departments you scrolled right
to reach the far agencies and the row's identity left the screen: you were ticking
anonymous checkboxes and counting rows to keep your place. That is the same
horizontal wall that killed the Scope Restrictions grid, except that grid had four
rows and this one had a row per entity in the system.

**Both of its jobs moved to where the question is actually asked.**

*"What is in Tax?"* is the **Agencies tab**. Each agency already expanded into a
read-only list of its contents; it is now an editor — members removable in place,
an add-picker per kind, the agency's name on screen the whole time. That last part
is the whole point: working agency-first keeps the thing being edited named.

*"Which agencies hold this secret?"* is an **Agencies column** on the entity's own
catalogue row — Variables, Secrets, SSH Keys, Scopes and Runners each gained one.
Deleting the matrix without these would have removed an answer people rely on, so
they ship together.

**A new endpoint, for a reason worth stating.** `PUT /agencies/{agencyId}/members`
replaces one AGENCY's member list; the existing `PUT /{kind}-agencies` setters
replace one ENTITY's agency list. The editor could have been built on those, by
reading an entity's whole agency list, modifying it and writing it back — and that
would have carried a silent lost-update bug. Two admins editing two *different*
departments feels independent and isn't: add a secret to Tax while a colleague
removes it from Finance, and whoever saves second sends a stale list and undoes the
other. The agency-scoped setter touches only rows with its own `agency_id`, so
edits to different agencies cannot interact by construction. It carries the same
RF-1b re-homing guard per added entity, the same RA-15 owner-removal refusal, and
the same session-epoch bump when a *scope* moves.

**Empty sets say what they mean.** An entity in no agency is *unrestricted* —
reachable from everywhere, which is more access, not less — and now reads that way
in words. On Runners the same state reads **general pool**, because an unassigned
runner may claim every department's unscoped and system work; it rendered as a bare
"—" before, which is how the most permissive state on the page looked like missing
data.

**Unchanged:** `GET /agency-matrix` stays — it is what the editor's add-picker
reads. The per-entity setters stay for that axis. `?tab=membership` deep links now
land on Agencies rather than falling through to Scopes.

**This closes the RBAC line.** RB-1…RB-32 and RF-1…RF-25 are complete.

---

## 0.57.8 — The two-axis model is gone (RB-19, RB-21)

**Date:** Aug 5, 2026

**Schema 850.** The departmental-RBAC programme's last structural debt is paid:
`ad_group_mappings` and `scope_restrictions` — the two tables that *were*
authorization until v0.56.5 — are dropped, along with every endpoint, resolver and
seed write that touched them.

**Why now, and what it cost to sequence.** RB-19 was never blocked on code. It was
blocked on ordering: `GET /rbac-preflight` READ both tables and was itself the gate
on deploying v0.56.4/.5, so dropping them early would have destroyed the tool that
authorized the releases the drop was supposed to follow. The soak between those
steps existed to provide a rollback window. With no production data to roll back
to, that window protects nothing, and the sequence collapses to its two real steps.

**Step 3 — the pre-flight stops describing a finished migration.** `losesExecute`,
`multiRoleUsers`, `grantlessMappings`, `wideningRestrictions` and `orphanScopes`
are removed. Each answered "what changes when we flip the switch", and both
switches are live. Keeping them would have meant a report that reads a table it
must not read, or one that reports a permanent zero — and a permanent zero reads to
an operator as an all-clear, which is the opposite of "this question no longer has
meaning". What remains is a current-state hygiene report: ungranted groups,
unscoped jobs and their share, unscoped schedules, parked runs, unmembered
entities. `unmappedGroups` becomes **`ungrantedGroups`** and asks its question
against the grants that actually decide access; `mappingsEvaluated` /
`restrictionsEvaluated` become **`grantsEvaluated`**.

**Step 4 — the drop.** Migration **850** removes both tables. `/ad-group-mappings`
and `/scope-restrictions` are retired from both OpenAPI copies, `auth.rolesForGroups`
and `auth.highestRole` are deleted, the seed stops writing two tables nobody read,
and the scope-rename cascade goes with them — grants key on agency id and
`scope_agencies` keys on scope id, so a rename cannot orphan a grant. It is
cascade-free by construction now rather than by remembering to write the `UPDATE`.

The down migration restores the two tables **empty**, and deliberately so. Grants
cannot be projected back onto the two-axis form: that form cannot express per-grant
scoping, so collapsing grants into two independent unions re-opens the exact
cross-product leak (viewer@Tax + operator@Finance ⇒ trigger Tax) the model was
built to close. A down migration that silently *widened* access would be far worse
than one that restores an empty shell. Roll back from a backup instead.

**RB-21 — Recent Logins stops naming one role.** The Honest View carried a single
`resolvedRole`, and under multi-grant that name was not merely terse but **false**.
"Alice: operator" is what an auditor reads as "Alice can operate", when the truth is
"Alice can operate Finance, and can only look at Tax" — on the one screen whose
entire purpose is answering who holds what. The column is now **Access**, listing
every grant as *role · where*. Unrestricted grants render as **All scopes** and are
styled apart, because those are the rows worth auditing first. A user no grant
names reads **No access** in words rather than as a dash: fail-closed means they can
do nothing, which is a real finding — usually a grant nobody wrote — and an empty
cell reads as missing data.

**Also corrected on that screen:** the Trigger jobs and Kill jobs permission hints
still read "NOT yet enforced on the run path (FR-M1)". That has been false since
v0.56.4 wired the verbs, and it is the worst possible place for a stale claim — the
screen where an admin decides what a role may do.

---

## 0.57.7 — The retired model leaves the screen (RB-19 partial)

**Date:** Aug 5, 2026

**No authorization change.** Nothing about who may do what moves in this release. What
moves is what the application *shows* you about it.

**The AD Group → Role Mappings card is gone.** It stopped deciding access at v0.56.5,
when Access Grants became authoritative, and spent every release since wearing a
banner that said so. A form that accepts edits and changes nothing is worse than no
form: the banner was an apology for a control that should not have still been there,
and an operator who skimmed past it saw a save succeed and no permission change. The
apology is replaced by the fix.

**The quieter half of the same lie is also fixed.** Recent Logins — the Honest View —
carries a **Resolved Role** column, and it was still deriving that role from
`ad_group_mappings`. It sat *above* the legacy card, in the same section, with no
banner, naming a role the user did not necessarily hold. It now resolves from
`access_grants`, the same source that decides access. The column had no test at all,
which is how it drifted for three releases; it now has one that fails in both
directions — a granted-but-unmapped user must resolve, a mapped-but-ungranted user
must not.

It remains a single lossy name under multi-grant — "Alice: operator" still hides that
she is operator only on Finance. Replacing it with the grant list is RB-21 and is
still open. This release makes the name honest about *which model answers*, not about
multi-grant.

**A first-boot lockout warning that read the wrong table.** The "NO ADMIN CONFIGURED"
startup warning counted admin rows in `ad_group_mappings`, so it was wrong in both
directions: an instance with admin grants and no legacy rows was warned it was locked
out when it was fine, and an instance with legacy admin rows and no grants was
genuinely locked out while the warning stayed silent. It counts `access_grants` now. A
lockout warning that reads the wrong table is worse than none, because it is trusted
at exactly the moment it misleads.

**What deliberately did NOT change.** The `ad_group_mappings` table, the
`/ad-group-mappings` endpoints, and `auth.rolesForGroups` all remain. `GET
/rbac-preflight` reads that table and is the gate on the deploy that authorizes
dropping it, and `rolesForGroups` is the legacy oracle in the grant-conversion test
that proves the two-axis leak is closed. Removing them is RB-19 step 4, which is
sequenced *after* a deployed release soaks — that soak is the rollback window the
tables exist to provide, and a down-migration cannot losslessly re-derive a grant set.
This release removes the SPA's dependency on the endpoint, which is what turns that
future drop into a cleanup rather than a breaking change.

---

## 0.57.6 — Run-as credentials: the authoring UI (RA-23, RA-20d)

**Date:** Aug 5, 2026

**The programme's two headline mechanisms were API-only until now.** Phase A shipped
aliasing in v0.57.0 and Phase B shipped become passwords in v0.57.3 — both built so a
department could run a shared job with *its own* credential, and neither reachable
without curl. Against the founding ask that was a larger gap than any of the
permission work.

**The alias, in both surfaces that need it.** The reference-bindings editor (Jobs and
Scripts) and the Run dialog's per-run additions both gain an optional **"inject as"**
field, with a live preview of the key the value will land on. They ship together
rather than in sequence because they share the same validation plumbing.

An aliased binding now shows **both** names — the row it resolves and the destination
it lands on — because each answers a different question: the row says *whose*
credential this is, the destination says what the job body reads. A chip showing only
one of them cannot answer both.

The alias is also now part of a binding's **identity**, matching dispatch's own
`kind\0name\0as` key. One row bound twice under two destinations is a legitimate pair
(it lands two keys); keying on kind+name alone silently collapsed them, so the second
binding lost its verdict and inherited the first's — showing a green tick over a
reference that would not resolve.

**The become password reaches the Composer**, ansible-only (the field is hidden for
every other run type, since the server refuses it there) and gated on Manage Env Vars,
matching the rule v0.57.4 put behind it. The helper line states the two things an
author needs: the value is delivered as a wiped file rather than an environment
variable, and the job will *wait* for a runner with ansible-core ≥ 2.12 rather than run
without escalation.

**Ownership is now visible where it is reasoned about.** The Env Vars create/edit forms
show the owning department beside the key. Display-only, deliberately: ownership is
fixed at creation and there is no transfer action, so an editable-looking control would
promise what the API cannot do.

**Capability chips explain themselves** (RA-20d). `become-file`, `vault`, `checkout` and
`collection:*` carry a hint naming what the token permits — a chip an operator cannot
interpret is a chip that does not help them fix the queued run that sent them there.

**A rendering defect the tests could not see.** Added to the bottom of the Env Vars edit
form, the owner line landed exactly at the modal body's fold and rendered *shaved in
half* behind the pinned footer. tsc passed and 617 unit tests passed. Screenshotting
the real dialog caught it; the fix was placement, not size — owner is row identity, so
it now sits beside the key where it cannot reach the fold.

**Docs.** The user manual gains the alias in §11.6 (with the rule that an alias is a
destination, never a selector — it cannot reach a row you could not already bind) and
the become-password field in §10.1. These were deliberately deferred from v0.57.5
because documenting a field nobody could reach would have been worse than the gap;
they close the last RA-13 item.

---

## 0.57.5 — Run-as credentials: runs that say why they aren't running (RA-24, RA-20b)

**Date:** Aug 5, 2026

**Two failures that both presented as silence.** A run that consumes a department's
credentials but carries no scope resolves nothing and can be claimed by nobody; a
run whose fleet has no eligible runner simply sits in `queued`. Neither said
anything. Under the operations-team model the person who must diagnose that is the
one furthest from the fleet — the agency user only knows their job did not run.

**RA-24 — an unbound run that consumes department-owned credentials is refused.**
An unbound run carries an empty agency snapshot, so an agency-*owned* row (which has
membership, and therefore intersects nothing) resolves for no department. The run
would reach dispatch and die with a 409 that reads as a permissions problem, or — on
a departmentalised fleet — queue forever, because the general-pool rule is
*disjoint*: an untagged run is claimable **only** by a runner with no agencies.

Counter-intuitively, being **unrestricted makes this more likely, not less**:
unrestricted is exactly what permits an unbound run in the first place.

The check is deliberately **precise rather than blunt**. The plan specified "a job
with declared bindings triggered with no effective scope ⇒ 422", which would have
refused jobs that work perfectly well today — anything binding a *global* row. So
the probe asks the real question instead: which of this job's declared bindings
actually fail to resolve, through the same predicate dispatch uses, so the guard
cannot drift from the failure it predicts. A job binding only global rows is
untouched, and so is any bound run.

It covers **every** path that builds a run, not just the trigger. The plan named
only the trigger boundary; there are three, and the trigger is the least dangerous
because a human is watching it:

| Path | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| Ad-hoc trigger | **422**, naming the reference and the remedy |
| Scheduled fire | terminal **skipped** run recorded with the reason — visible in History, not lost to a log line |
| Workflow step | terminal child run carrying the reason (a workflow has no per-run scope override, so the remedy is to scope the constituent job) |
| `POST /references/validate` | the verdict is downgraded, so the Run dialog cannot show a green chip for a reference the trigger will refuse |

Under this deployment's model, admins wire jobs and **schedule** them — so the
scheduled path is the common case and the one that fails with nobody watching. A
trigger-only guard would have covered the exception and missed the rule.

**RA-20(b) — a queued run now records why nothing can claim it.** Computed at
enqueue and **stored**, because the question is usually asked in the past tense:
"why didn't it run last night?" cannot be answered by probing today's fleet, since
the runner that was missing may be online now. The diagnosis narrows through
claimRun's own gates in the order an operator would check them and names the first
thing that is actually wrong:

- *no runner is online*
- *no online runner can run ansible jobs*
- *no online runner belongs to Tax*
- *this run has no scope, so only a runner with no agencies can claim it, and every
  online runner belongs to one*
- *this run carries credentials, and no eligible runner is flagged for secret
  injection* — the gate a newly-added runner most often trips
- *no eligible runner advertises `become-file`*

The hint is advisory: it never blocks an enqueue, never affects claiming, and a
runner appearing a moment later claims the run normally. It is only ever written to
a run still in `queued`, so a run already claimed is never stamped with a stale
complaint.

**No schema change** — `queued_reason` already existed; it simply had nothing to say
about eligibility before now.

### Documentation (RA-13, RA-20c, RA-Q8, RA-Q18)

The run-as programme shipped four releases with a changelog entry each while the
guides still described the world before it. That is closed.

**The Bash half of the original ask finally has a story.** The `bash-guide` gains
*"Privilege escalation: `sudo -S`, and its one sharp edge"* — the stdin idiom, and
the caveat that matters most: `sudo -S` is safe because the value crosses a *pipe*,
but the moment it reaches a command line it lands in `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` **on the
target**, where **Cronomicon's redaction cannot reach it**. Redaction masks the run log;
it has no visibility into a remote process table. Passwordless sudo is named the
preferred arrangement in both guides — this is the exception path, not an endorsement.

**The `ansible-guide`'s become section was rewritten**, not extended: it predated
Phase B and described only the runner-local `secrets.env` route. It now leads with
the job-level `become_password_secret`, keeps inventory lookup for per-host variation,
and explains the `become-file` routing consequence. A new section, *"One playbook,
every department's credential"*, documents per-department rows under one name and
aliasing — including that which row a run gets is decided by its **scope**, not by who
triggered it, which is what lets a central operations team run a department's job with
that department's credential without ever being able to see it.

**The administrator manual gains the Phase D and E material it never got**: §6.1f on
membership (with the silent-shadow case — a forgotten membership row makes a scoped
credential shadow the global one for *every other department*) and §6.1g on per-agency
ownership and the fail-closed ambiguity refusal. Plus four troubleshooting entries,
including the `ambiguous_reference` row that keeps a correct refusal from being filed
as a bug — it says **ambiguous**, not *unavailable*, because sending someone to hunt
for a missing row when the problem is *two* rows is unrecoverable.

**Runner guides get the fleet rule** (RA-20c): an **agency is a provisioning domain** —
a department's runners carry that department's key-dir, secrets and templates, and
claim-gating guarantees a run only lands where its names resolve. `runner-install`
gains a new-runner checklist stating what breaks if each step is skipped; `runner-manage`
gains *"Online, but nothing runs on it"*, mapping each queued reason to the setting
that fixes it. The most-forgotten step has a name now: enrolling a runner in its agency
feels like the whole job, but binding-bearing runs stay invisible until the **Secret
injection** flag is on too.

**Both manuals are stamped v0.57.5** — the user manual had never received a run-as
stamp at all, stopping at v0.56.10 — and carry the new queued-reason vocabulary in
user language. The alias field remains undocumented on purpose: there is still no UI
for it, and documenting a field nobody can reach is worse than the gap.

---

## 0.57.4 — Run-as credentials: the gate the contract already promised (RA-21)

**Date:** Aug 5, 2026

🔴 **A security fix for a hole this programme opened.** v0.57.3 shipped
`becomePasswordSecret` on the Job Composer with **no authorization check of any
kind** — no permission, no department check, no run-type validation, and no
existence check. `sshCredential`, two fields above it in the same handler, had all
four. Anyone who could compose a job could point it at **any department's** Secret
and have the runner write that value to a file for `--become-password-file`.

**What made it worse than an ordinary gap: the contract documented the gate as
present.** The shipped OpenAPI said the field *"carries the same ManageEnvVars rule
as sshCredential"*. A reader auditing the API would have concluded the surface was
protected and moved on. An unenforced gate is worse than a missing one, because a
missing one is at least visible to anyone looking.

The dispatch-side resolution gate always applied — the named row still had to
resolve for the run's scope and departments — so this was never unbounded. But it
bypassed the *authoring* gate entirely, and "binding secret material to a job is a
grant" (CA-Q1) is the rule every sibling field enforces.

**The gate now mirrors `sshCredential` exactly.** Manage Env Vars, plus membership
of the agency owning the row — and it authorizes **the row dispatch will actually
inject**, resolved through the shared `runref` predicate rather than a hand-written
lookup. That distinction is the whole point once two departments can own the same
key: a `SELECT id FROM secrets WHERE key = ?` would authorize one department's row
while the injector delivered another's. It fires only when the field is **set or
changed**, so a full-replace PUT of an unchanged job stays free for unrelated edits
and clearing the field needs nothing.

Two validation halves ship with it. A become password on a non-Ansible job is now
**422** rather than silently inert — the misconfiguration that looks like it worked.
And through the Composer the row must resolve: an unresolvable name is 422 at
authoring time, and a name owned by two of the scope's departments is 422 as
**ambiguous** rather than settled by a silent pick, surfacing RA-17's fail-closed
arm where it is actionable instead of at 3am on somebody's run.

**Git sync is deliberately left advisory** (RA-Q19). A synced job naming a missing
Secret still produces a warning, never a sync failure — failing the sync would take
every other job in the repo down with it, and the catalogue row is often created
minutes later by a different person. Repo write already implies job authorship
throughout this codebase; narrowing that is a change to the sync trust model, not to
this fix.

**Also in this release: the agency-delete refusal now names what blocks it.**
`DeleteAgency` counts four independent reference classes and collapsed them into one
error, which the API rendered as *"agency is still referenced by one or more
scopes"* — **unconditionally**, and therefore wrong whenever the blocker was a
runner, a membership row, or an owned entity. An operator retiring a department was
sent to audit the one class that was already clean. Each blocker is now named with
its remedy, and ownership — the one class with no clearing path — says plainly that
the row must be re-created and that deleting a stored Secret destroys its value.

While there: the M1 scope guard in that function had been **dead since migration
700**, which dropped the `scopes.agency_id` column it queried. Its error was
discarded, so the count silently stayed zero. Nothing was unprotected — scope
references are counted through `scope_agencies` like every other membership — but a
guard that reads as enforced and counts nothing has been removed rather than left to
mislead the next reader.

**No schema change.** Contract text corrected in both spec copies; frontend types
regenerated.

---

## 0.57.3 — Run-as credentials: a become password that is never an environment variable (RA Phase B)

**Date:** Aug 4, 2026

**A job can now name the Secret that supplies its Ansible become password.** Since
v0.55.3 the admin manual has said outright that *"a become password is deliberately
not a field, being secret material"* — and that position is **preserved, not
reversed**. The new `spec.become_password_secret` holds a **name**, never a value.
The password lives in the Secrets catalogue with every control that implies (KEK or
Vault at rest, scope and department resolution, reveal auditing, log redaction) and
is resolved at dispatch through the same reference path as any other secret. Run
inputs remain the wrong channel and this does not open one: prompt answers land in
`runs.env_json` in plaintext and are log-visible by design, which is exactly where a
password must never be.

**It is delivered as a file, not an environment variable.** The agent writes the
resolved value to a `0600` file on tmpfs *off the run tree*, exposes only the
**path** under the reference, passes that path to
`ansible-playbook --become-password-file`, and wipes the file when the run ends. An
environment variable is readable from `/proc` by anything that can see the process,
and an operator piping one into `sudo -S` puts it in the *target's* process table
where redaction cannot reach. A wiped file is a materially smaller window.

Per RA-Q9 the mechanism is **general** rather than become-specific: any secret
binding can request file delivery, and the become password is simply its first
consumer. It mirrors `AMADEUS_KEY_*`, where the reference has always resolved to a
path rather than to material. A file-mode binding is deliberately **not** also
placed in the environment — shipping both would leave the value exactly where file
delivery exists to keep it out of — and binding one secret both ways on one key is
refused, because the two would land on the same env key with different contents and
whichever the agent wrote last would win.

**The permission rationale it invalidates has been rewritten, not extended.** The
manual argued that `--become` needs no extra gate because *"a playbook can already
declare `become` itself, so the toggle grants nothing the caller could not already
run."* That is true of the *toggle*; it is not true of a run carrying a credential
the caller supplied. The gate is now secret-read entitlement — the named row must
resolve for the run's scope **and** department, failing closed if it does not — plus
an injection-flagged runner at protocol v9. Setting the field is itself a grant over
stored secret material and carries **Manage Env Vars**, the same rule as
`spec.ssh_credential`.

**The run waits for a capable runner rather than failing after assignment.** A job
with a become password automatically declares the `become-file` requirement token,
which only an agent with `ansible-core ≥ 2.12` advertises — the release where
`--become-password-file` landed. The token is *injected at enqueue*, not left to the
author, because a requirement an operator can forget is a requirement that does not
exist. With a fleet of one this is indistinguishable from refusing at manifest time;
with five, a manifest-time refusal burns an assignment a capable runner could have
taken. The protocol v9 gate remains as a backstop: an older agent drops the field, and
`become: true` with no password does not fail cleanly — it hangs on a sudo prompt or
escalates through whatever passwordless rule happens to exist.

**Two limitations, documented rather than solved.** The flag is *global to the run*,
so it cannot vary per host the way an inventory-authored `ansible_become_password`
can; a fleet with heterogeneous become passwords should keep the inventory pattern.
And passwordless sudo remains the preferred arrangement for both run types — this is
the exception path, not an endorsement of password-based escalation.

The value is written **byte-exact**, unlike delivered key material, which is
normalized for line endings. A password is an opaque byte string: appending a newline
would change what Ansible sends, and trimming one would break a password that
legitimately ends in whitespace.

**Schema.** Migration 840 adds the nullable `jobs.become_password_secret`. NULL —
every existing job — means no become password and behaviour identical to before.

---

## 0.57.2 — Run-as credentials: two departments, one name (RA Phase E)

**Date:** Aug 4, 2026

**Two departments can now each hold `BECOME_PASSWORD` in `prod`, and a run gets its
own.** Until this release `UNIQUE (key, scope)` meant one department's row was the
only row: the second department's create collided, and the workaround was the
naming convention Phase A exists to support — `TEAMA_SUDO`, `TEAMB_SUDO`, each
aliased to the destination the playbook reads. That is still the right answer when
rows genuinely cannot share a name. This is the other half: let them share it
outright. Entities gain an **owner**, uniqueness becomes
`(key, scope, owner_agency)`, and resolution prefers your department's row over a
shared one before falling back.

The same applies to SSH key labels (which have no scope dimension at all, so
uniqueness there is `(label, owner)` and a department may shadow a global label).

**The refusal is what makes it safe.** A run's agency snapshot is a *set* — a scope
can belong to several departments — so a run can see both owners of a name at once.
There is no defensible pick: whichever row an `ORDER BY` happened to put first, the
run would escalate with somebody's credential and the audit would record an intent
that never existed. So it resolves to **nothing**, with an operator message that
says *ambiguous* rather than *unavailable* — sending someone hunting for a missing
row when the problem is two rows is a diagnosis they cannot recover from. Which two
departments own it is withheld at dispatch and reported by the authoring-time
surfaces instead, where precision is already bounded by the caller's own visibility.

Because that refusal will otherwise be met as a run that mysteriously will not
start, it is surfaced before anyone hits it: the Env Vars list marks a
multi-department name with a **⚠ N owners** badge, every row carries an **owner
chip** so a same-key pair can be told apart at a glance, and `GET /agency-preflight`
reports the whole set. The likeliest victim is an unrestricted admin's ad-hoc run —
restricted users rarely carry multi-department snapshots — which is exactly the
person who would file it as a bug.

**Ownership only ever narrows.** It selects among rows a run could *already* reach;
it can never make one visible that membership excludes. A row whose ownership has
drifted away from its membership is dropped rather than resolved. The owner is
enrolled in its own row's visibility set at create, the Membership matrix refuses
to remove it (422 `owner_removal`), and an agency that owns anything cannot be
deleted.

**One duplicated predicate is gone.** The per-run attach gate carried a
hand-transcribed copy of the resolver's SQL under a comment promising it "mirrors
`runref.lookupScoped` exactly" — a promise no comment can keep. Phase E would have
broken it silently: the copy has no owner tier, so with two departments' rows
present the gate would have authorized one row while dispatch injected the other.
Both now call one exported function. The pre-flight report's in-memory resolver was
brought into step for the same reason — a report that describes a system which does
not exist is worse than no report.

**Schema.** Migration 830 rebuilds `secrets` and `env_vars` to widen the uniqueness
key and adds `owner_agency` to all three tables (`ssh_credentials` needed only a
column and an index swap). It is a **pure widening** — `owner_agency` is
`NOT NULL DEFAULT ''`, deliberately not nullable and deliberately not a
`COALESCE()`-based index:

- a *nullable* owner would silently regress the constraint, because SQLite treats
  NULLs as distinct in a UNIQUE and two unowned rows could then share a scope —
  precisely the ambiguity this phase exists to make well-defined;
- a NULL-safe index over `COALESCE(scope,'')` would be a *narrowing*. Global scope
  is stored as SQL NULL, so today two global rows may share a key. That is a real
  pre-existing hole, but closing it here would make this migration able to fail on
  live data. It is left to be closed on its own terms.

**A data-loss bug was caught by the migration's own test, not in production.** The
rebuild drops and recreates `secrets` and `env_vars`, and this pool opens with
`_foreign_keys=on` — so `DROP TABLE` fires `ON DELETE CASCADE` into
`secret_agencies` and `env_var_agencies`, and `ON DELETE SET NULL` into
`gitlab_config.pat_secret_id`. Every department's membership would have been erased
and the GitLab PAT unlinked, silently, on upgrade. Migration 490's note that
"PRAGMA foreign_keys is a no-op" was written about tables with no inbound
references and does not transfer. Each is now stashed and restored around the
rebuild, and the round-trip test asserts membership survives, the PAT link survives,
and the KEK-sealed blobs come back byte-identical through adversarial bytes
(embedded NUL, 0xFF, invalid UTF-8) — a rebuild that re-encoded a BLOB would destroy
every stored secret in the installation and nothing else would have noticed.

**Rolling back drops data, and says so.** The down migration collapses two
departments' same-named rows to one deterministic survivor rather than aborting
half-way. Roll back before departments start sharing a name, or export first; an
unowned catalogue rolls back losslessly.

---

## 0.57.1 — Run-as credentials: membership stops being paperwork (RA Phase D)

**Date:** Aug 4, 2026

**A department-scoped operator no longer has to ask for their own department.**
Creating a Secret, Variable or SSH key as a restricted actor used to be refused
with `agency_required` unless the request named an agency to place the row in.
The requirement was right — an entity with no membership is shared
infrastructure, unrestricted-only for writes and reveal, so a restricted creator
who omitted it would be locked out of the row they had just made — but it made
the safe outcome something you had to opt into on every single create. It is now
the default: a creator holding the permission on exactly one department gets that
department. Holding it on several still returns 422, because "their department"
then has no single answer and silently enrolling the row in all of them would
widen it past what anyone meant; the message now names the candidates so the
refusal is a decision rather than a dead end. Unrestricted admins are unchanged —
creating a row that belongs to nobody remains a deliberate statement only they can
make.

**And the catalogue now admits when one row is quietly overriding another.**
Reference resolution prefers a scope-exact row over a global one of the same key.
That is the override feature working. But an empty membership set means "no agency
restriction", so a scoped row created without a department wins for *every*
department's runs in that scope:

| Row | Scope | Membership | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `X` | *(global)* | none | shared infrastructure, reachable by all |
| `X` | `prod` | **none** | **every** department's `prod` run silently resolves this instead |

Nothing errored. Nothing warned. Nothing in the run log said which of the two rows
was injected — and because migration 670 backfills no membership at all, that
second line is not an exotic misconfiguration but the default outcome of adding a
scoped row and not thinking about departments. The Env Vars view now marks a
shadowing row in place, and it distinguishes the two cases rather than flattening
them: a row belonging to no department is called out as a warning, while one that
belongs to a department is noted quietly, because that one wins only for its own
department's runs and is usually exactly what was intended. Flattening them would
have made the badge noise in precisely the catalogue where it matters most.

The same findings are available as `GET /env-var-shadows` — session-gated and
scope-filtered to the caller's grants, so a finding never names a row in a scope
their own Env Vars list hides — and are folded into `GET /agency-preflight`, so an
operator reviewing membership before a tightening sees, in one report, the rows
whose resolution is *already* ambiguous. SSH keys are absent by construction:
`ssh_credentials` has no scope column, so there is no scope-exact-beats-global tier
for a key label to be caught in. Kinds are never compared against each other
either — a secret and a variable of the same name resolve through different tables
under different prefixes, so neither can shadow the other.

**Why now.** Phase A made it easy for departments to point one shared job body at
their own credential, which makes same-purpose rows in shared scopes far more
common; Phase E will make same-*named* rows a supported pattern outright. This
failure mode goes from latent to probable, and it is a hard prerequisite for E,
which is meaningless on an all-global catalogue.

**Not changed.** The A13 cross-kind conflict message (*"an env var already uses
this key in this scope"*) still tells a restricted actor about a row they cannot
see. That was reviewed and deliberately left alone (RA-Q7): the message is hit
constantly by legitimate authors, a vaguer one is materially harder to act on, and
Phase E narrows the collision to same-owner anyway, which moots most of the leak.

---

## 0.57.0 — Run-as credentials: one job body, every department's credential (RA Phase A)

**Date:** Aug 4, 2026

**A reference can now say what name it arrives under.** Until this release a
binding injected under its own row name and nothing else: bind the secret
`DB_PASS` and the run received `AMADEUS_SECRET_DB_PASS`, full stop. That made a
shared job body consumable by exactly one department's credential — a playbook
that hardcodes `lookup('env','AMADEUS_SECRET_BECOME_PASSWORD')` could only ever
be fed the row literally named `BECOME_PASSWORD`, so two departments wanting to
run the same automation with their own escalation password needed two jobs, two
playbooks, and two copies of whatever drifted between them. A binding now carries
an optional alias — a destination name — and the same job body resolves per
department:

```
TEAMA_SUDO (agency TeamA) --as--> AMADEUS_SECRET_BECOME_PASSWORD
TEAMB_SUDO (agency TeamB) --as--> AMADEUS_SECRET_BECOME_PASSWORD
```

This is the delivery half of the model that was already 80% built: agency-exclusive
Secrets, Variables and SSH Keys shipped with the agencies program, per-run
credential selection shipped as V2-11, and the departmental gate on attaching one
shipped as RB-32. What was missing was the last mile, and it was one field.

**The alias is a destination, never a selector.** The entire security argument
rests on that sentence, so it is worth stating plainly: `name` still identifies
the row, the row is still resolved by the one visibility predicate under the run's
scope and its **frozen** agency snapshot, and the alias is applied at the last
step where the injected key is built. An out-of-department secret dressed in a
harmless-looking alias still returns 403 at attach and still fails closed at
dispatch. Aliasing to another row's name yields *your* row's value under *that*
key. There are regression tests for each of those, because an implementation that
resolved *by* alias would invert the model while passing any naive "does it inject
under the new name?" check.

**Two credentials cannot quietly become one.** A run whose binding set has two
different rows targeting one key is refused, not resolved by whichever map write
landed last — with secret material a silent winner means the run escalates with
somebody's credential and the audit implies an intent that never existed. The
refusal fires at the authoring write, at the trigger boundary (422, naming the
contested `AMADEUS_*` key), and at dispatch, which is the only place the full
union of job bindings, script bindings and per-run additions actually exists. The
same row deliberately bound twice under two aliases stays legal: it lands two
keys and means what it says.

**The audit records both names.** A dispatch-injection row that said only
`BECOME_PASSWORD was injected` could not answer the one question aliasing makes
it possible to ask — whose credential ran. The change_log payload, the run's
override envelope and the binding-set audit line all carry `name → as`; an
un-aliased reference is recorded byte-identically to before, so nothing that
reads these payloads has to change.

Both executor seams apply the alias — the runner manifest and the in-process SSH
executor — so Bash and Ansible are at parity, which is what makes the "as long as
they are written to support this model" half of the ask true for both. Log
redaction is keyed by value rather than by name, so masking follows an aliased
secret for free; that is now test-enforced at both seams rather than assumed,
since the two have drifted before.

**Schema.** Migration 820 adds `alias` to `reference_bindings` and widens the
primary key to include it (SQLite cannot alter a key in place, so the table is
rebuilt; every existing row copies across with an empty alias, and a widening
cannot reject data). The 590 cascade triggers are dropped and recreated around
the rebuild — they name the table in their bodies and are re-parsed during the
rename, which is a quieter version of the migration-200 caveat than it first
looks.

**Not in this release.** The alias field is API-only for now: the Run dialog and
the References editor do not yet offer an input for it, and `spec.references[].as`
in job/script YAML is not implemented because reference bindings have no YAML
authoring surface at all today — adding one is a sync-side feature, not an alias
field. Phase D (membership hygiene), Phase E (per-agency same-name rows), Phase B
(`--become-password-file`) and Phase C (the `useEnvVars` permission split) remain
as planned in the runas-update plan.

---

## 0.56.10 — Departmental RBAC: the way back in, and the paperwork (RF)

**Date:** Aug 4, 2026

**A locked-out instance now has a supported way back in.** On OIDC deployments
the documented recovery lever — the bootstrap admin environment variable — has
never done anything: it applies only to proxy-header logins, and the manual did
not say so. Until now the honest answer to "we renamed our admin group in the
IdP and nobody can get in" was to edit the database by hand. The new offline
subcommand, `amadeus grant-admin <ad-group>`, writes an unrestricted admin grant
for a group with the server stopped: idempotent (running it twice mid-crisis is
expected), audited (a break-glass grant that leaves no trace is
indistinguishable from an attacker's), and visible afterwards as an ordinary
grant the recovered admin can review and remove. Passing an email instead
*looks up* that user's recorded groups and writes nothing — granting admin to a
group grants it to everyone in it, so choosing which group must be done with the
name in view. This closes the last precondition for deploying the two
access-narrowing releases.

**And the documentation now describes the system that exists.** The
architecture document had not been told about any of this — it still said the
trigger permission "remains deferred" and showed a permission matrix with two
columns that were deleted five releases ago. Both manuals were worse: stamped
eleven releases back, they told operators that trigger and kill are not enforced
("control access via your Authelia policy instead"), described the deleted
Scope Restrictions matrix as the access model, and documented the
lockout-recovery procedure that does not work on OIDC. All corrected, and the
three postures this programme decided are now written where operators will find
them: a scheduled run of a department-less job runs unrestricted on the shared
pool (which is why schedule authoring is admin-only); a scheduled ad-hoc run
fires with the authorization it was created under, so offboarding means revoking
the grants *and* sweeping the user's parked runs; and a secret or key belonging
to no department is shared infrastructure that only unrestricted operators may
change or reveal.

The changelog itself gets two corrections rather than rewrites: the 0.56.5 entry
overstated which banners shipped, and the removal of the Scope Restrictions
matrix happened with no entry at all — both are now recorded, dated, in place.
The README, the agent-context file, and the planning documents' own status
tables are reconciled to what actually shipped.

**Still gated, deliberately:** v0.56.4 (viewers lose execute; unscoped jobs bind
a scope) and v0.56.5 (grants become authoritative) deploy only after the
pre-flight report is read against production data. The legacy access tables
remain until both have shipped and soaked.

---

## 0.56.9 — Departmental RBAC: saying what is true (RF)## 0.56.9 — Departmental RBAC: saying what is true (RF)

**Date:** Aug 4, 2026

**No access changes.** This release fixes what the system *says* about itself, and
finishes one catalogue column.

**The API reference contradicted itself about the rule it was documenting.**
The trigger endpoint's description had grown a correction rather than a rewrite,
so it stated both that stopping an unscoped job "is triggerable by anyone today"
and, four paragraphs later, that it is not; and both that the trigger permission
"is checked nowhere" and that it is enforced. Anyone reading it to find out
whether a permission is real found both answers. It now states the two live rules
once, together, and explains why they are different questions: whether you can see
a department, and whether you may act in it. Both must pass.

**The endpoint the whole interface reads to decide what to show you was
undocumented.** It had been widened twice while missing from the API reference,
with the frontend keeping its own hand-written copy of the shape — so a renamed or
dropped field would have gone unnoticed until something quietly stopped appearing.
It is documented now, and the interface derives its copy from that document rather
than duplicating it. The description also spells out the two things easy to get
wrong: those flags mean "somewhere", never "here", and one of them describes reach
rather than permission.

**Workflows now show which departments they touch**, as jobs have since 0.56.3 —
the two halves of the same catalogue had been answering that question
differently. A workflow belongs to no department of its own, so it shows the
union across the jobs it runs, which is exactly the set its permissions are
checked against: one that spans two departments says so rather than picking one.
Searchable, like the jobs column.

**The screen that decides access got the search, filters and sorting every other
table already had.** It is also the table that grows fastest — roughly a row per
group per department — and it replaced a grid that grew sideways, so a list you
cannot search was only half the fix. The department filter has a dedicated entry
for grants that reach *everything*: those are the rows worth reviewing first. The
controls stay hidden until there are enough rows to need them.

---

## 0.56.8 — Departmental RBAC: the regression fence (RF)

**Date:** Aug 4, 2026

**No behaviour changes — this release is the tests the previous four were
supposed to ship with.** Each one covers a rule that was already live and
already relied upon, and that nothing would have noticed breaking.

**The stop-a-running-job route had never been called by a single test.** That is
the route carrying the most security-sensitive decision in the whole programme:
stopping a run is authorised against the department the *run* was launched into,
not the one its job belongs to — and for a job with no department of its own,
every run has a different answer. It now has one: a shared job whose runs were
launched by two departments can be stopped by each of them and by neither of the
others; a system run with no department at all can only be stopped by an operator
with unrestricted reach; and someone who can see everything but holds no
stop-jobs permission is refused, because seeing is not authority. Pausing and
resuming gained the same coverage for the case added in 0.56.4.

**"Revoking someone's access does not cancel the runs they already scheduled"**
is a deliberate decision, and it was written down nowhere but prose. A test now
deletes every grant a user had and asserts their parked run still fires, with a
failure message explaining that re-checking at fire time is the alternative that
was considered and rejected — so anyone "fixing" it has to argue with the
decision rather than quietly reverse it. Its companion covers the recourse that
makes the posture defensible: finding and cancelling a departing user's parked
runs.

**A scheduled run of a department-less job stays department-less**, reaching only
the shared runner pool. This is the one execution path deliberately left untouched
when the rest tightened — a cron fire has nobody to attribute it to — and it
looks exactly like the hole that was closed everywhere else. It is now pinned in
both directions: the department-less job stays unbound, and a job that *does*
belong to a department still carries it, so the rule cannot drift into "scheduled
runs ignore departments entirely".

**The two screens that actually control access had no tests**, while the page's
only test covered the retired one. Both are covered now — including the "no
longer controls access" notice, which is exactly the sort of thing that goes
missing for three releases when nothing checks for it. The department picker
added last release is covered too, including the case that matters most: when the
server cannot be reached to ask whether you are department-scoped, the picker
appears rather than hiding, so you can still comply.

---

## 0.56.7 — Departmental RBAC: finishing what 0.56.6 started (RF)

**Date:** Aug 4, 2026

**The departmental boundary now actually covers the things it claimed to cover.**
A review of the whole RBAC programme against the code found that the previous
release delivered about half of what it announced, and that one of its gates had
been attached to the wrong door. This release closes every gap that review found.

**The SSH key gate was on the wrong route.** It guarded key *creation* — a route
where there is no key to look up yet, so the check could only ever conclude "this
belongs to no agency" and demand an unrestricted operator. Meanwhile the route
that **rewrites key material**, which is the one the whole departmental-keys story
was about, had no check at all. Both are fixed: updating a key now requires
holding it in your own department, and creating one no longer requires
unrestricted access.

**Variables and runners were never covered.** The promise was that a department
owns its own secrets *and* variables; only secrets shipped. Runners were named
explicitly in the plan and got nothing. Both now check the agency that owns the
thing being changed — for runners that means drain, resync, managed settings,
secret-injection, host-key approval, deregistration, tags and the connection
test. A runner in **no** agency is the shared fleet every department depends on,
so changing it takes an unrestricted operator, the same rule already used for
shared secrets.

**Moving something between departments is itself a departmental act.** The
membership screens asked only for the general configuration permission, with no
check on the thing being moved — so every gate above could be sidestepped in
three requests: take another department's key, move it into yours, then edit it.
Re-homing now requires authority on both sides of the move, and claiming
something shared requires unrestricted access, for the same reason changing it
does. This was the most consequential thing the release's own review turned up.

**Attaching material to a one-off run is a grant over that material.** Three
in-handler checks — per-run references, per-run SSH credential selection, and the
job composer's credential binding — asked only whether the caller could manage
variables *somewhere*. They now also ask whether they may manage **this** one, so
someone holding the permission in Finance and only the ability to run jobs in
Production can no longer pull a Production secret into a Production run. Shared,
department-less material stays attachable: injecting it into a run whose scope you
already hold is consumption, not a write, and it is what "shared" means. The
Run dialog's preview now applies the same rule, so it cannot green-light something
the trigger will refuse. A reference that matches nothing behaves exactly as
before, so the trigger route still cannot be used to probe which names exist.

**Runner registration is fleet-wide, so it takes the fleet-wide bar.** A new
runner joins the general pool and serves every department, which made minting
enrolment tokens a way for one department's admin to reach all of them from the
other direction. Minting and revoking now require unrestricted access.

**New in this release: creating a departmental thing binds it to a department.**
A scope-restricted operator creating a secret, variable or SSH key must now say
which of their agencies owns it. This is what makes the boundary liveable: without
it, anything they created would immediately count as shared infrastructure and
lock them out of their own work a second after making it. The Variables, Secrets
and SSH Keys dialogs grew the picker to match, shown only to the operators the
rule applies to. Unrestricted operators are unaffected, and creating something
with no department remains how you deliberately make it shared.

**Two execution routes were guarded with the wrong verb, or none.** Pausing a
workflow asked for "trigger jobs" where pausing a *job* asks for "kill jobs", and
cancelling a running workflow asked for no permission at all — every other
execution route got one in 0.56.4 and this one was missed. Both now match their
siblings.

**A workflow of unscoped jobs was authorised by nothing.** The scope list a
workflow's guard iterates over silently dropped jobs that have no scope, so a
workflow built entirely from them produced an empty list and the guard's loop
never ran — any signed-in user could trigger it. The rule that unscoped work is
unrestricted-only now applies inside workflows as it already did for single jobs,
and a workflow whose jobs have all been deleted is no longer a free pass either.

**Deleting a role could silently revoke access.** The guard that refuses to delete
a role while it is still in use counted only the old mappings table, never the
grants that actually control access today — so deleting a granted role left those
grants pointing at nothing, which resolves to no permissions at all. It now
refuses, naming the number of grants in the way.

Also: the module comments that described grants as "inert" and the execution verbs
as "unenforced" have been corrected — they described a system three releases out
of date, on exactly the files someone reads to learn how authorisation works. The
superseded scope resolver is deleted rather than left beside its replacement, and
denials on unscoped work now name the permission they wanted.

**Still to come:** the contract, catalogue and documentation half of the review —
including the manuals, which currently describe trigger and kill as unenforced.

## Unversioned chore (Aug 3, 2026) — the Scope Restrictions matrix is removed

Recorded retroactively (Aug 4): this change shipped without a changelog entry,
and it removed a surface the 0.56.5 entry had promised would remain visible for a
release.

The Scope Restrictions matrix — the role × scope grid that stopped deciding
anything at 0.56.5 — is gone from Users & Access. Its replacement is the Access
Grants list above it, which had been the live model for two releases. The same
change added the "no longer controls access" notice to the AD Group → Role
Mappings card, which was written for 0.56.5 but had never landed — so for three
releases that card looked like a live control whose edits quietly did nothing.
The API endpoints and tables behind both surfaces are untouched; they remain
until the legacy model is retired.

---

## 0.56.6 — Departmental RBAC: departmental secrets and keys (RB)

**Date:** Aug 3, 2026

**A Tax admin now owns Tax's secrets — and cannot touch Finance's.** That was the
last unkept part of the departmental promise, and the sharpest one: revealing a
secret is gated on the same permission as editing a variable, so while that
permission was global, anyone trusted with *any* department's variables could read
*every* department's credentials.

Secret writes, secret **reveal**, secret deletion and SSH-key changes are now
checked against the agency that owns the thing being touched. SSH keys have no
scope of their own at all — agency membership is their only isolation — which is
why they were the highest-consequence gap left in the program.

**Shared infrastructure is deliberately unrestricted-only.** A secret or key
belonging to *no* agency is not unowned; it is the one every department's jobs
consume. So changing or revealing it now requires an operator with unrestricted
reach, rather than any one department's admin. A test that previously asserted the
opposite has been inverted, because that behaviour was the thing being decided
against: reading what everyone depends on is not a departmental act.

Restricted operators keep everything inside their own department, and unrestricted
ones are unaffected — this is a boundary, not a lockout.

**Still to come:** retiring the previous access tables. They are kept
deliberately: the pre-flight report reads them, and that report is what authorises
deploying the two access-narrowing releases before it. They can only be dropped
once those have shipped and soaked — the rollback window is the entire reason
they still exist.

---

## 0.56.5 — Departmental RBAC: the predicate switch (RB)

**Date:** Aug 3, 2026

🔴 **The leak closes.** Authorization ran on two axes resolved *independently* and
both OR-unioned — permissions over roles, scopes over roles. A user who was a
viewer on Tax and an operator on Finance resolved to permissions `{trigger}` and
scopes `{tax, finance}`, and could therefore trigger **Tax** jobs that nobody ever
granted her. Invisible with one department; the default outcome with two dozen.

Access is now decided by **grants**: one row saying *this AD group has this role
here*. A permission and a scope must come from the **same** grant, so the strongest
verb no longer floats free onto the widest reach. Alice keeps Finance, loses the
ability to act on Tax, and still *sees* both — visibility stays unioned on purpose,
because the alternative is a far larger and riskier change and is not what anyone
asked for.

**Settings → Users & Access gains an Access Grants card**, and "Operator, but only
for Tax" is finally one row. It is a list rather than a matrix, deliberately: the
role × scope grid it replaces grows a column per scope and becomes a horizontal
wall at two dozen departments.

**The old surfaces are labelled, not deleted.** The AD-group mappings list and the
scope-restrictions matrix now carry a "no longer controls access" banner. They stay
visible for one release so the previous configuration can be read alongside the new
one — but an operator who edits them out of habit is told immediately, instead of
watching a save succeed and quietly change nothing.

> **Correction (Aug 4, 2026):** the paragraph above overstated what shipped. The
> matrix carried its banner; the mappings-card banner was written but never landed,
> and that card presented itself as a live access control until the Aug 3 chore
> that also removed the matrix (see the entry below 0.56.6). Recorded rather than
> rewritten, because a changelog that quietly edits its own past is worse than one
> that was briefly wrong.

**A grant is now the only thing that confers access.** An identity with no grants
has no authority at all, which is why the break-glass path was taught about grants
a release early and why the demo seed had to learn to write them: the migration
that converts old configuration into grants runs before the seed exists, so a
freshly seeded database would otherwise have had none.

**Every seeded scope now belongs to an agency.** A grant applies to an agency, so a
scope in none produces no grant and its access disappears silently — the report
calls these orphans and treats them as a blocker. The development database now has
zero, which is what "ready to switch" looks like.

**Not in this release:** the reworked Recent Logins (one role name is a display-only
simplification under multi-grant), and departmental ownership of secrets, variables,
SSH keys and runners. That last one is the promise that a Tax admin owns Tax's
secrets; it is additive rather than load-bearing for the switch, and it is the next
thing to build.

---

## 0.56.4 — Departmental RBAC: enforcement (RB)

**Date:** Aug 3, 2026

🔴 **The first release that takes access away.** Everything before this changed no
authorization decision; this one changes two, and both were deliberate holes.

**The permission matrix stops being decorative.** `triggerJobs` and `killJobs` have
been computed, displayed in the roles UI, and checked *nowhere* for the life of the
project — so a Viewer with scope access could run and stop jobs, and the role you
gave someone described what they could do only by coincidence. Both verbs are now
enforced at every execution route: run, kill, pause, resume, workflow trigger and
workflow pause. **Viewers can no longer execute.**

**An unscoped job stops carrying authority of its own.** A job with no declared
scope used to be triggerable by anyone, dispatched to the general runner pool, with
its declared target host validated against nothing — which is the hole through
which "scoped to Tax" quietly stopped being true. A restricted operator must now
bind a scope they hold; only an unrestricted operator may run it unbound, which is
the genuinely global case ("back up the database"). Binding is not a formality: the
run records that scope, reaches that department's runners instead of the general
pool, and can finally use host-subset targeting.

That reframes an unscoped job as a **template** — one `restart-service`, run by Tax
against Tax and Finance against Finance — rather than one catalog entry per
department, which at two dozen departments is the larger practical win.

**And the binding is real, not nominal.** A job's declared target host is now
checked against a newly bound scope: an unscoped job pinned to `finance-db-01` and
bound to Tax is refused. Without that the scope an operator was forced to name
would have meant precisely nothing.

**A rule you can comply with.** The Run dialog opens on the scope picker when a
choice is required, preselects it when there's only one, and blocks with *"Choose a
scope to run against"* rather than letting the request go and come back refused. A
rule whose only compliance path is an error message is the worst possible shape for
a change to a job that worked yesterday.

**Two things fixed along the way.** Stopping a run is now authorized against *that
run's* scope rather than its job's — the two differ whenever a run was launched
with a scope override, and always differ for a bound unscoped job. And the workflow
guard no longer short-circuits for unrestricted callers, which would have skipped
the new verb check entirely: being unrestricted describes how far you can reach,
not what you may do, and an unrestricted viewer holds no verb at all.

**Deliberately unchanged:** a *scheduled* fire of an unscoped job still runs
unbound and unchecked, because a cron fire has no actor and inventing one would be
fiction. That is safe only while schedule authoring stays admin-only — a fact now
written at both ends and guarded by a test named after the reason, so widening it
fails loudly rather than silently becoming a way around the new rule.

---

## 0.56.3 — Departmental RBAC, phase 3: orientation (RB)

**Date:** Aug 3, 2026

Once access is departmental, "show me my department's jobs" is the first thing
anyone asks — and the Jobs catalog did not mention agencies at all. This release
is the orientation half of the UI work: the parts that are useful now and do not
depend on either of the two gated switches. **No authorization behavior changes.**

**Jobs gain an Agency column.** It is *derived* from the job's scope, never
stored: a job carrying its own agency would be a second source of truth that can
disagree with the first — a job labelled Tax whose scope belongs to Finance — and
every access decision would then have to pick a winner. The run path already
settled this by snapshotting the derived set onto each run rather than letting a
job carry one. Display and search only; a scope can belong to several agencies,
so a job can show several.

The column has an immediate diagnostic use it was not designed for: scopes with
no agency render an em-dash, and those are exactly the scopes whose access would
silently vanish when grants become authoritative. The pre-flight report
enumerates them; the catalog now shows them at a glance.

**Run and Kill now ask the server per row.** The `/capabilities` flags are a flat
union — "may trigger *somewhere*" — which cannot answer per-row truth: an operator
scoped to Finance reports `triggerJobs: true` and still may not touch a Tax job.
Each job row now carries the caller's actual authority for that job, computed
server-side. Consuming it is what stops the UI re-deriving authorization and
drifting from what the API will really do; the regression test reports the union
as true while a row says false, because a client that keeps trusting the union
looks correct on every single-department install and only breaks once departments
exist.

**403s now name the permission.** "insufficient permissions" is unactionable — the
reader cannot tell whether to ask for a role change, a scope grant, or neither.
The permission has been in the audit trail since the denial-auditing work; it was
simply never shown to the one person who most needs it.

**Deliberately not in this release:** the Access Grants table and the reworked
Recent Logins are gated on grants becoming authoritative — a UI that edits grants
while the old tables still decide access would show operators making changes that
do nothing. Dropping the legacy tables waits a further release after that, so a
rollback window exists. The scope/secret membership matrix rework is deferred on
scope, not blocked.
