## 0.56.2 — Departmental RBAC, phase 2: grants (inert) (RB)

**Date:** Aug 3, 2026

Authorization ran on two axes resolved **independently** and both OR-unioned:
permissions over roles, scopes over roles. A user in `tax-viewers` (viewer→tax)
*and* `finance-operators` (operator→finance) resolved to permissions `{trigger}`
and scopes `{tax, finance}` — and could therefore trigger **Tax** jobs. The axes
never met, so any multi-role user got the strongest verb applied to the widest
scope set. Invisible with one department; the default with two dozen.

Migration **810** introduces `access_grants` — one table, `ad_group → role →
where` — which keeps the association the two flat lists destroy: *this* role,
*here*. `where` is an **agency** or the `*` sentinel, nothing else: the agency
list is the department taxonomy, so a narrow need gets a deliberate narrow
agency rather than a loose per-scope grant.

**Nothing authorizes against it yet, and that is the point.** The table is
created, backfilled, resolved at login and carried on the session — but every
authorization decision still comes from the old two-axis model, and the legacy
endpoints remain what the UI uses. A test pins this as a contract rather than a
comment: an identity whose *grants* say "operator on tax only" while its legacy
fields say "operator + viewer over tax and finance" must still answer from the
legacy fields. The predicate flips one release later, alone, after
`/rbac-preflight` has been read against real data — the same choreography the
agencies program used, and for the same reason: a deployed installation cannot
change behavior on upgrade.

**Author on agency, evaluate on scope.** A grant naming Tax expands through the
agency's scopes at login, so a scope added to Tax next month is covered with no
grant edit. Because that expansion happens at login rather than per request,
agency-membership writes now bump the session epoch — otherwise the change would
never reach a signed-in operator. That means membership edits sign everyone else
out, which is worth knowing before it becomes a routine surface.

**Deleting an agency is now refused while any grant references it.** The foreign
key cascades, so the alternative was silently revoking every grant authored
against it — the quiet revocation this whole surface exists to make visible.

**One re-login, paid a release early.** The session cookie version bumps because
the identity gained a grants field. A session frozen before this release would
carry no grants, which is indistinguishable from "resolved to no access" — and
that becomes an authorization answer the moment the switch lands. Taking the
re-login now means there are no stale cookies to reason about in the release
where a bad resolution could actually lock someone out.

**Verified against real data.** Run against the development database, the
backfill produced exactly what `/rbac-preflight` predicted: the three scopes it
flagged as belonging to no agency were the three that produced no grant. That
correspondence is what the phasing exists to buy — the report is a reliable
predictor of the switch, so the next release is a decision rather than a
discovery. On that data it also says plainly that the switch is *not* ready:
one role would lose everything until its scopes are assigned to agencies.

---

## 0.56.1 — Departmental RBAC, phase 1: roles become data (RB)

**Date:** Aug 3, 2026

The permission matrix was a compiled-in Go literal, so "our Tax agency needs an
Operator and a Viewer scoped to just Tax" could not be expressed without a
recompile. Migration **800** makes it a `roles` table, and **Settings → Users &
Access gains a Roles card** where an operator can define one.

**Roles stay pure permission templates.** A role says what you may *do*; the
scope matrix beside it says *where*. That separation is the whole reason Tax
needs zero new roles — two grants against the existing `operator` and `viewer` —
rather than one role per department per level, which at two dozen departments
would be 96 roles and four more for every department added. Custom roles are
selectable in the AD-group mapping dropdown the moment they exist; that control
previously read from a hardcoded list pinned to a frozen enum, so the page had
two disagreeing answers to the same question.

**Six permissions, not eight.** `viewDashboard` and `editSchedules` are deleted.
Neither had an enforcement point anywhere, and neither could get one:
`viewDashboard` gates nothing a session does not already reach, and the only
schedule-authoring surface is admin-gated by a mechanism that must stay that way.
A permission that cannot be enforced must not be displayed as though it were.
They are omitted from the new table rather than created and dropped, since
removing a SQLite column is a table rebuild.

**`viewer` therefore holds nothing at all** — correct, not an oversight. Its only
entry was `viewDashboard`. A viewer's access is *visibility*, resolved from its
granted scopes, and visibility is not a verb. The Roles card says so in place
rather than rendering an empty cell.

**Built-ins are editable but not deletable**, with two floors that have no
recovery path if they are wrong: the `admin` role can never give up
`manageRoles` (nothing could restore it), and no edit may leave zero roles
holding it. Deleting a role is refused while any AD-group mapping still uses it,
mirroring agency deletion — cascading would silently strip access from everyone
whose only role it was. Every role write signs out all other sessions, because a
role's permission set changes what its holders may do on their next request.

**A fixed bug, carried in for free.** The old hardcoded precedence map omitted
`approver` entirely, so an approver-only user ranked zero and rendered a blank
role in Recent Logins. The seeded ranks include it.

**Still no enforcement change.** `triggerJobs` and `killJobs` remain checked
nowhere (that is the next release, gated on reading `/rbac-preflight` against
real data), and the `Can` seam still has no call sites. Editing a role changes
what the four *enforced* permissions grant, exactly as before — the difference is
that the answer now comes from a row instead of a recompile.

---

## 0.56.0 — Departmental RBAC, phase 0: the enforcement seam (RB)

**Date:** Aug 3, 2026

Cronomicon cannot express "Operator, but only for Tax," and no number of new roles
would fix it. Authorization runs on **two axes resolved independently and both
OR-unioned** — permissions over roles, scopes over roles — so a user in
`tax-viewers` (viewer→tax) *and* `finance-operators` (operator→finance) resolves
to permissions `{trigger}` and scopes `{tax, finance}`, and can therefore trigger
**Tax** jobs. The axes never meet, so any multi-role user gets the strongest verb
applied to the widest scope set. Invisible with one department; the default
outcome with two dozen.

**This release changes no authorization decision.** It is the seam, the report,
and the truth — the two narrowing releases that follow are deliberately separate
so their blast radius can be read against real data instead of discovered in
production. That phasing is copied from the agencies program, which did the same
thing and worked.

**The seam.** `Identity.Can(perm, scope)` ORs over grants where *the same grant*
carries both the permission and the scope — that single conjunction is the whole
fix. In this release grants are **synthesized** from today's `Roles ×
AllowedScopes`, so every outcome is bit-identical to before, verified across 3,120
role×scope×permission×target combinations. Phase 2 swaps the synthesis for real
per-grant rows, and *that* is when the leak closes. Three siblings ship with it:
`CanAnywhere` (holds the verb somewhere — what a scope-less settings route
actually asks), `CanUnbound` (only an unrestricted actor may act on an unscoped
object — what RB-2/RB-26 will need), and `CanAgency` for the entities isolated by
agency rather than scope. Nothing calls any of them yet.

**Half the permission matrix was decorative, and now says so.** Only four of eight
permissions had a predicate at all; `viewDashboard`, `triggerJobs`, `killJobs` and
`editSchedules` were enforced **nowhere** — a Tax Viewer could already trigger Tax
jobs. `/capabilities` now reports `triggerJobs`/`killJobs` so the SPA can gate on
what the server actually computed, and Jobs/Workflows now gate Run/Kill/Pause on
that flag instead of a **hardcoded client-side role list** that duplicated the
matrix (identical today; wrong the moment custom roles exist). `viewDashboard` and
`editSchedules` are deliberately *not* exposed — they are deleted outright in
phase 1 rather than advertised as if they were real.

**`GET /rbac-preflight`** (ManageRoles) is the gate on everything that follows: who
loses execute, who benefits from the cross-product leak today, which unscoped jobs
and schedules and parked runs are affected, which secrets have no agency
membership — and the two hazards in converting today's scope-shaped restrictions to
agency-shaped grants: conversions that **widen** access (the agency holds scopes the
role was never granted) and **orphan scopes** belonging to no agency, which the
conversion drops silently. The second is a hard blocker. An empty report is expected
on a fresh install; the `*Evaluated` counters say whether it had anything to bite on.

**Contract truth.** The run-path description claimed scope enforcement "is not yet
wired." It has been since F-R — the guard is `ScopeReadable` on the effective
scope. Corrected, along with an explicit statement of what is still *not* enforced
(the `triggerJobs` verb) and what an unscoped job means today.

**Also:** the role/permission matrix moved from `internal/api` to `internal/auth`
(the seam needs it and the import can only point that way), re-exported as type
aliases so all 75 route gates and the wire shape are untouched; its struct literals
became keyed, so the phase-1 field deletions cannot silently permute a role's
grants.

**Not in this release, on purpose:** enforcing the verbs, the unscoped-job binding
rule, roles-as-data, and grants. Read the preflight first.

---

## 0.55.20 — "When to run": deferred ad-hoc runs (AR)

**Date:** Aug 3, 2026

v0.55.18/.19 taught *schedules* about time. This teaches the *Run dialog*: a
fourth section, **When to run** — Now (default, unchanged) or **At a specific
time**. "Run this backup at 5pm, with these variables, on these hosts, as this
user" is now one dialog, not a conversation with an admin about a one-shot
schedule entry.

**The shape: a pending run, not a schedule and not a queued run.** A deferred
trigger is a fully-validated manual run parked in a new `pending_runs` table
(migration **790**): the frozen `EnqueueParams` — env snapshot, override
envelope, targeting, connect-as identity, everything the dialog collected —
ride the row, and a 15-second promotion loop in the scheduler replays them
through the ordinary enqueue seam at `run_at`. The two obvious designs were
rejected deliberately: a one-shot *schedule entry* mutates the job definition,
is Admin-gated (requireCompose), and cannot carry the run envelope; a *runs
row* with a not-before would thread a new predicate through both hot claim
queries and count against the concurrency cap from the moment of insert.

**Permissions by construction.** A pending run is created by the run-trigger
endpoints, so it carries the run-trigger gate — session + CSRF + scope access —
not Compose. Scheduling a run for later requires exactly the power of running
it now, time-shifted.

**Backpressure at the honest moment.** The concurrency cap and the Forbid
policy are judged at *promotion*, when the run actually enters the system —
"the system is busy now" says nothing about tomorrow 5pm. A blocked row stays
pending and retries each tick.

**Catch-up, bounded — and deliberately different from cron.** A cron fire
missed during downtime is lost (unchanged, and documented as such). But an
operator who chose a specific instant almost certainly wants it to fire after
a restart: a due pending run found **≤ 24 hours late fires**; later than that
it is marked `missed` and *kept visible* rather than silently vanishing or
firing a day-old run.

**Where you see it.** Until it fires: **Schedules → Upcoming**, interleaved
with the cron projections and badged **ad-hoc** (hover for who scheduled it),
with a **Cancel** button; missed runs get a dismissible notice on the same
tab. On the job's expanded row: a *Scheduled ad-hoc run* line
(`Job.pendingRunAt`). In the dialog: a set instant is a deviation, so the
confirmation window restates it. After it fires: an ordinary manual run in
History whose envelope records `scheduledFor`/`scheduledBy` — the audit trail
distinguishes "clicked at 5pm" from "scheduled at 10am for 5pm". Workflows get
the same through **⏱ Run later** beside the Run button.

**Lifecycle details.** Cancel is `DELETE /pending-runs/{id}` (session + CSRF;
SU-2 scope-gated), and the promote/cancel race resolves to whoever acts first.
Deleting a job or workflow cascades its parked runs. runAt must be in the
future and within a year (422 otherwise — a run parked two years out is a typo
or a job for real schedules). Dates are entered browser-local with the
app-zone equivalent shown, same as activation windows.

**Contract.** `runAt` on the job-run and workflow-trigger bodies, the
`PendingRun` 202 schema, `DELETE /pending-runs/{id}`, `Job.pendingRunAt`, and
`adHoc`/`pendingId`/`scheduledBy` on upcoming items — both byte-identical
`openapi.yaml` copies, client regenerated. No wire-protocol change; the claim
queries are untouched.

Design discussed and approved 2026-08-03 (the pending_runs option over the
one-shot-schedule and deferred-runs-row alternatives); both open questions
resolved as recommended: bounded startup catch-up (24h), one-year horizon.
`make verify` green; `tsc -b && vite build` green.

---

## 0.55.19 — Anchored intervals and one-shot schedules (Phase 2)

**Date:** Aug 3, 2026

v0.55.18 gave schedules a start date. This makes that start date do a second
job: it becomes the **phase anchor** an interval schedule counts from. "Every
10 days" is genuinely inexpressible in cron — it has no weekly or monthly
position to sit at — so it needs a date to measure from, and now there is one.

**Three modes.** A schedule entry fires by exactly one rule:

- **cron** — a cron expression, optionally window-bounded. Unchanged, and still
  the right answer for anything tied to a clock or a weekday.
- **interval** — every N from `startAt`: a Go duration (`36h`, `90m`) or a day
  count (`7d`), minimum one minute. `startAt` is **required**, because that is
  what the interval is measured from.
- **once** — a `startAt` with neither cron nor interval: one fire, then never
  again. The one-off migration or cutover you want scheduled rather than
  remembered.

Cron and interval are mutually exclusive, enforced identically at the API
(422), in Git YAML (validation error) and in the composer — one
`cronutil.Spec.Validate` shared by all three, so a Git-authored schedule is
held to the same contract as an in-app one.

**One seam.** `cronutil.ParseSpec` resolves the mode and applies the activation
window, returning a `cron.Schedule` for all three. The scheduler registers them
identically and the timing wheel never learns there is more than cron; the
projections (`nextRunAt`, the inventory, `/schedules/upcoming`) go through the
matching `NextSpec`/`NextNSpec`, so the UI shows what will actually happen in
every mode. The Phase 1 window decorator moved into `cronutil` as part of this,
leaving one implementation instead of two.

**Storage.** Migration **780** adds `interval` to `schedules` and
`definition_schedules`. Because `cron` is `NOT NULL` on both, an interval or
one-shot entry stores `cron = ''` rather than forcing a two-table rebuild —
empty cron has always been this system's "no cron" convention, and every read
path resolves the mode through `ParseSpec` rather than reading either column
alone. The `interval` segment joins `content_hash` only when set, so plain-cron
rows keep their stored digest exactly as they did across v0.55.18.

**DST, stated plainly.** Interval arithmetic is on absolute instants — pure
duration addition, no calendar walk — so an interval is immune to DST but does
*not* hold a wall-clock time-of-day across one. That is the correct semantic
for "every 36 hours"; an operator who means "every day at 5 p.m." wants cron,
and the mode picker says so where they choose.

**Authoring.** A *How it runs* mode picker in the Schedule Builder and in the
Composer's inline-schedule rows, with interval presets, a live plain-words
reading and next-three-fires preview for every mode, and the anchor requirement
surfaced where an operator hits it. Switching modes clears the other mode's
field, since an entry fires by exactly one rule. Git YAML gains `interval` on
both an inline entry and a `schedules/*.yaml` spec. The Schedules inventory now
shows whichever rule an entry uses rather than an empty cron cell — the same
`preservedInline` trap as v0.55.18, caught this time by extending the workflow
round-trip in the same change.

**Contract.** `interval` (nullable) and the derived `mode` enum
(`cron|interval|once`) added to `Schedule`, `ScheduleInput`, `ScheduleEntry`,
`ScheduleEntryStatus` and the compose inline-schedule schemas, in both
byte-identical `openapi.yaml` copies; client regenerated. No wire-protocol
change — the runner path is untouched.

Deferred at planning as AW-Q6 and tracked as backlog item V2-20, now shipped. Still deferred: missed-fire policy
(V2-21), per-schedule timezone (V2-22), blackout windows (V2-23), per-entry
pause (V2-24). `make verify` green; `tsc -b && vite build` green.

## 0.55.18 — Schedule activation windows: start later, stop at a date (AW-1…AW-19)

**Date:** Aug 3, 2026

Cron says *when in the week* a job runs; it could not say *"not until August
5th."* Until now the only way to stage a schedule was to create it paused and
remember to resume it. Schedule entries gain an optional **activation window** —
`startAt` / `endAt` — that bounds when the cron is permitted to fire without
touching the expression itself.

**The model.** Both bounds are optional RFC3339 instants stored on the
first-class `schedules` catalog and on the runtime `definition_schedules`
expansion (migration **770**); a ref expansion copies the window down with
cron/env so the runtime row stays self-contained and the scheduler never joins
back to the catalog. A NULL window is exactly the old behaviour, which every
pre-existing row keeps — the upgrade is a strict no-op.

Enforcement is a `cron.Schedule` decorator wrapped around the parsed expression
at registration, so the timing wheel, the reload path and the fire path are
untouched: before the window opens the decorator advances the query instant to
the start (a cron match landing exactly on the boundary still fires); past the
end it returns the zero time — robfig's "never again" contract — leaving the
entry registered but permanently silent.

**Three semantics worth knowing.** A `startAt` already in the past is **inert**:
no catch-up, no backfill, no thundering herd on reload. An elapsed window never
deletes the entry — it stays listed as `expired`, since git-source rows must
round-trip regardless. And the window gates **scheduled fires only**; manual
runs, run-now and webhook triggers bypass the scheduler and are unaffected,
which is what makes a deferred schedule safe to test.

**Projection parity.** `cronutil` gained `NextWindowed` / `NextNWindowed`, and
every read path that projects future fires — per-entry `nextRunAt`, the schedule
inventory, and `/schedules/upcoming` — now runs through them. Without this the
UI would have advertised phantom runs before a start date and after an end date.
Entries also report a derived `windowState` (`pending` / `active` / `expired`),
orthogonal to `enabled`/`paused`, which stay definition-level and still take
precedence in the collapsed display status.

**Authoring.** The Schedule Builder and the Composer's inline-schedule rows get
an **Active period** pair. Dates are entered in the *browser's* timezone and
stored as UTC, with the resolved app-zone equivalent shown beneath the field
when the two differ, so there is no ambiguity about which 5 p.m. was meant. The
live cron preview clamps to the window. Git YAML accepts the same `startAt` /
`endAt` on both an inline schedule entry and a `schedules/*.yaml` spec; a
malformed window there is an advisory validation error that syncs the entry
unbounded rather than wedging the repo.

**Two fixes found while building this.** The Workflow Editor round-trips inline
schedule entries it cannot author, and its preserved copy picked fields
explicitly — so saving a workflow would have silently cleared any window on
those entries; it now carries them. And `cronutil` had been accepting robfig's
`@every <duration>` descriptor through the API and Git YAML while every UI
surface rejected it as invalid — an unanchored interval arriving through a back
door. `@every` is now rejected with a clear message; the calendar descriptors
(`@daily`, `@weekly`, …) stay valid, since they have exact cron equivalents.

**Contract.** `startAt`/`endAt` added to `Schedule`, `ScheduleInput`,
`ScheduleEntry`, `ScheduleEntryStatus` and the job/workflow compose inline-schedule
schemas, plus the `windowState` enum, in both byte-identical `openapi.yaml`
copies; frontend client regenerated. The schedule `content_hash` includes the
window **only when set**, so every unbounded row keeps its stored digest and no
recompute pass or first-sync drift blip occurs. No wire-protocol change — the
runner path is untouched.

Planning decisions AW-Q1…AW-Q7 are resolved.
Deferred to V2: anchored intervals and one-shot schedules (V2-20), missed-fire
policy (V2-21), per-schedule timezone (V2-22), blackout windows (V2-23),
per-entry pause (V2-24). `make verify` green; `tsc -b && vite build` green.

## 0.55.17 — Parallel arms may be sequences: concurrent serial chains (PS-1)

**Date:** Aug 3, 2026

The second half of Automate-suite parity. A parallel block's arms were
restricted to plain leaf jobs, which made the most common big-suite shape —
several independent serial chains fanning out from one point and running
concurrently — inexpressible in a single workflow. That restriction is lifted.

**The model.** A new `sequence` step type (`{type:"sequence", steps:[…]}`)
holds an ordered serial chain. As a parallel arm it becomes one concurrent
lane: the engine walks each sequence arm in its own goroutine against a clone
of the results map (sibling arms can't observe each other mid-flight,
mirroring validation's scoping), merging the arm's produced results back at
the join — so an output captured inside a chain is consumable after the block,
and a chain's failure fails the block. Standalone, a sequence is just an
inline chain. Sequences may nest parallels and branches (and vice versa), so
image-4-shaped suites — fan-out → chain → nested fan-out — compose directly.

**Everything that walks the graph learned the type.** Validation (arms are
plain jobs or sequences; per-arm upstream scoping), node-id minting, branch-ref
collection, skipped-arm marking, the same-path duplicate guard, the run-detail
serializer and step-type container map, both OpenAPI spec copies, and the
regenerated TS schema.

**The frontend speaks it end to end.** Canvas tree/serializer round-trips
sequences (path ids `s1.j0.q1`); the flow graph draws a sequence arm as a
chained lane between fork and join; validateTree/upstreamProducers mirror the
engine's new rules; the canvas editor gets a SEQUENCE card with its own lane
and a "+ Sequence" button on parallel arm lanes (arms offer job/sequence; a
sequence's own lane offers the full palette); graphView maps statuses onto
chain nodes and sends sequence-bearing graphs to the canvas renderer.

Race-detector-clean engine tests drive real concurrent chains end to end
(ordering inside each chain, the post-block barrier, chain-failure halting);
validation and frontend model tests lock the scoping rules. Verified live:
a seed → three-concurrent-chains → join suite authored via the API renders on
the expanded-view canvas, the run graph, and round-trips through the editor.

## 0.55.16 — Complex workflow graphs render on the dagre canvas (WC-R1)

**Date:** Aug 3, 2026

Groundwork for Automate-scale job suites: the read-only React-Flow/dagre
canvas the editor already had is now the renderer for any workflow graph the
numbered chain can't draw honestly.

**Chain or canvas, decided per graph.** The expanded row's Steps section and
the run drill-down's Step Graph both keep StepChain for small, flat
workflows — its numbering is earned there — and switch to the pan/zoom/minimap
canvas when the graph nests containers inside branch arms (which StepChain
flattens into anonymous chips) or grows past ten nodes (where the chain
becomes a blind horizontal scroll). The canvas loads lazily and shares its
chunk with the editor, so the Workflows page bundle doesn't grow.

**Run graphs carry status onto the canvas.** Job nodes tint by their child
run's outcome (the same statusTone vocabulary as every badge; skipped arms
dim), refreshed live while the run polls. To make that possible the run-detail
serializer now preserves the FULL nested step structure in branch arms —
previously arms were flattened to their leaf jobs — and ships the structured
condition alongside its display label. A new pure `graphView` module
normalizes the two wire shapes (raw definition vs. run graph) into the canvas
model and owns the chain-vs-canvas rule, unit-tested for both shapes.

**Minimap themed.** xyflow's default white minimap card read as a hole in the
dark theme; it now follows the palette in both modes, sized and moved so it
stops colliding with the canvas content.

## 0.55.12 — Variables and run inputs are visible in logs; redaction narrowed to secrets

**Date:** Aug 1, 2026

Operators kept hitting `[REDACTED]` in run logs where their own plaintext
values should have been — a Variable from the Env Vars page, or an answer they
had just typed into the Run dialog. Those values were never secret by design
(they inject as `AMADEUS_VAR_<key>` un-masked, and schedule/job env was always
plaintext), yet the ingest redactor still masked them anywhere they happened to
match log text. That half-redaction is gone:

**No longer redacted.** Single-line Variables (the Env Vars → Variables tab)
and per-run inputs — prompt answers and ad-hoc environment overrides — now
appear raw in run logs, matching how they are stored and delivered everywhere
else.

**Still redacted, unchanged.** Stored and Vault-backed Secrets, SSH key
credentials, integration credentials (GitLab PAT, SMTP password, Vault AppRole
secret ID), and dispatch-time injected values/key material — including the
fail-closed `redactor_unavailable` guard for secret-bearing runs.

**One deliberate carve-out.** A *multi-line* Variable value stays masked: hosts
may reference an SSH private key stored under Variables by name
(`authKeyEnvVar` / `@variable:` references), and a PEM body must never surface
in a log even though it lives in the plaintext table.

UI copy now says so instead of promising best-effort masking: the Run dialog's
environment-overrides helper and run-inputs caveat, the Job Composer's
credential-shaped-prompt warning and scope-context blurb, and the workflow
step's resolved-context label ("secrets redacted").

## 0.55.10 — Server-side sorting for the paged History tables

**Date:** Aug 1, 2026

The sorting plan's final phase. The five server-paged surfaces — Executions,
Workflow Runs, Change Log, Schedule Pushes, and Git Sync — now sort **in the
database, before pagination**, via allowlisted `?sort=&order=` parameters on
their endpoints. Clicking "Duration ▲" on Executions finally means the shortest
run in the filtered set, not the shortest run on the current page — retiring a
page-scoped quirk that had shipped with the original Executions sort. The four
other tabs, which until now had no sorting at all, get the full header
affordance (carets, `aria-sort`, per-table persistence), and a sort change
snaps back to page 1.

Under the hood: each endpoint declares a column allowlist mapped to SQL — an
unknown sort key or direction is a 400, never interpolated. Result/status
columns rank by severity in SQL (worst first ascending), matching the client
tables; empty cells sort last in both directions; and every sorted query
carries a deterministic tiebreak so pages never shear under equal values.
Defaults are unchanged — a request without a sort key behaves exactly as
before. The excluded columns stay excluded: Details, Files Changed, Schedule
Change, Commit, and Trace IDs.

## 0.55.9 — Column sorting on every table

**Date:** Aug 1, 2026

The product owner's ask, plainly: "most windows are missing the feature to allow a user to
sort by the various columns." Now they have it. Seventeen tables across the app
gained clickable column headers — Jobs, Scripts, Workflows, Schedules (Catalog,
Inventory, Upcoming), Env Vars (Variables, Secrets, SSH Keys), Scopes,
Agencies, SSH Targets (hosts and bastions), Recent Logins, AD Group Mappings,
Alert Rules, and the Runner Registry — all speaking the one sort idiom built in
the shared-primitive refactor: ▲/▼ carets, `aria-sort`, hover titles, and a
per-table remembered choice (localStorage, mirroring column widths).

**The rules, everywhere the same.** First click on a text column sorts
ascending; on a date or count column, descending (newest/largest first) —
second click flips. Empty cells sort last in both directions, so a job that
never ran can't top "Last Run". Status columns sort by *meaning*, not
alphabet: one click floats the broken things — failures before warnings before
healthy — with each table's vocabulary ranked worst-first (SSH targets rank
`reachable` and `verified` equal, per v0.55.8). Catalogs default to Name
ascending; History keeps Started, newest first; Upcoming keeps soonest-first.

**What deliberately doesn't sort:** action/expand gutters, multi-value columns
(Tags, Capabilities, Agencies, AD Groups, Channels, Recipients), free-text
(Description, Details), identifier noise (Trace ID, fingerprints), and cron
expressions — the Next Run/When columns are the sortable form of that
information. Browse mode on the four catalogs keeps its folders-first tree:
the shared header renders without carets there, because sorting columns
against a folder grouping would mean nothing. The five server-paged History
tabs stay unsorted rather than misleadingly page-sorted — their real fix is
the Phase 3 server sort parameter.

**Found along the way (TS-15):** Workflows' search mode rendered every
matching row with no pager at all; it now pages 25 at a time like its three
catalog siblings.

## 0.55.7 — Two-tier SSH connection test: keyless targets report Reachable

**Date:** Jul 31, 2026

Since the "connect as" work (v0.54/v0.55), a target's SSH identity can come
entirely from a job or run override — a target row with no key of its own is a
legitimate configuration. But its *Test* button still demanded one: with no key
configured the probe returned `cred_error` before opening a socket, so a
keyless target could never demonstrate reachability or pin its host key.

**The keyless tier (TT).** When a target (or bastion) has no auth credential
and no key name, *Test* now runs an unauthenticated probe instead: it dials the
SSH endpoint, verifies the host key exactly as a job would — strict compare
when pinned, TOFU-capture-and-persist when not — and then aborts the handshake
before authentication, borrowing the runner keyscan's sentinel pattern. No
credentials are needed, nothing authenticates, and no ICMP is involved: the
probe proves the actual SSH port answers and establishes the host's identity,
which is the part only the target row can carry. The result is the new
`reachable` status — "endpoint answered, host key pinned, authentication not
tested" — a good outcome, not an error: it lands as a *success* ssh-test run in
History, shows a primary-colored *Reachable* badge (with its own summary tile),
and the inline result names the presented host-key type and fingerprint.

A keyed target still gets the full tier — a real login as before, byte-for-byte
— and the pin-mismatch (possible MITM) refusal applies on both tiers. One edge
is refused loudly: a keyless target routed through a *keyless* bastion returns
`cred_error` naming the bastion, because the bastion hop must authenticate
before the target can be reached at all.

## 0.55.6 — Two-tier run confirmation: press-again for defaults, a window for deviations

**Date:** Jul 31, 2026

The product owner's hybrid design from the confirmation discussion: routine runs deserve the
cheapest possible confirm, unusual runs deserve a loud one — and the split is
decided by whether the run's settings deviate from the job's defaults.

**Default settings → press again (RC).** The first press of *Run now* arms the
button into a one-line recap — *"Press again — all 4 hosts in Cluster-A via
SSH"* — and the second press runs it. The armed state reverts after six seconds,
and **any settings change disarms it**, so a stale recap sentence can never be
confirmed. The recap phrase reflects the *effective* targeting (a host subset
reads "1 selected host", not "all 4 hosts" — caught by the screenshot sweep).

**Deviations → a confirmation window.** When the operator changed anything from
the job's defaults — scope, executor, host/group subset, raw `--limit`, connect
as, check mode, diff, tags, verbosity, become, extra variables, env overrides,
added references — the press opens a window instead: one sentence of what will
happen, then each deviation named against the default it replaces ("Scope:
Production — job default: Staging"). *Back* returns to the form untouched;
*Confirm & run* commits and records `confirmation` in the run's audit metadata
(the server's known-names filter gains the token). Check mode gets its callout
here too — the last thing on screen before a dry run commits says it is one.

**What deliberately is NOT a deviation:** the run-anyway escape for unfilled
answers. It already carries its own explicit acknowledgment checkbox, and
warning twice for one act teaches operators to stop reading warnings.

Confirmations keep their meaning by being proportionate: the double-press is
half a second of friction on every run; the window appears only when the run is
genuinely unusual — which is exactly when it should be read.

## 0.55.5 — The Run dialog becomes three sections, with a review gate

**Date:** Jul 31, 2026

**Three sections (RV).** The Run dialog is now three stacked disclosures:
**Required variables** (the answers panel, open by default when the job declares
inputs — it is the one part that genuinely needs the operator), **Where it
runs** (scope, references, executor, Connect as, targeting), and **Advanced
options** (the Ansible flags, previously nested inside Where it runs, plus the
per-run environment overrides). Every collapsed section keeps a one-line
summary, so the RD1 rule — targeting is never hidden, check mode is never
hidden — now applies three times. The answers panel suppresses its own headline
when embedded (the section header and summary carry the title and ready-count),
and the extra-vars editor's distinct "+ Add extra-var" label earns its keep now
that both editors live in the same section.

**The review gate (visited-gating, RV-Q1).** When a job declares run inputs,
the Run button stays disabled until *Where it runs* has been open at least once
— the button reads **Review where it runs** until then, so the gate names its
own remedy. "Visited" means has-been-open-ever: closing the section after
glancing is fine, and the sections that auto-spring open on a problem
(incompatible scope, unresolved reference) satisfy it naturally. A job with
**no** declared inputs keeps its one-click run (RV-Q2) — the gate exists for
runs that already demand operator attention, and the wrong-scope mistake on a
var-less job was judged not worth taxing every routine rerun.

**Recorded, not just enforced (RV-Q3).** The sections the operator had open ride
the run's audit envelope as `reviewedSections` (server-filtered to the known
section names, since the envelope is displayed verbatim) — the same T2.4 channel
as the prompt metadata, so History can tell a reviewed manual run from an API
call. Client-side only as a guarantee, audit-honest as a record: absence means
the caller wasn't the dialog.

## 0.55.3 — Advanced Ansible run options, and env passthrough in the Composer

**Date:** Jul 31, 2026

Phase 3 (RP-15..RP-19) and RP-14 of the run-parity plan — the two
items deferred out of the parity work, now scoped and shipped.

**Advanced Ansible options (Phase 3).** The Run dialog grows an *Ansible options*
block — collapsed, ansible-only — carrying `--check`, `--diff`,
`--tags`/`--skip-tags`, verbosity, `--become`/`--become-user`, and `-e`
extra-vars. These are **per-run only** and live solely in the run's override
envelope: no columns, no migration, no scheduler/workflow fold. That is the
design, not a shortcut — they are the flags an operator reaches for *at* trigger
time ("dry-run this once", "just the certs tag"), and a job-spec layer would need
a real precedence story of its own.

**Check mode is the reason the protocol moved to v8.** An older agent drops an
unknown manifest field, so a run the operator asked to *dry-run* would apply for
real while the console labelled it a check — and a `--skip-tags` exclusion would
run the very task it was meant to skip. Rather than encode which individual
flags are dangerous (a matrix that rots as flags are added), **any**
option-carrying run assigned to a protocol < 8 agent is refused with
`409 agent_too_old`. Slightly over-strict for a verbosity-only run, and that is
the correct trade. A run setting no option is wire- and behavior-identical to a
pre-v8 run.

**Extra-vars cannot forge the run's identity.** `-e` is the same precedence tier
Phase 2 uses for `ansible_user`/`ansible_ssh_private_key_file`, and ansible takes
the *last* occurrence of a repeated variable. So the two identity names are
refused at the trigger boundary (422, pointing at **Connect as**), *and* the
agent emits the identity pair after any operator extra-vars — two independent
locks, because either a validation gap or an ordering regression alone would
otherwise let a run connect as someone other than what its own audit record
claims. Every other `ansible_*` name stays allowed: `ansible_python_interpreter`
and friends are legitimate.

Two things stated plainly in the UI and both manuals: `-e` values land in the
runner's **process table**, readable by any local user there — a weaker position
than the env channel, so never a place for secret material; and `--become` gets
no extra permission gate, because a playbook can already declare `become` itself,
so the toggle grants nothing the caller could not already run. A become
*password* is deliberately not a field.

**Composer env passthrough (RP-14).** `spec.env_passthrough` had been
Git-YAML-only since protocol v3, so an in-app-composed ansible job could never
read a runner-local variable. The Composer now authors it (Advanced → *Runner
environment passthrough*), writing the same serialization the sync path does,
with the env-namespace rules applied: POSIX name charset, `AMADEUS_*` refused
(those are injected references, not the runner's environment), local-toolchain
run types only.

Also: the two "+ Add variable" buttons that would have sat in the same dialog are
now distinct (*+ Add extra-var*), and a negative `ansibleVerbosity` is a 422
rather than being silently swallowed — caught by its own test.

Manuals restamped v0.55.3; runner-security guide **R7.6** with the v8 gate and
the argv-exposure note.

---

## 0.55.2 — SSH ↔ Ansible run parity, part 2: "connect as" works on Ansible runs

**Date:** Jul 31, 2026

Phase 2 of the run-parity plan (RP-6..RP-11). The per-run and
per-job **connect-as identity** shipped in v0.54.0/v0.55.0 was refused for
ansible at every layer. It now works there — and the reason it took a protocol
change rather than deleting a few `422`s is the interesting part.

**Delivered as extra-vars, not CLI flags (RP-Q1).** An ssh-family run is dialled
by Cronomicon's own SSH client, so an override is applied by rewriting the resolved
target list. `ansible-playbook` dials for itself, and the agent never reads
`targets[].user` — so the manifest now carries the identity in two explicit
fields (`sshUser`, `sshKeyRef`, protocol **v7**, names only) which the agent
turns into `-e ansible_user=…` / `-e ansible_ssh_private_key_file=…`.
Extra-vars are ansible's *highest*-precedence source, so the override beats an
inventory-authored `ansible_user` on every host in the run — matching how the
SSH executor's override replaces per-host wiring outright. The obvious-looking
`-u` / `--private-key` flags sit in the *lowest* tier and would have lost to the
inventory on exactly the hosts an admin had bothered to wire: applying silently,
and only sometimes.

**Fail-closed in three places.** An identity-carrying ansible run assigned to a
protocol < 7 agent is refused (`409 agent_too_old`) — an older agent would drop
the unknown fields and run as the inventory's identity while the run record and
the console showed the operator's. The agent refuses a run whose `sshKeyRef`
names material that did not arrive, rather than falling back to the inventory's
key. And an override key **suppresses** the `--private-key` auto-wire, so one
run can never carry two keys through two precedence tiers.

**One predicate, five call sites (RP-7).** `execspec.IdentityCapableRunType`
replaces the ad-hoc `SupportedRunType` checks at both authoring boundaries and
all three enqueue folds (manual trigger, scheduler, workflow engine), so a
scheduled ansible run and a manually-triggered one cannot disagree about whose
identity they use. It is deliberately neither "ssh-family" nor "anything but
terraform": an unknown run type answers **false**, because identity support is
granted by something having been taught to apply it.

**Terraform stays excluded** (RP-Q2) at every layer — 422 at both authoring
boundaries, dropped at every fold, never set on a manifest, ignored by the agent
branch. Its providers authenticate, not SSH, so the fields could only no-op.

**Hardening carried by construction (RP-8).** The manifest identity overlay was
never run-type-gated; it was merely *unreachable* for ansible because every
producer zeroed the columns. Lifting the producer gates would have made it fire
and silently drop the username half. The overlay is now explicitly branched per
run type with a test pinning each branch.

**UI (RP-10):** the Run dialog and Composer offer Connect as for ansible jobs,
worded for the mechanism ("overrides `ansible_user` from the scope's
inventory"), and the Composer clears a typed identity when a job is re-bound to
a terraform script rather than submitting a hidden value the server would 422.

**Contract (RP-11/RP-13):** OpenAPI gains the two manifest fields and the
long-missing protocol v3/v6 surface — `envPassthrough`, `checkout`, `secrets`,
`keys`, plus the `ManifestCheckout` / `ManifestKey` schemas — and `Run.overrides`
now documents `groups`, `ansibleLimit`, `sshUser` and `sshCredential`, which the
server has always written. Both manuals restamp to v0.55.2 and the
runner-security guide goes to **R7.5** with the v7 gate and the extra-vars
rationale.

## 0.55.1 — SSH ↔ Ansible run parity, part 1: the same options, in the same shape

**Date:** Jul 31, 2026

Phase 1 of the run-parity plan (RP-1..RP-5) — presentation parity.
Frontend only: no API, schema, or executor change. An ansible run and a shell
run now offer the same targeting controls, worded for what each one actually
does, instead of the ansible run quietly hiding half the form.

**Host targeting for runner runs (RP-1):** the host-subset picker was gated on
`executor === "ssh"` and replaced, for every runner run, with a static note
("Host selection applies to SSH runs…"). It is now offered for all run types —
the API has accepted `targetHosts` for runner runs since V2-12, and the server
folds the selection into the pinned ansible `--limit`. What differs per type is
the *wording*, not the control: SSH connects to the selection, ansible passes
it as `--limit`, terraform records it for audit without consuming it.

**Honest helper text (RP-2):** the group picker told every runner run "Ansible:
passes N groups as --limit" — including terraform runs, which never see a
`--limit`. Helper lines are now keyed on run type rather than executor.

**Raw `--limit` is mutually exclusive with the pickers (RP-Q4):** setting a raw
pattern disables the host/group chips and vice versa, and submission enforces
the exclusion rather than trusting the disabled attribute. Ansible's `:` unions
patterns, so any silent combination of a pin and a subset could target *more*
hosts than either input alone suggests.

**Auto executor stops lying (RP-3):** a job with no pinned executor resolves to
a concrete one in the dialog (a run is always concrete), but the dialog now
says so — "Auto → Runner" in the collapsed summary, "job default (Auto)" on the
card, and the resolution spelled out in the helper. Picking a card drops the
Auto wording, because that is a real override.

**One form idiom (RP-4):** `fieldLabelStyle`, `FormField` (label + control +
helper, with a danger tone for inline verdicts) and `Disclosure` now live in
`components/ui.tsx`. The Run dialog's local `labelStyle` const and the
Composer's local `Field`/`input()` are retired onto them, so the two authoring
surfaces read as the same form. Style functions, not frozen consts — the theme
tokens mutate in place on toggle.

**One run-type vocabulary (RP-5):** the closed run-type list was retyped in four
files (runner provisioner, Scopes capability editor, History filter, Publish
builder). It is now authored once in `runtypes.ts`, and a new unit test pins it
against the OpenAPI `RunType` enum so a backend addition fails the build instead
of silently missing from a picker.

Connect-as identity stays hidden for ansible/terraform — the server still 422s
it. Lifting that is Phase 2 (RP-6..RP-11), which needs the decided `-e`
extra-vars delivery to beat inventory-authored identity.

## 0.55.0 — Per-job SSH identity: declarative "connect as" on the job spec

**Date:** Jul 31, 2026

Phase B of the ssh-user plan (CA-7..CA-12): the "connect as"
identity v0.54.0 gave the Run dialog is now a **declarative job property** that
applies on **every** run path — manual, scheduled, and workflow steps.

**Authoring:** Git YAML gains `spec.ssh_user` / `spec.ssh_credential`
(credential by **label**, names only); the Composer gains a matching
"Connect as / SSH key" row next to the host pin. Validation is
posture-appropriate per surface: the Composer hard-422s a bad username,
unknown label, or an ansible/terraform script (authoring can be actionable),
while Git sync **warns and still writes the row** — a sync must never wedge a
repo over one field, and dispatch fails loudly anyway. Setting or *changing*
the credential from the Composer requires **Manage Env Vars** (the V2-11
grant rule); an unchanged full-replace resend or a clearing edit does not, so
compose-only editors aren't locked out of unrelated edits.

**Enqueue fold (the TG lesson, applied by construction):** the job identity is
frozen onto the v0.54.0 `runs` columns at every producer — the manual trigger
defaults beneath the operator's per-run override (per field, override wins;
the audit envelope keeps recording only what the operator typed), the
scheduler's per-fire read (edit applies on the next fire, no reload), and the
workflow engine's hand-built child-run INSERT. All three gate the fold to
ssh-family run types, so a stored identity on an ansible job is ignored
rather than frozen onto a run that can't honor it. Migration 760 adds the two
`jobs` columns.

**Run dialog (CA-11):** a job's declared identity shows as the displayed
defaults — "svc-report (from job)" / "Job default (prod-key)" — and
submitting them untouched sends nothing, keeping envelopes honest.

**Docs (CA-12):** both manuals now document the feature and stamp v0.55.0 —
User Manual §6.5 (the fifth override card + precedence callout) and §10.1
(Composer field row); Administrator Manual §6 (the "who may point a run at a
stored key" record); the Runner Security guide gains the CA-3b trust-model
section and bumps to R7.4.

Tests: YAML validation, sync-fixture columns, Composer CRUD + clearing PUT,
producer folds on all three paths (scheduler/workflow/manual, including the
ansible not-folded guards), schema-version bump to 760. Full backend +
frontend suites green; Composer row and dialog prefill verified on screen in
both themes.

## 0.54.0 — Per-run SSH identity: "connect as" user + stored-key picker

**Date:** Jul 30, 2026

The ad-hoc Run dialog can now override **who a run logs in as**: a "Connect as"
username field and an SSH-key dropdown (the stored credentials list) sit next to
the executor picker, overriding each resolved target's per-host identity for
that run only. Precedence is per-run override > per-host record > `root`;
bastion hops are never touched. This is Phase A of
the ssh-user plan (CA-1..CA-6 + CA-3b; decisions CA-Q1..Q5 locked
2026-07-30). Phase B — the declarative job-spec `ssh_user`/`ssh_credential`
layer — is next and will carry the manual updates.

**Wire & storage are names-only (CA-Q2):** `POST /jobs/{id}/run` gains
`sshUser` + `sshCredential` (the credential's **label**, never bytes), recorded
in the F3 override envelope and frozen onto two new `runs` columns (migration
750) at enqueue. Dispatch applies them as a target overlay
(`execspec.ApplyIdentityOverride`) after the shared `ResolveRun` in **both**
executors; the SSH executor resolves the label to a credential id at dispatch
and fails the run loudly if it was deleted or renamed since queueing.

**Runner runs get the full mapping (CA-Q3):** the frozen credential rides the
existing D8 key-delivery channel as an implicit `key` binding — agency
membership check, `injects_secret` arming, and lockstep log redaction all
inherited — while each manifest target's `authKeyEnvVar` becomes the derived
`AMADEUS_KEY_<label>` reference the agent resolves to the delivered 0600 key
file. The secret-injection claim fence now also covers the per-run credential
column (a non-flagged runner leaves such a run queued), and a local-inventory
runner refuses an identity-carrying run (409) rather than silently running as
the wrong identity.

**Authorization (CA-Q1):** picking a stored key requires **Manage Env Vars** —
the shipped V2-11 rule that a reference is a grant over stored key material; a
username alone needs no extra permission. The dialog renders the key dropdown
disabled-with-tooltip without the permission; ansible/terraform run types 422
both fields (identity comes from inventory/toolchain). History's expanded run
view shows a "Connected as" line from the audit envelope.

Tests: overlay/charset units (`execspec`), trigger validation + RBAC gate
(`api`), D8 delivery / claim-fence / local-inventory refusal (`runner`), plus
the schema-version bump. Full backend + frontend suites green; Run dialog
verified in both themes.

## 0.53.6 — Vault settings take effect without a restart

**Date:** Jul 30, 2026

Editing the Vault connection in Settings — configuring it for the first time,
rotating a token or `secret_id`, fixing the address — previously reached only the
per-request surfaces (`/capabilities`, run-detail redaction), because the runner
service, the SSH executor, and the API's secrets service wire their Vault client
**once at construction**. Dispatch kept resolving vault-source secrets with the
stale credentials until a process restart, while the status badge probed the new
stored config and read "ok" — and the documented recovery for a lapsed static
token ("store a fresh one") silently didn't work. Nothing in the UI said a
restart was needed.

**`WireVaultClient` now installs a dynamic client** (`settings/vault.go`): a thin
indirection that resolves the current env-or-DB config through the existing
H4 config-keyed process cache on **every Vault operation** and delegates. An
unchanged config hits the cache and keeps its client, token cache, and single-use
`secret_id` unwrap — the H4 singleton guarantee is untouched — while a changed
config keys a fresh client, so a settings edit takes effect on the next reveal
across every subsystem, first-time setup included. The per-operation cost is two
SQLite point reads ahead of a Vault HTTP round-trip.

Consequences kept honest along the way: `secrets.Service.VaultConfigured` (the
L7 "actually usable" signal) now asks the dynamic client, so it tracks live
config in both directions instead of freezing the construction-time answer; the
stub's error is exported as `secrets.ErrVaultUnavailable` and the dynamic client
fails unconfigured operations with exactly it; and the invalid-hardening-config
error log is deduped per config key so a persistently bad CA bundle logs once,
not once per secret resolution (the build itself is still retried, since the CA
file can be fixed in place). Regression test
`TestVaultConfigChangeReachesWiredServices`: one long-lived wired service
observes unconfigured → configured → rotated, no re-wire, no restart. Full
backend suite green.

## 0.53.5 — A run can borrow a stored reference without editing the job

**Date:** Jul 29, 2026

The Run dialog's "Where it runs" fold gains the counterpart of the job editor's
reference pickers (V2-11, narrowed to stored-reference additions): two dropdowns
that attach an existing Secret, Variable, or SSH Key to **this run only**, beside
the plaintext env overrides that have carried one-off values since F1. The job's
declared bindings render read-only above them — additive only, a run can widen
the injected set but never shrink what the author declared.

**Names ride, values never do.** The trigger records only `{kind, name}` pairs in
the run's `override_json` envelope (the JC12 rule — the envelope is un-redacted
audit metadata). Dispatch reads them back via `runref.OverrideBindings` and unions
them with the declared set at every seam that matters: the SSH executor's stdin
prelude, the runner manifest's Secrets block, the ingest-log redaction dictionary,
and the H2 output-masking pass — so an added secret is resolved, delivered,
audited and masked exactly like a declared one. An added key on an SSH-executor
run is skipped in-band with the same warning a declared key gets (P1.4), and the
dialog says so before the operator commits.

**The gate is the binding gate, not the trigger gate.** Attaching a reference is
a grant over stored secret/key material, so the server requires ManageEnvVars on
the run body (403 without it, audited like every permission denial) — the same
bar as editing a job's declared bindings. Without the permission the dialog keeps
its read-only preflight and shows no pickers; an operator who can merely trigger
cannot route a secret into a one-off run. Additions are validated at the boundary
with the stored-binding rules (422 `invalid_binding` for a bad kind or bare name)
and pre-checked live against the effective scope via the existing
`POST /references/validate`, whose verdict chips now cover added rows too — an
unresolvable addition springs the fold open just like a declared one.

Both `openapi.yaml` copies document the new `references` request field and its
envelope echo; the frontend client is regenerated. `make verify` green;
`tsc -b && vite build` green; embedded dist rebuilt.

## 0.53.4 — A job's SSH key stops hiding in a list of twelve

**Date:** Jul 29, 2026

Two findings from the product owner's read of the expanded views (EV-6): the section ⓘ looked
like a capital I, and the SSH key a job consumes sat as one chip among a dozen
optional variables.

**The ⓘ is a drawn glyph now.** The character was already a lowercase `i` — at
`fontXs`/700 inside a 16px circle its tittle antialiased into the stem at 1x, so
the badge rendered as a solid bar and read as "I". It is a path now (dot plus stem
with a whole-pixel gap, `currentColor` so the muted → primary toggle is unchanged),
which makes it case-correct at any DPI rather than at the sizes that happen to
hint well. One component, so all seven ⓘ across Jobs, Runners and Workflows change
together.

**A job's SSH key is its own field, beside Executor.** It is the field Executor
completes: one says how the job runs, the other what key material the run gets. It
also never belonged in the References list's scope model — `ssh_credentials`
carries no scope column, so a key is agency-filtered rather than scope-filtered
and never gets a resolved-scope pill, while the section around it explains itself
in terms of scope. The list keeps secrets and variables and is titled for them.

**The key picker finally has a source.** The add control fed its datalist from
`/env-secrets` and `/env-vars` and nothing else, so the one kind a job nearly
always wants was the one you typed from memory — and `unknown()` skipped keys, so
a mistyped label got no warning either, only a ✗ after save. Both surfaces read
`/ssh/credentials` now; the promoted field is a single-select over stored labels
that applies on change, since a draft plus a Save button is ceremony around
picking one name.

**Writes preserve the kinds they do not show.** Two surfaces editing one
whole-set endpoint is the one way this split could lose data rather than merely
look wrong, so each write re-reads the set, merges its own kinds over the fresh
copy, and aborts if the re-read fails. A stale in-memory copy would have let a
secrets save silently revert a key assignment made a moment earlier.

**The delivery caveat is stated rather than implied.** Only the runner path
materializes a declared key (D8); the in-app SSH executor skips key references and
says so in-band (P1.4), and in-app SSH auth uses the key on the SSH *host* record,
not the job's binding. The field says which path honours it instead of presenting
every executor as equal — and the first cut of this work gated the field's
visibility on "can this job SSH", which is exactly backwards: it hid the field on
the runner jobs where a declared key works. It is ungated now, which also keeps a
key declarable on every job now that the list below no longer offers the kind.

**A reference row's × is anchored, not pushed.** `marginLeft: auto` put it at the
end of the flex flow, so a verdict reason long enough to wrap — routine in the
narrower key column, where every row states one — carried the × down with it. In a
two-row list the control then sat *between* the rows and read as the neighbour's.
It is absolutely positioned at the row's top-right now, on the line whose reference
it deletes. The reason stays inline rather than being forced onto its own line,
which would have doubled the height of every row in a healthy list. Shared row, so
the secrets list gets the same fix.

Verified in the running app in both themes, and end-to-end against the real
backend: assigning persists, saving a secret keeps the key, removing the key keeps
the secrets, and with two keys and two failing secrets bound, every × measures
inside its own row's band on its own first line. `tsc -b` clean; 508 frontend tests
pass, 7 of them new — the promoted row and its verdict, the caveat appearing only
off the runner path, the field rendering on every job, the picker offering only
unbound labels, both preservation directions asserted on the PUT body, and the ×
anchoring (jsdom cannot measure a wrap, so the screenshot is that one's real
proof).

## 0.53.3 — The Dashboard answers "is everything okay?" in words

**Date:** Jul 29, 2026

The dashboard-update plan (CS-0..CS-6), from the product owner's review of the
Score: the panel's most important fact was rendered at the smallest size on the
page, and ~300px of viewport below it was empty.

**Coincident runs are a chord now, not a numeral.** Seven failed runs sharing a
cluster used to collapse into one 10px notehead with an 11px "7" above it — the
single fact a non-technical viewer must not miss, drawn smaller than anything
else on screen. They now stack: one pip per member, severity-sorted with the
worst on the staff line, sharing a single stem sized by the longest member, the
way notation draws simultaneous notes. Magnitude becomes geometry. Each pip also
keeps its **own** outcome's colour, which fixes something the worst-status rule
(VU-21) hid: a cluster of six successes and one failure used to paint entirely
red — the failure was guaranteed visible but the successes were not. The stack
caps at 8 with a `+k` overflow that folds from the *mildest* end, so an overflow
can never hide a failure. Time is untouched — this changes y, never x, so the
recorded no-jitter decision is not reopened.

**A Current Status section fills the space below.** The Score answers *when*;
nothing answered "is everything okay?" in words, and the resting readout said
*"Hover the timeline"* — so a reader who never hovers got zero sentences from the
whole panel. Two blocks now sit below it, in the order a glance wants them.
**Up next** names the next scheduled run with its zoned time and a relative
delta, and opens Schedules → Upcoming. **Recent errors** folds the failure and
warning feeds per job (a flapping job is one row carrying a count, not seven
identical rows), failures before warnings, each row opening that job's own
History. When there is nothing wrong, it becomes the verdict in plain language:
*"All 13 jobs healthy."*

**The failed-run banner is gone** — a behaviour change worth noting if you look
for it. It named only the *latest* failure and truncated the rest to "+6 more",
which is strictly less than the per-job list now says, so a bad day was
double-red for no added information. Its one unique behaviour — re-showing after
dismissal when a genuinely new failure arrived — has nothing to replace it
because Current Status has no dismissal to recover from; a new failure simply
sorts to the top.

**History gained a `?job=` deep link** to land those rows somewhere useful. It is
applied **server-side** (the endpoint already supported an exact `job` filter —
no backend change), which matters: the free-text search beside it refines the
current page only, so a job whose runs sit past page 1 would have rendered a
confident "No matching runs" while the pager still counted every run in the
system. The filter shows as a clearable chip, because a short table with no
stated reason is the failure mode of arriving pre-filtered.

Verified in the running app in both themes across three states — failures,
all-clear, and arrived-via-deep-link — with the pager reading "1–6 of 6 runs" on
the filtered view, which is the visible proof the filter reached the server.
`tsc -b` clean; 501 frontend tests pass, 17 of them new: the chord's stack order,
per-pip colouring and overflow folding; that the anchor survives the severity
sort (the group's identity key is what hover and the keyboard cursor are held
by); that no banner renders even with failures present; that the next run is
stated exactly once; and that a row navigates to `/runs?job=…`.

**Docs note:** user-manual §5.2 is now stale twice over — it documents the
failed-run banner and the count-numeral collapse the chord replaced. Left for
the next manual-reconciliation pass rather than renumbered here.

## 0.53.2 — The wordmark stops being a picture

**Date:** Jul 29, 2026

Part C of the ux-fixes plan (LG-1..LG-3), from the product owner's report that
switching Dark → Light replaced the sidebar logo with a smaller one. It did —
and the size was only the visible half of it.

**The two marks were different pictures, not differently-styled ones.** Both
themes rendered at the same `width: 158`; nothing in `Shell.tsx` was
theme-conditional except which file to load. The dark asset was 368×335 with its
artwork filling 92% of the canvas; the light one was 676×369 filling 41%. From
identical CSS that drew the light artwork at roughly 65px against the dark one's
146px, in a box 40% shorter. They also disagreed on the tagline — "CONDUCTING
AUTOMATION" versus "CONDUCTING YOUR AUTOMATION" — so toggling the theme on the
login page changed the words as well as the size.

**The collapsed rail was worse, and this one was a real defect (LG-2).** It
cropped to the emblem through a hardcoded window — `width: 55.5, left: -9.1,
top: -1.8` inside a 40×34 box — with a comment recording the source pixels it
was tuned against. That arithmetic belonged to the 368px asset. Applied to the
676px one it resolved to a region wider than the emblem and taller than the
image, so collapsed dark showed the emblem while collapsed light showed the
*entire* logo, wordmark and all, squeezed into 40×34 and unreadable.

**Fixed by deleting the problem rather than re-tuning it.** The request was to
use the dark logo in both themes; that specific mechanism is the one that must
not be taken, because the dark asset's lettering is white and the light rail is
`#ffffff` — the brand would vanish. That exact regression already happened once,
and the comment explaining why sat in `Shell.tsx`. So the *goal* is adopted and
the mechanism is not: the wordmark is no longer baked into a bitmap at all. One
emblem-only asset now serves both themes, and "AMADEUS / CONDUCTING AUTOMATION"
renders as real DOM text in the sidebar's own tokens — which in dark mode makes
the wordmark the brand gold, where before it was flat white.

That fixes the whole class rather than the three symptoms. There is one asset,
so nothing can drift; one size, because it is the same DOM in both themes; one
tagline string, so LG-3 cannot recur; and the crop window is **deleted**, not
retuned, because collapsing now just hides the text. The wordmark is also
themeable, selectable and available to a screen reader for the first time.

The emblem artwork needed no per-theme variant, which was worth checking rather
than assuming: it is a colour badge with dark outlines inside a gold ring, and it
was composited against both rail colours before being adopted. `Login.tsx` ran
the same per-theme switch over the same two assets and now shares the component,
re-toned for a card rather than the rail. Both retired assets are gone from the
frontend (the standalone prototype at the repo root keeps its own copies).

Verified in the running app across all four sidebar states — expanded and
collapsed × dark and light — plus login in both themes, with zero console
errors. `tsc -b` clean; 486 frontend tests pass, four of them new: that exactly
one image renders and it is never the white-lettered asset (the LG-Q1 hazard),
that the wordmark is real text with one canonical tagline, and that collapsing
hides the lettering instead of cropping a bitmap.

Part B of the ux-fixes plan (EV-1..EV-5), from the product owner's report that the
expanded rows on Runners, Jobs and Workflows read as a wall of text. Runners was

copies, an envvars `DetailLabel`, and two diverging `Field` variants. Four of the
five `SectionLabel`s were byte-identical; the fifth had drifted to a different
colour token and margin. Nobody decided that — it was a copy that aged, which is
the whole argument. There is now one `Section` (header, hairline, ⓘ disclosure,
actions slot), one `SectionLabel` (the flat caption, with the optional
right-aligned action the env-var tabs needed), and one `Field`, all in

**Runners' left column reordered (EV-5).** Registration and Managed settings —
the two read-only blocks — move above the four editable controls, so the column
reads "what this runner *is*, then what you can *change*", and the ⚙ Settings

Two things the screenshots caught that neither `tsc` nor the tests could. The
recent-runs table, now in a narrower column, was clipped at the column edge with
no way to reach the cut-off columns — it scrolls now. And the new actions strip,

Workflows where nothing sits to its left; the rule is unchanged but the bar is

## 0.53.0 — The target host a job was pinned to is now the host it runs on

**Date:** Jul 29, 2026

Part A of the ux-fixes plan (TG-1..TG-4), from the product owner's report that jobs
scoped to specific hosts were not honored at run time. They were not. A job
definition can pin a single target host, and that pin was honored on exactly one
of the four paths that can start a run — the one where a human presses Run.

**⚠️ This narrows what scheduled and workflow runs execute on.** If a pinned job's
cron fire or workflow step has been running across a whole scope, it will now run
on the pinned host only. That is what the pin has always claimed to mean, and the
change moves in the safe direction — it shrinks blast radius, never widens it. If
you were relying on the fan-out, the remedy is one edit: clear the job's target
host and it fans out again, deliberately this time. Unpinned jobs are unaffected
on every path.

**A cron fire ignored the pin entirely (TG-1).** `scheduler.fire()` assembled its
enqueue params from the job's name, scope, env, executor and agencies — and not
its target host. The struct had the field; the manual trigger handler was the
only caller in the tree that ever set it. So the run row landed with a NULL
target host and both executors resolved that to "no target", which
`ResolveTargets` reads as *fan out across the entire scope*. A job pinned to one
host ran on every host in its scope, every time its schedule fired. The fix rides
the per-fire job read that was already there for job-level env, so editing a pin
takes effect on the next fire with no scheduler reload — identical freshness
semantics to env.

**Workflow steps had the same hole, by a different route (TG-2).** The workflow
engine builds its own `INSERT INTO runs` rather than going through the scheduler's
params struct, and the column list simply omitted `target_host`. The comment above
that INSERT already warned this is exactly the kind of thing it is easy to miss —
the agency snapshot was missed there once before. It now carries the pin, on the
first attempt and on every WB-R1 retry, and skipped-step rows carry it too so
History shows what the step *would* have targeted.

**Ansible runs ignored the pin even when a human triggered them (TG-3).** For an
ansible run the blast radius is the inventory plus `--limit`, and the manifest
computed `--limit` from the per-trigger override envelope alone. The pin never
reached it. That produced the worst possible split: the SSH executor dialed
exactly the pinned host while the runner shipped the full inventory with no limit
at all — the two-executor drift the execspec module exists to prevent, on a
manual run. Both routes now compute the limit through one new shared
`execspec.RunLimit`, so they cannot disagree. A raw `ansibleLimit` passthrough
still wins outright; otherwise the pin applies.

**The pin wins outright over a host subset, rather than unioning with it** —
because that is what `ResolveTargets` has always done on the SSH side, returning
the single pinned target and ignoring the subset. Unioning would have made
`--limit` *broader* than the set SSH dials, since a comma in an ansible pattern is
a union and not an intersection. That is the same drift in the same dangerous
direction the fix set out to remove, so the two now mirror each other by
construction. In practice the two are never both set — the trigger boundary
clears the pin whenever a subset is supplied — but the limit no longer depends on
that holding.

**And a pin that could not be expressed had to fail loudly, not widen (TG-4).**
`AnsibleLimit` silently refuses any name carrying an ansible pattern
metacharacter — correct for its original inputs, because the trigger boundary
422s those first. But a job's target host had no such boundary: the Composer
accepts free text and Git YAML is arbitrary. Folding the pin into `--limit`
without a guard would have meant a pin like `web[01:50]` getting dropped, leaving
no limit, leaving a full-inventory run — the precise silent widening the fix was
written to remove. Guarded at every boundary that can introduce one: the Compose
endpoint 422s such a job at authoring time, the manual trigger 422s such a target
before a run is enqueued (the same rule its sibling host-subset check has always
enforced, on the field next to it), and the manifest hard-fails the run with a 409
for Git-synced and pre-existing rows that reach neither. Git sync itself only
warns and still writes the row — a bad pin in one file must not wedge a whole
repo's sync — and the 409 is what makes that advisory posture safe.

All three guards deliberately stand down when a raw `ansibleLimit` is supplied:
there the passthrough wins and the pin is never folded in, so there is nothing to
widen, and refusing would have broken the documented escape hatch.

A pin naming a host that has left the scope was already handled and still is: it
surfaces as a per-host resolve error, which is a loud failure, not a quiet
widening.

No migration, no wire-protocol change, no frontend change — every column already
existed and the manifest's `Limit` field is long-standing, so old agents need no
lockstep. Definition-level *multi*-host and group pinning (V2-13 / JC13–15)
remains deliberately out of scope; this closes the runtime gap for the scalar pin
that already existed.

Tests: scheduler fires persist the pin, leave NULL alone, and carry it onto
Forbid skip records; workflow child runs carry it on first attempt and on retry,
and skipped rows too; the limit helper covers pin-alone, pin-over-subset parity,
raw-passthrough precedence, and the metachar case that yields an empty limit; the
manifest ships the pinned limit in both inventory modes, 409s a metachar pin, and
does *not* 409 when a passthrough makes the pin unused; the trigger boundary 422s
a metachar target and enqueues nothing; Compose 422s one on create and update and
writes nothing; a synced job with a bad pin is still written and warns. Full Go
suite passes.

Found by an adversarial review of the fix itself, which is where the union bug,
the missing trigger-boundary guard, and a sync warning sitting on a code path the
sync never executes all came from — each is now fixed and covered by a test that
fails against the version of this change that shipped without it.

## 0.52.38 — A visual sweep, and the loading migration finished properly

**Date:** Jul 29, 2026

A whole-app screenshot sweep across every view Phases A–H touched, in both
themes, driving the app rather than reading the diff. It found three things.

**FX-15 was only half-applied, and I had claimed otherwise.** v0.52.36 said "the
thirteen table-shaped views now reserve their layout". Thirteen was what the
migration script covered — not what the inventory listed. Missing: the three
tables in Users & Access, the alert-rules table, the Dashboard, Publish Builder,
scope Membership, and the five table consumers of History's shared `Loading()`
(Executions, Change Log, Git Sync, Schedule Pushes, Workflow Runs). All now use
`SkeletonRows`. Every remaining site — forms, detail panes, dropdowns, inline
values — is `InlineLoading`. The only bare "Loading…" left in the app is
`App.tsx`'s full-viewport auth gate, which is deliberately its own state.

**One site got the wrong treatment.** The Run Notifications card is a form, and
the regex gave it a table skeleton — five shimmer bars promising rows that were
never coming. It is `InlineLoading` now.

**Verified the way the state actually behaves.** A loading state that lives for
300ms cannot be checked with a screenshot of a loaded page, so the sweep holds
every view-data response for three seconds and photographs what is on screen.
That is also what caught the first run being wrong: delaying *every* API call
stalls `/me`, so the app-level auth gate renders and no view ever mounts —
the probe was measuring App.tsx on all fourteen views. Narrowed to view data
only, every table view shows its skeleton in both themes.

The rest of the sweep was clean, and it was checking for the failure modes a
scripted 30-file edit actually has: **zero console errors** across 28
view/theme combinations, no surviving legacy chevrons (`▸`, `⋯`), and no
`span[onclick]` copy affordances — the FX-13 defect cannot have crept back.
History renders 25 `CopyText` buttons, one per trace id, which is the migration
visible in the aggregate.

No behaviour changed beyond the loading states; 456 frontend tests still pass.
