## 0.52.37 — Fixes Phase H: the workflow-pause authz hole, and a status that finally exists

**Date:** Jul 28, 2026

Phase H of the fixes plan (FX-19, FX-18) — the only backend work in
the plan, and the last of it. Both items were found by grounding Phase B's own
premises against source rather than trusting them. Built to the recommendations
recorded under FX-Q7/FX-Q8.

**Any authenticated user could pause any workflow, in any scope (FX-19).**
`PATCH /workflows/{workflowId}` was `requireSession` + `requireCSRF` and *nothing
else*: no role check, and — the exploitable part — no scope check. Pausing a
workflow suppresses its schedule, so this was a denial of service on someone
else's automation, available to the lowest role and to any scope.

Both its siblings guard. `triggerWorkflow` enforces scope over **every
constituent job** (WB-S1/D1) — a workflow has no scope of its own, so that is the
only correct shape — and `pauseJob`/`resumeJob` enforce `auth.ScopeReadable`
(SU-2, the July security update). This route was missed by both sweeps. That
guard is now extracted as `workflowScopesReadable` and applied to both handlers;
it writes its own failure response and returns a bool, so a handler that forgets
to check the result cannot silently continue.

The regression test is written to fail loudly against the old code, and does:
without the guard a scope-restricted caller pausing an out-of-scope workflow gets
**200 and the `paused_jobs` row is written**. With it: 403, no row, and the
in-scope and unrestricted paths still work.

**A role gate was deliberately not added here.** `TriggerJobs`/`KillJobs` are
enforced on no route today and `/capabilities` does not expose them, so gating
this one route would put the API and the UI on two different sources of truth —
the frontend's `canTriggerJobs` is a hardcoded role list, the backend's is the
DB-driven mapping. That is **FR-M1** (the 2026-07-07 review), which covers
the whole execution surface and is where it belongs (FX-Q8).

**`degraded` is a runner status that now exists (FX-18).** The OpenAPI enum has
always promised it and the UI has always drawn a Degraded tile, but nothing could
produce it: every write is online/offline/draining and the table's CHECK
constraint forbids more, so the tile read 0 forever.

The gap it names is real and was invisible. `last_seen_at` is written on every
long-poll, and the reaper waits `RunnerOfflineAfter` (5m) before calling a runner
offline — so for up to five minutes a runner that had already died read **Online**
in its row, in the tile counts, and to anyone deciding where to send work.
`degraded` is that window: reported once a heartbeat is more than two minutes old
(agents poll once a minute, so two missed polls — late enough not to flag
jitter), and for a runner that registered but never polled or whose heartbeat
will not parse.

**Derived at read time, not stored** (FX-Q7). The stored status is the runner's
*lifecycle*; this is a freshness reading on top of it. Storing it would mean
widening the CHECK constraint — a SQLite table rebuild — *and* teaching the
reaper's `WHERE status IN ('online','draining')` sweep about the new value, or a
degraded runner would never be offlined or deregistered again. One function in
the shared response mapper, revertible in one commit, and no migration. Only
`online` degrades: `draining` is already leaving and `offline` has been reaped.

No spec change — the enum already promised this — and no frontend change: the
Degraded tile, the colour branch and FX-7's `isReachable` were all written for
this in Phase B and light up as they are. Verified end to end in the running app:
a runner stored `online` with a 3-minute-old heartbeat reports `degraded`, the
tile reads 1 for the first time, its stored status is untouched, and its recovery
actions are present exactly as FX-7 intended.

Tests: the scope guard (403 out of scope with nothing written, 200 in scope with
the row written, unrestricted never gated) and the derivation (fresh, just inside
the window, stale, past the offline threshold, never polled, unparseable, and
both non-`online` states left alone), plus one proving the derived value is never
written back. Full Go suite passes.

## 0.52.36 — Fixes Phase G: four vocabularies collapse into four components

**Date:** Jul 28, 2026

Phase G of the fixes plan (FX-13, FX-15, FX-16, FX-17) — the
consistency families, and the last frontend phase in the plan. Four things the
app said four different ways now have one spelling each, held by a component so
they cannot re-drift.

**Copy to clipboard — nine implementations, five styles (FX-13).** The finding
counted seven; the sweep found nine. The user-visible defect was the runner-ID
copy: a bare `<span onClick>` with no role, no tab stop, no keyboard path and —
uniquely — **no feedback at all**, so clicking it told you nothing about whether
it had worked. Three more sites were the same span pattern, and two flashed
"Copied" on a promise they never awaited, so they claimed success even when the
browser rejected the write.

`CopyButton` and `CopyText` replace all nine. Always a real `<button>` with an
accessible name, always an awaited write, always an `aria-live` confirmation, and
they hide themselves when the browser withholds the clipboard API — in a
non-secure context that affordance can only fail. `CopyText` is the sibling for
where the *value* is the affordance (a runner id, a fingerprint), so it stays
monospace and readable while still being one tab stop. Three separate flash
timers (1200/1500/2000ms), two `copied` string-union states, `flashCopied`,
`upgradeCopiedId` and `copyText` are all deleted — the component owns that now.

**Success feedback (FX-16).** The toast was hand-inlined identically in Jobs and
Workflows and the two copies had already drifted — one set `color: c.text`, the
other inherited whatever it landed on. Both now render the shared `Toast`, which
is also `role="status"`. Runners' hand-rolled **success banner** became a toast
too, and its hand-rolled error banner became the shared `AlertBanner`: banners
are for conditions that persist and need dismissing, and "connection verified" is
neither. Six redundant "clear the old success message" calls went with it.

**Loading (FX-15).** `SkeletonRows` existed and was used by 2 of ~20 sites. The
thirteen table-shaped views now reserve their layout instead of popping in and
shifting the page. For the rest — forms, detail panes, inline values — one
`InlineLoading`, because there were eight wordings ("Loading…", "Loading runs…",
"Loading tokens…", "Loading steps…", …) in four paddings and two colours.

**Expand/collapse (FX-17).** Five glyph pairs meant one thing: `▲/▼` on
Workflows, Schedules, Scripts and the workflow-runs table, `▾/▸` on Scopes, `▼/▶`
on the Disclosure fold and the Score, `▾/⋯` on the canvas editor. All now render
`ExpandChevron`. **`▼/▶` wins for a reason rather than by vote:** it is the
disclosure triangle every OS and `<details>` uses, it is what the app's own
`Disclosure` already drew — and it frees `▲/▼`, which the registration-token
table uses for **sort direction**. Two meanings were sharing one pair of arrows.

Deliberately left alone: `TagFilterSelect`'s `▾`, which is a dropdown caret
(`aria-haspopup="listbox"`), not a disclosure — the same glyph a native `<select>`
draws; and the two *text* toggles that carry information a glyph cannot ("+3
more", "Details").

One accessibility catch worth recording: moving the upgrade-command button onto
`CopyButton` initially gave it the accessible name "Copy **the** upgrade command
for runner-a" while its visible label read "Copy upgrade command" — a WCAG 2.5.3
(label in name) violation, where a voice-control user saying what they can see
fails to hit the button. The existing Phase A test caught it. The name is now the
visible label plus the runner it targets, which is also more useful when three of
these are on screen at once.

Tests: 8 new on the copy components — real button with a name, copies, refuses to
claim success on a rejected write, renders nothing with nothing to copy or no
clipboard API, reports to a caller that shows its own notice, and keeps its click
off the clickable row behind it. 456 frontend tests pass. Verified in the running
app in both themes: the runner-ID copy is focusable (`document.activeElement` is a
BUTTON) and flashes its check, and a list view now shows exactly one expand glyph.

## 0.52.35 — Fixes Phase F: Save stops scrolling away, in every modal

**Date:** Jul 28, 2026

Phase F of the fixes plan (FX-10) — the propagation Phase A's FX-6 fix
was always meant to become.

**The defect, once, everywhere.** `Modal` caps its panel at 84vh and scrolls it.
So in every long modal in the app, Save/Cancel — *and the validation error
explaining why Save was disabled* — slid below the fold on a short viewport. The
Jobs run dialog had grown a hand-rolled sticky bar for exactly this; nothing else
had anything.

**`Modal` grew a `footer`, and it is not the sticky bar copied eight times.**
FX-6 found what sticky costs: a bar pinned by its *bottom* edge grows **upward**
over the content once it outgrows the scrollport, which is how the run dialog
ended up painting over its own questions. So with a footer the panel becomes a
flex column and the footer sits **outside** the scrollport entirely — it cannot
overlap anything, however tall either part gets. A modal that passes no footer
renders exactly as it did, so nothing changed by being recompiled.

**Migrated:** the eight sites the finding named (Scopes, Runners ×2, Secrets,
Variables, SSH Keys, Agencies), plus four the sweep turned up that are in the same
defect class — the Vault-migration dialog, the SSH-key result dialog, "Add a
Runner", and the publish confirmation. Each keeps its validation error pinned with
the buttons it explains, because an error you cannot see while the disabled button
is on screen is not doing its job.

**`ConfirmDialog` was a one-line change** that fixes all eleven of its call sites
at once — including the AD-mapping removal shipped in Phase E, whose message names
three separate consequences and is the longest confirm text in the app.

**Two sites needed more than a mechanical move**, and are worth knowing about: the
host-key scan dialog is a two-branch ternary, so its footer is one too (queued vs
form, each with its own action, and the Done button lifted out of a paragraph it
was nested inside); and "Add a Runner" only has a trailing bar once a token has
been minted, so its footer is per-branch rather than a bar that renders empty half
the time.

**Jobs' hand-rolled sticky bar is gone**, replaced by the same prop. That also
closes the residual FX-6 exposure noted when Phase A shipped: the "answers still
missing" warning lists every unfilled input and is unbounded, so inside a sticky
bar a long list could still regrow over the answers. Outside the scrollport it can
only shrink the body — pinned in a way that cannot come back.

Tests: the Modal contract is pinned structurally, which is the form jsdom can check
exactly — the footer is not inside the element that scrolls, the body carries
`minHeight: 0` (without it a flex item refuses to shrink and pushes the footer off
the panel), a footerless modal keeps its old structure, and backdrop-close still
works. The run dialog's layout assertions moved from "has a sticky ancestor" to
"is not in the thing that scrolls" — a stronger property — with a new case proving
twelve missing answers cannot push the action row over the form. 448 frontend
tests pass. Four migrated modals were driven at a 620px viewport in both themes,
where the 84vh cap bites hard: every action row measured fully on screen without
scrolling.

## 0.52.34 — Fixes Phase E: two deletes that never asked, and a button that never worked

**Date:** Jul 28, 2026

Phase E of the fixes plan (FX-9, FX-12).

**Removing an AD group → role mapping now asks first (FX-9).** It fired on the
first click. This is the most consequential delete in the app and it was the only
one with no guard at all — removing an SSH *host* asked for confirmation;
removing the thing that grants Admin did not. The dialog names the group and the
role, and states the two consequences an operator cannot see from the row:

- **Everyone else is signed out.** `DELETE /ad-group-mappings/{id}` calls
  `RevokeOtherSessions` (SU-5) — a role change invalidates existing sessions, so
  every other signed-in operator has to sign in again. Confirming without saying
  so would have been a surprise.
- **The self-lockout path, when it is actually yours.** `/me` already carries the
  caller's AD groups (`auth.Identity.Groups`); the frontend type simply never
  declared them. It does now, so when the mapping being removed is one of the
  caller's own groups the dialog says so — and says it accurately: the current
  session survives (the endpoint keeps the actor logged in), but the next sign-in
  will not grant that role, and if nothing else grants it the action cannot be
  undone. Matched case-insensitively, because AD group names are not
  case-sensitive and the claim's casing belongs to the identity provider.

**Deleting an alert rule now asks first (FX-9).** Also instant, also
irreversible: one click and the thing that tells you a job failed is gone, with
nothing naming what went. The dialog names the rule, its trigger and its
channels, and distinguishes an active rule (something stops being sent) from an
inactive one (nothing was being sent anyway).

**The alert-rule Edit button works on every row it renders (FX-12).** `editing`
compared `editId` — set from `r.id ?? null` — against `r.id ?? ""`, so a rule
without an id could never match: `null === ""` is false, and the button did
nothing, forever. Investigating what an id-less rule *is* answered the question
the finding left open: it is not a real state. `alert_config.id` is the primary
key, `settings.AlertRule.ID` is a non-pointer string so a null would fail the
scan, and the spec marks it `readOnly` — the guard was never exercised, which is
exactly why nobody noticed it was broken. The typed id stays optional, so the
impossible row is now handled by not offering an action that cannot work: editing
keys on the id itself, and a row without one renders no Edit button rather than a
dead one. That is the Phase B house rule from the other side — preconditions
disable with an explanation, and irrelevance hides.

Not in scope, deliberately: converging the app's other three confirmation styles
(`window.confirm`, inline two-step) onto `ConfirmDialog`. That is recorded under
FX-17's family; this phase is only about the two that had nothing.

Tests: both delete flows require confirmation, name what is being deleted, delete
the right thing once confirmed, and leave it alone on cancel; the self-lockout
warning appears for the caller's own group, stays quiet for somebody else's, and
survives a case-only difference; and Edit opens the editor for every rendered
rule while a row that could not be edited offers no button. 443 frontend tests
pass; both dialogs verified in the running app in both themes, including the
self-lockout warning firing on the dev identity's own `amadeus-admins` mapping.

## 0.52.33 — Fixes Phase D: the Score stops smearing near-coincident runs

**Date:** Jul 28, 2026

Phase D of the fixes plan (FX-5), to the recorded decisions: FX-Q4
**clustering only**, FX-Q6 **worst-status notehead + count badge** (the rendering
was already right — this phase changes grouping math and nothing else).

**Why it piled up.** Grouping merged marks only on **exact millisecond equality**.
That caught `0 6 * * *` firing two jobs and nothing else — so runs launched
seconds or minutes apart drew separate noteheads at indistinguishable x and
smeared into each other. Marks now merge by **rendered proximity**: the bucket is
derived from the geometry rather than picked, at one notehead plus its gap (12px),
which on the fixed 36-hour window is ~18.5 minutes. Marks closer together than
that already overlapped on screen; the only question was whether they overlapped
as one honest mark carrying a count or as a smear.

This does not reopen the recorded "no jitter / no beeswarm" decision. That
decision refused to move a mark off its true time to make room; a cluster is drawn
within one notehead-width of every member, so nothing moves further than the width
of the mark itself — and the overlap is removed rather than arranged around.

**A cluster anchors on its earliest member, not its mean.** The plot holds hover
and keyboard selection by `${tense}@${at}`, and the Dashboard rebuilds the marks
array every four seconds — a mean would shift each time a run joined the cluster
and drop the operator's selection mid-poll. Anchoring also leaves a lone mark
exactly where it has always been. The sweep admits members within the bucket of
the *anchor* rather than of the previous member, so a dense train of marks breaks
into bounded clusters instead of chaining into one arbitrarily wide one.

**What this actually fixes, seen rather than argued.** Driving the app with three
bursts of near-coincident runs (4, 3 and 5 jobs launched within ~2 minutes of each
other, two bursts containing a failure): before, 12 separate past noteheads, and
**two of the three bursts rendered green** — the failure inside each was painted
over by a later success, which is precisely the defect grouping exists to prevent
(VU-21), just at a separation exact-instant matching could not see. Playwright
could not even hover the covered marks: *"win-update-check … intercepts pointer
events"*. After, the three bursts are three noteheads carrying counts 3, 4 and 5,
coloured amber, red and red. The mix stays available on hover, where the readout
lists every member.

FullScore's per-job staves get the same clustering — they call the same function.

Tests: nine new on the clustering (merges runs seconds apart; leaves marks beyond
the bucket alone; the distortion bound; no chaining; anchor stability across a
poll; tenses still never merge; worst-status and longest-stem now holding across a
cluster; the `clusterMs: 0` escape hatch; and the constant pinned to its geometry
so it cannot drift into an arbitrary number of minutes). Two older fixtures were
re-based rather than weakened: instants a second and a minute apart were being
used to mean "distinct", and they are now one mark by design — the properties they
tested (nearest-mark resolution reaching a covered neighbour) are re-pinned at a
separation that is still adjacent but genuinely two marks.

**Also fixed, out of scope but caused to matter here:** `Notifications.Transports`
waited for the card title rather than the config fetch, so every assertion about
`lastSent` raced that promise — and the negative assertions passed trivially
whenever the data had not landed. It usually won the race; under this phase's
fuller test run it intermittently did not. It now waits for the readiness marker
the component already exposes. Eight consecutive full-suite runs are clean.

431 frontend tests pass; both themes verified in the running app.

## 0.52.32 — Fixes Phase C: the full score is the Score, expanded

**Date:** Jul 28, 2026

Phase C of the fixes plan (FX-1), built to the two decisions recorded
there: FX-Q1 **replace**, FX-Q5 **shared-shell swap**.

**One panel, two depths.** "Full score" was already an inline toggle rather than a
separate window, but it read as a separate window anyway: the button sat alone in a
right-aligned row *below* the compact Score, and clicking it appended a second,
detached panel underneath. The operator ended up reading one view stacked on
another with the control stranded between them. The control now lives in the
Score's own header, beside the legend, and expanding **replaces** the single lane
with the per-job staves inside the same bordered surface — one view at a time, one
panel, and the header, caption and legend stay put across the swap.

**How it is built matters here.** `Score` and `FullScore` were not merged into one
bimodal component — that was flagged in the plan as the riskiest change available,
two render modes sharing one keyboard and ARIA contract. Instead the panel chrome
(section, header, caption, legend, control) became a thin shell that swaps which
body renders inside it. The compact plot moved into its own `ScorePlot` with every
line intact, `FullScore` is untouched, and neither knows the other exists. The
expansion is opt-in at the call site: pass no `jobNames` and the panel is exactly
what it was, with no control at all.

**Accessibility.** The control carries `aria-expanded`, and when expanded its
accessible name is "Collapse the full score" rather than the bare "Collapse" — the
sidebar has a Collapse button too, and a screen reader listing buttons would have
read the same word twice with nothing to tell them apart. The name still contains
the visible label (WCAG 2.5.3). `Btn` grew `ariaExpanded`/`ariaLabel` props for
this, named after `HoverTr`'s existing pair rather than spreading arbitrary props.
No height animation is involved — whole bodies are swapped — so there is no
reduced-motion question to answer.

Tests: the control is inside the Score region and names its job count; expanding
removes the compact listbox and mounts the staves in the same panel (FX-Q1's
"replace", pinned so a future change back to stacking fails); header and legend
survive both modes; the panel is controlled, reporting the toggle to the Dashboard
rather than holding the state; and no control renders when there is nothing to
expand into. Dashboard's own half — that the job list reaches the staves and the
click round-trips — is covered by rendering the view. All 34 pre-existing Score
tests pass unchanged, which is the evidence the compact path was not disturbed.
421 frontend tests pass; both themes verified in the running app.

---

## 0.52.31 — Fixes Phase B: actions that were offered on the wrong condition

**Date:** Jul 28, 2026

Phase B of the fixes plan — three controls gated on something that was
not their precondition. Frontend only; no backend change (FX-Q2).

**A paused job can always be resumed (FX-2).** Pause is a row in `paused_jobs`,
and nothing about removing a schedule clears it — not the composer, not a
schedule-definition delete, not a GitLab sync; the migration-200 cascade fires only
on job *deletion*. But the whole pause/resume ternary sat behind `isScheduled(j)`,
so the moment a paused job's schedule went away its Resume button went with it. The
job stayed paused, the status badge said so, and the only ways back were re-adding a
schedule, `curl -X POST /jobs/{id}/resume`, or deleting the job. Resume now renders
on `status === "paused"` alone; Pause keeps the schedule gate, which was always
fair for it (pausing a manual-only job suppresses nothing). The backend `resumeJob`
never had a schedule precondition, so this was purely a frontend asymmetry —
verified end to end in the running app: Resume on a scheduleless paused job returns
200, drops the `paused_jobs` row and clears the badge.

**Workflow Pause/Resume is gated like its siblings (FX-8).** Run is gated on
`canRun`, Edit and Delete on compose + source; Pause/Resume had no gate at all. It
now carries `canRun`, matching Jobs. Deliberately *no* source gate: unlike DELETE,
`PATCH /workflows/{id}` has no amadeus-only guard, so a git-sourced workflow really
can be paused in-app and hiding the button would have removed a working action.

**One flag, one word (FX-8).** `w.disabled` rendered as a badge reading
"disabled", a Result pill reading "Paused", and a button reading "Pause"/"Resume",
with a toast saying "Workflow paused" — an operator scanning the row for the state
the button names never found it. The badge now reads Paused, from the same
`jobStatusLabel` source Jobs uses.

**Runner recovery actions no longer hide behind a protocol version (FX-7).**
Resync, Scan keys and Drain were gated on `status === "online"`; they are now gated
on the runner being *reachable* (`online || degraded`) — health is not the
precondition for recovery, and a degraded runner still heartbeats and still holds
work. Offline keeps hiding them: there is no one there to ask. The visible half of
this today is Scan keys, which used to *vanish* below protocol v5 with no
explanation while Resync, on the same bar, disabled itself with a sentence saying
why. Scan keys now does the same. That establishes the house rule the rest of this
plan follows: **a precondition disables with an explanation; only irrelevance
hides.**

One honest caveat on the degraded half: the OpenAPI `Runner.status` enum promises
`degraded`, and the UI has a Degraded tile and colour branch, but no backend path
can currently produce it — every write is online/offline/draining and the table's
CHECK constraint forbids anything else. So that part of the fix is forward-looking
rather than a live repair; the runner status derivation it waits on is noted as a
follow-up in the plan.

Tests: a paused scheduleless job renders Resume and POSTs `/jobs/{id}/resume`; a
scheduled job still gets Pause and only Pause; an unpaused manual-only job gets
neither; a viewer sees no workflow Pause while an operator does; a git-source
workflow keeps it; the disabled flag reads "Paused" in both columns; a degraded
runner keeps all three recovery actions; Scan keys is disabled-with-title rather
than absent below protocol v5; an offline runner still hides them. 414 frontend
tests pass; both themes verified in the running app.

## 0.52.30 — Fixes Phase A: a fold that stopped covering the form

**Date:** Jul 28, 2026

Phase A of the fixes plan — the five items that live in files already
open together. Nothing here reopens the v0.52.13–.24 visual design.

**The run dialog no longer paints over its own questions (FX-6).** "Where it runs"
sat *inside* the pinned commit bar at the bottom of the Run modal. That bar is
opaque and pinned by its **bottom** edge, so the moment the fold opened — scope
picker, preflight, executor, host/group chips, `--limit`, env overrides — the block
grew taller than the modal's 84vh scrollport and its top edge was forced up over
"Answers this run needs". The comment in the source predicted it would "simply
scroll"; sticky doesn't scroll, it clips and occludes. The fold now sits in normal
flow directly under the answers, and the pinned bar keeps only what belongs pinned:
the run error, the missing-answers warning and Cancel/Run. The collapsed summary
still states scope and executor, so the one fact a collapse must never hide is
still never hidden.

**Run logs can be copied (FX-3).** A copy button overlays the log body — the
clipboard glyph already used by the trace-id copies in the same rows, flipping to a
green ✓ Copied for a second and a half. All four log surfaces (Jobs, Runners,
Workflow steps, History → Executions) render one shared `RunLog`, so all four
gained it at once. It hides itself when there is no log to copy, and when the
browser withholds the clipboard API — a button that can only fail is worse than no
button.

**An expanded log is no longer trapped in a shorter box (FX-11).** The recent-runs
list caps itself at 340px and scrolls; the log inside it is 400px tall. Expanding a
run therefore nested one scrollport inside a shorter one — double scrollbars, the
clicked row shoved out of view by its own expansion, and the sticky column header
painting over the top of the log. The cap (and the sticky header with it) now
applies to the collapsed list only: a log you deliberately opened is the thing you
came to read, so the container grows to it.

**'Copy upgrade command' moved up into the runner action bar (FX-4)**, beside
⚙ Settings / Resync / Scan keys / Drain, instead of sitting below the fold in the
version section. It stays offered whatever the version badge says — it is also the
reinstall command, and `behind` compares version *strings*, so a locally-built agent
reads "up to date" while speaking an older protocol. The version section keeps the
version string and the "Upgrade available" badge and now points at the button.

**Runner detail states its registration facts once (FX-14).** Registered/Protocol
were rendered twice under different labels ("Protocol" + "Registered" in the field
grid, "Protocol version" + "Registered at" under Registration), reading as two
separate facts. The Registration section is the surviving copy — it is where the
token that created the runner already is.

## 0.52.29 — Vault token auth actually works

**Date:** Jul 28, 2026

Adding a HashiCorp Vault with **Auth Method = token** failed with a 500:

```
upsert vault_config: NOT NULL constraint failed: vault_config.role_id
```

`vault_config.role_id` is `NOT NULL DEFAULT ''` (migration 060), and token auth
supplies no Role ID — so the upsert bound a nil `*string`. A column DEFAULT does
not apply when a value is given explicitly, and `NULL` is a value, so the very
first save under token auth always failed. It is now bound as a string.

That was the crash. Behind it, token auth was **enum-only**: the API accepted it,
the DB stored it, the spec advertised it, and nothing read it. The client logged
in with AppRole unconditionally, `ResolveVaultRuntime` refused to wire anything
without a role_id, and the status badge demanded both AppRole halves — so a
token-auth deployment that got past the 500 would have sat at "Not configured"
with every reveal failing. Token auth is now wired end to end:

- `secrets.VaultOptions.AuthMethod` — under `token`, the stored credential *is*
  the Vault token: presented as `X-Vault-Token` directly, with no
  `auth/approle/login` call. Static tokens are not renewed; when one lapses Vault
  answers 403 and the operator stores a new one.
- `ResolveVaultRuntime` returns a `VaultRuntime` (addr, auth method, credentials)
  and resolves per method. Env `AMADEUS_VAULT_*` still wins and is always AppRole.
- One `vaultCredsComplete` shared by the status badge and the client wiring, so
  the badge cannot read "ok" while the client is still a stub.
- Response-wrapped credentials stay AppRole-only; pairing them with token auth is
  refused at construction rather than sending a single-use wrapping token as
  `X-Vault-Token` and 403ing on every read with nothing to explain why.

**Switching auth method now clears the stored credential.** An AppRole secret_id
is not a Vault token; carrying one across a switch built a client that failed
every read. The switch requires the new credential, and the UI says so — the
write-only field is now labelled **Token** or **Secret ID** to match the selected
method, and its placeholder distinguishes set from unset.

Spec: `roleIdSet` / `secretIdSet` were returned by the API but undeclared, so the
generated frontend types lacked them; both are declared now, and `secretId` says
what it carries under each auth method.

## 0.52.28 — Scaffolding out, strict build back

**Date:** Jul 28, 2026

Closes the deploy incident. A deploy came up with no `/build-error.txt`, meaning
the in-image build ran and the container is serving a bundle built from source —
so the v0.52.26 diagnostic scaffolding has done its job and is gone.

Removed: the fallback `COPY backend/web/dist /repo/backend/web/dist-committed`,
the failure branch that swapped in the committed dist and wrote the build log to
`dist/build-error.txt`, and the `.dockerignore` exemption that made the committed
dist available. `backend/web/dist` is excluded from the build context again, so
the image can once more only ever embed a bundle built from source HEAD (B.1).

Stage 1 is now a plain `RUN mkdir -p /repo/backend/web && npx vite build`.

**Kept:** `vite build` instead of `npm run build` (v0.52.27) — that was the fix,
not the scaffolding. Type-checking stays a source gate, in the local build and in
CI, where a type error should fail. The Dockerfile comment records why, including
the orphan file that made the difference matter.

**Findable if needed:** the fallback and the log-to-a-URL trick live in git at
`a8c594e`, and the Dockerfile says so at the site. `git show a8c594e` has both
halves. That was the only channel that worked in an environment with no CI, no
host shell, and a deploy tool that shows an exit code but not the output behind
it — worth not having to reinvent.

### Still open, unrelated to the build

The deploy checkout still contains a file git deleted in v0.41.6. Nothing breaks
today, because an unimported stray file cannot fail `vite build` or enter the
bundle — but a stale file that *is* imported would be bundled silently, which is
a worse failure than the one this incident produced. And
`AMADEUS_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_GROUP` is unset in the deploy environment.

## 0.52.27 — Type-checking leaves the image build

**Date:** Jul 28, 2026

The root cause of the v0.52.25 deploy failure, found by the scaffolding added in
v0.52.26, and the fix.

### The cause: an orphan file from v0.41.6

The deploy host's checkout still contained
`frontend/src/views/envvars/ScopesTab.tsx` — **deleted from git in `b384ad2`
(v0.41.6)**, when Scopes was promoted to its own top-level page. Eleven minor
versions ago. It is in no clean checkout, which is why the build passed from a
fresh clone, in a replica of the Docker stage's exact filesystem, and locally.

It never mattered because `vite build` only bundles what the entry reaches, so an
unimported file is invisible to it. But the image ran **`npm run build`**, which
is `tsc -b && vite build` — and `tsc -b` type-checks **every file under `src/`**,
imported or not.

The orphan passes a scope id into `/scopes/{scopeId}`. That parameter was declared
`integer` in `openapi.yaml`, so `number` matched and the file compiled for eleven
versions. **K-3 (v0.52.24) corrected it to `string`**, because scope ids are
UUIDv7 — and a file nothing imports failed the deploy with seven type errors.

Also worth recording: `tsc -b` exits **1** on diagnostics, where plain `tsc`
exits 2. That cost a wrong inference along the way — exit 1 was read as "the
failure is in vite, not the type-check", when it was the type-check all along.

### The fix

Stage 1 runs **`npx vite build`** instead of `npm run build`. Type-checking is a
source gate: it belongs where a type error should fail — locally and in CI — not
in an image build. `npm run build` is unchanged for those.

Verified both directions with the orphan file restored: `npm run build` → exit 1,
`vite build` → exit 0 with the orphan contributing **zero bytes** to the bundle.
Dropping the type-check also takes ~700 MB of peak RSS and ~14 s off the image
build.

**This does not make a dirty deploy checkout safe.** A stale file that *is*
imported would still be bundled, shipping old code silently. The checkout should
still be cleaned; this only stops an unimported leftover from breaking a deploy.

### Also — the fallback marker now says when it was written

`dist/build-error.txt` records the image-build timestamp and says what it means
if that timestamp predates your last deploy: the image was **not** rebuilt and
nothing re-ran. Bringing a stack down and up does not rebuild an image whose
source has not changed, and an unchanged marker file reads exactly like a
repeated failure.

### Still temporary

The v0.52.26 fallback scaffolding stays until a deploy comes up with no
`/build-error.txt`. Removing it: restore
`RUN mkdir -p /repo/backend/web && npx vite build`, drop the `dist-committed`
COPY, and re-add `backend/web/dist` to `.dockerignore`.

---

## 0.52.26 — A deploy that can tell you why it broke

**Date:** Jul 28, 2026

Not a feature. Temporary scaffolding in `backend/Dockerfile` so a failing
frontend build stops being a dead end.

### The problem

Deploying v0.52.25 failed at stage 1 with `exit code: 1` and **no way to see
why**: the deploy tool surfaces only BuildKit's summary — the Dockerfile context
and the exit code — not the failing step's output. There is no CI pipeline
(`backend/.gitlab-ci.yml` exists but sits outside the root where GitLab looks for
it, and no pipeline has run), and no shell access to the docker host. So the one
artifact that would name the cause was the one thing unreachable.

Everything checkable from outside the container was checked and cleared:

- a clean clone of `main` builds — `npm ci && npm run build`, exit 0;
- a **replica of stage 1's exact filesystem** — only the paths the Dockerfile
  COPYs, nothing else — builds, exit 0;
- the lockfile carries all 25 rollup and 23 esbuild platform binaries, so a
  missing native binding is not it;
- `.dockerignore`'s `index.html` / `*.js` entries are root-anchored and aim at
  the real root-level prototype files, so nothing under `frontend/` is stripped;
- the deploy did build the merge commit (pushed 19:11:11 UTC, deploy 19:13:19);
- and it is **not** memory: a node heap OOM exits 134, a cgroup kill 137.

That last check also narrows the stage: `npm` propagates exit codes verbatim
(verified), `tsc` exits **2** on type errors and `vite build` exits **1** — so
the failure is inside `vite build`, not the type-check.

### The change

Stage 1 now builds as before, and on failure:

- falls back to the dist committed at `backend/web/dist`, so the image builds and
  the container comes up working;
- writes the build log to `dist/build-error.txt`, which the SPA handler serves —
  **the error becomes readable at `/build-error.txt` in a browser.**

`.dockerignore` had to stop excluding `backend/web/dist` for the fallback to
exist. Both branches were verified by extracting the real `RUN` body and
executing it: success embeds the fresh dist and leaves no marker file; failure
leaves the committed dist plus the log, and the layer exits 0 either way.

### What to know while it is in place

**The fallback can serve a dist older than source HEAD** — the trade this makes
against B.1's "never ship a stale dist". The presence of `/build-error.txt` is
the only signal that it happened, so check for it after a deploy. It is currently
byte-identical to a fresh build of this commit.

**That file is as public as the SPA is** — the same unauthenticated static
handler serves it. A vite log carries file paths, not secrets, but it should not
outlive the investigation.

### Removing it

Restore `RUN mkdir -p /repo/backend/web && npm run build`, drop the
`dist-committed` COPY, and re-add `backend/web/dist` to `.dockerignore`. The
Dockerfile comment says the same thing at the site.

### Not changed

The manuals still say **v0.52.25**. Nothing an operator can see changed, and
bumping a version line the app does not reflect would be noise.

---

## 0.52.25 — A button that answers "can this reach anyone?" (visual update, Phase K-5)

**Date:** Jul 28, 2026

The gap v0.52.24 exposed and could not close from the inside. Phase K moved the
per-transport "last sent" signal onto the transports that actually send — but it
only fills in after a real run fails, so an operator configuring notifications
had no way to find out whether their SMTP relay or Apprise gateway worked without
waiting for something to break. Verifying that release needed a throwaway helper
to stamp the columns by hand, which was the tell.

`tsc` clean, **396 frontend tests across 39 files**, `make verify` green.

### Added — Send test

A button beside **Save Changes** on Settings → Notifications.
`POST /settings/notifications/test` delivers a fixed message over every
configured transport and returns what happened to each one.

**Three states, not two.** `sent`, `failed`, and **`not attempted`** — with the
reason. On a half-configured install the third is the answer most of the time
(*"No SMTP host is configured"*, *"Apprise is switched off"*, *"No Apprise
targets are configured"*), and it tells the operator what to fix where a bare
failure does not. This is why the response is a per-transport list rather than
one verdict.

**Parameterless on purpose.** Every recipient, gateway and target comes from
stored settings; the request carries nothing. The endpoint cannot be used to mail
an arbitrary address by anyone who reaches it, and the Apprise leg goes through
the same SSRF-guarded client as a real dispatch, so it grants no egress an
operator did not already have. `configureApp` + CSRF, and audited — "who sent the
3am test mail" is a question someone will ask.

**200 whenever the attempt was made.** A refused SMTP connection is a true
answer to the operator's question, not a server error; only a failure to *read*
the config is a 500.

**A test does not borrow an alert rule's recipients.** Email goes to the default
recipients on the notification config and nowhere else. If there are none, the
transport is skipped even with a working SMTP host — a rule naming someone must
not cause a test click to mail them.

**A successful test stamps `lastSent`**, and the card re-reads the config so the
line updates in place. That field answers "when did this transport last reach
anyone", and a test is a real answer; a successful test that left the line empty
would be the confusing outcome.

### Changed — the last-sent line got a neighbour, so it got a label

Driving the button showed the two lines sitting adjacent and both starting
*"Email —"*, reading as a contradiction when one said *sent 6:56 PM* and the
other *failed*. The report now sits under a **TEST SEND** heading: one is the
transport's history, the other is the attempt you just made.

### Note — verified against a real receiver

Not only mocks. A throwaway SMTP sink on `127.0.0.1:2525` received the actual
message with the right From, To, Subject and body; the run after the sink was
gone produced the failure path in the real UI with the real error
(`dial tcp 127.0.0.1:2525: connect: connection refused`). Both outcomes were seen
on screen in both themes.

### Known — two things it does not do

No rate limiting: it is admin-only, one click is one message, and the button
disables itself in flight. And no per-transport selection — it tests everything
configured, because an operator asking "does this work" rarely means "does
exactly one leg work".

---

## 0.52.24 — One address book, and ids that admit what they are (visual update, Phase K)

**Date:** Jul 28, 2026

Phase K of the visual-update-followups plan — VF-16 and VF-17, both
found while shipping Phase J. Same move twice: delete or correct a thing that
lies.

`tsc` clean, **392 frontend tests across 39 files**, `make verify` green, driven
against a fresh database.

### Removed — the Alert Destinations section, which routed nothing

It had full CRUD, four endpoints, and a UI offering Webhook / Email / In-App
destinations with URLs and enable toggles. **No code ever read it to deliver
anything.** Routing came from `notification_config` — the SMTP relay and the
Apprise target list — plus each rule's `channels`. The only read stamped
`last_fired_at` on *every* enabled destination of a matching type whenever any
rule sent, so the "last fired" signal an operator read as *this destination
delivered* only ever meant *something delivered over this transport*.

So the app had three address books and two of them delivered. Deleting the one
that didn't is the smallest change that ends the ambiguity.

**Not deleted:** the `alert_destinations` table, migration 004, and
`alert_config.destination_id`'s foreign key. That FK is what the
rules-target-destinations design was for — it was specced into the schema and
never finished — and building it properly is a feature (a join table, plus
webhook and in-app transports that do not exist) rather than a cleanup. The data
survives, the seed still populates it with a comment saying why, and the design
is not foreclosed.

### Added — "last sent", per transport, where it is true

Migration **740** puts `last_email_at`/`last_apprise_at` and their statuses on
the `notification_config` singleton, and the Run Notifications card reads
*"Email — sent 7/28/2026, 10:00 AM"* against the transport that actually sent.

Three details worth keeping. **"Never" is absent rather than blank** — an
operator asking why an alert did not arrive needs to tell "nothing has ever
sent" from "the last send failed", so a failure is red and says so. **No
backfill**: mapping a per-destination stamp onto a transport means deciding
which destination "won" a send, and inventing history is worse than a field that
fills in on the next dispatch. **`markTransport` upserts** rather than updates,
because an install that has never opened Settings has no config row and can
still have sent — an Apprise gateway configured by `AMADEUS_APPRISE_URL` alone
needs no row at all.

### Fixed — ids that claimed to be integers

`openapi.yaml` declared `id: { type: integer }` on fifteen schemas. **Seven
return a UUIDv7 string** — `Scope`, `EnvVar`, `EnvSecret`, `SshHost`,
`SshBastion`, `AlertRule`, `AdGroupMapping`: every settings-family entity, since
those endpoints shipped. The other eight are genuinely integers (`Job` → `11`,
`ActivityEntry` → `67`, rowid-keyed tables) and were left alone. This is a
correction, not a sweep.

It was **three copies of the same lie**, and fixing one would have fixed
nothing:

1. The schema declarations.
2. The **reusable path parameters** — `scopeId`, `envVarId`, `secretId`,
   `alertId`, `hostId`, `bastionId`, `mappingId` all `type: integer`, so every
   `DELETE /scopes/{scopeId}` passed a string into a number-typed slot.
3. **Hand-written local interfaces** — `EnvVarRow`, `EnvSecretRow` and
   `ScopeRow` restated `id?: number` in TypeScript, independent of codegen.

Correcting them surfaced 29 type errors across six files, which is the point:
every one was a place that had been told an id was a number. Including a
`Record<number, string>` keyed by secret id, and a test asserting
`scopeId).toBe(1)` — a fixture faithfully reproducing the defect, which is the
best evidence that nobody had read the declaration as a claim.

Harmless at runtime today, because JS compares two identical strings happily.
The `?? -1` idiom at six call sites is what a `number` declaration on a UUID
talks people into.

### Added — the guard, again the durable part

`TestIdTypesMatchTheSpec` seeds a test server, GETs ten collections, and asserts
the JSON type of `items[0].id` matches what the spec declares. It probes the wire
rather than reflecting over Go types, because the wire is what a client sees and
what the generated frontend types are built from.

It lists the **integer** schemas alongside the string ones, so it cannot be
satisfied by turning everything into a string, and it fails on an empty
collection rather than passing vacuously. Verified to fail on the regression:
reverting `Scope.id` produces *"Scope.id is declared "integer" in openapi.yaml
but /scopes returns string."*

### Note — a guard from months ago earned its keep

Removing the four destination handlers without removing their two spec paths
fails `TestSpecRouteConformance`, which asserts every spec operation has a route.
That is why this could not be a UI-only deletion — and it is the same shape as
the two guards added in v0.52.23 and here.

### Known — one gap this work exposed

There is **no "send a test notification" button**. Seeing the populated
last-sent line in the real app required stamping the columns with a throwaway
helper. An operator debugging "why did no alert arrive?" has the same problem,
and now has a signal that only fills in after a real run fails.

*Closed in 0.52.25.*

---

## 0.52.23 — Every Notifications control does something (visual update, Phase J)

**Date:** Jul 28, 2026

Phase J of the visual-update-followups plan, and the one that should
not have been needed. Phase F2 established a rule — *every control on the
Settings pages does something* — by auditing the two files a finding had named.
This is what was on the page nobody opened.

`tsc` clean, **382 frontend tests across 37 files**, `make verify` green.

### Fixed — five controls that collected input and threw it away

Settings → Notifications' alert-rule form offered five things the dispatcher had
no branch for. Each one persisted, listed, and produced nothing:

- **By Tag** targeting — `targetMatches` returns `false` for it, and `job_tags`
  was never even selected by the dispatcher's query.
- **N failures in window**, with its count and window inputs — `triggerMatches`
  compares the trigger against a run's *terminal status*, so a literal
  `n-failures-window` could never match. Nothing implemented a window.
- **Slack**, **Webhook** and **In-App** channels — three of the four offered.
  The dispatcher only ever spoke `email`/`smtp` and `push`/`apprise`.
- **"Also notify the user who started the run"** — stored, never read.

This is worse than the settings VF-2 found in v0.52.19. An unenforced session
timeout can be discovered by testing whether your session locks; a notification
rule that matches nothing is invisible from inside the product. There is no log
line, no error, and no destination stamp — the absence of an alert looks exactly
like the absence of a failure. In the demo seed, **three of four rules were in
this state.**

### Added — Apprise is selectable on a rule for the first time

The removal that adds a capability. Slack and Webhook were never missing
features, they were duplicates: Apprise already fans one event out to Slack,
Discord and webhooks, and the app configures it two panels up the same page. The
channel list is now the one the notifier actually speaks — **Email** and
**Apprise** — which means the working non-email transport finally appears on a
rule.

### Fixed — a stored trigger is no longer eaten on save

`ruleToForm` assigned the stored trigger straight into the form. When that value
was not one the dropdown offered, the `<select>` matched no option and pressing
**Save** silently rewrote the rule to *Job fails*. The seeded `backup-warnings`
rule stores `warning`, which is real and does fire, so this was live data loss.
An unoffered value now keeps its own option and round-trips.

The dropdown still offers only *Job fails* and *Job succeeds*. Widening what an
operator can create is a capability decision, deliberately not taken here —
`warning`, `killed`, `skipped` and `any` all work and remain API-only.

### Fixed — the API refuses inert rules too, not just the UI

Narrowing a form does not narrow a contract. `POST /alerts` accepted every one
of the removed values, so a script, a curl, or an old bundle in a cached tab
could still create a rule that never fired. The removed values now return
**422** with a code naming the field (`invalid_target_mode`, `invalid_trigger`,
`invalid_channel`) and a message pointing at what to use instead.

### Changed — the contract says what is true

`AlertRuleInput`'s enums are narrowed to what the dispatcher honours, and its
`trigger` enum is **corrected rather than trimmed**: it claimed
`[failure, success, n-failures-window]` while `triggerMatches` matched any
terminal run status plus `any`. It now lists the real vocabulary.

`AlertRule` — the response — stops inheriting those enums and declares tolerant
`targetMode` and `channels` strings instead. **Read is deliberately laxer than
write**, which is why narrowing the contract needed no migration: rules stored
before this release still validate, and the rule table marks a dead channel
**struck through** so an operator can see which rules to re-point.

`jobTags`, `triggerCount`, `triggerWindow` and `notifyTriggerer` stay in the
spec and in the database, marked `deprecated` — v0.52.19's precedent: an unused
optional field breaks no client, and removing one costs both byte-identical spec
copies plus a regeneration for no gain.

### Fixed — one false sentence

The In-App destination type claimed *"In-app notifications are delivered to all
active sessions. No additional configuration required."* No in-app delivery path
exists anywhere in the backend. It now says so, and points at the two transports
that work.

### Added — the guard, which is the durable part

`TestAlertEnumsAreHonoured` reads `openapi.yaml` and asserts that **every value
`AlertRuleInput` accepts has a live branch in the dispatcher** — and the
converse, that behaviour the dispatcher honours is reachable from the API. Both
directions matter: the first is the original defect, and the second is how
Apprise stayed unselectable while working perfectly.

Verified to fail on the regression it exists to catch: re-adding `tag` to the
spec enum produces *"openapi.yaml accepts targetMode "tag" but
notify.targetMatches has no branch for it."* The guard also self-checks, so
deleting the enums cannot make it pass vacuously.

The dispatcher's inline channel switch became `channelTransport`, so validation,
the guard and delivery cannot disagree about what a channel means. An unknown
channel on a legacy rule now logs a warning instead of being skipped in silence.

### Changed — demo data that shows the product working

`seed.go` seeded `target_mode = "scope"` and the slack/in-app/webhook channels,
so three of its four rules demonstrated the defect. Every seeded rule would now
genuinely fire. `backup-warnings` keeps its `warning` trigger on purpose: it is
the fixture for the round-trip fix above.

### Known — two things left open on purpose

- **The Alert Destinations section routes nothing.** It has full CRUD and a UI
  offering Webhook / Email / In-App destinations, and no code reads it to
  deliver anything; the only read stamps `last_fired_at` on every enabled
  destination of a matching type whenever *any* rule sends. Either it becomes
  the routing table it looks like, or it goes — both are design work, tracked as
  **VF-16**.
- **`openapi.yaml` declares `AlertRule.id` as `integer`;** it is a UUID string,
  and the frontend's `editId` is typed `number | null` on the strength of it.
  Harmless at runtime, wrong on paper. Tracked as **VF-17**.

## 0.52.22 — A button that leads somewhere, and a question answered (visual update, Phase I)

**Date:** Jul 28, 2026

Phase I of the visual-update-followups plan — the last one, and the
smallest. One page disagreeing with itself, and a question that had been open
since the visual update began.

`tsc` clean, **382 tests across 37 files**.

### Fixed — a primary button that led to a refusal

Jobs and Workflows both gated their empty-state "Create a job" / "Create a
workflow" on the **Compose** capability, and left the toolbar's `+ Create`
ungated — so one page said two different things about who may author, and a
Viewer got a primary-styled button leading straight to the composer's "requires
the Compose capability" notice. Both are gated now, matching **Schedules**, which
has always done this.

### Answered — production has no egress to fonts.googleapis.com

Open since the original plan (VU-Q7, then VF-14). The answer is the unlucky one:
**there is no egress**, so before v0.52.13 the console rendered in the browser's
default sans, in production, for its entire life — with nothing anywhere to say
so. Self-hosting the fonts in Phase A fixed a live defect rather than removing a
precautionary dependency, and Phase C's type scale was the first time the
intended type system had actually been on screen.

Since the answer alone changes nothing, the failure mode became a test. The docs
drift-guard covered `documentation/*.html` and **not `frontend/index.html`** —
the file the original defect was in, protected only by a sentence in AGENTS.md.
It is guarded now, in both directions: no font CDN, and the self-hosted
`@font-face` declarations must still be present, so "fixing" it by deleting the
fonts fails too.

Verified by measurement rather than assertion: ten routes driven in a real
browser — the login page, seven views, both manuals and a wrapped runner guide —
requested **zero external origins**.

### Not done — the casing drift (I-2)

Deliberate, on the plan's own recommendation and the audit's. Most of it is
invisible because those labels are uppercased in CSS. Recorded so it reads as a
decision rather than an oversight.

## 0.52.21 — The Score is reachable, and motion is finally opt-in (visual update, Phase H)

**Date:** Jul 28, 2026

Phase H of the visual-update-followups plan — the two gaps the
keyboard and motion work of Phase D left behind. Both were half-finished in the
same way: the mechanism shipped, the part that tells assistive tech or the
operating system about it did not.

`tsc` clean, **379 tests across 37 files**, and both halves driven in a real
browser — the roles read out of the live DOM, the motion rule checked under an
emulated `prefers-reduced-motion` in both states.

### Fixed — the Score's marks were a mouse-only affordance

D-5 built a real keyboard contract (one tab stop, arrows step, Home/End jump,
Escape clears) and nothing announced it. The plot was `role="group"` — not a
widget role, so a screen reader had no reason to say the arrow keys did
anything — and each notehead was a bare `div` with an `onClick`, no role and no
name.

The plot is a **listbox** now and every mark an **option** with an accessible
name: *"nightly-backup, Success, ran Jul 28, 16:00"*. The name is built from the
same `statusLabel` and the same zoned stamp the visible readout uses, so the two
cannot drift apart, and a coincident group announces its count and its **worst**
outcome — the colour the mark is already painted.

`aria-activedescendant` tracks the **keyboard cursor**, deliberately not the
hover: pointing it at whatever the mouse is over would narrate forty runs to
someone sweeping the plot.

### Fixed — reduced motion stopped at the keyframes

`prefers-reduced-motion` covered the two `@keyframes` and nothing else. Every
transition in the app is an *inline* style — a chevron rotating 180°, a settings
toggle's knob sliding, a Dashboard tile lifting — which is precisely the
transform-based motion the preference exists for, and it all kept running.

One stylesheet rule now neutralises transitions and animations under `reduce`.
It needs `!important` to do it, because that is the only way a sheet beats an
inline style — and one rule no future component can forget to opt into is worth
more than four that each have to remember. Near-zero rather than `none`, so
`transitionend` still fires for anything sequencing on it.

**The one case CSS cannot reach** is a scroll requested from JavaScript:
`scrollIntoView({behavior:"smooth"})` passes the behaviour as an argument, and an
argument beats the property. Runners' token highlight — the app's only
smooth-scroll call — now asks first via `utils/motion.ts`, and jumps instead. It
still scrolls: reduced motion removes the animation, never the navigation.

## 0.52.20 — One word per concept (visual update, Phase G)

**Date:** Jul 28, 2026

Phase G of the visual-update-followups plan — the vocabulary pass, and
the guard that stops it regrowing. Every item is one screen agreeing with itself
and disagreeing with the next screen over.

`tsc` clean, **364 tests across 36 files**, backend green, every changed surface
driven in the app, and a raw-wire-value sweep across nine routes returning
nothing.

### Changed — the ten contradictions

Each of these was two words for one thing. The winner is in bold; the losing word
was in the product.

- **Paused** — a Jobs row said `⏸ paused` in Schedule and **Paused** in Status.
- **Success** — the Jobs status tab said **Healthy** where Workflows' said Success.
- **Result** — Workflow Runs was the only run surface that called the outcome
  *Status*, in both its column and its filter.
- **"Run queued"** — one `▶ Run` button produced two different sentences,
  "Run queued" on Jobs and "Workflow triggered" on Workflows.
- **When** — Notifications used *Trigger* as a noun for a rule's condition, in an
  app where "trigger" is the verb for starting a run. The column holds a *when*:
  "Job fails".
- **Pause / Resume** — Workflows said Enable/Disable for a state its own badge
  called **Paused**, and which is stored in the same `paused_jobs` table a job's
  pause is. Dropping `▶` from Resume leaves the play glyph meaning "run now".
- **Kill run / Cancel run** — a destructive action now names its object, so the
  bare **Cancel** stays what every modal means by it.
- **History** — Activity's empty state offered "Open run history" for a
  destination whose nav item and page title are History.
- **Waiting because** — a Jobs field labelled **Queued** (a *state*) held a
  *reason*, and printed `runner_lost` raw. `RecentRuns` had the same raw reason,
  missed when E-3 fixed its twin.
- **SSH · Runner · Local inventory · Cronomicon inventory · Not configured** — five
  raw wire values on screen, each with a tooltip beside it already spelling the
  word properly.

One more turned up while re-running the audit by hand: a notification rule's
trigger fell back to the raw value, so a seeded rule that genuinely fires read
`warning` in a column where the rest of the app says **Warn**.

### Fixed — reference errors named a database table

`no SSH key **credential** named "x" exists` — surfaced verbatim in the References
editor and the Run dialog's preflight. "Credential" is the `ssh_credentials`
table's name leaking into a sentence an operator reads; the UI's word is **SSH
key**, and the message now takes it from the same function every other reference
error uses.

### Changed — "Write Branch" is now "Working Branch"

It governs sync **reads** as much as schedule writes, so the old label named half
of what the setting does — an operator had no reason to think changing it would
re-point where definitions are read from. Both the app and the user manual.

### Added — a drift guard for the status vocabulary

The reason the list above exists is that these words were typed rather than
produced. `status-vocabulary.test.ts` fails if a string literal's entire value is
one of the canonical labels — `statusLabel` and `jobStatusLabel` are the only
things allowed to turn a wire status into a word.

It is deliberately narrow: case-sensitive, so wire values (`status === "paused"`)
stay legal, with one case-insensitive exception behind a leading glyph, because
`"⏸ paused"` is exactly the drift that shipped. Its own word list is derived from
the canonical functions rather than retyped — a hand-written list would be this
file's own defect, one level up.

## 0.52.19 — Every control on the Settings pages does something (visual update, Phase F2)

**Date:** Jul 28, 2026

Phase F2 of the visual-update-followups plan — the two decisions
recorded on 2026-07-28, plus the one item that turned out to need a migration.
Five settings accepted input and enforced nothing. Four are gone; the fifth
guarded a feature that genuinely works, so it got the join it was missing.

`make verify` green, **361 frontend tests across 35 files**, and F2-3 driven
end-to-end in the real binary rather than only in tests.

### Fixed — the GitLab webhook flags now decide whether a delivery is acted on

**Webhook Enabled** and **Webhook Events** were parsed, persisted and shown in
Settings → Integrations, and read by nothing: the handler validated its token and
synced whatever they said. They now govern delivery. Disabled → **403**, with the
reason named, because GitLab's own hook log is where an operator debugging "why
did my push not sync" looks. An event whose flag is off → **202 and no sync** —
the delivery is not an error, it is simply not one we react to. The token is
validated first, so a 403 is unreachable without the secret.

**This needed a migration, and that is the part worth reading.** All four columns
default to `0`, and nobody had a reason to switch on a toggle that did nothing —
so enforcing the stored value would have silently stopped every working webhook
on upgrade. Migration **730** back-fills existing rows to the policy every install
has effectively been running (enabled, all three events), and the policy read
**fails open** — no row, no table, any read error → enabled. What changes is only
what an operator can now turn *off*.

### Removed — four controls that enforced nothing

**Session Idle Timeout**, **Require re-auth for sensitive actions**, **Job
Timeout** and **GitLab Token Expiry Notice**. An operator could set a session idle
timeout, watch it persist, and believe their console locked; session lifetime is
the fixed 8h `auth.sessionTTL` and `sessionPolicy` was read by nothing. A security
control that silently does nothing is worse than an absent one.

The stored fields and their OpenAPI schema are untouched — the form still
round-trips them through the PUT, so nothing stored is lost and no client breaks.
Only the controls are gone. Re-add each with its enforcement, not before.

The principle that falls out, and the one worth protecting: **every control on
the Settings pages does something.** If one must ever ship ahead of its
enforcement, label it in the UI rather than leaving it silently inert.

### Removed — the reserved display face

The app carried a `c.display` token for Fraunces that styled nothing. VU-Q1 put
the serif on the login page and the sidebar wordmark, and both render the wordmark
as a raster asset, so there was no text for it to set — leaving a reserved token
as an attractive nuisance for the next person wanting a serif page title. Three
faces now, not four, and `type-scale.test.ts` fails if one comes back.

**Fraunces itself stays**, as a docs-only face: the user manual's hero is set in
it, the `.woff2` files still ship, and the docs drift-guard records the exemption
by name instead of being weakened. Confirmed in the app — the manual's hero
renders in Fraunces while the console loads only the three Plex faces.

## 0.52.18 — Filters that agree with the rows they return (visual update, Phase F)

**Date:** Jul 28, 2026

Phase F of the visual-update-followups plan — the follow-ups where
the console misinforms the operator. Four items, all of them the same shape: a
surface saying two words for one thing.

`tsc` clean, **361 tests across 35 files**, `make verify` green, and the filter
round-trip driven in the running app rather than only in jsdom.

### Fixed — the Workflow Runs status filter spoke the wire's vocabulary

The dropdown offered `queued`, `danger`, `warning`. You picked **danger** and got
rows whose Status column said **Failed**. It now offers the same labels the rows
carry — All · Running · Success · Warn · Failed · Skipped · **Cancelled** — and
sends the wire value behind each one. `queued` is not a separate option because a
queued run's badge already reads Running; picking Running returns both.

**Cancelled is new, and making it work needed the server.** Cancellation is not a
status in `workflow_runs`: migration 260 keeps the CHECK-legal terminal
(`failure`) and carries the fact in a flag, so the old filter disagreed with its
rows in both directions — `status=cancelled` matched nothing at all, and
`status=danger` returned soft-cancelled runs whose own Status column read
Cancelled. The endpoint now folds the flag in, with a case per branch under test.
Driven in the app against a seeded cancelled run: every option returns rows
labelled with that exact option, and the pager total narrows with it.

### Fixed — a mark's tooltip in the full score showed a raw UTC instant

`2026-07-28T23:00:00.000Z` in an app where every other timestamp follows the
application timezone — so hovering one mark in the condensed staff and the same
mark in the full score gave two different times for one event. Both now read
`Jul 28, 16:00`. The stamp is a required prop, not an optional one with a
fallback: a default is how the raw instant would come back.

### Changed — one status vocabulary, not four copies of it

The contradictions above are what a duplicated vocabulary produces, so the copies
are gone. `matchesStatus` is now the single filter predicate, derived from
`statusLabel` — which makes "the filter and the row can never disagree" true by
construction rather than by everyone remembering. It replaces `ExecutionsTab`'s
`matchesResult`, its `RESULT_PARAM` deep-link table, and `Workflows`' four tab
predicates; `Score`'s `markColor` is now `statusTone`.

Two of those copies had already drifted, which is the argument: the Workflows
tabs matched a bare `danger`, so a **killed** workflow run read "Failed" in its
own Result column and was missing from the **Failed** tab — and `running` missed
queued the same way. Both tabs now count what their label promises.

### Note — no "Cancelled" on the Executions tab

The plan called for one there too. It would have been a dead option: cancellation
is a workflow-run display status and the `runs.status` CHECK has no such value,
so nothing on that tab could ever match it. The gap was real but it was on the
Workflow Runs filter, which now has it.

## 0.52.17 — Content, copy and one merged row (visual update, Phase E)

**Date:** Jul 27, 2026

Phase E of the visual-updates plan — the last one. Nothing structural:
this is the pass over what the console actually *says*, plus the References merge
that has been annoying anyone who opened a job's expanded row.

`tsc` clean, **353 tests across 34 files**, build clean, all 13 routes swept in
both themes with zero console errors and every rendered size on the type scale.

### Changed — Activity collapses repeats

Nine consecutive `AMADEUS_GITLAB_BASE_URL not configured` rows was the default
view on a dev install: the signal is "this happened nine times", and the feed
buried it in nine identical lines. Consecutive identical events now collapse into
one row with a count and a time range — on the seeded install the wall becomes
**`×19 · 18:16 – 23:21`**.

**Consecutive only.** `A A B A A` renders three rows, not two — collapsing
non-adjacent events would misrepresent order, which is the one thing a
chronological feed must not do. The count is a button: expanding lists every
member's instant, so nothing is lost. Grouping is keyed by what the row
*displays*, and group identity survives a refetch rather than being an array
index — the same lesson Phase D learned the hard way.

### Changed — every empty state offers a next step

They stated a fact and stopped. Now they point at the control that resolves them
— "No steps yet" gets an add-step button, "No registration tokens yet" gets the
mint control, and the catalogs link to Compose, the Schedule Builder or the
workflow editor.

Two rules shaped this more than the copy did. **Actions are capability-gated**:
in-app authoring is Admin-only, so an empty state never offers what the viewer
cannot do. And **"nothing exists yet" is not "nothing matches your filter"** —
those get different copy and different actions, a create control versus a clear
button.

That distinction turned up a real bug. Four History surfaces send their filters
to the *server*, so an empty result under an active filter rendered the
never-happened copy: **searching the change log for a target that had never been
touched claimed the audit trail was empty.** All four now branch correctly.

### Changed — Settings copy describes what you get, not the mechanism

"Global concurrent-run cap across all runners" → "The most jobs that can run at
once, across every runner." Fifteen strings in that register.

Three of them are **factual corrections**, each verified against the Go source
rather than reworded by feel: the GitLab write branch also governs sync *reads*;
the change-log retention setting also prunes sign-in events, and its old text
contradicted the neighbouring field; and the metrics path only takes effect after
a restart, which nothing said.

**Security-relevant help was left exactly as written** — token validity, secret
handling, TOFU host-key pinning, audit retention. A friendlier sentence that is
wrong is much worse than an ugly one that is right.

### Changed — References is one row per reference (VU-20)

The Jobs expanded row rendered every reference **twice**: once as a chip, once as
a line beneath. With two unresolved references you read the same failure in a
capsule and then again as a sentence. They are now one row carrying the kind dot,
the `AMADEUS_*` name, the verdict, the state pill, the reason and the remove
control.

**Rows render for healthy references too.** The old list filtered to failures, so
dropping the chips instead would have made a fully-resolving job show an *empty*
References section — losing the inventory of what the job consumes, which is the
section's whole purpose. The screen-reader-only reason became the row's
`aria-describedby`: one node, visible and announced, which was the point.

### Fixed — one word per concept (E-4)

An audit of every user-visible status word found the console using several
vocabularies at once. The contradictions fixed here:

- **The Score's own legend disagreed with its readout** — hovering a projected
  run gave "Queued" under a legend that said "Scheduled", and "Queued" was
  false: a projection has not been enqueued. This shipped in Phase D **and the
  test asserted it as correct**; both are fixed, and the test now pins the
  legend and the readout to each other rather than to a literal.
- **Workflows had three words for one outcome** — a "Healthy" tab filtering rows
  labelled "Passing" whose steps said "Success". The local status map is deleted;
  everything routes through the canonical vocabulary.
- **Expanding a run row changed its result from "Failed" to `danger`**, with a
  raw `runner_lost` appended. Same class of bug on the runner rows, where the
  expanded view printed lowercase `online`.
- A local `statusLabel` was **shadowing the imported canonical one** in Runners —
  harmless today, a live footgun for the next caller.

Casing drift (Title Case modals next to sentence-case ones, four spellings of
"run type") is catalogued in the audit and deliberately **not** fixed: it is
cosmetic, and most of it is invisible because the labels are uppercased in CSS.

### Known, and deliberately not papered over

The Settings pass found **three settings that are stored but enforced by
nothing**: Session Idle Timeout, "Require re-auth for sensitive actions", and the
global Job Timeout. The plan's own worked example for E-3 was to relabel the
first as "Sign out after this long without activity" — **that would have been a
false claim**, so their help text is unchanged and the finding is recorded here
instead. Session lifetime is the hardcoded 8-hour TTL.

## 0.52.16 — The Score replaces four dashboard cards (visual update, Phase D)

**Date:** Jul 27, 2026

Phase D of the visual-updates plan. The dashboard's histogram,
Upcoming, Recent Completions and Currently Running were **one dataset split by
tense**, each rendering it as a different list, leaving the operator to
reassemble "what happened, and what is about to" in their head. All four are
replaced by a single timeline. No API change — both endpoints already supported
what the component needed.

`tsc` clean, **334 tests across 33 files** (49 new), build clean, dashboard swept
in both themes at 1280 / 1366 / 1366-with-rail-collapsed / 1600 with **zero
console errors**.

### Added — the Score

A fixed **24 hours back, 12 hours ahead** window with hour ticks, six-hour bar
lines, day boundaries in the application timezone, and a gold playhead. Each mark
is a stem and a notehead: **filled means it ran, hollow means it is scheduled**,
and the stem's height is the run's duration on a **log** scale — linear is
useless here, because real durations cluster at 2–3 minutes against a 14-second
outlier and every stem would be the same height.

**There is no range picker**, and that is deliberate (VU-Q8). The old histogram
had one because a bar chart needs several scales to be useful; a timeline showing
both tenses does not. The fixed window also keeps the forward half inside the
projection caps — at the 7d horizon a picker would have needed, a `*/30` schedule
alone projects 336 fires against a per-entry cap of 200 and is **silently** cut.

### Fixed — a failed run could be hidden behind a successful one (VU-21)

Marks sharing an instant paint in array order, so the last one drawn covers the
others. On the seeded install that is not a rare edge: **7 of the 26 marks on the
dashboard right now are coincident groups**, because `0 6 * * *` fires two jobs
and `*/30` collides with every top-of-hour schedule.

Coincident marks now collapse into **one notehead carrying a count, coloured by
the worst outcome in the group** — so a failure sharing a minute with a success
can never be painted over. Not the first status, not the most common: the worst.
They are deliberately **not** dodged apart, because this is a time axis and
moving a mark off its true time trades one inaccuracy for another. The stem uses
the group's longest run.

### Added — interaction that reaches every mark

- **Hover resolves pointer → time → nearest mark on the track**, not per-mark hit
  boxes. At notehead size, marks minutes apart overlap and the one painted last
  swallows its neighbours; in the prototype three of six seeded runs were
  literally unhoverable.
- **The readout is a fixed slot below the staff**, not a floating tooltip. It
  never moves, so the eye does not chase it, and it has room to enumerate a
  coincident group's members by name — which a tooltip pinned to a 10px notehead
  does not.
- **One tab stop, arrow keys step through marks** (Home/End jump, Escape clears).
  Per-mark tab stops would have added 60+ stops to the dashboard.
- **Full score** behind a toggle: one staff per job, grouped by run type, sharing
  the axis and playhead. This is where `disk-usage-audit` firing every 30 minutes
  stops being a repeated table row and becomes a visible pulse. Jobs with no
  events render as empty staves, which reads correctly as a rest.

### Changed — the stat row encodes urgency (VU-12)

Four equal tiles stretched edge-to-edge gave a zero the same presence as a
five-alarm failure. The row is now left-aligned and content-sized, and **Failed
(24h) and Running now carry a tint only when they are non-zero**; the two
reference counts stay quiet always. `StatTile`'s `tint` prop already supported
this — the dashboard simply never used it.

### Notes

- **The window is fetched as 24h and trimmed to 12h client-side**, because
  `/schedules/upcoming`'s `window` is an *enum* (`24h` | `7d`), not a duration —
  anything else is silently coerced. And `/runs` filters on **enqueue** time, not
  start time, so the request asks for an hour more than the plot shows and clips
  on `startedAt`; without that margin a run queued just before the window but
  started inside it would be missing.
- **The end-of-projection terminator is inferred, not reported.** The API has no
  truncation signal at all — the response is `{ window, items }` and both caps
  are silent — so a full 500 items is the only available inference. A false
  positive is harmless; the forward half trailing off with no explanation is not.
- **Selection is keyed by instant, not by object identity or index.** The
  dashboard polls every four seconds and rebuilds the marks array, which would
  otherwise drop the highlight on every poll and slide the keyboard cursor onto a
  different run whenever a new mark arrived.
- The freed vertical space (D-9) went into a **taller plot** — at 190px the stems
  had too little travel for a log scale spanning 14 seconds to an hour. The full
  score stays behind its toggle rather than being forced inline.
