## 0.52.15 — New type system, new palette, true light mode (visual update, Phase C)

**Date:** Jul 27, 2026

Phase C of the visual-updates plan — the phase the plan calls the
point of no return, because a palette everyone hates is a full revert. It
replaces the console's faces and its colours, and rebuilds light mode as a real
light mode rather than a dark rail with white panels. No IA change.

`tsc --noEmit` clean, **285 tests green across 31 files** (14 new), build clean.
All 13 routes driven in both themes plus Login and the three published documents:
**zero external requests, zero console errors**, and every rendered font-size on
the six-step scale.

### Changed — the type system is four faces and six sizes

The app's type lived entirely in a **10–14px band in one family**. With four
sizes covering everything from a page title to a chip, hierarchy had nowhere to
go and fell to colour instead. Outfit and JetBrains Mono are retired; the console
now runs on **IBM Plex**, self-hosted like everything else:

| Role | Face |
| --- | --- |
| Body, page titles | IBM Plex Sans |
| Column heads, eyebrows, labels (uppercase) | IBM Plex Sans **Condensed** |
| Cron, trace IDs, timestamps, durations | IBM Plex Mono |
| Reserved for brand surfaces | Fraunces |

Condensed on column heads is structural rather than decorative — it buys real
characters-per-pixel in History's nine-column table, and it gives the eye a
second axis of hierarchy (width) in an app whose type otherwise sat in a 4px
range. Sizes are now six tokens — **36 / 24 / 16 / 14 / 13 / 11** — and **10px is
gone** (with a stray 9px), because below 11 the uppercase stopped being legible
on a dense row. Page titles finally have their own step at 24px.

`frontend/src/type-scale.test.ts` fails on any hardcoded `fontSize`. Its first
version only caught a leading digit and **four off-scale buttons slipped through
as `small ? 12 : 13`** — the browser sweep caught them, and the guard now scans
the whole value expression.

### Changed — gold is the brand, warning is orange

`accent` and `warning` were **the same hex**, which meant the logo's gold could
only ever read as a warning. They are now distinct: gold `#c9a227` is the brand
(active nav, and Phase D's playhead), warning moves to orange `#d98a2b`. **Every
existing warning badge, alert banner and the Runners "Degraded" tile changes
colour** — if you have muscle memory for gold-means-warn, this is the release
that breaks it.

The ground is deeper (`#0a1119`), `primary` is brighter (`#4da3d9`) so it carries
on it, and the three desaturated blue-greys become two greys plus an emphasis
near-white.

### Changed — light mode has a light rail

The sidebar stayed dark in light mode — the classic bootstrap-admin split, and
the most dated thing about the theme. It is now a **true light rail**: white,
hairline border, gold-tinted active item, so the brand reads identically in both
modes. Light-mode `primary` is a luminance sibling of the dark one rather than a
navy, so the two themes are one product with the lights on instead of two.

That change had a consequence worth stating: the rail's wordmark was the
**white-text** logo, hardcoded because the rail used to be dark in both modes. On
a white rail the brand would have vanished. Shell now picks the asset per theme,
as Login always has. The Dashboard's histogram tooltip had the same latent bug —
white text on `c.sidebar` — and now uses panel tokens.

### Fixed — four WCAG AA failures, and two new tokens

Every text/background and control-boundary pair is checked to AA; the matrix is
recorded in the plan (§C-4) and is **62 pairs, 0 failures**. Four failures were
found and fixed rather than waived:

- **White on a solid fill failed in dark mode** — 2.78:1 on the brightened
  primary, 2.68:1 on success. New **`onSolid`** token: near-black ink in dark
  (6.83:1), white in light. A solid button no longer means white text.
- **A form control's boundary was effectively invisible** — the hairline is
  1.38:1 on panel, and in dark mode the field fill sat within ~1.1:1 of the card
  behind it, so a field had neither a visible edge nor a distinguishable fill.
  New **`borderStrong`** (3.24:1 / 3.29:1) on every input, select and textarea.
  Decorative separators between surfaces keep the quiet tone — 1.4.11 governs
  controls, not rules.
- Light-mode `textMuted`, `primary` and `accent` were 4.04–4.47:1 — near misses,
  invisible to the eye, real to a contrast checker. Darkened to clear 4.5.

Also fixed: `document.body` had no font-family and computed to **Times New
Roman**, so anything rendered outside the Shell's root landed in serif.

### Changed — the manuals and runner guides follow the app

`documentation/*.html` hardcoded the old palette as hex literals and imported
Outfit, JetBrains Mono and Fraunces **from Google's CDN** — the same egress
defect Phase A fixed in the app, in documents the binary serves to operators.
Both manuals now use the theme's colours and the self-hosted Plex faces (the
three runner guides inherit the user manual's stylesheet at wrap time, so they
follow automatically). Fraunces stays on the user manual's hero, which is a
brand surface and its one legitimate use.

`frontend/src/documentation-palette.test.ts` guards both directions: a hex absent
from `theme.ts` fails, a CDN reference fails, an unknown family fails, and a
document that drops its `@import` **without** adding `@font-face` fails too —
that last one would otherwise pass every other check and still ship a fontless
page.

## 0.52.14 — De-boxed surfaces, three radii, two chip shapes (visual update, Phase B)

**Date:** Jul 27, 2026

Phase B of the visual-updates plan. Where Phase A fixed defects under
the existing design, this one changes it — by **deleting**, not adding. Three
habits made the console read as a 2018 bordered-admin template: everything was a
box three levels deep, nine radius values were in play with no system behind
them, and one table row could carry four chip shapes at four radii. All three are
gone. No information architecture changed: same nav, same tabs, same columns.

`tsc --noEmit` clean, 270 tests green across 29 files, `npm run build` clean, and
all 13 routes driven in both themes with **zero console errors**.

### Changed — a surface gets a border OR a shadow, never both

`Card` and `StatTile` carried a border *and* a shadow *and* a fill that differs
from the page — three ways of saying the same thing, and the reason the app read
as a stack of boxes rather than a document. The border stays (it is the one that
survives both themes); the shadow is gone.

The one exception is **overlays** — `Modal`, the tag-filter popover, the
`SearchSelect` dropdown, the toasts. Their shadow separates them from whatever
arbitrary content is beneath, which is work, not decoration. Nothing in normal
page flow keeps both, and the sweep verifies it against computed styles rather
than against the source: **zero in-flow elements carry a border and a shadow.**

### Changed — the middle framing layer is deleted

Two new atoms in the kit replace what nested `Card`s were doing:

- **`Rule`** — a hairline, now the single grouping primitive. A line plus some
  leading groups content as well as a box does, without adding a third frame
  inside two existing ones.
- **`TableSurface`** — a table's frame. Tables previously sat inside a `Card`;
  they now sit on the page between a top and a bottom rule, which removes a whole
  level of nesting from every catalog view.

Applied to the Dashboard's Upcoming / Recent Completions / Currently Running
lists (per-row borders gone, hairline-separated), the Jobs and Scripts catalogs,
all four History tabs, Workflow Runs, the Schedules inventory and upcoming tabs,
the Runner Registry, the pending-host-keys list, the workflow editor's step
cards, and Notifications' Apprise targets.

**A status-coloured left accent bar is information, not framing, and was kept
everywhere it appears** — on a Recent Completions row it is the only outcome
signal in the row's left half. Same for borders that encode selection or input
state. Where a border was carrying meaning it stayed; where it was decoration it
went.

One latent bug fell out of the Dashboard work: those row-cards were filled with
`panel2`, which is the *same hex* as `panelHover` in both palettes, so their
hover state had never been visible. With a transparent resting state it works.

### Changed — nine radius values collapse to three tokens

Measured before: `6`×92, `4`×50, `8`×29, `3`×25, `10`×12, `20`×9, `5`×7, `2`×3,
`7`×2, `14`×1 — 243 uses, no system. Now three tokens on the palette, reached
like any other token:

| Token | Value | For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `c.radiusChip` | 4 | chips, tags, buttons, inputs, small controls |
| `c.radiusSurface` | 8 | cards, panels, modals, banners, tiles |
| `c.radiusPill` | 999 | **status pills only** |

Verified in the browser, not just the source: across all 13 routes, **every
rendered element's computed border-radius is one of the three tokens** (or a 50%
dot). `frontend/src/radius-tokens.test.ts` now fails on any numeric
`borderRadius:` literal, so this cannot re-fragment; AGENTS.md records the rule.

Two deliberate exceptions, both geometry rather than vocabulary, commented where
they live: the maintenance-mode **toggle tracks** (a chip radius on a 36×20 track
with a round knob reads as a broken button) and the workflow canvas's **start/end
anchor nodes**, where the stadium shape is the flowchart terminator and the only
thing distinguishing them from a job node.

### Changed — two chip shapes, not four

A single Jobs row carried a status pill (r20), a type chip (r4), tag chips (r3)
and a source pill (r4): four shapes, four radii, three tint systems, in one
horizontal scan. Now there are two — a **pill** for status, a **tag** for
everything else — and the pill is reserved so that status is the thing that pops.
Measured on a live Jobs row: four r4 chips, one pill, one dot.

That reservation drove several small calls, each recorded in place: the executor
badge, the role badge, the runner `HealthPill` (three of its four uses carry a
measurement, not a status) and the "Lost" indicator all became **chips**, because
a kind or a measurement wearing the status shape reads as a status. The schedule
inventory's `StateBadge` became a **pill**, because it is one.

### Fixed — two module-level style objects that froze the palette

`scheduling/ui.tsx`'s `btn` and `Shell.tsx`'s top-bar control style were plain
module-level objects capturing `c.*` at load time — the exact pattern that breaks
the Light/Dark toggle, and which this repo has been bitten by before. Both are
now functions evaluated during render. They surfaced because they were also the
last radius literals: a token cannot be read from a frozen object.

## 0.52.13 — Self-hosted fonts, keyboard focus, button hover (visual update, Phase A)

**Date:** Jul 27, 2026

Phase A of the visual-updates plan. Nothing here changes the design;
it fixes five things that are wrong *under* the current one, so that the phases
that do change it start from a sound base. The phase was specified as
no-visual-change, and the sweep confirms it: the only differences on screen are
focus rings and hover states that were previously absent.

Frontend `tsc --noEmit` clean, 267 tests green across 28 files (5 new),
`npm run build` clean. Verified in the running app in both themes across ten
routes plus the unauthenticated Login page.

### Fixed — the fonts were CDN-only, and a blocked CDN takes the whole type system with it

`index.html` pulled four families from `fonts.googleapis.com`, and nothing was
self-hosted. On a deployment with no egress to Google — which, behind Traefik and
Authelia with internal-only GitLab and Vault upstreams, is the likely case — that
stylesheet never arrives, every family silently falls back to `system-ui`, and
the console does not look like the thing anybody designed. There is no error and
nothing in the UI says so.

Outfit and JetBrains Mono are now served from the binary. The files are Google's
own latin and latin-ext variable-font subsets, so the rendering is unchanged; only
the origin moved. Two of the four requested families — **DM Sans** and **Source
Sans 3** — were never referenced by `theme.ts` at all and are simply gone. Net
effect on a cold load: four files from our own origin (~90 KB) instead of a
render-blocking round trip to a third party.

Vite copies `public/` into `backend/web/dist` verbatim and `//go:embed all:dist`
is recursive, so this needed no Go change. Confirmed by driving the real app and
asserting on the request log: **zero requests leave the origin**, and
`document.fonts.check()` reports both families loaded.

### Fixed — keyboard operation was effectively invisible

`focusRing()` existed but reached only `Input`, `Select` and `SearchSelect`. There
was no `:focus-visible` anywhere in the frontend, so buttons, tabs, pager
controls, sidebar links and clickable table rows gave a keyboard user nothing to
follow — and because the field styles suppress the browser's default outline, the
fallback was suppressed too. This was the one finding in the review that is an
accessibility failure rather than a matter of taste.

The fix is one rule in one place rather than per-component state, because a rule
cannot drift out of sync with a component that was added later. The global
stylesheet moved out of `main.tsx` into `global-css.ts` so it can be tested, and
`applyTheme` now publishes the ring colour as the `--am-focus` custom property —
the bridge a static stylesheet needs to read a mutable token object, so the ring
repaints on theme toggle like everything else.

**Clickable table rows are now keyboard-reachable at all.** A ring on an element
that cannot take focus is decoration, so `HoverTr` rows carrying an `onClick`
default to `tabIndex=0` and activate on Enter or Space; before this, a mouse was
the only way to expand a row. Callers that already manage their own tab order
(FolderBrowser, Runners) pass their own and are untouched. Fields keep their
existing border-and-glow treatment and never show two rings at once — their
inline `outline: none` outranks the sheet, which is deliberate.

### Fixed — primary and secondary buttons did not respond to the cursor

`Btn` tracked hover state and then used it for exactly one variant. `primaryHover`
was defined in both palettes and referenced nowhere in the codebase. Primary
buttons now light to `primaryHover` and secondary buttons to `panelHover`;
`dangerQuiet` keeps the behaviour it already had.

### Changed — numeric columns are tabular and right-aligned

Proportional digits make a live-refreshing column jitter, because a `1` is
narrower than a `0`. `tdStyle()`, `thStyle()`, the mono atom and the pager label
now request `tabular-nums`, and the numeric columns are right-aligned so the
digits actually form a column: **Duration** in History (Executions *and* Workflow
Runs — the latter was inconsistent with its sibling tab) and **Load** in Runners.

### Changed — motion is explicit and respects the OS reduced-motion setting

`transition: all` on `Card`, `Btn`, `TabBar`, `AlertBanner`, the sidebar `NavItem`
and the dashboard expander is now a list of the properties actually animated —
`all` also animates layout-affecting properties, so an unrelated re-render paid
for a paint it never asked for. The `pulse` and `shimmer` keyframes are now
defined only inside `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)`: under
*reduce* the animation name resolves to nothing and the element renders its static
state. The running-status dot keeps its colour and glow, so "running" stays
distinguishable with motion off.

Two known gaps, both deliberately out of Phase A's scope and recorded here rather
than fixed quietly: the smooth `scrollIntoView` in Runners' token highlight is JS
motion that a CSS media query cannot gate, and the transform-based toggles and
chevrons still animate under *reduce*.

## 0.52.12 — Documentation reconciliation and two drift guards (logging update, Phase E)

**Date:** Jul 27, 2026

Phase E of the logging-update plan — the cross-cutting item (LU-14)
that ran alongside the other four and closes out afterwards. No behaviour change:
this is documentation, plus the two tests §7.1 and §7.3 asked for and that had
never been written.

Backend `make verify` clean with 5 new Go tests, each mutation-verified against
the regression it claims to catch; frontend `tsc --noEmit` clean, 262 tests
green. All three byte-identical mirror pairs (the spec, both manuals) verified.

### Added — an environment drift guard, which found seven undocumented knobs

Every knob the process reads is part of its operator contract, and one nobody
documented is one nobody can find. The failure is silent in both directions: the
operator doesn't know the setting exists, and nothing notices the reference has
gone incomplete. The security plan asked for this guard months ago and it was
never written.

It asserts both directions. Forward: every `AMADEUS_*` name read by `config.go`
has a row in the env matrix. Reverse: every name the matrix has a **row** for is
read by some binary — because a row for a variable nothing reads is worse than a
missing row, since an operator sets it, sees no effect, and cannot tell whether
they typo'd it or the feature is broken. Renames leave exactly that residue.

It found seven variables that had never been documented, none of them from this
plan's work:

`AMADEUS_BACKUP_AT` · `AMADEUS_GITLAB_WRITE_BRANCH` ·
`AMADEUS_RUNNER_OFFLINE_AFTER` · `AMADEUS_RUNNER_DEREGISTER_AFTER` ·
`AMADEUS_SSH_EXECUTOR_ENABLED` · `AMADEUS_SSH_EXECUTOR_CONCURRENCY` ·
`AMADEUS_SSH_EXECUTOR_STALE_AFTER`

All seven are now documented from their actual behaviour rather than their
names — several have semantics that are not guessable, notably that
`AMADEUS_BACKUP_AT` is wall-clock UTC and therefore decides when *retention*
runs too, that the SSH executor's startup orphan sweep runs even when the
executor is disabled, and that `STALE_AFTER` must stay above the longest
plausible job or it will kill live runs.

The allowlist for deliberate omissions is empty and self-expiring: an entry that
becomes documented **fails** the test, so the list cannot rot into a permanent
set of exemptions.

The reverse check initially reported two false positives, which is worth
recording: `AMADEUS_GITLAB_TOKEN` and `AMADEUS_GIT_CACHE_DIR` are read with a
direct `os.Getenv` where they are used rather than through `config.go`. The docs
were right and the test was too narrow — it now scans the whole backend for that
direction, while the forward direction stays scoped to `config.go`, which is the
config contract.

### Added — the `paused_jobs` cascade test

`triggers_test.go` covered the `definition_schedules` trigger pair and not its
`paused_jobs` sibling, so a dropped `trg_paused_jobs_*` would have passed every
test in the repo.

That gap mattered because of what the missing cascade does. A paused definition
that is deleted — pruned from git, or deleted in-app — leaves its pause row
behind; when a definition of the same name returns, the scheduler finds it paused
and **silently skips every fire**. Nothing errors, nothing logs, the job just
never runs. Migration 200 exists to close that, and its own header warns that any
future table rebuild silently drops the triggers.

The test asserts source-qualification and cross-kind isolation as well as the
cascade itself, because `paused_jobs` keys on `source` where
`definition_schedules` keys on `owner_source` — migration 200 flags that trap
explicitly, and a trigger written against the wrong column would either not fire
or delete another source's pause. Verified by mutation: dropping the effective
trigger fails the test with exactly the diagnostic it promises. (The first
mutation attempt didn't fail, which was itself informative — migration 490
recreates that trigger, so 200's copy is not the effective one.)

### Fixed — a Phase D change that was reported as shipped and was not

The 0.52.11 entry above claimed free-text audit fields were masked and bounded
before the database insert. They were not: the edit was applied by a script whose
`cd` failed, so the script never ran — while the build-and-test line after it ran
independently and reported green, because nothing had changed and the existing
tests only ever inspected the emitted event. Both the commit message and the
changelog then described a fix that did not exist. Found by an adversarial docs
pass, not by me.

The behaviour it was supposed to fix was real. `WriteAuthEvent` masked before its
`INSERT`; `WriteChangeLog` and `WriteActivity` masked only on the way to the
stream. With a redactor installed that would scrub a secret out of `audit.log`
while leaving it verbatim in the `change_log` row — and `ExportAudit` reads those
rows straight into the CSV an auditor downloads, so the leak would survive in the
one artifact most likely to be handed to someone outside the team. Latent today
because nothing installs a redactor, live the moment anything does.

Now genuinely applied, along with the `summary` bound that was missing beside
`details`. Two tests pin it, and — unlike the ones that existed — they read the
stored **columns** rather than the emitted event, which is the only place the two
implementations differ. Both were verified to fail against the code 0.52.11
actually shipped.

### Fixed — documentation reconciliation across the four phases

Each phase's docs were written incrementally, so statements true in Phase A had
stopped being true by Phase D. `AGENTS.md` still claimed the latest migration was
710. Corrected there and across the env matrix, README, security review and both
manuals — including the statements about where logs live, what still requires a
restart, and how many retention knobs exist.

## 0.52.11 — The audit stream, and auth events that exist (logging update, Phase D)

**Date:** Jul 27, 2026

Phase D of the logging-update plan, the last one. Cronomicon gains a
compliance audit stream on disk, and — for the first time — records that anyone
logged in. Migration **720**, additive: one new table.

Backend `make verify` clean with 44 new Go tests (plus `-race` over the sink, the
event stream and the address parser); frontend `tsc --noEmit` clean, 262 unit
tests green. Verified against a running server: the stream file appears at mode
0640, a CSRF failure is attributed to its user, and the corrected export filter
returns auth events instead of config changes.

### Fixed — no authentication event was recorded anywhere

Not login success. Not login failure. Not logout, session creation, RBAC denial,
or CSRF rejection. Nothing, to either audit table. `recent_logins` is not a
substitute and its own code says so: it is an UPSERT keyed on the user, so login

# 2 destroys the record of login #1, and its write error is swallowed

A new `auth_events` table records `login`, `login-failed`, `logout`, `denied`,
`csrf-failed`, `dev-auth`, `bootstrap-admin` and `session-revoked`. It is its own
table rather than a reuse of the existing pair for two reasons that both would
have forced a table rebuild or a lie: `activity.kind` has a `CHECK` limited to
seven values with no `auth`, and `change_log.actor` is `NOT NULL` — while the
events that matter most here are precisely the ones with no known identity.

Three things made this larger than "log the OIDC callback":

- **trusted-header is the default mode**, and it has no callback and no login
  event at all — identity is minted per *request*. An implementation written only
  against the OIDC path would have audited nothing in the deployment that
  actually ships. Login events there are throttled to one per user per five
  minutes, reusing the throttle `recent_logins` already needed; unthrottled, one
  idle browser tab would write thousands of identical rows a day.
- **Nothing in the codebase had ever looked at a client address.** Zero
  `X-Forwarded-For` handling, zero `User-Agent` extraction.
- **Scope denial was ~20 copy-pasted 403s**, not one helper. The predicates are
  centralised but the responses were not.

### Added — the client address, derived correctly

Two columns, `remote_addr` and `client_ip`. Behind a proxy the first is the
proxy's address on every request; recording only that would have answered
nothing, and the operator asked to observe what this collects in practice.

`client_ip` walks `X-Forwarded-For` **right to left**, discarding trusted-proxy
hops, and only when the immediate peer is itself a trusted proxy. The header is
append-only and every hop appends to whatever arrived, so the left-most entry —
the one most code reaches for — is simply what the caller chose to send. An audit
trail carrying an attacker-supplied address is worse than one carrying none: it
actively misleads whoever reads it. A malformed entry ends the walk rather than
being skipped, so garbage cannot be used to shift which hop is believed.

`AMADEUS_TRUSTED_PROXIES` therefore has a second job now. With none configured
there is nothing to strip and the peer is used verbatim.

### Added — `audit.log`

A JSON Lines stream, one record per line, keys fixed by a versioned schema
(`"v": 1`). Deliberately **not** routed through slog: consumers live outside this
repo and need stable keys and types, which a general-purpose logging handler
does not promise — and routing through slog would put audit records at the mercy
of the process log's level, format and destination, none of which are the
auditor's to change.

Content is the `change_log` spine plus a named subset of `activity` kinds. The
line is drawn at "would an auditor ask about this?": `run-end`, `workflow-end`,
`config`, `gitsync` and `push` are in; `run-start` and `workflow-start` are out,
being the announcement half of a pair whose other half already carries the
outcome. Neither table alone would do — `activity` holds no secret, role or
credential events at all, and `change_log` loses runner token mint/revoke and
every execution outcome.

Rotated **daily by UTC date** rather than by size, because the question asked of
it is "what happened on the 14th". Generations are `audit.log.YYYYMMDD`, which
don't end in `.log`, so the run-log reaper skips them; the live file is excluded
by name. A restart across midnight rotates on open, from the file's mtime — so a
file named for a day contains that day.

**The database is authoritative and the file is an export stream.** They are not
written in one transaction, so a crash between them can leave a row with no line.
That asymmetry is deliberate: the row goes first, a missing line is recoverable
by re-exporting, and the reverse is not.

### Added — a seventh retention knob

`auditLogFiles`, default **730 days** — deliberately longer than `changeLog`'s
365, which is the entire point: it preserves a tamper-evident tail after the rows
themselves have been pruned. It gets its own reaper pass, matching only
`<base>.<8 digits>` so nothing else in the directory can be caught.

`auth_events` rows are pruned on the `changeLog` window rather than gaining an
eighth knob — they are change-log-class audit data, and the file stream already
carries the longer window.

### Fixed — the `authEvents` export filter was a lie

Selecting *Auth Events* alone in the export returned every config change and not
one auth event: the filter was a pure alias for `configChanges`. It was correct
in the only sense available at the time — there were no auth events — but the
spec advertised it without caveat. It now streams the real table.

### Changed — `internal/auditlog` is finally the single writer it claimed to be

Its package comment claimed single-writer status for both audit tables. That was
true of `change_log` and false of `activity`: **16 sites** bypassed it with raw
`INSERT INTO activity`, which is a third of the feed — and any tee hooked to the
writer would have silently missed all of it.

All 16 now route through it. Two changes made that possible without altering
behaviour: `ActivityParams` gained an `At` field, because most callers
deliberately share one timestamp with the `runs` row they describe (the reaper's
`completed_at`, the claim's `started_at`, the probe's `CheckedAt`) and stamping a
fresh `time.Now()` inside the writer would have desynced the pair; and the
writers now take an `Execer`, so the demo seeder can use them inside its own
transaction with its backdated timestamps intact.

That conversion surfaced a real latent bug: a test fixture's hand-rolled
`activity` table was missing the eight columns migration 030 added, and because
these writes are best-effort (`_ =`) it had been failing **silently**.

### Deferred

Free-text audit fields are masked and length-bounded before the database insert,
so a row and its stream line always carry the same text. **This did not actually
ship in 0.52.11** — the edit was silently skipped and the claim above was wrong;
it landed in 0.52.12, which describes what happened.

**The audit stream is not redacted.** A masking hook exists on the writer but
nothing installs one, so treat `audit.log` like the process log. The exposure is
narrower — audit rows are assembled from structured fields rather than arbitrary
process output, and the one genuinely free-text field is `details` — but it is
real, and a 730-day window means anything that lands there persists for two
years. The shape of a fix is not obvious: run logs are masked by a per-scope
redactor that needs a database and a context, so it cannot simply be handed over
as a process-wide masker. Recorded in `deploy/security-review.md`.

The stream also carries no cryptographic chaining or external anchoring — it is
tamper-*evident* only in the sense that it lives outside the database and
outlives it. Signing or hash-chaining the records is its own piece of work.

## 0.52.10 — Run logs grouped by entity (logging update, Phase C)

**Date:** Jul 27, 2026

Phase C of the logging-update plan. Run logs move from one flat
directory into a folder per job or workflow, addressed by a stable code that
survives everything that destroys a SQLite rowid. Migration **710**, additive
only — one new table and one new column, no table rebuild.

Backend `make verify` clean with 31 new Go tests (plus a `-race` pass over the
allocator); frontend `tsc --noEmit` clean, 262 unit tests green (4 new). Verified
against a populated database: the migration backfilled 16 codes, left all 50
pre-existing runs on the flat path, and a freshly triggered run picked up its
job's code.

### Added — a stable entity code, and the folder it names

`{logDir}/{traceID}.log` becomes `{logDir}/{code}/{traceID}.log`, where `code`
is an opaque 8-hex-character identifier for the owning job or workflow. SSH
connection tests, which record a run but belong to no job, go in `_system/`.

**Why a registry table and not a column.** `jobs` and `workflows` have no
surrogate key: what the API exposes as `id` is SQLite's implicit rowid, a
physical storage address. It is destroyed by a sync prune-and-re-add, by any
table-rebuild migration (170 and 490 both did `INSERT INTO jobs_new SELECT …;
DROP TABLE jobs;` without preserving rowids, and the next CHECK-widening one
will do it again), and potentially by the nightly `VACUUM INTO` restore path. A
directory tree keyed on rowid would silently reshuffle under all three.

The obvious alternative — add an `AUTOINCREMENT` column — is **illegal here**:
it requires the column be `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`, there can be exactly one per
table, and both tables already have `PRIMARY KEY (source, name)`, which is the
entire premise of the dual-source model. Hence a separate table whose sole
integer primary key can carry it.

`AUTOINCREMENT` is load-bearing rather than decorative: SQLite never reuses a
freed value, so a newly created entity can never inherit a dead one's folder.
That is what makes it safe to leave dead folders in place.

Keyed on `(kind, source, name)`, all three required — the git and amadeus
namespaces are deliberately disjoint, and a job and a workflow may share a name,
so `job/git/deploy`, `job/amadeus/deploy` and `workflow/git/deploy` are three
entities with three codes.

### Added — `_meta.json`, so a folder can explain itself

`logs/0000a3f2/` tells a human nothing, and since a deleted entity's folder stays
exactly where it is there is no naming convention separating a live one from a
dead one. Each folder carries a sidecar naming the kind, source and name that
own it, plus `createdAt` and — once deleted — `deletedAt`. It is the only way to
answer "what is this, and does it still exist?" from the log tree alone, which
matters because that tree can be archived or mounted where the database isn't.

Deliberately not named `*.log`: the retention reaper only removes `.log` files,
so a folder's explanation outlives the logs it explains.

### Changed — the code is stamped at enqueue, not resolved at write time

`runs` has no foreign key to `jobs` — it references `job_name` + `job_source` —
so resolving the folder when a log line arrives would break for a job deleted
mid-run. Stamping at enqueue makes the destination a property of the run, fixed
for its whole life.

This is also what makes the migration free. **Existing logs are not moved.** Runs
enqueued before 710 carry a NULL code, their logs stay at the flat path, and the
path builder reads NULL as "flat" — so the two layouts coexist permanently with
no fallback search and no probing of the filesystem.

### Changed — deleting an entity keeps its logs

The folder stays. Destroying an audit trail as a side effect of a delete is the
wrong default, and the no-reuse guarantee above is what makes retaining it safe.
A recreated entity of the same name gets a **new** code and a new folder, so it
can never read as a continuation of the old one. The reaper still collects the
old folder's *files* by age, so growth stays bounded.

**A sync prune is not a delete.** Only an explicit operator delete stamps the
registry. A git job disappears from a sync for reasons nobody chose — a repo
reorganisation, a rename, a transient YAML validation failure, a branch switch,
a partial clone — and returns on the next good sync; treating that as a deletion
would strand a folder and split the job's log history on every such cycle. This
is why the stamp is written explicitly in the two delete handlers rather than by
an `AFTER DELETE` trigger, which could not tell the two apart.

### Changed — log-storage stats say what each file actually is

The Settings panel reported one undifferentiated "N log files · X" that counted
run output, the process log, its rotated generations and the folder sidecars
together. A deployment with 5 GB of run history and one runaway process log
looked identical to the reverse.

`fileCount` now means **run logs only** — roughly the number of runs on disk —
and `oldestLogAt` is the oldest **run** log, where it previously pinned to the
process log's mtime and became meaningless exactly when someone was trying to
judge whether retention was working. A `classes` breakdown (run logs, process
log, audit log, other) partitions the whole tree, so the sizes sum to the total.
The panel lists a class only when it has files, so a deployment with no audit
log doesn't read a permanent "Audit log 0 B" that looks like a fault.

### Security

Git-sourced job and workflow names are entirely unvalidated: the sync inserts the
YAML's `metadata.name` verbatim — no regex, allowlist, length limit or trim — so
a name like `../../etc/cron.d/x` is reachable by anyone with merge rights on the
synced repo, and an empty name falls back to a value that yields `"."`.

Naming folders after entities would have made log storage the enforcement point
for that. Using an opaque server-assigned code sidesteps it entirely, and the
path builder validates the code's shape as well as the trace ID's before joining
them. The underlying gap is unchanged and recorded in `security-review.md`:
those names still flow unchecked into the database, the API and the UI, and
deserve their own validation work.

### Notes

The ingest path retries once on `ENOENT` when opening a run's log. The nightly
sweep prunes directories it finds empty, and a run that has created its folder
but not yet its first file is momentarily exactly that — microseconds against a
once-a-day sweep, but the cost of losing the race is a failed ingest.

Rolling **back** past 710 is unusually lossy and the down migration says so: it
resets the `AUTOINCREMENT` counter, so re-running the up migration will not
reproduce the same codes. The logs themselves survive — only the mapping is
destroyed, and the sidecars still record what each folder was.

## 0.52.9 — A process log on disk (logging update, Phase B)

**Date:** Jul 27, 2026

Phase B of the logging-update plan. Cronomicon now keeps its own log on
disk instead of relying on whatever is collecting stdout, the run-log directory
can be moved without a restart, and trace IDs are validated before they become
filenames. No schema change, no new migration.

Backend `make verify` clean with 29 new Go tests (including a `-race` pass over
the new writer); frontend `tsc --noEmit` clean, 258 unit tests green. Verified
end-to-end against a running server: the log file appears at mode 0640, follows
a directory change live, and the malformed-trace-id path returns 400 while a
well-formed but missing one still returns 404.

### Added — `amadeus.log`

The process log was stdout only, so on a host where nothing collects stdout a
crash left nothing behind to read. It is now also written to a file — stdout is
kept as a tee, never replaced, so journald/docker deployments lose nothing.

Four new knobs, all with working defaults:

| Var | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AMADEUS_LOG_FILE_ENABLED` | `true` | Set `false` for stdout only. |
| `AMADEUS_LOG_FILE` | *(derived)* | Absolute path. Empty ⇒ `<run-log dir>/amadeus.log`. |
| `AMADEUS_LOG_FILE_MAX_MB` | `64` | Rotate at this size. |
| `AMADEUS_LOG_FILE_KEEP` | `5` | Generations kept as `amadeus.log.1` … `.N`. `0` keeps none. |

Disk is bounded by `(KEEP+1) × MAX_MB`. Rotated generations deliberately do not
end in `.log`, so the run-log reaper added in 0.52.8 ignores them — process-log
retention is the keep count, not the run-log retention window, because the two
answer different questions. The live `amadeus.log` is excluded from that reaper
outright: it is held open for the process's lifetime, so deleting it would free
no space and would send every later line to an unlinked inode.

Rather than rebuild the logger, the one slog handler is built over a swappable
writer. The logger is stored on 12 structs across as many packages with ~193
uses of `s.log` in `internal/api` alone; re-wiring them was never on the table,
and a writer swap reaches 100% of server logging for free — which is also what
makes the live re-point below possible.

`KEEP` is taken literally: `0` means keep no generations, not "use the default".
The default is applied in the config layer, which is the only place that can
tell an unset variable from one deliberately set to zero — an early cut of this
had the sink treat `0` as unset, so an operator asking for no rotated copies
would silently have got five. That is the same class of defect Phase A existed
to remove, so it is now pinned by a test.

Two failure modes are handled deliberately. A file that can't be opened degrades
to stdout with a rate-limited notice on stderr rather than failing startup — and
because slog discards the error a handler's `Write` returns, reporting it any
other way would make it vanish. And a handle lost mid-run (a full disk, a
briefly unavailable mount) is retried on the same throttle, so a transient
problem self-heals instead of silently disabling the file for the rest of the
process's life — the worst possible outcome for a file whose purpose is being
there when something breaks.

**Not redacted.** Run logs pass through `runner.NewRedactor` with a documented
fail-closed path; the process log has no redactor. That was already true of
stdout, but persisting it raises the stakes: a credential that reaches an error
string is now a durable artifact, and lands in volume backups. Recorded as
accepted residual risk in `deploy/security-review.md`, with the mitigations that
do apply (mode 0640, dir 0750, bounded size, and the off switch).

### Changed — the run-log directory applies immediately

Saving Settings → Log Storage wrote the row and nothing reacted;
`ResolveLogDir`'s own doc comment conceded "path changes take effect on
restart", and the PUT handler logged a warning saying so.

The catch was that neither consumer could be reached: the runner service and the
SSH executor were both built inside `mountRunners` and dropped, so there was
nothing left holding them. They are now retained on the Server, and a saved path
is pushed to both — plus the SSH-test writer and, when it is derived rather than
pinned, the process log.

This also settles an inconsistency: the runner and executor resolved the
directory once at mount while `writeSSHTestLog` resolved it per request, so
after a change the three disagreed until a restart. All of them now read one
in-process value.

In-flight runs keep writing to the handle they already opened; only the next run
lands in the new directory. Existing log files are **not** moved — the panel
says so, rather than leaving it to be discovered.

### Fixed — a deleted job was unfindable in Activity

`deleteJob` and `deleteWorkflow` wrote an activity row with `Kind`, `Actor`,
`Category`, `Action` and `Target` and nothing else. Every omission had a visible
cost, and the Activity view was innocent — it read fields the writer never set:

- **No `summary`.** It is one of three columns the server-side `?q=` filter
  searches (`job_name`, `workflow_name`, `summary`) and one of five the client
  filter checks — so the deleted entity's name was **unsearchable** — and it is
  the only descriptive line the card renders, so the card had no body text.
- **No `job_name`/`workflow_name`.** These drive the card title, so a deletion
  rendered with the literal word **"config"** as its headline. The name appeared
  nowhere; `target` is neither searched nor rendered.
- **No `outcome`.** The row was invisible to success/failure filtering and drew
  with a neutral border and no status badge.

Both handlers now route through one helper that fills all of them, plus the
scope. `target` and `action` are kept alongside `summary` — the settings package
folds them into the summary and leaves both NULL, the compose mounts did the
inverse; writing all three is what search, filters, cards and the export each
actually want. The rowid is deliberately not recorded: this delete destroys it,
and SQLite reassigns rowids.

The `"Deleted"` vs `"deleted"` casing split is **not** changed here — see below.

### Security — trace IDs are validated before becoming filenames

A trace ID arrives as an unvalidated path parameter and is concatenated straight
into a log path. `openapi.yaml` declares `format: uuid` but nothing enforced it
at runtime, and while Go's `{traceId}` wildcard is single-segment — so a `/`
can't get through the router — that is a property of the current routing, not a
guarantee the path builders hold themselves.

All three sites that turn an ID into a filename now check it, and both log
endpoints return **400** `invalid_trace_id` for a malformed one: path
separators, `..`, a leading `.`, over 64 characters, or anything outside
`[A-Za-z0-9._-]`.

The check sits *before* the run lookup, not at the path build. Placed at the
build it was dead code — the lookup 404s on a nonexistent run first, so a
malformed ID could never reach it. A well-formed but missing ID still returns
404; only a malformed one is a 400.

Deliberately shape-based rather than a UUID match: a UUID regex would reject the
short literal IDs used throughout the existing suite and would need relaxing the
moment the trace-ID format changes, while adding nothing to the traversal
defence this exists for.

### Deferred

The plan also asked to normalise `"Deleted"` → `"deleted"` on the two delete
handlers, on the grounds that every other category is lowercase. That premise
does not hold: the casing splits by package, not by category — `internal/api`'s
compose and execution mounts capitalise every verb (Jobs, Workflows, Schedules,
Scripts), `internal/settings` lowercases them. Changing only these two would put
`Jobs/Created` and `Jobs/deleted` in the same category. The full sweep is ~14
call sites plus a decision about already-stored rows, so it is left as its own
piece of work.

## 0.52.8 — Retention actually retains (logging update, Phase A)

**Date:** Jul 27, 2026

Phase A of the logging plan: close the two
structural gaps that made every later logging feature unsafe to build, and give
the retention knobs a home in the UI. No schema change, no new migration.

Backend `make verify` clean with 20 new Go tests; frontend `tsc --noEmit` clean,
258 unit tests green (5 new). Verified end-to-end against a running server in
both themes.

### Fixed — nothing ever deleted a log file (LU-1)

`{logDir}/*.log` grew forever. The `logFiles: 90` setting was read by no code,
and the nightly sweep pruned database rows only — so a run's log outlived its
`runs` row by an unbounded margin, and the orphans were invisible to every
cleanup path. On a busy fleet this ends in a disk-fill incident.

The sweep now reaps run-log files by **file mtime** — not by joining against
`runs`, since the owning row is usually pruned first and those orphans are
exactly what needs collecting — then removes any directories left empty. Three
safety properties, each covered by a test:

- **Only `*.log` files are candidates.** The log directory is operator-set, so a
  mistyped path must not turn the reaper loose on unrelated files. This mirrors
  the snapshot GC, which matches `amadeus-*.db` and nothing else.
- **It never returns an error.** `runSweep`'s deferred hook fires
  `metrics.BackupFailed()` on any non-context error, so an unreadable log mount
  would otherwise abort the nightly backup *and* raise a false backup alarm.
- **It runs before the backup, not after.** `VACUUM INTO` needs free space; a
  full disk fails the backup, and reaping afterwards would skip the one step
  that reclaims any.

The walk is recursive and the root log directory is never removed.

### Fixed — every knob in Audit & Compliance was inert (LU-2)

`RetentionPolicy` was built from `AMADEUS_RETENTION_RUNS_DAYS` /
`AMADEUS_RETENTION_CHANGELOG_DAYS` at boot; `settings.GetAuditCompliance` was
never called outside its own GET handler. Saving the settings blob changed
nothing. This is the same "configured it but it did nothing" trap that got the
inert `Backup` and `sensitiveLogging` fields deleted in PP-M9 — this was the
surviving instance.

The stored blob is now **authoritative**, and the sweeper **re-reads it at the
top of every sweep**, so a retention change lands on the next nightly run
instead of the next restart.

Retention is also genuinely per-table now. Two env vars used to cover five
tables, which left three of the six settings knobs with no field to map onto;
`RetentionPolicy` gained one field per pruned table, so `changeLog` can outlive
`runs` the way the UI always implied it could.

**Upgrade safety.** On the first boot that finds the blob unset, it is seeded
from the current environment — the coarse env values fanned out to their member
tables, reproducing the old behaviour exactly. Without this, a deployment that
set `AMADEUS_RETENTION_RUNS_DAYS=30` and never opened the UI would silently
jump to 90 days on upgrade. The seed is a single `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`
statement, so concurrent boots cannot double-seed and an operator's saved values
are never overwritten.

The env vars keep working as the **bootstrap default for fresh installs**; after
seeding they have no effect. New: `AMADEUS_RETENTION_LOG_FILES_DAYS` (default
`90`).

### Added — the Data Retention panel (LU-15)

`GET/PUT /api/v1/settings/audit-compliance` existed and worked, but no component
called them — wiring the knobs up without this would have delivered controls
nobody could reach.

*Settings → Audit & Compliance* gains a **Data Retention** card above the
existing export: the six windows (Run History, Activity Log, Workflow Runs,
Change Log, Schedule Pushes, Run Log Files), each with a hint saying what it
governs. `0` reads as `∞` rather than a bare zero, because 0 means *keep
forever* — the opposite of what a bare zero suggests — and the card states
plainly that a change applies on the next nightly sweep.

`useSettingForm` / `SaveBtn` / `Status` moved from `Integrations.tsx` into the
settings `ui` kit now that a third panel uses them.

### Added — validation on the retention knobs

The PUT accepted anything. A **negative** window is silently absorbed by the
sweep as *keep forever* — both prune paths gate on `days <= 0` — which is the
exact opposite of what someone typing `-1` is asking for, and nothing tells
them. It now rejects negatives and anything above 10,000 days with a `422` the
form renders inline, and the client clamps at 0 so it never posts a value it
knows will be refused. Those `days <= 0` guards are also the only thing between
a negative and a delete-everything cutoff, so keeping bad values out of the
store is worth doing independently of them.

Note this validates on write only — `GetAuditCompliance` does not re-validate,
so a hand-edited blob still reaches the sweeper.

### Changed — the runner long-poll no longer floods the access log (LU-3)

`requestLogger` demoted only `/healthz` and `/readyz`. At the agent's 60s poll
default each runner emitted ~1,440 access lines a day — ~14k/day across ten
runners, and roughly 95% of everything a process log would contain.

`GET /api/v1/runners/{id}/poll` now logs at Debug alongside the health probes,
matched on the resolved `ServeMux` pattern rather than the raw path so a runner
id can never be mistaken for the route. No diagnostic signal is lost: the poll
handler still logs its own failures at Error.

### Docs

`AMADEUS_RETENTION_*` documented as bootstrap-only in the env matrix,
`amadeus.env.example` and the backend README, with the new log-files knob added.
The user manual's "Retention & backup have no UI" callout was true and is now
half-wrong — retention has a panel; the S3 backup still doesn't — so it says
that instead. Dropped the stale ", backup" from the audit-compliance endpoint
summary in both spec copies, and corrected the latest-migration number in
`AGENTS.md` (630 → 700).

## 0.52.7 — Delete from the expanded row (Jobs, Workflows, Scopes)

**Date:** Jul 27, 2026

Cronomicon-authored jobs and workflows can now be deleted from the list view's
expanded row, instead of only from inside their editor.

Frontend `tsc --noEmit` clean, 253 unit tests green (16 new). No schema change,
no API change, no backend change — all three DELETE endpoints already existed.

### Added — a row-level Delete for in-app definitions

**Jobs** and **Workflows** gain a quiet-danger `Delete` in the expanded row's
action strip, gated exactly like the neighbouring Edit — `canCompose &&
source === "amadeus"`. Both go through the shared `ConfirmDialog`, then
`DELETE /jobs/{jobId}` / `DELETE /workflows/{workflowId}` — the same endpoints
the editors call. On success the row collapses, a toast fires and the list
refetches; the confirm copy states what survives (run history) and what does not
(the definition, its schedule, its references).

This reverses the earlier decision (D4 for jobs, its workflow equivalent) that
delete should live only in the editor. The editor delete is unchanged and still
works; this is an additional entry point, not a move.

The button gate is UX only — the server remains the guard, rejecting git-source
rows with a 409. That 409 is translated to "Only amadeus-source jobs/workflows
can be deleted in-app." rather than surfacing a bare status code.

### Fixed — the Scopes delete was offered to users who could not use it

`Delete Scope` in the scope detail panel was gated on `isLocal` alone, so a
viewer without `configureApp` saw a button whose only possible outcome was a
server 403 — every other mutation control in that view was already `canEdit`
gated. It now carries the same gate, and drops from solid `danger` to
`dangerQuiet`, matching the VC.6 convention that reserves the loud fill for the
confirm button.

### Tests

New `Jobs.Delete.test.tsx`, `Workflows.Delete.test.tsx` and
`scopes/ScopesTab.test.tsx` cover, per view: the button shows for an
amadeus row with the capability; hides for a git row; hides without the
capability; the click confirms before sending anything; the confirm DELETEs the
right id; and a 409 reads as the amadeus-only sentence rather than the server's
raw message. The capability-off cases assert against a positive control so they
cannot pass vacuously on a not-yet-rendered row.

## 0.52.5 — Runner E2E flake fixed at root cause

**Date:** Jul 27, 2026

A long-standing intermittent test failure, chased to root cause rather than retried
away — plus the class of false run-failure it turned out to be sitting on.

Backend `go test ./...` + `go vet` green. No schema change, no API change, no UI
change; the manuals are unchanged and still document v0.52.4 accurately.

### Fixed — the runner E2E flake, and the false-failure class behind it

`TestRunnerAgentE2EHappyPath` had failed roughly **1 run in 4** for a long time, but
only when the whole package ran — in isolation it always passed. Chased to root cause.

**What was happening.** The run reached `status="failure"` with a NULL exit code and,
in the per-run log file, this:

```
[web01] [REDACTED]
[web01] amadeus: EOF
{"exitCode":1,"durationMs":3,…}
```

So the SSH session connected, produced its output (correctly redacted), and then
`session.Run` returned a bare `io.EOF` rather than an `*ssh.ExitError` — which the
executor scores `-1`, giving a failed run. Instrumenting `Start`/`Wait` separately
pinned it to `Wait()`, and since stdout/stderr are attached as pipes, the **stdin**
copy is the only `copyFunc` that can produce that error. x/crypto/ssh returns it in
place of a clean exit status:

```go
waitErr := <-s.exitStatus            // nil on a clean exit
for range s.copyFuncs { … copyError … }
if waitErr != nil { return waitErr }
return copyError                     // ← a successful run, reported as an error
```

**Why stdin was even in play.** Since H1 the injected environment is delivered on
stdin, never argv, so `remotecmd.Render` invokes the interpreter as `bash -s` — which
reads its *program* from stdin. The manifest here carries a 282-byte export prelude.

**The flake itself was the test fixture.** Its in-test SSH server replied to `exec`,
wrote a canned stdout line, sent `exit-status` and closed the channel **without
reading a byte of stdin** — modelling a server no real interpreter resembles, since
`bash -s` cannot run at all without consuming stdin first. Under load the close beat
the client's in-flight write and the copy failed. The fixture now drains stdin, which
is what any real remote does. **Verified: 20/20 clean package runs, against a ~1-in-4
baseline** (and 12/12 with this change alone, isolating it as the cause).

### Changed — executors no longer let a stdin-copy failure override a clean exit

Both SSH executors now write stdin through an explicit `StdinPipe` and **discard the
write error**, rather than handing the reader to `session.Stdin` and letting `Wait()`
surface its failure as the run's result. A non-zero exit is unaffected — `Wait()`
returns `waitErr` in preference to any copy error — so this discards only the case
where the command succeeded by its own account.

This is separate from the flake fix and did not cause it (reverting it leaves the
suite green). It removes the class of false failure the flake exposed: `bash -s` reads
its program *incrementally*, so a script with an early `exit 0` leaves its tail unread
and the remote closes while the client may still be writing. Go's own `os/exec`
ignores exactly this class of error for exactly this reason
(`skipStdinCopyError`, issue 9173).

**Stated plainly:** the production case is argued from the mechanism and the
precedent, not from a reproduction. The race is too tight to force synthetically
without racing library internals, and two attempts at a regression test passed with
*and* without the fix — a test that discriminates nothing is worse than none, so
neither was kept. The reasoning is recorded in the code instead.

## 0.52.4 — The at-a-glance surface (Agencies Phase 4)

**Date:** Jul 26, 2026

Phase 4 — the final phase — of the agencies plan (tasks T4.1–T4.4). **No
schema change.**

Phases 1–3 unified the mechanism; this makes it readable. The plan opens with an
operator losing a debugging session to a model that was *correct at every step* and
unreadable as a whole — four entity types carrying isolation by four different
mechanisms on two unrelated axes, with nothing that answered **"what belongs to
DSS?"** in one view. Answering it meant holding five facts at once. Now it is a tab.

Backend `go test ./...` + `go vet` green; frontend `tsc -b`, **233** vitest (7 new) and
full build green; both `openapi.yaml` copies byte-identical + client regenerated;
`backend/web/dist` rebuilt; both manuals updated; verified in the running app in both
themes.

### Added

- **The Membership matrix — Scopes → Membership (T4.1).** Rows are every scope, secret,
  variable, SSH key and runner; columns are the agencies; a cell is the membership,
  ticked in place (ConfigureApp). Sections are ordered the way the model reads: where a
  run happens, then what it can reach, then who executes it — each with a one-line
  statement of what membership *means* for that kind, because the rule differs
  (dispatch requirement vs injectability vs claim eligibility).

  **Rows with no membership are listed and labelled `unrestricted`.** That is the point
  of the view, not a rendering detail: an empty row is not missing information, it is
  the statement "reachable from everywhere", and it is exactly what an admin needs to
  see *before* ticking the box that narrows it. A grid showing only assigned rows would
  hide precisely what is about to break. A secret or variable also shows its own scope
  (`DB_PASS@prod`), so two same-named rows are never confused.
- **`GET /api/v1/agency-matrix`** — the whole grid in one read. One endpoint rather than
  nine client-side catalog + membership reads, because the entity-id → name join a
  client would have to perform is the bookkeeping this view exists to spare someone.
- **Per-agency detail (T4.2).** Each row on the Agencies tab expands into what the
  agency contains, grouped by kind, plus the two numbers that decide whether work placed
  there actually moves. Backed by `GET /api/v1/agencies/{agencyId}`.
- 🔴 **The queue-forever trap is stated on the agency itself (T4.3).** An agency with no
  online runner queues every run targeting it **indefinitely** — the runs are not
  failed, so nothing alerts, no notification fires, and no dashboard tile counts them.
  This is the trap the entire program came out of, and until now it was observable only
  on one run's status line at a time. The expanded agency says it outright and reports
  **how many runs are already waiting**, turning a prediction into a count.

  `queuedRuns` is derived from the same `run_agencies` index `claimRun` probes, so the
  number and dispatch cannot disagree.

### Changed

- **The Agencies tab explains the model it now owns.** Its blurb still said runner
  membership and hard-isolation dispatch "arrive in later milestones" — three releases
  after they arrived. It now states the actual rule, and its delete-guard note covers
  secrets, variables and keys.
- **Stale singular phrasing in the user manual** (`"no online runner in agency 'X'"`)
  corrected to the set form v0.52.3 actually emits.

### Deviation from the plan

- **T4.1 specifies `ManageEnvVars` for the cells; they ship ConfigureApp-gated** — the
  same deviation, for the same reason, as the Phase 2 setters they write through.
  Membership is an isolation-zone assignment, and every sibling operation on that axis
  is ConfigureApp. Gating the matrix lower than the endpoints behind it would just
  produce cells that look editable and 403.

### The plan is complete

All four phases of the agencies plan have shipped: authoring-time reference
validation (v0.52.1), the membership tables and pre-flight report (v0.52.2), the
predicate switch and the SSH-key tightening (v0.52.3), and this surface. Agency is now
the single membership axis for scopes, secrets, variables, SSH keys and runners, and the
originating failure — *"reference `AMADEUS_SECRET_RH8_BECOME_PASS` is unavailable for
this run"* with no way to tell a typo from a scope mismatch — is visible in the job
editor before a run is ever triggered.

Explicitly still out of scope, as the plan states: per-agency RBAC (who may *administer*
an agency), Vault-side path isolation per agency, agency-aware log redaction, and
jobs/workflows as direct agency members (AG-Q7(b)/(c), deferred pending a real case).

## 0.52.3 — One membership axis, switched on (Agencies Phase 3)

**Date:** Jul 26, 2026

Phase 3 of the agencies plan (decisions **AG-Q1b**, **AG-Q2b**, **AG-Q3a**,
**AG-Q5**, **AG-Q8**; tasks T3.1–T3.10). **Schema v700** (migrations
`690_run_agencies_index`, `700_drop_legacy_agency_columns`).

The tables Phase 2 built now decide things. Dispatch matches a run's agency **set**
against runner membership, reference resolution gains the agency clause, SSH keys stop
being the one entity type with no isolation at all, and the 1:1 columns those replaced
are gone. Agency is now the single membership axis for scopes, secrets, variables, SSH
keys and runners — which is the whole point of the plan.

Backend `go test ./...` + `go vet` green; frontend `tsc -b`, **226** vitest and full
build green; both `openapi.yaml` copies byte-identical + client regenerated;
`backend/web/dist` rebuilt; verified end-to-end in the running app (a multi-agency scope,
the key tightening refusing an out-of-agency binding, the set snapshot and its
materialized index, and the stuck-run reason naming both agencies) in both themes.

> ### ⚠️ Upgrade note — read the pre-flight report first
>
> - 🔴 **AG-Q5 is a tightening: SSH-key bindings that work today can stop.** Until now
>   any job could bind any key. Now a key binding resolves only if the key's agencies
>   intersect the run's. **Run `GET /api/v1/agency-preflight` (shipped in v0.52.2)
>   BEFORE upgrading** — its `keyFindings` are exactly the bindings this release breaks.
> - **Nothing breaks on deploy by itself.** An EMPTY membership set means "no agency
>   restriction", and migration 670 deliberately assigned no key membership — so every
>   existing key stays reachable until an operator assigns one. The same convention
>   applies to secrets and variables, which is why AG-Q1(b) is additive rather than a
>   cliff: an unscoped, unassigned row is as reachable as it ever was.
> - **`runs.agency` and `scopes.agency_id` are DROPPED (migration 700).** Both were
>   dual-written through v0.52.2 precisely so this release could remove them. Rolling
>   back past v0.52.2 after upgrading is not supported: the down migration restores the
>   columns and re-derives them, but a scalar cannot hold a set — a scope in two
>   agencies collapses to one (deterministically, the alphabetically first).
> - **The general-pool rule is UNCHANGED (AG-Q3a).** An untagged run is still claimable
>   only by a runner belonging to no agency. It is an isolation invariant, not an
>   implementation detail, and it was deliberately not relaxed inside a refactor.
> - **The `agency` field on a run is now `agencies` (an array)**, and a scope's `agency`
>   object is now `agencies`. Both were undeclared or singular before.

### The benchmark gate — and what it actually found (T3.1/T3.3)

The plan made the predicate change conditional on a benchmark: measure the scalar
predicate as the baseline **first**, and accept the set predicate only within a ≤15%
p99 budget. The measurement is checked in (`internal/runner/poll_claim_bench_test.go`,
10k queued × 50 runners × 20 agencies) and it failed, repeatedly:

| predicate | before index | after index |
| --- | --- | --- |
| scalar `agency IN (…)` — the baseline | 4.47 ms | **0.336 ms** |
| naive `json_each(agencies_json)` ∩ | 19.9 ms **(+350%)** | — |
| correlated join via `run_agencies` | 18.8 ms **(+320%)** | — |
| correlated probe | 13.9 ms **(+210%)** | — |
| uncorrelated `IN` | 13.4 ms **(+200%)** | — |
| **shipped** | 8.4 ms (+87%) | **0.338 ms (~0%)** |

Two findings, in the order that matters:

1. 🔴 **`claimRun` had no usable index at all.** `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` showed `SCAN runs`
   plus `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY` — every poll, from every runner, examined the
   entire runs table and sorted it. That scan *is* the 4.47 ms baseline, and it is why
   every candidate predicate looked catastrophic: each was multiplying work that should
   not have been happening. Migration 690's `idx_runs_claimable (status, executor,
   created_at)` removes it and makes the hot path **~13× faster than before this
   release**, for the old predicate and the new one alike. This was found by
   benchmarking the predicate change, not by going looking for it.
2. **The predicate's cost was concentrated in the general-pool branch**, not the
   membership one: a correlated `NOT EXISTS (… WHERE run_id = runs.id)` ran for every
   row the first branch rejected — most of the queue in a multi-agency fleet — where the
   legacy predicate short-circuited on a plain column. The shipped clause keeps both
   branches uncorrelated and tests the compact-JSON column with a byte comparison.

Net: the new predicate ships at **parity** (~0.6%, inside the noise band and far inside
the budget) and the hot path is an order of magnitude faster than it was. A
`TestClaimQueryPlan` test now asserts the PLAN, not just the timing — a benchmark tells
you something got slow, the plan tells you why, and it is the thing that silently
regresses when a later migration touches an index.

### Added

- **Migration `690_run_agencies_index`** — the `run_agencies` materialized index
  (T3.3's documented fallback) plus the claim-query index above. `runs.agencies_json`
  stays authoritative; this is derived from it, written in the same enqueue, and exists
  only so the membership probe is a keyed lookup rather than a per-row JSON parse.
- **Migration `700_drop_legacy_agency_columns`** — `runs.agency` and
  `scopes.agency_id`, once every reader was converted. Leaving them would leave a
  second, quietly-diverging answer to "which agency is this?", which is the exact
  confusion this plan exists to remove.
- **`execspec.SyncRunAgencies`** — materializes the snapshot at enqueue, shared by all
  **three** enqueue paths. A failure here fails the enqueue: a run missing its index
  rows looks like general-pool work to the claim predicate and would be offered to
  runners outside its agency. That is an isolation breach, not a performance blip.
- **Tests.** The AG-Q1(b) truth table (8 cases over {unrestricted, agency} row ×
  {general-pool, matching, non-matching, multi} run × the scope clause); the AG-Q5
  tightening including its M2-safe generic operator message; predicate agreement between
  the legacy and shipped claim clauses over an identical fixture; the query-plan
  assertion; migration-700 round-trip including the deliberate lossiness of its down.

### Changed

- **`claimRun` matches the agency SET (T3.2/AG-Q2b)** — the run's snapshot intersected
  with `runner_agencies`, via the materialized index. General-pool branch unchanged.
- **Reference resolution applies AG-Q1(b) (T3.4)** — `(row has no membership OR row
  ∩ run ≠ ∅) AND (row.scope IS NULL OR row.scope = run.scope)`. The scope half is
  untouched, so nobody loses a control they had; the agency half narrows only rows an
  operator explicitly assigned. Both clauses live in `lookupScoped`, the ONE query
  dispatch and the authoring-time validator share — an inlined copy is exactly how the
  clause would come to be enforced on secrets but silently not on variables.
- **Resolution reads the run's frozen snapshot, never live membership (AG-Q8).**
  Resolution happens at manifest fetch, after the claim; reading live membership would
  mean re-homing a scope silently retargets what an in-flight run can reach.
- **SSH keys gain agency membership (T3.5/AG-Q5)** — closing the G3 hole where three
  entity types gave three different answers. Keys are agency-filtered, still not
  scope-filtered (`ssh_credentials` has no scope column; the host/bastion FK is the
  narrowing signal). The out-of-agency message stays **generic** on the run surface, so
  a run cannot become an existence oracle for key labels either — the authoring
  validator is where the precise reason lives.
- **Stuck-run reasons name the SET (T3.7)** — *"Waiting: no online runner in agencies
  'agency-alpha', 'agency-beta'"*. The old singular phrasing is actively misleading once
  a run can require any of several.
- **Scope detail shows full membership (T3.8).** The 1:1 picker remains for the common
  case; a scope in several agencies gets a read-only summary instead, because the picker
  would silently truncate the set. Runner detail already showed a set.
- 🔴 **A third enqueue path was found and fixed.** The workflow engine builds its own
  child-run `INSERT` rather than going through `scheduler.EnqueueParams`, so Phase 2's
  dual-write never reached it. Harmless while the snapshot was inert; under Phase 3 every
  workflow child run would have been stranded — snapshot empty, claimable only by
  general-pool runners, refused by the agency its scope actually belongs to.

### Retired

- **`TestPhase2ChangesNoResolution` did its job and became its own inverse.** It asserted
  that assigning membership changed nothing; Phase 3 makes it change something, so it
  correctly began failing and now ships as `TestPhase3AppliesTheAgencyPredicate` — same
  setup, opposite expectation. It stays live because it is the only test that would
  notice the agency clause being quietly dropped from resolution while the membership UI
  kept pretending it meant something.
- `execspec.ScopeAgency` (→ `ScopeAgencies`), `execspec.AgencyHasOnlineRunner` (→
  `AgenciesHaveOnlineRunner`), `EnqueueParams.Agency` (→ `AgenciesJSON`), and the
  git-sync `scopes.agency_id` preservation test (superseded by the join-table one, which
  additionally covers the multi-agency case the scalar structurally could not).

### Not in this phase

Phase 4 — the at-a-glance membership matrix (rows = scopes/secrets/variables/keys/
runners, columns = agencies), the per-agency detail view, and the empty-state warning
for an agency with no runners — is untouched. Membership is still assigned through the
API and the per-scope/per-runner controls.
